title: Address from the TDWG Chair: highlights of the year and TDWG at a crossroads
session: Monday plenary programme
summary: TDWG chair David Bloom reviewed the past year's highlights: ratification of the Darwin Core Data Package, progress of the Biodiversity Data Quality and MIDS standards toward public review, a completed Darwin Core public review affecting the Humboldt and new mineralogy extensions, a new Image Quality and AI Readiness task group, Community Support Fund awards, Living Data 2025 in Bogotá, and a new editor-in-chief for the BISS journal. He then traced TDWG's history from a taxonomy-focused group in the 1980s, through the occurrence-data and portal era, to a new focus on linked open data. He set out current challenges (documentation and archives, participation, volunteer succession, sustainable standards maintenance, finances, and AI) and appealed to attendees to get involved.
takeaway: TDWG has had a productive year, but a growing, more diverse community and the rise of AI put it at a crossroads that needs more volunteers, better documentation and more sustainable maintenance and funding.
whyItMatters: It is the organisation's own view of where its standards work stands and what it needs next. It flags upcoming public reviews, new groups and elections that community members can join, and names the structural risks: volunteer burnout, maintenance load and documentation debt.
keyPoints: The Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP) has been ratified after a multi-year effort led largely by the Darwin Core Maintenance Group.
The Biodiversity Data Quality Interest Group's standard is heading toward public review, and the Minimum Information about a Digital Specimen (MIDS) standard is about to enter public review.
The second Darwin Core public review of the year passed all proposals, leading to significant changes to the Humboldt extension and a new mineralogy extension (pending Executive Committee approval).

A new Image Quality and AI Readiness task group has formed. The TDWG Community Support Fund made four awards totalling just over US$15,000 (mineralogy, sensitive species, invasive species in environmental samples, eDNA).
Living Data 2025 in Bogotá had more than 900 participants, over 700 of them in person.
BISS (Biodiversity Information Science and Standards, hosted by Pensoft) has a new editor-in-chief and will expand to peer-reviewed papers. Discounted fees for TDWG members are being considered.
TDWG's focus has moved from taxonomy/names (1980s) to primary occurrence data and portals such as GBIF and VertNet (2000s, both marking 25 years), and now to linked open data and data packages.

Challenges named: archival and online documentation (a new task group will review documentation tools and processes), participation (Executive Committee elections, subcommittees, working groups), succession in an all-volunteer organisation, a maintenance load that now needs four or five people per standard, finances (a new donate button), and AI.
Bloom argued that the use of AI makes TDWG's work even more important.

moments.description: Announcement that the Darwin Core Data Package has been ratified.
History of TDWG from 1980s taxonomy through the occurrence-data era to linked open data.
Start of the challenges: documentation, participation, volunteer succession, maintenance and funding.
AI described as 'a disturbance in the Force' and a challenge for the community.

title: AI for Nature at Large Scale and High Resolution
session: Monday plenary programme
summary: Berger-Wolf argued that computation does not change the scientific method but lets scientists 'look at more things, more carefully', at larger scale and higher resolution. Biodiversity data, however, are heavily biased toward where wealthy people are, and AI methods tuned to benchmarks tend to learn more about what we already know. She presented Imageomics work that builds biological knowledge into machine learning. The examples were BioCLIP (a foundation model trained on 214 million images of about a million species captioned with full taxonomy), biologically meaningful interpretability with attention and sparse autoencoders, automated trait measurement of NEON ground beetles, and drone-based behaviour data. She then showed that AI agents fail mainly at finding and preparing data rather than at analysis. She ended on data readiness: the FAIR for AI checklist and agent, sovereign data supply chains, and infrastructure that returns value to primary data collectors.
takeaway: AI can help fill biodiversity knowledge shortfalls only if biological knowledge is built into the models and the data infrastructure is FAIR for AI and returns value to primary data collectors, because 'there is no AI without data'.
whyItMatters: The keynote connects state-of-the-art machine learning to TDWG's core business. Its evidence that AI agents fail mostly at data discovery, API construction and data preparation, rather than at analysis, argues that standards, metadata and provenance are the bottleneck for AI in biodiversity science. It also calls for provenance and attribution to flow back from ML-derived products to the original data providers.
keyPoints: Following Poincaré's Science and Method, computation lets scientists look at more things more carefully, but data remain strongly skewed geographically, taxonomically and by wealth. Observations track where rich people are, not where biodiversity is.

Estimated species numbers have risen to roughly 30-50 million while only about two million (perhaps 1.5 million unique) are named, so the Linnean shortfall is growing. A recent prospective paper maps each biodiversity shortfall to AI research that could help fill it.
'AI' here means mostly (about 99%) machine learning, not LLMs. Benchmark-driven ML improves performance on the data-rich bulk of skewed distributions rather than the long tail where discovery lies.

BioCLIP was trained on about 214 million images of about a million species (sources include EOL, GBIF, iNaturalist, FathomNet and BIOSCAN), simply captioned with full taxonomic strings. It learns taxonomy implicitly and can classify at any rank.

BioCLIP's embedding space holds biology it was never given: clusters for life stage, sex and disease, a Darwin's finch axis aligned with beak size, and a freshwater versus marine split in fish. Similarity search surfaces diseased plants and pollinator interactions.

Biologically meaningful interpretability: attention-based part highlighting, and sparse autoencoders that manipulate features to show what about a trait (for example the shape of a house sparrow's beak) distinguishes a species. This supports trait discovery, dichotomous keys and separating mimic species.

An imaging pipeline for NEON ground-beetle bycatch segments specimens and measures landmark distances more accurately than calipers. The traits are being tested as predictors of drought and soil moisture.
Drone-based systems collect population-level behaviour and movement data. This work motivates FAIR-for-AI drone data standards.

In a benchmark of about 300 data-driven ecological questions split into four stages (find data, extract/API, organise, analyse), AI agents failed badly at building the right API and preparing data. With data and method given they reached about 60% accuracy at a cost of thousands of dollars in tokens.

'AI-ready' is question-specific. FAIR for AI is the general layer between FAIR and task-specific readiness. A community-built FAIR for AI checklist (90+ criteria) is assessed by an agent that gives constructive feedback.

Data flow one way toward aggregators. ML-derived improvements (bounding boxes, deduplication, updated taxonomy, provenance) should flow back to primary data providers through lightweight AI-ready infrastructure layered on existing repositories.

moments.description: Poincaré's Science and Method: computation lets scientists look at more things, more carefully.
Geographic and income bias in GBIF, iNaturalist and eBird data.
How BioCLIP was built by captioning images with full taxonomy.
Emergent biological structure in BioCLIP's embedding space (life stages, sex, disease, finch beak size).
Sparse autoencoders showing what about a house sparrow's beak makes it distinctive.
AI agent benchmark: agents fail at data discovery and preparation, not at analysis.
'There is no AI without data': FAIR for AI and returning value to primary data collectors.
Q&A on where AI-ready datasets should live and how to keep provenance.

title: Sámi perspectives on biodiversity data governance: when biodiversity data travel, does their governance travel with them?
session: Monday plenary programme
summary: Máret Heatta, a Sámi biologist, uses lichen monitoring data she helped collect on NINA permanent plots on the Finnmark Plateau in 2005 as a thought experiment for Indigenous data governance. She shows how an apparently simple lichen occurrence record is also information about Sámi reindeer winter grazing lands, and how a report finding of increased lichen cover became a newspaper headline of 'better grazing' without reindeer herders' knowledge of snow, ice and access. She grounds Indigenous data sovereignty in UNDRIP and self-determination, contrasts FAIR with CARE, and surveys Sámi and international initiatives (GIDA Sápmi, the 2023 Tromsø conference, SODA, Finnish Sámi research ethics guidelines, IEEE 2890-2025, the GBIF Indigenous data governance task group, Māori data infrastructure), closing with questions for biodiversity infrastructures about existing, reused and newly collected data.
takeaway: Biodiversity data about lands, ecosystems and species can be Indigenous data, so infrastructures must ask whether context, authority and responsibilities travel with the data as FAIR makes them easier to reuse.
whyItMatters: For GBIF and TDWG, the talk challenges the assumption that species occurrence data are neutral and 'not about people', and sets out concrete questions (recognising the significance of existing data, keeping context attached on reuse, building CARE in at collection) that the GBIF Indigenous data governance task group and standards such as Local Contexts labels and IEEE 2890 are starting to address.
keyPoints: The same lichen occurrence record is an occurrence for an infrastructure, ecological evidence for a researcher, land-use evidence for a planning authority, and pasture information for a reindeer herder.

Indigenous data include data about individuals, about collectives, and about non-human relations (land, water, ecosystems, plants, animals); biodiversity data need not mention a Sámi person to be relevant to Indigenous data governance.
Indigenous data sovereignty begins with rights and self-determination (UNDRIP, especially Articles 11-13), not with data; Indigenous data governance is putting that authority into practice.
Two dimensions: data for governance (access to data for own decision-making) and governance of data (authority over how data are governed).

FAIR assessment can largely be a technical exercise, whereas CARE requires engagement with people across the whole data lifecycle; technically reusable is not the same as appropriate or ethical reuse.

The NINA report's measured increase in lichen cover and thickness was communicated publicly as 'better grazing', although grazing conditions for herders also depend on snow, ice, access and reindeer land use; more lichen does not by itself mean better grazing.
Sámi historical experience of being researched, including racial biology and the extraction of remains and objects, explains caution towards data sharing; trust must be earned, not requested.

Sámi and international developments are moving from principles to practice: GIDA Sápmi (2021), the 2023 Tromsø conference on Sámi research data governance, the 2024 Finnish Sámi research ethics guidelines, the Sámi Council's SODA principles, IEEE 2890-2025 on provenance of Indigenous peoples' data, the GBIF Indigenous data governance task group (2025), guidelines for Indigenous data in scholarly publishing, and Māori-controlled data storage.
The CARE Data Maturity Model is presented as an iterative way to operationalise CARE rather than something done at the end of a project.

For infrastructures such as GBIF there are three situations: existing data that may have Sámi significance, reuse of those data after aggregation, and new data collection where CARE can be designed in from the start.

moments.description: One lichen record viewed from four perspectives: infrastructure, researcher, planning authority, reindeer herder.
What counts as Indigenous data: individuals, collectives and non-human relations.
How 'more lichen' became the headline 'better grazing' and the knowledge gap this reveals.
Three situations for GBIF-type infrastructures: existing data, reused data, new data collection.
Closing question: when biodiversity data travel, does their governance travel with them?

title: From biodiversity data to knowledge in the age of AI: where do ontologies and standards fit?
session: Monday plenary programme
summary: Ramona Walls, now leading the Data Collaboration Center at C-Path in the biomedical regulatory world, argues that the path from observation to data to evidence to knowledge depends on meaning, trust (provenance, context) and relevance ('context of use'). Using the Information Artifact Ontology's definition of data, examples such as a feather versus a paw print as evidence, and DNA analysis of 'Yeti' specimens, she asks whether AI generates data and knowledge, concluding that it generates data and candidate knowledge that only becomes knowledge when supported by trusted evidence. She stresses the roles of standards bodies, governance ('good governance makes altruism possible') and ontologies (Plant Phenology Ontology, BCO), and offers biomedical models (OMOP CDM and vocabulary, FHIR, European Health Data Space, a C-Path knowledge graph) as potential lessons for biodiversity, concluding that TDWG builds the infrastructure that turns data into evidence.
takeaway: AI can generate data and candidate knowledge, but only standards, ontologies, provenance and governance let data become trusted evidence and therefore knowledge, which is why TDWG matters more than ever.
whyItMatters: It reframes TDWG's standards and ontology work as infrastructure for evidence generation in an AI era, and brings an outside perspective from biomedical regulation, where independent, long-lived standards bodies and portable governance determine what regulators will trust.
keyPoints: Data are the result of an observation or measurement, almost always a sample, and are intended to represent the truth; this aligns with the Information Artifact Ontology definition of a data entity as a subclass of information content entity.
The knowledge pyramid places information above data, the opposite of IAO's hierarchy, illustrating that how terms are defined determines how entities are understood within a worldview.
Transforming data into knowledge requires meaning, trust (provenance, context) and relevance (context of use), which together produce evidence.
Different kinds of data carry different strengths of evidence (a feather versus a paw print).

AI generates data (text, images, synthetic data, predictions, classifications, inferred values) but not new empirical observations; it reproduces knowledge and creates candidate knowledge, which becomes knowledge only when supported by trusted evidence.
Secondary reuse of data is the only way to scale inquiry, so collectors' minimal notes are insufficient without standards and context.
Regulators such as the FDA trust international, independent, long-lived standards organisations rather than individual academic ontology projects; TDWG (since 1985) plays that role for biodiversity.

Governance controls access and use; C-Path's strong, flexible governance lets partners share data they would share with nobody else, and portable governance travelling with data may be feasible in three to five years.
Standards and controlled vocabularies improve interoperability but have loose semantics; ontologies are human- and machine-readable artifacts that encode domain semantics.

Biomedical models (OMOP Common Data Model and vocabulary, FHIR, European Health Data Space) and C-Path's ontology-annotated knowledge graph enabling cross-dataset queries are offered as possible models for biodiversity data.

moments.description: Information Artifact Ontology definition of data.
Data-to-knowledge chain: meaning, trust, relevance (context of use), evidence.
Yeti specimens sequenced: bears and a dog, plus new bear evolutionary history.
Does AI generate data? Does AI create knowledge?
Why independent standards bodies like TDWG matter, seen from the biomedical regulatory world.
Summary: AI raises the stakes; TDWG builds infrastructure for evidence generation.

title: Building a New Foundation for the Biodiversity Heritage Library
session: Monday plenary programme
summary: Nicole Kearney told the story of how the Biodiversity Heritage Library (BHL) survived the Smithsonian's 2025 decision to stop hosting it from 1 January 2026. BHL moved its financial and legal home to the Council on Library and Information Resources (CLIR), the Field Museum took over web and technical hosting, and new members supplied technical support. Public fundraising now matters for the first time. She said BHL is only secure through 2027, described the platform modernisation now under way, and asked the community for partnerships and funding.
takeaway: BHL has survived losing its Smithsonian home by becoming an independent, globally governed consortium, but its future is still not secure and it needs community support.
whyItMatters: BHL is a core infrastructure for taxonomy and biodiversity knowledge, and its near-collapse shows how fragile long-running community infrastructures are when they depend on one institutional host.
keyPoints: BHL is a consortium of 684 contributing organisations with more than 64 million freely accessible pages, full-text search and taxonomic name recognition.
BHL has added article data to scholarly articles and assigned DOIs to more than 80,000 of them, including retrospective DOIs for historic species descriptions.
In April 2025 the Smithsonian said it would stop hosting BHL (secretariat staff, technical team, seven servers and the website) from 1 January 2026.
BHL moved to CLIR as its financial and legal home, which lets it accept donations, apply for grants and manage staff contracts on its own.

New members stepped in: University of South Florida Libraries (three years of support for BHL's metadata collection workflow system), Vanderbilt University (an associate cloud engineer) and a third organisation (ASR 'Zenberg Nature Support', probably Senckenberg). The Field Museum now hosts the website and infrastructure; the move from Washington DC to Chicago finished at the end of June.

BHL's July user survey put enhanced text search first, then image search and a better page viewer. These drive a platform modernisation towards a cloud-based, machine-actionable, linked-data platform with better APIs and persistent identifiers.

Public fundraising: the Give BHL Wings campaign reached US$50,000 on New Year's Eve, a Guardian feature brought in more than US$10,000 in one day, and online donations have passed US$100,000 from more than 1,750 donors in 48 countries.
BHL is secure only through 2027. Kearney said the community must stop taking BHL for granted.

moments.description: The Smithsonian's decision to stop hosting BHL puts it at risk
BHL is secure only through 2027
User survey priorities and the platform modernisation project
Call to stop taking BHL for granted

title: Reducing the lag from observation to action
session: Monday plenary programme
summary: Quentin Groom looked at the delay between a biodiversity observation and the moment someone can act on it, with a focus on early detection of invasive species. He showed that recent GBIF monthly observation counts drop because data has not yet been mobilised, and used iNaturalist data to show that identifications can take months to become stable. He separated unavoidable lags from operational choices such as embargoes, unconnected systems and waiting for a dataset to be 'finished'. He then proposed a new 'Wangari Maathai shortfall' for timeliness, to add to the known biodiversity knowledge shortfalls. Q&A covered publishing data directly instead of through papers, and data valuation mechanisms.
takeaway: Timeliness is a missing biodiversity knowledge shortfall: publish soon, publish often, and improve continuously.
whyItMatters: For invasive species, pests and conservation action, data that arrives years late loses much of its value. As automated sensors take over from human observers, alert systems are needed so that unexpected species are noticed at all.
keyPoints: GBIF monthly observation counts fall off over the last two years because observations have not been mobilised yet, not because people stopped observing. The lag goes back further and covers tens of millions of records.
For invasive species, delays let a species establish and spread, raising the cost of eradication until it is no longer feasible.
Informal networks (emailing someone you know) work locally but do not scale.

Within about five years, data from eDNA, camera traps, acoustic sensors and automated imaging may outnumber human observations. Without a human in the loop, invasive species that are not specifically looked for will go unseen.
Lag builds up across observation, identification, digitisation, standardisation, validation, publication, aggregation, analysis, alerting and action.
In iNaturalist, bird identifications are right on day one about 50% of the time, but plants only about 10%. Identifications can take months to years to stabilise.
Some lags are real difficulties (remote fieldwork, taxonomic uncertainty). Others are operational choices (embargoes, unconnected systems, waiting for a dataset to be finished).
Groom argued for a publish, improve, update cycle instead of collect, clean, validate, analyse, then publish.

The OneSTOP project is building an open-source GBIF alert system (by Nico, of Binary Forest) for customised invasive species alerts by species and area. A Norwegian implementation exists but is not yet public.
He proposed a 'Wangari Maathai shortfall': the delay between an observation being made and the information becoming accessible for action. It would sit alongside the seven shortfalls of Hortal et al.

moments.description: GBIF monthly observation curve and the publication lag
iNaturalist analysis of time to stable identification by taxon
OneSTOP GBIF invasive species alert system
Proposal of a timeliness shortfall named after Wangari Maathai
Ramona Walls asks about publishing data directly instead of papers

title: Keeping Colliders in Physics: Rebuilding the ALA taxonomic backbone
session: Monday plenary programme
summary: Cameron Slatyer explained how the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA) rebuilt its taxonomic backbone. It had been assembled by an automated 'large taxon collider' that merged the ABRS National Species List with the Catalogue of Life, the New Zealand Organism Register and ad hoc sources. He argued that a backbone for matching data is different from a taxonomic checklist, and that a fully automated, human-free backbone is a fiction. ALA stopped the colliding: it now adds sources one at a time around the NSL, with metric checks and feedback loops through ChecklistBank and data matching. This sharply cut duplicates and unmatched records.
takeaway: Taxonomic checklists are not backbones: data aggregators need a curated single hierarchy with quality-control feedback loops, not automated merging of checklists.
whyItMatters: Names matching decides whether millions of occurrence records can be found and used, including for threatened species assessments, sensitive data handling and AI. ALA's metrics-driven approach is a practical model for other aggregators.
keyPoints: ALA holds more than 184 million records. Its backbone is built on the ABRS National Species List because of endemism, Australia-specific taxonomy, undescribed phrase-name species, names fixed in legislation, invasive species risk and traditional ecological knowledge.
The large taxon collider merged checklists automatically. It relied on consistent hierarchies and complete name combinations; any variance produced errors and duplicates.

Example: records of the endangered common bent-wing bat, long misidentified as Miniopterus schreibersii, did not connect to the endemic species because the misidentification was not a synonym in the NSL.
Listing a misapplied name both under the taxon it was misapplied to and in its correct place, which is common in checklists, is a disaster for data matching.
The old backbone had jumbled concepts and duplicates. More than 10 million records (10% of holdings) matched nothing, and one name had 78 variants.

A backbone needs a single hierarchy, not necessarily a fully scientifically valid one. It needs names inserted (prioritising legislated species), concepts removed or moved to avoid mis-routing records, and sometimes a commonly accepted name used over the best current name.
ChecklistBank metrics (duplicates, orphan taxa) plus data matching (higher matches and no matches) guide curation. The team extracted all 2.06 million names-match parameter combinations.
The collider code is still used, but sources are now added one at a time around the NSL core, bottom up, with feedback loops at every step.

moments.description: Bent-wing bat example of a missing misidentification link
State of the old backbone: 10 million unmatched records, 78 variants of one name
Metric checking and feedback loops with ChecklistBank
Results: 380,000 to 233,000 accepted taxa, under 1.5% of records affected

title: DwC-DP Integration at GBIF
session: Monday plenary programme
summary: Federico Mendez and a GBIF colleague (introduced as Nikolaj) described how GBIF is integrating the Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP) into its publishing and ingestion infrastructure. Mendez stressed that Darwin Core Archives are not going away. He explained that DwC-DP adds a Frictionless-style datapackage.json with typed fields, constraints and referential integrity, and that the IPT will support mapping and publishing DwC-DP. Nikolaj covered the stricter validation, metadata synchronisation to the registry, and a new ingestion that maps DwC-DP into GBIF's internal model, with examples from the Nice Botanic Garden herbarium. Everything is currently only in GBIF's test environment.
takeaway: GBIF is close to supporting Darwin Core Data Packages end to end, with typed and stricter validation, while keeping Darwin Core Archives fully supported.
whyItMatters: DwC-DP is the biggest change to the Darwin Core publishing model in years. How GBIF validates, ingests and displays it will decide how data publishers can express richer, relational biodiversity data.
keyPoints: Darwin Core Archives (core plus extensions, meta.xml and EML) will stay supported. Publishers who are happy with them can keep using them.
GBIF's 20-year review found that publishing around central entities (occurrences, events, taxa) was not enough for existing data or for engaging new communities.
The DwC-DP conceptual model was ratified in May 2026. The final review's no-dissent period ended on 15 September, and ratification and release by the TDWG Executive is expected soon.
A DwC-DP has data files, the same EML, and a new datapackage.json (from the Frictionless Data specification) that describes tables, fields, constraints, data types and relationships between tables.
The IPT will support mapping, metadata editing, validation and publishing of DwC-DP, but only in the test environment for now.

Validation checks the datapackage.json against its schema and against the standardised TDWG definitions, then checks unique and primary-key constraints and referential integrity, and reports statistics such as unique and populated values per column.
Metadata synchronisation mainly uses EML, falling back to datapackage.json where needed.

The new ingestion maps DwC-DP into GBIF's internal structure so it can be shown on gbif.org next to DwC-A data without loss. Richer views will follow. Examples used the Nice Botanic Garden herbarium, including material, media and usage-policy links that were not possible before.
Authenticated publishers will be able to see validation results, and simplified navigable table views of the raw published data are planned.

moments.description: Darwin Core Archives will stay supported
Anatomy of a DwC-DP and datapackage.json with data types
Validation steps for DwC-DP
Ingestion examples from the Nice Botanic Garden herbarium
Roadmap and the versioning challenge

title: Using automation to consolidate biodiversity occurrence data in South African National Parks
session: Monday plenary programme
summary: Judith Botha presented the SANParks Biodiversity Information Management System (BIMS), built with the Freshwater Research Centre and technical partner Kartoza. It brings together GBIF occurrence data, SANParks monitoring data and data captured from literature for South Africa's 21 national parks. The system produces annotated species checklists (needed for five-yearly park management plans), summary dashboards, Red List status and Red List Index trends, and climate station dashboards. Harvesting, taxonomic checks against the GBIF backbone, value assignment and dashboard generation are all automated.
takeaway: Automating the harvest, integration and summary of biodiversity data lets park staff get evidence-based species lists and dashboards without laborious manual compilation.
whyItMatters: This shows aggregated biodiversity data and standards reaching conservation managers and rangers as practical decision-support tools, and replacing the manual work behind statutory species lists.
keyPoints: SANParks manages 21 national parks (about 4.4 million ha terrestrial plus about 370,000 ha of marine protected areas). Kruger National Park is about 2 million ha and turned 100 this year.
South Africa has about 67,000 animal species, many poorly known and highly endemic.
Park management plans every five years need updated species lists, which used to be compiled by hand from literature.

BIMS harvests species and occurrence data from GBIF (occurrences for each reserve plus a buffer and catchment) and adds unpublished literature, databases, books, reports and theses captured by dedicated staff.
The GBIF taxonomic backbone keeps names to accepted names.

Users filter by taxon, space, time, Red List status, origin and endemism, and download annotated checklists (Excel, PDF, CSV). The checklists include coordinate uncertainty and precision, record counts, most recent record date, and an include/exclude flag for known misidentifications.
The dashboards show endemism, origin and conservation status. A Red List view uses SANBI's Red List Index by taxonomic group, and a climate dashboard summarises station data by time period.
Partner data has access restrictions but is available to SANParks staff.

moments.description: Introduction of the SANParks BIMS and its partners
Generating and downloading an annotated Kruger bird checklist
Red List Index dashboard
Where automation and AI are used in the system

title: Extending Darwin Core to Represent Sociobiodiversity and Traditional Knowledge
session: Monday plenary programme
summary: Clara Baringo Fonseca described Brazil's work on a Darwin Core extension for sociobiodiversity data: the relationships between biodiversity and sociocultural diversity, including traditional uses, practices and knowledge of Indigenous peoples, local communities and family farmers. A 2024 project with Colombia and Argentina produced draft terms (such as use-to, use-form, used-by holder) that were tested in three case studies. The case studies exposed missing fields, ambiguous terms and questions about who should be the data publisher. She also covered the new Entre Ciências intercultural project and templates for registering associated traditional knowledge under Brazil's biodiversity law.
takeaway: Representing traditional knowledge in biodiversity standards needs new terms, knowledge-centred (not species-centred) models, and careful governance of who holds and publishes the data.
whyItMatters: It extends Darwin Core towards Indigenous and local knowledge in a way that respects community data ownership and consent, and links to benefit-sharing law, data sovereignty and Darwin Core Data Package work.
keyPoints: Sociobiodiversity data is defined (Brazilian National Sociobiodiversity Plan) as data on the interrelationship between biodiversity and sociocultural diversity: resources, traditional practices, uses and knowledge.
Communities and territories are the main source and are knowledge holders and data owners. Data should be shared only with their consent and under their governance.

Other sources include scientific articles, collections (often in occurrence remarks), 17th–19th century naturalists' works, market inventories and films. These are produced in different contexts and make it hard to identify the knowledge holder.

A 2024 project with Brazil, Colombia and Argentina produced draft extension terms, with controlled vocabularies (use-to, used-by type, source type) and free text (used-by holder, use-form, use-to description), kept on GitHub.
Three case studies: translating a 17th-century book, working directly with a community on the Rio de Janeiro coast, and a living collection of medicinal plants at the Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden.

Findings: missing used-by holder and used-where data, ambiguous interpretation of use-to, and debate over whether the researcher or the community is the publisher, which matters for GBIF citation tracking.

The GEF-funded Entre Ciências project (started two months ago, three years) works with eight territories, six in the Amazon and two in the Cerrado, on data sovereignty, governance and locally chosen monitoring.

Under Brazil's biodiversity law, research on genetic heritage and associated traditional knowledge must be registered for benefit sharing. The team built templates, based on Colombia's, that put the knowledge rather than the species at the centre.

moments.description: Definition of sociobiodiversity data
Draft extension terms and controlled vocabularies
Case study results and the publisher question
Knowledge-centred rather than species-centred templates

title: What if biodiversity data systems were designed to behave like ecosystems?
session: Monday plenary programme
summary: Kit Lewers used the 1995 reintroduction of wolves to Yellowstone and the trophic cascades that followed as an analogy for biodiversity information infrastructure. The argument was that system-level behaviour emerges from interactions between loosely coupled components, not from any single blueprint. Lewers proposed event-driven, modular, microservices-style architectures in which new data arriving triggers workflows and updates that cascade through the system. They framed Darwin Core as an existing 'data contract' that already lets diverse institutions interoperate, and suggested making that implicit modularity explicit. NASA remote sensing processing levels were given as an example of adding data without changing the whole paradigm.
takeaway: Biodiversity information systems should be designed like ecosystems: loosely coupled, event-driven components linked by shared standards, able to reorganise as conditions change.
whyItMatters: It offers a conceptual design pattern for bringing new data types (such as remote sensing) into biodiversity infrastructure without monolithic redesign, and treats standards like Darwin Core as connective infrastructure.
keyPoints: Molly Beattie (US Fish and Wildlife Service director from 1993) oversaw the 1995 reintroduction of 14 wolves to Yellowstone, with 17 more the next year, despite opposition and uncertainty.
Trophic cascades are nonlinear, spatially uneven and still debated. Change came from networks of interactions, not simple chains.

An ecosystem can be seen as information unfolding in real time. Biodiversity information systems are likewise interdependent, loosely coupled, heterogeneous and only partly coordinated information ecosystems.
Data gains value through interaction: a new dataset arriving is an event that triggers workflows, updates products and recalibrates models, and the outputs become new events.
Lewers proposed event-driven modular systems based on microservices, where ingestion, processing, analysis, transformation and dissemination run independently through well-defined interfaces.
Loosely coupled does not mean structureless. Shared standards and governance let components understand each other.

Darwin Core already works as a data contract that lets museums, the NEON Biorepository, iNaturalist and NASA contribute without the same internal systems. Making this explicit prompts questions about translation, embedded assumptions, provenance and who maintains interfaces.

NASA data passes through L0 (raw), L1 (calibrated radiance) and L2 (reflectance) before derived products. Darwin Core would represent biodiversity observations derived from imagery, not the imagery itself.
The goal is not to eliminate complexity or 'solve' the information ecosystem, but to create conditions in which it can keep evolving.

moments.description: Central question: design information systems like ecosystems respond to disruption
Data arrival as an event that cascades through the system
Darwin Core as an existing data contract enabling modularity
Restoring infrastructural relationships can change what a system can do

title: Mainstreaming high-throughput biodiversity monitoring using AI
session: Monday plenary programme
summary: Niels Raes, coordinator of the Horizon Europe project Biodiversity Meets Data (BMD), described how the project is scaling AI-based high-throughput monitoring (camera traps, audio and eDNA) to site managers across Natura 2000 and Emerald Network sites. He showed Naturalis's ARISE platform: 4G sensor upload, data management, a library of image and audio AI models, overnight processing on supercomputers, and export as Camtrap DP for publication to GBIF matched to the Catalogue of Life. He also gave compute and cost figures for inference and for training Naturalis's multi-source model. Q&A covered invertebrate monitoring, the cost of deployment on devices, and human-in-the-loop verification.
takeaway: AI identification platforms like ARISE can take sensor data automatically to GBIF-published, standardised data for protected-area managers, but training costs are high and human verification still matters.
whyItMatters: It shows a working, continental-scale pipeline from automated sensors to standardised GBIF data and management tools, with rarely shared figures on the compute cost of the AI involved.
keyPoints: BMD is a Horizon Europe innovation action that mainstreams existing technology to new stakeholders. The primary audience is natural resource site managers, then policymakers, with academia last.

Scope: better implementation of the EU nature directives across about 27,000 Natura 2000 sites, extended to the Emerald Network (UK, Norway, Switzerland, Ukraine), about 30,000 potential sites, as a pilot. The project is in month 19.

'Virtual research environments' were renamed 'biodiversity analysis tools' because the term did not resonate with stakeholders. The tools are co-designed with stakeholders, for example a biodiversity status tool showing which directive-listed species were observed.
The target workflow is 4G-connected sensors with solar or battery power, automated upload, remote status control, archiving, AI identification and publication to GBIF.

ARISE (Authoritative and Rapid Identification System for Essential biodiversity information, Naturalis) offers audio models developed under MAMBO (birds, bats, frogs, insects, cicadas/crickets) and image models (MegaDetector, SpeciesNet, and Naturalis's multi-source model).
MegaDetector runs first to remove humans and licence plates for GDPR. Processing is batched overnight on supercomputers because on-the-fly processing is costly.

Results are exported as Camtrap DP, mapped to Darwin Core, published to GBIF and matched to the Catalogue of Life, then feed analysis tools such as species distribution models of climate change effects.

Image recognition takes about 0.03 s per image on GPU (0.06 s on CPU); training takes about 8 s per image. The multi-source model covers about 44,000 taxa, was trained on 42 million labelled images, combines 39 models, serves 100 million requests a year, and takes five months to train plus one month of validation each year, costing roughly €93,000–130,000 on Snellius.

moments.description: The ARISE platform and its library of AI models
MegaDetector plus SpeciesNet identification and GDPR filtering
Export as Camtrap DP to GBIF and the Catalogue of Life
Compute and cost figures for training the multi-source model
Human-in-the-loop verification before publishing AI identifications

title: Governance as a Foundation for Resilient Biodiversity Data Infrastructures: Lessons from DiSSCo
session: Building resilient data infrastructures for biodiversity science
summary: Eva Alonso argues that governance is a "connective tissue" that makes research infrastructures resilient, distinguishing operational governance (budget, legal form, decision processes) from strategic-capability governance. Using DiSSCo, which becomes operational next year, she shows how inclusiveness is built into its statutes through a Nodes Advisory Committee and strategic agreements with third parties, and how keeping funders close (Funders Forum, then an Interim Council of more than 18 countries) brought nodes into national roadmaps. She also points to a Dutch coordination of 15 health and life-science infrastructures as a way to counter funding fragmentation.
takeaway: Inclusive, funder-connected governance designed into a research infrastructure from day one is a core ingredient of its resilience.
whyItMatters: Most resilience talk focuses on technology; this frames governance structures, funder relations and cross-infrastructure coordination as practical levers that decide whether infrastructures like DiSSCo survive political and funding shocks.
keyPoints: Governance has two layers: operational mechanics (budget cycle, regulations, legal form, who decides how) and strategic-capability governance that lets infrastructures underpin competitiveness, innovation and resilience.

Three governance elements matter most: inclusiveness of key actors from day one, facilitating translation of science into societally beneficial measures, and advocating against funding fragmentation and bias.

DiSSCo's governance looks conventional (General Assembly, Director General, Executive Board, advisory bodies, national nodes), but its Nodes Advisory Committee is written into the statutes and advises on strategic direction.
The statutes allow strategic agreements with third parties that are neither members nor funders but want to contribute to the mission.
Keeping funders close took at least five years, moving from a non-decision-making Funders Forum to a decision-making Interim Council of more than 18 countries.
Funding fragmentation pushes institutions into opportunistic behaviour; coordinated advocacy by several infrastructures (e.g. 15 Dutch health and life-science RIs) can counter it.
Trade-offs remain: uncertain durability of joint governance, preserving uniqueness, tracing impact in short political cycles, and keeping people engaged.

moments.description: Two levels of governance: operational versus strategic capability.
Governance framed as internal and external connective tissue; three key elements listed.
DiSSCo's Nodes Advisory Committee as statutory inclusiveness.
Interim Council of 18+ countries and resulting national investments.
Key messages and trade-offs of governance for resilience.

title: Resilience of Research Infrastructures through knowledge and engagement
session: Building resilient data infrastructures for biodiversity science
summary: The talk argues that resilience is not only a technical reaction to disruption but a pre-emptive strength that comes from being used, valued, understood, connected and relevant to a broad community. Jose describes a communication loop (visibility turned into understanding, use and reported impact, which builds community support) and an engagement loop (dialogue with other initiatives leading to alignment and expanded relevance). Mareike Petersen adds that infrastructures need sustained, user-centred training adapted to how users want to learn, and should treat training of end users as reinvestment in the infrastructure.
takeaway: Communication, engagement and continuous user training make an infrastructure relevant enough that a community will want it to survive.
whyItMatters: It gives technically minded infrastructure teams a concrete model for how outreach and training contribute to resilience, and argues that investment in people and users should match investment in servers.
keyPoints: Two kinds of resilience: reactive/technical (respond to disruption) and pre-emptive, community-based resilience built on solid foundations.
A resilient infrastructure is technically robust but also used, valuable (with demonstrable value), understood, connected/interoperable and relevant to a broad community.
Communication loop: make work visible, turn visibility into understanding of why it matters, drive use, then report impact so a community supports you.
Engagement loop: communications staff can initiate dialogue with other initiatives, enabling technical alignment that expands the infrastructure into new ecosystems.
Training must be user-centred: know who users are, how they want to be trained (week-long workshop vs. scattered sessions), and which skills suit self-paced courses vs. interactive workshops.
Infrastructures need not train in everything (e.g. general research data management) that other parties already cover.
Past training mostly targeted infrastructure builders or single tool launches; continuous end-user training is needed for sustainability.

moments.description: Reactive technical resilience contrasted with pre-emptive community-based resilience.
The double loop of communication and engagement.
Interoperability expands an infrastructure into a new ecosystem and wider relevance.
Mareike Petersen on user-centred training portfolios.
Summary recommendations.

title: Adopting Environmental Sustainability as a Strategy to Build Resilient Data Infrastructures in Biodiversity Science
session: Building resilient data infrastructures for biodiversity science
summary: Giuditta Parolini argues that environmental sustainability, rarely discussed in research data management, should be treated as a risk-management strategy rather than a nice-to-have. Drawing on the International Energy Agency (growing demand, geopolitical fragmentation, grid limits strained by AI data centres, pressure on critical materials such as rare earths and lithium, slow climate mitigation) and a 2023 ESFRI report on energy and supply challenges, she defines resilience as continued availability of core services under political, legal, financial and technological change. Frugal infrastructures that need fewer resources are better placed to face rising hardware and energy costs and growing EU environmental reporting duties, and biodiversity data are especially at risk because they are politically contentious.
takeaway: Building frugal, environmentally sustainable data infrastructures is a practical risk-management strategy for resilience.
whyItMatters: It reframes green IT from a values question into a resilience argument that infrastructure managers and funders can act on as energy, hardware and compliance risks grow.
keyPoints: Sustainability in RDM is usually discussed in financial or social terms, rarely environmental, even though IT infrastructure use of electricity, hardware and e-waste keeps growing.
The IEA identifies growing energy demand against geopolitical fragmentation and grids not keeping pace, partly due to generative-AI data centres.
Supply chains for critical materials are under pressure (e.g. the 2025 Chinese export restrictions on rare earths; lithium provisioning).

Resilience = continued availability of core services under political, legal, financial and technological change; build it by defining core services, identifying risks and adopting a risk-management strategy.
ESFRI (2023, after COVID and the Ukraine invasion) recommended greening operations, including materials, reuse and recycling, as risk management.
Biodiversity data are politically contentious and face energy/hardware cost risks plus EU environmental regulation and reporting duties.

moments.description: International Energy Agency risk analysis.
Definition of resilience as continued availability of core services.
ESFRI 2023 report on energy and supply challenges.
Take-home message.

title: Supporting resilient data infrastructure in a changing environment
session: Building resilient data infrastructures for biodiversity science
summary: Rachael Blake reviews how sudden US funding and personnel changes in 2025 exposed fragile environmental data systems, with examples such as EJSCREEN, the NOAA Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters database and Columbia's SEDAC being lost or rehosted. She describes how panic copying without metadata or context fragmented data, while informed rescuers rebuilt datasets on Zenodo, domain repositories or bespoke hosting (e.g. EPA Risk Management Plan data via Datasette). She then surveys efforts toward long-term resilient systems and argues for investing in human infrastructure, interoperability, federated networks and purpose-driven data products.
takeaway: Technical copies are not enough: durable data infrastructure depends on preserved human expertise, messy maintenance work and data standardized close to collection.
whyItMatters: It distils lessons from the 2025 US data-rescue wave that biodiversity infrastructures can apply before a crisis hits.
keyPoints: In early 2025 the US community risked losing entire archives and repositories; patched fragile systems broke when funding and staff changed.

Examples: EJSCREEN (now hosted by Public Environmental Data Partners), the Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters database (now at Climate Central), SEDAC (shut down; data archived at NASA and Harvard Dataverse).
Panic copying without context or metadata fragmented data and did not support long-term interoperability or reuse.
Short-term recovery used domain and generalist repositories (much went to Zenodo) and bespoke architectures; EPA RMP data served via Datasette as SQLite.
Longer-term efforts: repository crisis scorecards, Climate Reserve at the Aspen Global Change Institute supporting former federal staff, the Council of Data Facilities on replication.
Coalitions: Coalition for Resilient Research Data Infrastructure, AGU Global Data Convening, Semantic Commons for Climate, Nature and Economy, World Ocean Database resilience effort.
Training the next generation of data stewards (e.g. an ocean data stewardship programme launched this year).

moments.description: Examples of US environmental datasets lost or rehosted in 2025.
Why panic copying without metadata hurt reuse.
Argument for investing in human infrastructure, interoperability, federated networks and purpose-driven products.
Final thoughts on durable infrastructure.

title: From Pixels to Policy: Closing the Gap between In Situ Monitoring, Earth Observation, and Policy Actionability
session: Building resilient data infrastructures for biodiversity science
summary: Claus Weiland presents a "Pixel to Policy" approach for making endangered earth and environmental data rescue-ready, within the new DFG-funded SEND Earth Data project that aims at preservation workflows with legal guidance, resilient storage and a national data-sovereignty network grounded in NFDI4Earth and aligned with the AGU global data resilience framework. Use cases include camera-trap data from Polissya (Ukraine) with the Frankfurt Zoological Society, multidisciplinary monitoring from Socotra (Yemen), and redundant storage for Movebank tracking data. Data, annotations, Earth-observation links, machine-readable policies and workflow provenance are packaged as FAIR Digital Objects built on web standards (schema.org, RO-Crate, Bioschemas, Croissant) - "WebFDO" - with a Wildlife Monitoring Ontology and ODRL-based policy objects serving as "data lifeboats".
takeaway: Packaging data with its semantics, provenance and machine-readable policy as FAIR Digital Objects makes it rescue-ready and redeployable elsewhere.
whyItMatters: It offers a concrete technical pattern for moving at-risk biodiversity and environmental data between infrastructures without losing the legal and policy context that makes it usable.
keyPoints: Data at risk from institutional defunding, reprioritization toward security and AI, and armed conflict.

SEND Earth Data (Secure Endangered Earth Data), DFG-funded and started two months ago, delivers preservation workflows with legal guidance and usage agreements, resilient storage and a national data-sovereignty network grounded in NFDI4Earth.

Use cases: Polissya camera traps (Ukraine, with Frankfurt Zoological Society), Socotra monitoring (Yemen, with the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature, Jordan), redundant storage for Movebank.

A capture event links images, ML annotations, DNA from samples, Earth-observation time series, machine-readable policies, licences and workflow provenance; drawing a software "box" around it with an identifier and type makes a FAIR Digital Object.
WebFDO uses schema.org/JSON-LD, RO-Crate, Bioschemas and MLCommons Croissant; DiSSCo digital specimens are the same concept.
Wildlife Monitoring Ontology (WLMO), derived from SOSA, with mappings to Camtrap DP via SSSOM.
Policy embedded with ODRL permissions and duties and the European Legislation Identifier ontology (from Biodiversity Meets Data), e.g. linking to the Nature Restoration Law.
Envisioned multi-tier resiliency network from national (NFDI) through European (DiSSCo, EOSC/Data Terra) to the AGU global framework.

moments.description: SEND Earth Data project and its objectives.
How a capture event aggregates images, annotations, EO data and policies.
WebFDO technology stack.
Embedding machine-interpretable policy with ODRL and ELI.
Data lifeboats and multi-tier resiliency network.

title: The GBIF data index: crawling and crawled
session: Building resilient data infrastructures for biodiversity science
summary: Matthew Blissett traces how GBIF moved from distributed DiGIR/TAPIR/BioCASe queries to a central occurrence index (2007) and now weekly Darwin Core Archive downloads and image caching, and then describes how usage patterns changed in the last two to three years. Search engines and self-identifying LLM crawlers can be rate-limited or blocked (one that ignores robots.txt was blocked), but 'vibe-coded' apps now hammer the GBIF API with millions of inefficient requests, and residential-proxy networks such as Bright Data send one or two requests per IP while posing as browsers. Cloudflare blocks less than half; GBIF has had to simplify and cache web pages, categorize traffic and push monthly cloud exports, while resisting API keys.
takeaway: AI-era crawling through residential proxies is a new, hard-to-block load that is forcing open biodiversity infrastructures and their publishers to spend effort on defence.
whyItMatters: It documents a concrete, growing operational threat to open biodiversity data services and to small publishers whose public image URLs are scraped directly.
keyPoints: Early 2000s DiGIR/TAPIR/BioCASe fan-out searches were unreliable; from 2007 GBIF built a central index, crawling publishers with a distributed lock of one request per server.
Now nearly all publishing uses Darwin Core Archives or data packages; GBIF checks weekly and respects HTTP Not Modified.
GBIF caches publisher images for at least a year; from early spring this year publishers were overwhelmed by probable LLM-training crawlers fetching public image URLs directly.
LLM services open thousands of simultaneous connections, unlike past crawlers.
Search engines and identifying LLM crawlers respecting robots.txt are manageable; one major crawler ignoring it was blocked outright.
Since March 2025 vibe-coded apps (e.g. "Bird.world", "BioTag") make inefficient API use; over 100 sites made more than 100,000 requests in recent months.
Residential proxy networks (e.g. Bright Data via apps on smart TVs) make crawling almost unidentifiable; Cloudflare blocks less than half.
Mitigations: simpler, daily-cached pages, request categorization, pre-calculated data, extended monthly cloud exports; GBIF does not want API keys.

moments.description: History: from distributed queries to a central occurrence index.
Publishers overwhelmed by LLM crawlers fetching images.
Vibe-coded apps hammering the GBIF API.
How residential proxy networks work.
GBIF reluctance to introduce API keys.

title: Resilient Attribution Infrastructures for Biodiversity Science: Archiving and Risk Mitigation in Bionomia
session: Building resilient data infrastructures for biodiversity science
summary: David Shorthouse describes Bionomia, which links more than 50 million biodiversity records to people via ORCID and Wikidata identifiers through automation and volunteer 'scribes', and the risks it faces: code and server upkeep, institutional oversight questions with his employer, and AI crawlers that took the site down dozens of times until Cloudflare was introduced. Resilience comes from simple design, standalone libraries (a Ruby gem ported to Go for parsing human names), and monthly archiving to Zenodo of a CSV graph and frictionless data packages for roughly 9,000 GBIF datasets, which institutions such as the Natural History Museum, University of Oslo reuse. Small projects can be resilient if they plan for decommissioning from the outset.
takeaway: Small niche infrastructures can be resilient by planning for their own end: keep things simple and push versioned data and reusable code outward.
whyItMatters: Bionomia is a widely used single-maintainer service; its approach shows how to protect volunteers' contributions and downstream users against a project's eventual loss.
keyPoints: Bionomia maintains over 50 million attribution links; interface translated into seven languages via Crowdin.
Runs on three DigitalOcean virtual machines with a Redis job queue.
Misbehaving bots and AI crawlers took the website down dozens of times; Cloudflare now gatekeeps, but its long-term sustainability is a worry.
Core functions are encapsulated in standalone libraries, e.g. a Ruby gem for parsing human names now ported to Go.

Monthly: a CSV graph structure pushed to Zenodo, and a frictionless data package for each of about 9,000 GBIF-publishing datasets, including logically incongruent records (e.g. collected before a collector's birth).
Data round-trips: e.g. NHM University of Oslo staff reuse the packages and publish ORCID/Wikidata identifiers to GBIF.
Individual researchers can archive their attributed records with DataCite DOIs via Zenodo integration.

moments.description: AI crawlers took Bionomia down dozens of times; Cloudflare as gatekeeper.
Monthly archiving of graph and data packages to Zenodo.
Plan for decommissioning from the start.

title: SYM18 discussion: who sustains biodiversity data infrastructures?
session: Building resilient data infrastructures for biodiversity science
summary: The discussion moved from where project materials should live after projects end to how to break down the divide between infrastructure providers and users. Speakers stressed that bottom-up volunteer effort cannot replace hardware, system ownership and stable funding; David Shorthouse urged every project to decide what is 'fail-safe' and what is 'safe to fail'. Audience members (Siobhan Leachman, Sharon from the Field Museum) lamented that Bionomia depends on one self-funded person and argued that data infrastructure needs its own governance and support distinct from transient research projects; others raised accreditation as a sustainability route, an impending 'tidal wave' of LLM-built fragile apps, the vulnerability of small data providers to crawlers, and whether infrastructures could recoup crawler costs.
takeaway: Volunteer and single-developer infrastructures deliver proven value, but the community lacks mechanisms and funding to protect them.
whyItMatters: It surfaces the unresolved gap between research-project funding and long-term infrastructure support that underlies many resilience problems in biodiversity informatics.
keyPoints: Plan from the start where project materials will live and in accessible formats; possibly in more than one place.
Bottom-up participation helps with intellectual work, but repositories and bot defence need hardware and system ownership beyond volunteers' time.
Project-to-project funding leaves infrastructures dependent on single people; consortia of research infrastructures can make joint value cases for sustained funding.
Decide what is 'fail-safe' and what is 'safe to fail'; Bionomia mints no new identifiers so its links persist if it ends.
Data infrastructure needs governance, resilience and support distinct from transient research; openness builds communities that step up in crises.
Accreditation (as used by UK cultural heritage) could help tap national funding; DiSSCo is still developing this.
LLM tools will let anyone build full-stack biodiversity apps; the community should anticipate thousands of fragile projects.
Established infrastructures could step forward to protect proven-value resources like Bionomia.

moments.description: David Shorthouse on 'fail-safe' versus 'safe to fail' and planning for Bionomia's end.
Siobhan Leachman on dependence on a single self-funded maintainer.
Sharon (Field Museum): data infrastructure needs its own governance and support.
The coming 'tidal wave' of LLM-built applications.
Which infrastructure will step forward to protect Bionomia?

title: An Introduction to the Biodiversity Data Quality Standard (BDQ)
session: Data Quality: From Standard to Practice
summary: Lee Belbin introduces the proposed TDWG Biodiversity Data Quality (BDQ) standard: a unified, transparent framework of 110 core single-record tests derived from reviewing over 500 tests run by aggregators. Tests take information elements (Darwin Core as example, but data-structure agnostic), parameters and source authorities, and are of four types (validations, amendments, issues, measures) described in seven vocabularies and one ontology. He stresses that data quality cannot be defined without a use case, that tests should be applied from the point of collection onward, and mentions using Gemini Notebooks with the ~800 pages of documentation to prepare the slides.
takeaway: BDQ provides 110 standard, use-case-linked tests so that data quality can be assessed consistently from collection to aggregation.
whyItMatters: A shared data quality test suite would let publishers, aggregators and users assess fitness for use consistently instead of each running idiosyncratic checks.
keyPoints: Work started from the idea at Woods Hole in 2010 and was convened from 2014; it took far longer than the expected year and a half.
Over 500 tests from aggregators (ALA, GBIF, iDigBio, BISON, etc.) were reviewed to build a single framework.
Output: 110 core single-record tests and four use cases; adding a test requires justifying it by a use case (tutorial and BDQUC vocabulary).
Tests use information elements, parameters and source authorities (e.g. ISO 3166) and are independent of Darwin Core, ABCD or data packages.
Four test types: validation (e.g. country found), amendment (e.g. month standardized, not to be applied without consideration), issue (e.g. annotation not empty, some tests aspirational) and measure.
Seven vocabularies and one ontology (BDQ FFDQ) underpin the standard.
Cradle-to-grave approach: ideally apply tests at collection (e.g. in Specify or field apps) as well as by aggregators.

moments.description: Using Gemini Notebooks with ~800 pages of BDQ documentation.
110 tests; data quality requires a use case.
The four test types with examples.
Cradle-to-grave application of tests.

title: GBIF Rule Based Annotations
session: Data Quality: From Standard to Practice
summary: John Waller presents experimental work at GBIF on rule-based annotations that capture 'rules in people's heads' about suspicious occurrences, e.g. 'amphibians in Antarctica are suspicious'. Rules are polygons plus taxon and optional scoping (dataset key, basis of record, fossils excluded) and apply to existing and future records. Examples include an elephant shrew record in Madagascar and axolotls outside Mexico; he argues that marking where a species is certainly not found (an 'anti-distribution') is much easier for non-experts than defining native ranges. A demo Download Annotator and an R package, gbifrules, apply rules to downloads.
takeaway: Simple, scoped negative-range rules let non-experts flag suspicious GBIF occurrences persistently, including future records.
whyItMatters: It offers a lightweight, community-driven way to capture expert knowledge about data errors that survives unstable occurrence identifiers.
keyPoints: Rules flag all current and future matching records (taxon within polygon) as suspicious.
Anti-distributions (where a species will not occur) are easier to define than native ranges and need little expertise.
Because GBIF occurrence IDs are not fully stable, single records are targeted by scoping rules to a small box plus dataset key and basis of record.
Complex rules allow exceptions, e.g. no non-human primates in Cuba except fossils.
Tools: an experimental web UI for making rules, a browser-based Download Annotator demo, and the gbifrules R package (GitHub, not CRAN).
Main challenge: recruiting rule makers; the feature is not yet visible on gbif.org.

moments.description: Elephant shrew record in Madagascar.
Axolotl anti-distribution rule.
Scoping rules to cope with unstable IDs.
Complex rule: primates in Cuba except fossils.

title: Interpreting the Responses from BDQ Tests
session: Data Quality: From Standard to Practice
summary: Arthur Chapman explains how to interpret the reports and responses produced by BDQ tests. The only normative output is the response, consisting of a status (e.g. run has result, internal or external prerequisites not met, amended, not amended), a result (compliant/not compliant, potential issue, a value) and a human-readable comment, plus an optional qualifier. Worked examples cover day-in-range validation, data-generalizations issue flags, day amendments and measures, with emphasis that amendments should never enter a database of record without human checking.
takeaway: Every BDQ test returns a status, result and comment, and understanding these lets users decide fitness for their own use.
whyItMatters: Implementers and data users need to read BDQ outputs correctly, e.g. distinguishing data problems from temporary external failures.
keyPoints: Report form is not specified by BDQ, but a report should include a response for every test run, in a strict order.
Response = status (operational metadata), result (core assertion from controlled vocabulary), comment (human-readable), optional qualifier.
Internal prerequisites not met: the data cannot be evaluated and will always give this result until the record changes.
External prerequisites not met: an external authority (e.g. a GBIF vocabulary) was unavailable; rerunning may succeed.
Validation example: day 30 with month 2 of 1952 is not compliant; day 31 without a month cannot be evaluated.
Issue tests (e.g. data generalizations not empty) raise warnings for human judgement.
Measures: single-record direct, single-record derived and multi-record.

moments.description: Status, result and comment of a response.
Internal versus external prerequisites not met.
Worked day-in-range validation examples.
Key takeaways.

title: The Swedish experience on verification and how to improve quality on observations
session: Data Quality: From Standard to Practice
summary: Mora Aronsson describes human verification of species observations in Sweden's Artportalen, as distinct from automated validation. Quality now covers not only identity but accurate positions, especially for red-listed, sensitive and EU-regulated invasive species. About 480-500 contracted, trained verifiers handle roughly 20,000 observations a day (about 7.5 million a year in Artportalen alone), aiming to verify around 10%, with focus on rare, threatened and invasive species. The main open problem is communicating verification status between databases and back to primary repositories, for which a standard is needed.
takeaway: Human verification remains essential, and the community needs a standard to exchange verification status between systems.
whyItMatters: Without a way to share verification results, corrected or doubtful records keep circulating uncorrected through aggregators.
keyPoints: Position accuracy has become as important as identification, driven by protected and invasive species legislation.
Verification focuses on rare birds, species new to the country, outliers, threatened and invasive species.
Verification classes range from expert-determined samples to trusted reporters; "not approved" is used sparingly after dialogue with reporters.
Verifiers receive education and sign contracts covering confidentiality of sensitive data and courteous behaviour.
Artportalen has had verification for about 25 years (initially birds).
Coverage is biased: birds and vascular plants have higher verification rates.
Verification results need to flow between databases and back to primary repositories.

moments.description: AI help and trust in AI identification.
Scale of verification: ~20,000 observations/day, 480 verifiers.
Need to exchange verification status between databases.
Verification versus validation defined.

title: Transitivity Failures in Taxonomic Name Resolution: Implications for Botanical Dataset Construction
session: Data Quality: From Standard to Practice
summary: Adam Richard-Bollans shows that resolving names to accepted names across taxonomy versions is not transitive: a name x resolved to y in one version may not resolve to where y resolves in a later version, e.g. because heterotypic synonyms are split. Comparing World Checklist of Vascular Plants versions (2022 vs 2025), about 13,000 of ~1.4 million names (≈1%) disagree, about half at species level, implying ~0.5% species-level error in datasets that kept only accepted names, rising to 0.7% by June 2026. Errors cluster in western and southern Europe (France, Italy, Spain).
takeaway: Always keep original verbatim names so datasets can be re-resolved against the latest taxonomy.
whyItMatters: Many secondary datasets discard original names after resolution; this quantifies the silent error that introduces and shows it grows over time.
keyPoints: Most aggregated botanical datasets resolve names to accepted names and often discard verbatim names.
Transitivity: x→y in v1 and y→z in v2 should imply x→z in v2; heterotypic synonym splits break this.
Example: Panicum nitidum resolved to Dichanthelium dichotomum in WCVP v10 (2022), but to Dichanthelium nitidum in v14 (2025).
~13,000 of ~1.4 million names disagree (≈1%); about half at species level, some at genus level.
Regional clustering of non-transitive resolutions in western/southern Europe.
Error grows with time since the original version (0.5% in 2025 to 0.7% by June 2026 for a 2022 dataset).
World Flora Online results are more severe; resolving to a different taxonomy likely increases error further.

moments.description: Definition of transitivity in name resolution.
Panicum nitidum example.
13,000 names (≈1%) disagree.
Error grows over successive versions.

title: How Darwin Core enables harmonizing Biodiversity Data via the OSCA Consortium
session: Data Quality: From Standard to Practice
summary: Cristian-Dan Bara presents OSCA (Open Scientific Collections Austria), a collaboration of 15 Austrian institutions digitizing preserved specimens into a shared cloud infrastructure built around a central Postgres cache aligned to Darwin Core and approved extensions. A streamlined pipeline with automated checks for Darwin Core validity and essential values gives scientists feedback before publication, keeping a human in the loop. Two public portals (v4 aggregating searches across international portals, v5 searching consortium data first with deep links outward) are being compared, and records are categorised by MIDS levels, targeting at least MIDS level 1.
takeaway: A shared Darwin Core-based cloud pipeline lets 15 Austrian institutions of very different IT capacity publish harmonised specimen data.
whyItMatters: It shows how a national consortium can use Darwin Core as a common language to pool capacity and publish comparable collection data.
keyPoints: OSCA digitizes preserved specimens across 15 museums, universities and scientific institutions.
Darwin Core is the shared language, enabling "micro infrastructures" where larger institutions support smaller ones.
Central Postgres table in the cloud follows Darwin Core and approved extensions.
Automated processing flags Darwin Core validity and missing essential values; scientists correct before publication.
Three pillars: search and discover, direct Darwin Core export (Excel), and a feedback loop on user needs.
Portal v4 compiles results from international portals; v5 searches consortium data first (harvested into DiSSCo) with deep links.
MIDS classes used to categorise records; MIDS level 1 minimum, level 2 (with media) desired for public value.

moments.description: Darwin Core as the enabler of collaboration.
Automated feedback loop before publication.
Portal v4 and v5 demos.
MIDS-based quality layers.

title: AURORA - A Shiny app designed to create Darwin Core Archives from messy biodiversity datasets
session: Semantic Interoperability and Standards Infrastructure
summary: Sara Araújo presents the AURORA Shiny app, a browser-based R Shiny workflow of eight steps that turns non-standard occurrence tables into Darwin Core tables ready for publication. It supports tidying, header-to-term mapping with suggestions, creating ID and dependent fields, repository-specific required-term validation (OBIS, GBIF, EMODnet Biology), date and coordinate conversion, taxonomic cleaning and matching against WoRMS or the GBIF backbone, event/occurrence restructuring, eMoF creation, quality control and IPT-style metadata. It does not build the archive itself (the IPT does) and currently supports only a limited set of cores and extensions.
takeaway: AURORA lowers the barrier to Darwin Core publication by guiding researchers step by step from messy tables to standard-compliant tables and metadata.
whyItMatters: Standardization is a main barrier to data publication; a free, guided tool can bring more datasets into GBIF, OBIS and EMODnet.
keyPoints: Eight-step workflow: upload/tidy, map headers to Darwin Core terms, create key fields, validate required terms, transform dates and coordinates, clean and match taxonomy, structure event core/occurrence/eMoF, quality control and metadata export.
Required terms adapt to the target repository (OBIS, GBIF, EMODnet Biology).
Taxonomic validation via WoRMS (marine) or GBIF backbone (terrestrial) retrieves scientificNameID and taxonRank.
eMoF measurements are assigned to events (e.g. temperature) or occurrences (e.g. life stage) and can use controlled vocabularies.
Quality control produces logs, summaries and issue flags.
Limitations: does not create the DwC-A (use the GBIF IPT); only event core + occurrence + eMoF or occurrence core + eMoF; users must know their data and basic Darwin Core.
Funded by the EU via the DTO-BioFlow project; user manual, video tutorial and source code on GitHub.

moments.description: Motivation and overview of the R Shiny workflow.
Taxonomic validation against WoRMS or GBIF backbone.
Creating eMoF tables.
Limitations and planned improvements.

title: Rebuilding core functionalities of the GGBN system: taxonomic alignment with international research infrastructures
session: Semantic Interoperability and Standards Infrastructure
summary: Walter Berendsohn describes replacing the outdated taxonomic component of the Global Genome Biodiversity Network (GGBN) portal, built around 2010. Incoming names from biobank datasets are first parsed (GBIF's parser chosen over Catalogue of Life's after testing), with pre-processing such as removing 'sp.' and flagging 'cf.', then matched via ChecklistBank name matching against the Catalogue of Life Extended Release to obtain synonyms and a standard higher taxonomy. Outcomes are qualified by match types and issues, with provider feedback for ambiguous cases, and the website documents how an accepted name was reached. He pleads for a universal homonym list.
takeaway: GGBN is rebuilding transparent automated name parsing and matching on GBIF parsing and ChecklistBank/Catalogue of Life XR to improve sample discovery.
whyItMatters: Reliable taxonomic alignment across all kingdoms is essential to find biobank samples, do gap analysis and link to other infrastructures.
keyPoints: GGBN is a community instrument for DNA-research samples, not only a data portal; a white paper on GGBN was published this month.
Names should be processed automatically so data go online fast, while feedback to providers continues transparently.
Goals: better searching by any related name and by higher taxa, and future gap analysis.
GBIF and Catalogue of Life parsers share a core but give different results; GBIF's was chosen.
Parser attributes (e.g. virus, cultivar, Candidatus) indicate the nomenclatural code.
ChecklistBank name matching against Catalogue of Life Extended Release provides synonyms, broad coverage and standard higher taxa.
Pre-processing (removing sp., flagging cf.) significantly improves results.
Ambiguous matches (homonyms) remain a problem; a universal homonym list would help.

moments.description: Choosing between GBIF and Catalogue of Life parsers.
Catalogue of Life Extended Release chosen as target.
Plea for a universal homonym list.

title: Bridging eLTER Data Reporting Format: enabling interoperable biodiversity and ecological data publication across research infrastructures
session: Semantic Interoperability and Standards Infrastructure
summary: Alessandro Oggioni presents the eLTER Research Infrastructure, a pan-European network of long-term ecological sites, and its Data Reporting Format: a zip of CSV tables (method, reference, station, event, sample, licence and data) described by a specification on Zenodo. To improve interoperability, eLTER built a vocabulary of its template terms mapped to Darwin Core where possible and an R function that converts reports into Frictionless data packages. In Q&A he said Darwin Core Data Package largely suffices, but the strong link between data and monitoring sites/facilities is missing.
takeaway: eLTER is aligning its CSV-based data reporting format with Darwin Core and Frictionless data packages to make long-term ecological data more FAIR.
