whyItMatters: Bridging long-term ecological monitoring data with biodiversity standards enables cross-infrastructure reuse.
keyPoints: eLTER RI studies structure, processes and functions of terrestrial, freshwater, coastal and transitional ecosystems; entered the ESFRI roadmap about 10 years ago.
Sites collect ecosystem, chemical, soil, atmospheric and biological parameters.
Data Reporting Format: relational-like CSV tables zipped together; specification published on Zenodo.
Vocabulary of template terms with Darwin Core matches and URIs where available.
R function generates Frictionless data packages from eLTER reports.
Future: automated publication workflows.

moments.description: Structure of the eLTER data template.
R-based data package generator.
Gap: site/facility relations in Darwin Core Data Package.

title: Infrastructure-driven solutions to strengthen semantic interoperability in ecology
session: Semantic Interoperability and Standards Infrastructure
summary: Cristina Di Muri presents LifeWatch services for semantic interoperability. EcoPortal, part of the OntoPortal Alliance and its federation, catalogues ecological semantic artefacts, integrates VocBench for collaborative editing, and offers FAIR assessment, annotator and recommender tools. Because semantic artefacts are scattered over many catalogs with redundancies, version mismatches, poor metadata and little use in annotation, they built a terminology service that federates search across 28 catalogs via 20 connectors, with discovery, version monitoring and embeddable search/annotation widgets, and produced over 3,000 new alignments across six artefacts using semi-automated tools.
takeaway: A federated terminology service over 28 catalogs plus community alignments tackles the fragmentation of ecological vocabularies.
whyItMatters: Semantic artefacts underpin FAIR data, but their fragmentation undermines interoperability; single-point access and alignments make them usable.
keyPoints: Semantic artefacts: ontologies, thesauri, glossaries and controlled vocabularies in SKOS, OWL, RDFS.
EcoPortal manages artefacts across their life cycle, with VocBench editing, FAIR assessment, annotator and recommender.
EcoPortal is part of the OntoPortal Alliance federation offering federated search and upcoming federated API across four catalogs.
Problems: many catalogs and technologies, redundant and unaligned vocabularies, divergent versions, missing metadata, underuse in annotation.
Terminology service: federated search over 28 catalogs via 20 configurable connectors, discovery alerts and version monitoring.
Search and annotation widgets tested in three metadata management systems.
Over 3,000 new alignments across six semantic artefacts via semi-automated tools.

moments.description: EcoPortal features.
Redundancy and versioning problems across catalogs.
Federated terminology service over 28 catalogs.
Over 3,000 new alignments.

title: The Triple A Principle: actionability, applicability and auditability for actionable biodiversity knowledge
session: Semantic Interoperability and Standards Infrastructure
summary: Lars Vogt argues that FAIR data and machine-actionability are insufficient for actionable knowledge in interventions such as restoring a degraded mangrove site. He proposes three nested criteria - actionability (procedural knowledge of what to do), applicability (explicit context conditions under which it works) and auditability (evidence of where it succeeded or failed, feeding back into conditions) - and a representation using the Semantic Units Framework: action units, applicable action units and audited applicable action units, plus conditional action units with question and directive units that turn a knowledge graph into a context-sensitive decision support system. The framework is conceptual, with a preprint on arXiv.
takeaway: Actionable biodiversity knowledge needs procedural content with explicit applicability conditions and evidence, not just FAIR metadata.
whyItMatters: It pushes knowledge-graph design beyond describing what is the case toward supporting decisions and interventions such as ecosystem restoration.
keyPoints: Many "FAIR" datasets have FAIR containers (metadata) but not FAIR content.
Machine-actionability usually means data transformation; human actionability includes epistemic and intervention operations.
Actionability: procedural knowledge (directives, steps toward a goal) is largely absent from FAIR infrastructures.
Applicability: actionability does not equal applicability due to context dependencies; explicit applicability conditions are needed.
Auditability: applicability reports feed back to refine conditions (e.g. salinity outside documented success range).
The three As are nested and proposed as necessary and sufficient for the representational side of actionable knowledge.
Semantic units make statements first-class typed, addressable units; action units link input, output, plan and objective units.
Conditional action units (if question unit then directive unit) give graph-native decision logic.

moments.description: Mangrove restoration problem space.
FAIR containers versus FAIR content.
The nested Triple A principle.
Conditional action units and graph-native decision logic.

title: SFBorg: a frictionless biodiversity data exchange
session: Semantic Interoperability and Standards Infrastructure
summary: Dmitry Mozzherin presents SFBorg and its Species File Group Archive (SFGA) format, an SQLite database schema used as an "active" exchange format that applications can use directly without importing, by analogy with MP3 files. SQLite is a single, fast, compressible file format with a stable format supported until 2050 and accepted by the Library of Congress for archiving. The ecosystem includes a shared library, the SF conversion tool (e.g. CSV, Darwin Core, ColDP via SFGA), a Harvester for idiosyncratic datasets, GNdb for building name-resolution databases, and Hive, a taxonomic viewer/editor/validator.
takeaway: Using an SQLite schema as the exchange format lets biodiversity datasets be used instantly by applications without import.
whyItMatters: Text-based exchange formats require database import skills; an active single-file format could enable many zero-effort applications for any dataset.
keyPoints: Darwin Core Archives, ColDP and Darwin Core Data Packages are inert text files that must be imported.
SFGA is a semantically versioned SQLite schema; version 1 will guarantee backward compatibility.
SQLite: single file, fast, scalable to terabytes, standard SQL, format stable for 30 years and supported until at least 2050.
SQLite is a Library of Congress recommended archival format alongside XML and JSON.
Used in production at Species File Group for harvesting, conversion (Darwin Core to ColDP and back), validation and aggregation (e.g. GN Verifier).
Tools: Species File Library, SF converter, Harvester, GNdb, Hive.
Ideas: instant websites, curation apps and AI interfaces for any SFGA dataset.

moments.description: Current exchange files are inert.
MP3 analogy for an active format.
Why SQLite.
SFGA as the core standard with semantic versioning.

title: Capitalizing the Invisible Ledger: A Cost-of-Production and Shadow Pricing Methodology for Valuing Open-Source Biodiversity Assets in India
session: Community-Powered, Research-Ready: Citizen Science for a Digital Future
summary: Ashwin A estimates the hidden production cost of India's roughly 2.8 million open-access citizen-science biodiversity observations, whose market price is zero. Building a cost model from field effort, taxonomic expertise, platform and data infrastructure and participant capital, he estimates about ₹137-676 per reusable occurrence record, compared with ₹700-3,500 for professional producers and ₹2,500-7,000 per institutional specimen output (not equivalent products). He argues open access removes the price of access, not the cost of production, and calls for recognising citizen science as productive data infrastructure and co-investing in validation and coverage.
takeaway: Open access removes the price of biodiversity data, not its production cost; citizen science is under-recognised national data infrastructure.
whyItMatters: Putting a shadow price on citizen-science records gives funders and policymakers an economic argument for investing in validation, coverage and platforms.
keyPoints: The economic asset is a reusable, identified, standardized and interoperable occurrence record, distinct from a photo or voucher specimen.
Cost components: core production (field effort ~₹104/hour, taxonomy expertise ~₹133/hour, platform ₹3-15/record), data infrastructure (+₹2-5/record), participant capital (₹80-160/record).
Estimated total ₹137-676 per record versus ₹700-3,500 for professional/NGO production and ₹2,500-7,000 per institutional specimen output.
Under-recognition leads to under-investment, spatial gaps, taxonomic biases and validation backlogs.
Citizen science redistributes production costs across citizens, experts and infrastructure rather than eliminating them.
Calls to standardize valuation and co-invest in platform, validation, coverage and capacity.

moments.description: Cost build-up of one biodiversity record.
Estimated ₹137-676 per record and comparators.
Open access removes price, not cost.

title: From citizen observations to long-term ecological knowledge: integrating iNaturalist records into LTER framework through automated enrichment
session: Community-Powered, Research-Ready: Citizen Science for a Digital Future
summary: Alessandro Oggioni presents an R package that treats iNaturalist as a service, downloading observations within eLTER site boundaries and automatically enriching them with IUCN Red List status, EU Habitats and Birds Directive annexes, nativeness from the EASIN database and standardised observation information. Outputs are research-ready interactive maps, charts and tables. The benefit is dual: eLTER sites gain additional observations and spatial coverage, while volunteers can engage in co-designed campaigns and see their observations gain scientific value.
takeaway: Rather than forcing citizens to produce structured data, automated enrichment elevates iNaturalist records into research-ready data for eLTER sites.
whyItMatters: It shows a low-burden route to integrate citizen observations into long-term ecological research infrastructures.
keyPoints: Vision: build workflows that structure citizen data instead of forcing citizens to produce structured data.
R package downloads iNaturalist observations by eLTER site boundaries.
Four enrichment pillars: IUCN Red List, EU Habitats and Birds Directives, nativeness (EASIN), standardised observation data.
Outputs: interactive map, analytical charts and tables.
Benefits for eLTER (more observations, expanded coverage) and citizens (co-design, future campaigns, elevated value).

moments.description: Elevate observations instead of forcing citizens to structure data.
Automated enrichment sources.
Dual benefit for infrastructure and citizens.

title: An eDNA Platform for Community-Powered LA River Restoration
session: Community-Powered, Research-Ready: Citizen Science for a Digital Future
summary: Ryan Martin describes how community groups, land managers and Indigenous groups monitoring removal of concrete from the heavily channelized Los Angeles River used eDNA metabarcoding (12 sites, seven months, six markers) and the eDNA Explorer platform. The platform handles sequencing processing, taxonomic assignment, GBIF comparisons, seasonal analyses and random-forest community models using about 400 Google Earth Engine variables, showing concrete as a strong predictor of community composition. The work, funded by Metabolic Studio with CALeDNA at UC Santa Cruz, founded eDNA Explorer and now supports ongoing restoration monitoring.
takeaway: An eDNA analysis platform let community groups without bioinformatics expertise measure how river channelization shapes biodiversity.
whyItMatters: It shows how packaging eDNA workflows makes advanced biodiversity monitoring accessible to communities and restoration projects.
keyPoints: About 95% of the LA River is channelized in concrete following 1930s flood control.
Protect Our River (from 2019) brought together community groups, land managers and Indigenous groups.
eDNA sampling at 12 sites over seven months with six markers across the tree of life.
eDNA detected taxa not in GBIF for the area, e.g. freshwater jellyfish in about a third of samples.
Seasonal patterns shown from CO1 marker data.
Random forest models on ~400 Earth Engine variables found concrete a strong predictor across most markers.
Results support restoration monitoring, a proposed pathogen baseline for the 2028 Olympics, and Indigenous revitalisation efforts; GBIF uploads have just started.

moments.description: Sampling design: 12 sites, seven months, six markers.
eDNA detects freshwater jellyfish missing from GBIF.
Concrete as a predictor of community composition.

title: Ground-Truth from the Ground Up: Community-Led Occurrence Data for Prosopis juliflora Restoration in Kutch's Climate-Stressed Drylands
session: Community-Powered, Research-Ready: Citizen Science for a Digital Future
summary: Pranav Jha describes Climitra's geospatial mapping of the invasive Prosopis juliflora in Kutch, Gujarat, which was planted from 1961 to hold back the desert and has spread to about 1.1 million hectares, depleting groundwater and raising soil salinity. Communities living with the invasion act as primary data producers through local-language voice agents and simple forms, confirming and correcting satellite classifier maps from geo foundation models in a loop that removes false positives. Locals are paid through restoration livelihoods, supported by a government mandate to remove the species.
takeaway: Community ground-truthing through voice-based, local-language tools makes satellite invasive-species maps reliable and restoration locally owned.
whyItMatters: It demonstrates inclusive data collection for low-literacy communities and links citizen data directly to large-scale restoration.
keyPoints: Prosopis juliflora is among IUCN's top invasive species; introduced in 1961 on about 31,000 ha and now covering about 1.1 million ha.
The species kills native vegetation, depletes groundwater and raises soil salinity; it is spreading across India's agroclimatic zones.
Classifier maps built with geo foundation models over a region larger than Sweden.
Voice agents in local languages and simple forms ("analog front end, digital back end") for largely illiterate communities.
Ground truths feed a loop of satellite confirmation, false-positive removal and hotspot benchmarking.
Datasets being prepared with Google for inclusion in Google Earth.

moments.description: Background on Prosopis juliflora invasion.
Voice agents and local-language forms for illiterate communities.
Communities as primary data producers.

title: The Asian Nature Challenge as a Beacon of Citizen Science: Regional Contributions, Macroecological Data Networks, and Strategies for Optimizing Taxonomic Identification Efficiency in India
session: Community-Powered, Research-Ready: Citizen Science for a Digital Future
summary: Ashwin A analyses two years (2024-2025) of the Asian Nature Challenge on iNaturalist, about 190,000 observations, asking how efficiently observations become research-ready. India contributed about 47,000 observations but only about 40% reached research grade, compared with 60-79% for other countries, revealing an identification deficit that is taxonomically graded: birds and mammals reach research grade easily while plants and fungi are around 4%, a 22-fold spread. He proposes an identification flywheel: target backlogs, build identifier networks, run targeted mobilisation such as identification-a-thons and use AI-assisted, human-verified identification.
takeaway: More observations do not mean more usable data; identification capacity is the bottleneck for India's citizen science.
whyItMatters: It pinpoints where citizen-science pipelines stall and suggests targeted interventions to turn volume into research-ready records.
keyPoints: Asian Nature Challenge aims to increase Asian representation on iNaturalist.
~190,000 observations in 2024-2025.
Research grade is a community-supported ID used as a proxy for data readiness, not a guarantee of correctness.
India: ~47,000 observations, ~40% research grade; other countries 60-79%.
Identification bottleneck varies by taxon: birds/mammals high, plants and fungi ~4%; ~22-fold difference.
Drivers: identifier capacity, photo-identifiability of taxa, and available evidence and digital support.
Identification flywheel: more IDs → more accurate data → more training data → better IDs → more observers.

moments.description: India versus other countries in research-grade rates.
Taxonomic gradient of the bottleneck.
Identification flywheel.

title: Growing Together: Community-Driven Conservation of Plant Genetic Resources
session: Community-Powered, Research-Ready: Citizen Science for a Digital Future
summary: Markus Oppermann presents the citizen science experiment of the INCREASE project, which sent well-defined sets of common bean varieties to citizens across Europe via a smartphone app with a material agreement. Participants grew the beans, recorded defined traits and images, and could exchange material (with DOIs assigned), producing more than 100,000 phenotypic observations from about 25,000 registered participants in nearly every EU country since 2021. National Facebook groups, native-language support and country-specific media worked best, and the project had to cap shipments at 5,000 in the third round due to demand; it also tested decentralized, community-based conservation as an alternative to gene banks.
takeaway: Giving citizens seeds, a good app and clear tutorials can yield large phenotypic datasets and community-based conservation of crop diversity.
whyItMatters: It demonstrates a scalable citizen-science model for plant genetic resources that both raises awareness and generates research data.
keyPoints: Aims: raise awareness of plant genetic resources, collect phenotypic data across Europe, and trial decentralized conservation.
Participants register in an app, sign an agreement, receive five bean varieties, grow them and record traits and images.
More than 100,000 single phenotypic observations; about 25,000 registered citizen scientists.
Material exchange between participants with DOIs assigned to material.
National Facebook groups (older gardener community) and native-language support were key; TV/radio worked in Italy, newspapers in Germany.
Data quality depends on a well-designed app and detailed tutorials.
Demand overwhelmed capacity; the third round was capped at 5,000 shipments.

moments.description: Decentralized conservation as alternative to gene banks.
National Facebook groups and language matter.
Overwhelming demand and capped shipments.

title: Introduction to the AI for Biodiversity Data session: what machine learning and LLMs actually do
session: AI for Biodiversity Data
summary: David Williamson opened the SYM30A session with a primer on AI for a biodiversity audience: machine learning as approximating an unknown function y = f(x) from many labelled examples, illustrated with his own herbarium-sheet phenology classifier (buds, flowers, fruits). He then described large language models as next-token predictors trained on large text corpora, argued that 'reasoning' models only re-prompt themselves, and used examples completing 'Hymenoptera is a...' to argue that hallucinations are indistinguishable from true statements in the text and that there is no objective way to score such outputs. He closed by previewing the session's talks on machine vision, audio and validation.
takeaway: LLMs are word predictors with no notion of truth, so their outputs, including hallucinations, cannot be objectively scored from the text alone.
whyItMatters: It frames the whole session with a sceptical, mechanistic understanding of AI, reminding biodiversity researchers that performance measurement and truthfulness are open problems when using LLMs.
keyPoints: Most talks in the session concern machine learning, specifically deep learning (neural networks, transformers, LLMs), a subfield of AI going back to the 1960s or earlier.
Machine learning approximates an unknown function y = f(x) by training on many annotated examples, e.g. detecting buds, flowers and fruits on herbarium sheets.
LLMs predict the next token given a system prompt, user prompt and conversation context; tool calls and 'reasoning' are bolt-ons or self-prompting.
LLM performance is intuitively easy to judge but hard to measure objectively; they need huge training data and are expensive.
Hallucinations are plausible sentences that may or may not be true; there is no way to tell from the text itself.

moments.description: Machine learning framed as solving y = f(x) with unknown f.
How LLMs predict the next word, with the 'grandmother exploded' example.
Hallucinations and why they cannot be objectively distinguished from true statements.

title: Delivering AI for biodiversity data in the public sector: data handling, security and humans-in-the-loop when small teams build at pace
session: AI for Biodiversity Data
summary: Rachel Wiles, product manager for the Natural History Museum's Data Ecosystem (a biodiversity data platform for largely urban UK nature built with AWS), described how a very small tech team uses AI tools to build at pace. She set out three boundaries of AI use: Claude Design for UI prototyping with dummy data, AWS Kiro as a code assistant running within the museum's AWS account for governance and logging, and GitLab agents for automated code review before deployment. She listed team rules (no AI acting on production data, no promoting unrewritten prototype code beyond dev, never bending the data model to a mock-up) and described human-in-the-loop verification tools (duplicate detection, PII/human detection, species clustering) surfaced as suggestions to expert verifiers. She asked the community for ideas on validation and provenance.
takeaway: Small public-sector teams can use AI tools productively if they set clear boundaries between prototype, dev, test and production and keep expert humans in the loop.
whyItMatters: Offers a candid, practical model of AI governance for under-resourced biodiversity data teams, and raises the open problem of preserving provenance and credit when AI assists data workflows.
keyPoints: The Data Ecosystem aggregates eDNA, environmental sensing, community science and camera trap data with quality checks; 10 million records in its first six months.
Built in a four-year AWS partnership by a tiny team (a data engineer, a senior engineer and a product manager) with consultants filling gaps.
Claude Design is used for wireframes and prototypes with generated dummy data, avoiding museum IP or real records.
AWS Kiro sits inside the AWS account, allowing central access control and logging of model use.
GitLab agents add automated code review before deployment.
Organisations without an AI policy should get one now; retrofitting code to a policy is hard.
AI-assisted outputs (duplicate detection, PII checks, species clustering) arrive as suggestions for Centre for UK Nature experts to action.

moments.description: The three boundaries of AI tool use: design, coding assistant, automated review.
Team rules for AI use.
Open call for ideas on validation and provenance.

title: Scalable Edge AI for Real-Time Biodiversity Monitoring: tracking invasive plant species in roadside imagery
session: AI for Biodiversity Data
summary: Giulio Martellucci presented work from a Biodiversa+ project in which vehicle-mounted cameras captured high-resolution roadside imagery across several countries (about 2,200 km of roads, 60 target alien plant species). Applying the Pl@ntNet classifier with multi-scale tiling works but takes around 10 seconds per image, so the team used knowledge distillation from the tiling 'teacher' to a global multi-label model: first the DINOv2 vision transformer, then a ConvNeXt (DINOv3-pretrained) model that scales linearly with resolution. The ConvNeXt model was both far cheaper (about 12 hours and 2.6 kWh versus 18 days and 138 kWh for the monitored roads) and more accurate on an expert-annotated test set.
takeaway: Distilling a tiling-based plant identifier into a single ConvNeXt model makes high-resolution roadside invasive-species monitoring fast, cheap and more accurate.
whyItMatters: Transport corridors spread invasive plants; efficient models that could run in real time and be released open source make continental-scale early detection feasible.
keyPoints: Invasive plants are among the top five drivers of biodiversity loss; roads and railways accelerate seed dispersal.
Multi-scale tiling with the Pl@ntNet API (~70,000 species) gives presence/absence but is slow and costly.
Knowledge distillation trains a student to mimic the tiling teacher's predictions on whole high-resolution images.
Vision transformers scale quadratically with resolution; ConvNeXt scales linearly.
ConvNeXt processes about 14 images per second and uses dramatically fewer GFLOPs than tiling.
ConvNeXt achieved the best mAP and ROC metrics on a test set of 36 monitored species annotated by experts; tiling ranks true occurrences but produces too many false alarms.
Grad-CAM and dense-feature analyses show the model localises species even with occlusion and overlap.

moments.description: Why tiling is too costly: ~10 s per image and ~70 days non-stop for all roads.
Compute and energy comparison of tiling vs ConvNeXt.
Conclusions and plans for open-source release.

title: AI-vision for integrated management of pest insects and their natural enemies
session: AI for Biodiversity Data
summary: Ritter Guimapi of NIBIO presented an idea and work in progress: extending precision sprayer robots, which in Norway have cut herbicide use by 40-90% by dropping herbicide only on detected weeds, to insect pests within conservation biological control. The vision is a robot that distinguishes pests from beneficial natural enemies (e.g. parasitoids) and applies insecticide only to pests. He described why collecting representative training images has proven much harder than for weeds: pest-enemy interactions are transient and hard to time, insects are mobile, damaging life stages sit on leaf undersides, affordable equipment is needed, and regulations restrict releasing natural enemies in controlled settings. He invited suggestions on equipment and approaches.
takeaway: Moving precision spraying from static weeds to mobile pests and their natural enemies is blocked mainly by the difficulty of collecting representative image data.
whyItMatters: Integrating AI vision into conservation biological control could reduce pesticide use while protecting beneficial insects, but data acquisition is the bottleneck.
keyPoints: Integrated Pest Management and conservation biological control aim to keep pests below thresholds while supporting beneficial organisms.
Precision sprayer robots in Norway reduce herbicide use by 40-90%, helped by regulations banning drone spraying.
Transfer learning was the first idea, but field data collection failed.
Challenges: timing of interactions, insect mobility, eggs and larvae on leaf undersides, cost of equipment, and national regulations.
A controlled environment is being explored but is not simple either.

moments.description: The core idea: robots that spray only pests, sparing natural enemies.
Why collecting representative pest images is harder than for weeds.

title: Soundscape China: Listening to the Sounds of Nature with AI
session: AI for Biodiversity Data
summary: Congtian Lin presented Soundscape China, a national initiative to build a passive acoustic monitoring network, a nature-sound database and AI models, while involving citizen scientists and sound artists. The project tests sound sensors from different companies against standards (4G/5G data transfer, solar power, over 50 days' storage); about 280 devices have been deployed by over 110 participating organisations at more than 260 sites, yielding over 3.6 million records in one year. The platform includes a citizen-science recording app, an annotation tool with volunteers, a localised extension of Audubon Core, and a self-supervised pre-trained spectrogram model for sound event detection and classification, illustrated with bird-call activity patterns at three sites in Shandong Province.
takeaway: Soundscape China is building a nationwide acoustic sensor network, database and AI models, gathering 3.6 million recordings in its first year.
whyItMatters: Standardised, large-scale acoustic data and open datasets are prerequisites for training reliable sound-recognition models and for using soundscapes as biodiversity indicators.
keyPoints: Soundscape ecology treats sound diversity as an indicator of biodiversity.
Framework: platform of sensors, models and database; services for data sharing, annotation, analysis and model training; audiences in monitoring, sound art and citizen science.
Device standards: 4G/5G automatic transfer, solar-powered, >50 days storage, plus plug-in microphones for citizen scientists.
About 280 devices, 110+ organisations, 260+ sites.
Audubon Core was used as the data standard but extended and localised, e.g. for equipment information.
Pre-training on time and frequency patches of spectrograms supports downstream sound event detection and classification.
The programme is endorsed by ISSP within the UNESCO science decade.

moments.description: Why Soundscape China: testing devices, building a database, training models and involving the public and artists.
Progress: devices, participating organisations and deployment sites.
Shandong case study of bird call events.

title: Cross-Modal Coordination for Biodiversity Monitoring at Scale: Lessons from SmartWilds
session: AI for Biodiversity Data
summary: Jenna Kline, a postdoc at MIT, presented her PhD work reframing ecological sensing as an adaptive edge-systems problem in which AI closes the sensing loop. She first described autonomous drone systems for tracking herds that redefine the target as the herd, add behaviour-adaptive flight to reduce disturbance, and adapt paths to capture views needed for individual identification (tested in Ohio and Kenya). She then argued for cross-modal coordination among drones, camera traps, acoustic monitors, citizen science and GPS, presenting the SmartWilds dataset from a summer-long campaign at The Wilds safari park in Ohio: nearly 400,000 occurrences across five modalities with metadata enabling temporal and spatial cross-referencing against a known census. Synchronised traces from such datasets can inform provisioning decisions (models, hardware, sensor configuration, thresholds) before expensive field trials.
takeaway: Coordinating multiple sensor modalities with AI at the far edge, informed by synchronised multimodal datasets like SmartWilds, can scale and adapt biodiversity monitoring.
whyItMatters: Moves monitoring from collect-then-analyse pipelines toward real-time adaptive sensing, and shows how multimodal benchmark datasets can de-risk the design of field systems.
keyPoints: Traditional workflows separate sensing, inference and analysis, preventing real-time adjustment and delaying insights.
'Far edge' means both remote field sites and constrained commodity hardware with latency and connectivity limits.
Autonomous drone work: herd tracking, behaviour-adaptive flight, and surface-of-interest-aware paths (e.g. elephant ears, zebra/giraffe flanks for individual ID).
AI in the loop increased the yield of usable data in field tests in Ohio and Kenya.
SmartWilds: 200-acre pasture with known census of milu deer, takin and Przewalski's horses; ~400,000 occurrences across five modalities.
Cross-modal triggers: a camera trap alarm could launch a drone; an acoustic event could activate camera traps; a citizen science observation could trigger other sensors.
Biodiversity datasets must be usable by robotics and AI research communities.

moments.description: Reframing ecological sensing as an adaptive edge-systems problem.
The SmartWilds field campaign and dataset.
Summary of benefits of cross-modal coordination.

title: Trapper 2.0: scalable, open-source platform for managing camera trapping projects with integrated AI pipelines
session: AI for Biodiversity Data
summary: Karolina Kuczkowska presented Trapper, a ten-year-old open-source data infrastructure for camera trapping projects, and its forthcoming version 2, which adds video analysis. Its customisable AI pipeline chains object detection (MegaDetector or YOLO models), species classification, multi-object tracking with custom post-processing, pose estimation and, in development, depth estimation for population density methods, with experts correcting results in the interface. New models can be added via a form or a Python connector class. Trapper runs wherever Docker runs, from cloud servers to NVIDIA Jetson or Raspberry Pi; the WildLabs-funded Trapper Keeper field box enables edge processing, which she argued is key for hotspots without infrastructure, data security and lower environmental impact. Data export in Camtrap DP allows publication to GBIF via the IPT, with direct publication planned.
takeaway: Trapper 2.0 offers an open, model-agnostic, edge-deployable pipeline for camera trap photos and videos with expert review and Camtrap DP export.
whyItMatters: Manual camera trap analysis can delay results by a year or more; an open, scalable pipeline that runs even offline in the field brings automation to where biodiversity is.
keyPoints: Trapper is a suite of tools (GUI, back end, AI components, command-line tools), fully open source on GitLab.
Version 2 supports videos and is planned for official release before the end of the year.
Video counts need tracking to determine whether detections in different frames are the same animal.
Pose tracking currently improves tracking accuracy; behaviour models are a planned next step.
Depth estimation, calibrated with objects at known distances, produces per-frame distance maps for population size estimation.
The full stack including AI runs on CPU, GPU or Hailo accelerators on microservers.
Over 40 million images processed by partner institutions; Slack community of almost 200 experts.
Camtrap DP export can be uploaded to the IPT without post-processing; direct GBIF publication is planned.

moments.description: Video of European bison with boxes, species labels and skeletons in Trapper 2.
Trapper Keeper field box running the full stack.
How depth estimation supports population size estimation.

title: Are plant image datasets ready for AI-enabled community assessment? A systematic review of bias, representativeness and annotation quality
session: AI for Biodiversity Data
summary: Yuchen Zhao (Newcastle University) argued that ecological AI is constrained less by model architecture than by the quantity and quality of training data. She presented a four-dimension framework, inspired by clinical reporting frameworks and FAIR, for assessing plant image dataset readiness: training-relevant characteristics, image acquisition characteristics, annotation protocol, and accessibility. A systematic review of in-situ, non-crop plant object detection and segmentation datasets screened 360 unique studies and found only 40 eligible datasets, with strong geographic bias toward Europe and Asia, a dominance of agricultural applications (19 of 40 focused on wheat), neglect of background plants, and generally unsatisfactory annotation protocols.
takeaway: Current plant image datasets are not yet ready for AI-enabled ecological monitoring, especially for spatially explicit tasks and annotation quality.
whyItMatters: Spatially explicit tasks (locating plants and estimating cover) are needed for ecological inference, and the review offers a framework for building and reporting datasets fit for them.
keyPoints: Imaging tasks: classification (present?), object detection (where?), segmentation (where exactly, and what cover?).
Framework dimensions: training-relevant characteristics; acquisition (growth stage, season, angle, location, protocol, weather); annotation protocol and QC; accessibility.
508 records, 360 unique studies screened, 40 eligible datasets.
Object detection datasets are increasing; segmentation less so; ground-level and UAV imagery dominate with growing use of consumer devices.
Datasets are uneven in size and concentrated in Europe and Asia, neglecting biodiversity hotspots.
Wheat (19/40) and tree crowns (8) dominate; only 3 on wildflowers.

moments.description: The four-dimension dataset readiness framework.
Review results: 40 eligible datasets and their biases.
Answer: datasets are not yet ready.

title: The WildLIVE Portal: Towards Scalable Wildlife Monitoring through the Integration of Citizen Science and Human-in-the-Loop AI Workflows
session: AI for Biodiversity Data
summary: Rajapreethi Rajendran presented the WildLIVE portal, which supports the lifecycle of camera trap wildlife monitoring: data management (Camtrap DP import/export, a Wildlife Monitoring Ontology built on SOSA and Web Annotation), a model registry supporting internally and externally hosted models ('bring your own model'), taxonomic name resolution through Catalogue of Life's ChecklistBank API, and human-in-the-loop verification by citizen scientists and experts. The ontology distinguishes classification from verification with full provenance, and project-level confidence thresholds can auto-approve high-confidence annotations. A GeoEngine-based virtual research environment connects results to Earth observation data, and data are published as FAIR digital objects with RO-Crate and FAIR Signposting.
takeaway: WildLIVE combines a model registry, provenance-tracked human verification and FAIR publication to move camera trap data from raw images to publishable data.
whyItMatters: It addresses trust in AI annotations by preserving the machine annotation and appending verification history, while making outputs machine-actionable.
keyPoints: Model registry versions models; currently SpeciesNet and a custom jaguar model (Bolivia, South Africa).
Catalogue of Life ChecklistBank provides stable species identifiers across models with different class names.
Each annotation has one provenance object to which verification steps are appended.
Consensus/threshold setting at project or capture-event level auto-approves annotations above chosen confidence.
Virtual research environment by GeoEngine gives access to Sentinel-2, Copernicus land cover, burn data, etc.
Planned: active learning, separating MegaDetector for blanks/humans, IUCN Red List-driven location obscuring, direct GBIF mobilisation.

moments.description: Model registry and bring-your-own-model approach.
Can AI annotations be trusted? Classification vs verification in the ontology.
FAIR publication with RO-Crate and signposting.

title: HerbAudit: Validating AI-Driven Herbarium Transcriptions
session: AI for Biodiversity Data
summary: Dilara Ağacık presented HerbAudit, a tool that both transcribes herbarium labels with a single multimodal AI call (after LeafMachine2 label detection) into Darwin Core, and evaluates transcriptions against manual annotations or GBIF records using field-specific scoring that avoids wrongly penalising AI: taxonomic synonym checks, order-independent collector matching, date-distance scoring, ISO country normalisation and transliteration, word-based locality matching and Haversine distance for coordinates. On a manually annotated benchmark of 90 specimens from 63 institutions, AI transcription averaged 94% accuracy; a Gemini 'Lite' model (ASR 'Gemini 3.5 Lite') offered the best accuracy-to-cost trade-off, the local Gemma model came close at zero API cost, and HerbAudit outperformed other tools with full extraction coverage. Handwritten labels scored lowest and most variably.
takeaway: HerbAudit shows AI herbarium transcription reaching ~94% accuracy and provides a fair, field-aware way to benchmark it.
whyItMatters: The community lacked a clear benchmark for AI transcription; field-aware evaluation and evidence that local models perform well help institutions adopt AI responsibly.
keyPoints: Manual databasing at NYBG averages 10 specimens per hour (130,000 staff hours for 1.3 million specimens).
GBIF records can be incomplete or wrong and are an imperfect ground truth.
Single-call transcription (no separate OCR) reduces time and cost and logs metadata such as model, tokens and cost.
Benchmark: 90 specimens, 63 institutions, handwritten/typed/mixed categories, annotated in Label Studio.
Interactive HTML reports show per-field and per-specimen scores; synonyms and doubtful taxonomy are excluded from scoring and flagged.
Error sources: hard-to-read cursive surnames, low resolution, crossed-out redeterminations and multiple labels.

moments.description: Example of GBIF record errors invisible without checking the label.
Field-specific evaluation logic.
Model cost-accuracy frontier results.

title: AI-assisted digitisation of printed identification keys: from book to structured data in minutes
session: AI for Biodiversity Data
summary: Wouter Koch explained why identification keys remain essential alongside image recognition (pictures often lack diagnostic characters, models do not explain why, and training needs labelled data) and showed combining image-recognition top-5 suggestions with digital keys to ask only the discriminating questions. He then described an LLM agent pipeline, demonstrated on a new key to Norwegian rodents compiled from six books none of which alone covered all species: local OCR, one agent per source extracting modular, precise statements (using both keys, descriptions and images), a fresh audit agent with 'nothing to defend', merging and harmonising characters (with documented decisions and moving shared traits to higher taxa, optional translation), and a grounding agent verifying every statement against the sources. A single key costs about $10 in an hour, six books under about $30, producing a draft for expert review rather than a finished key; generated illustrations still fail.
takeaway: An agentic LLM pipeline can turn printed keys and descriptions into a structured draft identification key for tens of dollars, shifting experts from transcribers to reviewers.
whyItMatters: Identification knowledge underpins observational data; cheaply mobilising keys from books improves accessibility, education and data quality.
keyPoints: Keys embed domain knowledge that image classifiers cannot provide.
Digital (multi-access) keys remove the linear dead-end problem of printed keys.
Image recognition can filter a key to the characters separating its top candidates.
OCR should be done locally and once, for cost and environmental reasons.
Compound statements (e.g. 'brown fur, white legs, short tail') are split; vague terms are replaced by measurements from the text.
A fresh audit agent works better than having the original agent correct its own work.
Merging treats indistinguishable descriptions (pale yellow vs whitish yellow) as the same and documents every such decision.
Grounding step checks all statements appear in original materials to prevent hallucination.

moments.description: Combining image recognition with keys to show only separating questions.
Why an independent audit agent beats self-correction.
Costs compared with expert time.

title: AI-assisted georeferencing a posteriori of herbarium specimens: a case study on Italian herbaria
session: AI for Biodiversity Data
summary: Matteo Conti described a workflow for retrospective georeferencing of specimens from a national project digitising 12 large Italian herbaria (about four million specimens). Standard tools performed poorly on historical, often Latin, handwritten localities (Nominatim georeferenced under 10% and Google Maps about 50%). The six-step workflow uses an LLM parser, with dynamically injected few-shot examples matched by language and spatial relation, to extract toponyms, habitats, elevations and relations; matches toponyms against three gazetteers; ranks and filters candidates; uses an LLM judge to accept, flag for review or reject; and adjusts coordinates and uncertainty for relational localities. Run locally with Gemma it produced more than double Google Maps' correct georeferences with fewer wrong ones, and Gemma and Gemini Flash Lite flagged all coarser and wrong results for human review.
takeaway: Combining LLM parsing and LLM judging with gazetteers more than doubles correct georeferences for historical herbarium localities compared with Google Maps, even with a local model.
whyItMatters: Coordinates are essential for analyses like species distribution models, and historical collections are hard to georeference with standard geocoders.
keyPoints: Italian project phases: imaging (Picturae), transcription, cleaning and Darwin Core alignment, publication.
About 20% of records are in Latin with historical toponyms and handwritten labels causing transcription errors.
Prompt: system instructions, dynamically inserted examples by pattern, then batches of localities.
Up to 10 candidates per toponym are retrieved and ranked with threshold filtering.
LLM judge returns accepted match, uncertain match flagged for review, or rejection with an explanation.
Results categorised as correct, coarser or wrong.
Gemini Flash Lite performed well at half the cost of Gemini Flash; Gemma 4 runs locally at almost no cost.

moments.description: Why standard tools fail on historical herbaria.
Dynamic example injection into the parser prompt.
Local Gemma workflow beats Google Maps.

title: Towards Scalable Trait Measurements from Digitized Specimens
session: AI for Biodiversity Data
summary: Kenzo Milleville presented a method to convert pixel measurements on specimen images into metric units by reading the ruler on the sheet. Instead of predicting scale directly, the ruler is detected and normalised, similar rulers are retrieved from an annotated reference set with a CLIP-like similarity model, and a keypoint-matching model transforms the known tick marks onto the new image, requiring in principle only one labelled example per ruler type. The reference set grew to about 2,000 rulers (21,000 annotated points, ~350 institutions), and 96% of predictions now have under 1% error (mean ~0.3%, below the ~0.8% manual annotation error). A proof of concept with Segment Anything 3 measured leaf sizes across taxa and geography. He recommended including ArUco markers or QR codes of known size during digitisation, and noted a proposal to Audiovisual Core to standardise such metadata and the idea of sharing length annotations via DiSSCo.
takeaway: Matching rulers to an annotated reference set lets specimen images be calibrated to real-world units with under 1% error in 96% of cases.
whyItMatters: Normalised measurements are a prerequisite for comparing traits across collections and at global scale from digitised specimens.
keyPoints: Rulers are highly diverse but frequently reused across institutions.
Pipeline: object detection, normalisation, similarity retrieval (top 3), keypoint matching, post-processing.
Main improvement over last year's Living Data version comes from a larger dataset and renewed models, especially keypoint matching.
Robust to lower resolution and partial occlusion; high-contrast popular rulers perform best; simple block rulers worst.
Annotation error is roughly constant in pixels regardless of image resolution.
No standard yet for storing calibration metadata; proposal submitted on GitHub for Audiovisual Core.

moments.description: Key idea: match rulers to known examples instead of predicting.
Accuracy improvements.
Recommendation to include ArUco/QR markers when digitising.

title: Introduction: Reimagining BHL
session: BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Reimagining BHL: Foundations, Partnerships and Future Infrastructure
summary: Nicole Kearney, BHL communications director, opened the BHL at 20 symposium with a recap of her previous-day talk: over 18 months BHL moved from being hosted administratively and technically by the Smithsonian Institution to an independent, globally governed consortium with new financial and legal homes, new technical hosting, strengthened governance, new members and a modernisation effort. She stressed that BHL's long-term future is not yet secure, outlined the two sessions' talks, and invited the audience to challenge ideas about BHL's next chapter.
takeaway: BHL at 20 has a new independent foundation but an unsecured future, and the symposium seeks ideas to shape what comes next.
whyItMatters: Provides the institutional context for the BHL talks: a major infrastructure's transition and search for sustainability.
keyPoints: 2026 is BHL's 20th anniversary and the beginning of a new chapter.
BHL has a new financial home, legal home and technical hosting after leaving Smithsonian hosting.
BHL described as a 'living bridge' still being built.
Extra discussion time was available because her talk moved to the taster session.

moments.description: Recap of BHL's transition from the Smithsonian.

title: Reconsidering the original vision for a global biodiversity information facility
session: BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Reimagining BHL: Foundations, Partnerships and Future Infrastructure
summary: Joe Miller, GBIF Executive Secretary, offered a 'provocation' for GBIF's 25th anniversary: a personal timeline of biodiversity infrastructures (LTER, GenBank, TDWG, the 1992 Rio conventions, TreeBASE, Species 2000/Catalogue of Life, OBIS, GEO BON, BHL, EOL) leading to the 1999 OECD Megascience Forum recommendation for a Global Biodiversity Information Facility. He revisited the report's figure: GBIF was to encompass names, specimen data, a 'species bank' and biodiversity literature, but funders narrowed it to occurrence data and the nodes network, and other initiatives (Catalogue of Life, BHL, EOL) filled the gaps. Today's landscape achieves 'synergisms among existing investments' through collaboration, but he asked whether that is enough. The Q&A debated how to make the case for closer BHL-GBIF links: Miller said the community, not the Secretariat, must bring such a case to the Governing Board; Donat Agosti argued literature data are already integrated at scale; and a commenter called for a new, AI-informed, impact-focused community vision.
takeaway: GBIF achieved its 1999 vision only partially and through a network of collaborating infrastructures; the community must decide whether that is enough and articulate the next vision.
whyItMatters: It reframes the relationship between GBIF, BHL and related infrastructures as an unfinished design question, relevant to their sustainability and future integration.
keyPoints: The 1999 OECD report proposed a distributed system of interlinked, interoperable databases and tools.
Original content areas: catalogue of names, specimen data, species bank, biodiversity literature, linked to sequence, geospatial, climate and ecological data.
Limited funding narrowed GBIF's scope to occurrence data and the nodes network.
GBIF now has 70 member nations and around 300 businesses sharing data.
Catalogue of Life collaboration ended duplication and benefits both organisations.
New paper 'GBIF After 25 Years' published in Biodiversity Data Journal (Pensoft).
Donat Agosti: 62,000 GBIF datasets derive from literature; new Pensoft/EJT publications reach GBIF within 24 hours with material citations linked to text positions.
Miller: CBD focal points at the Kunming dialogue cannot get usable data from their own countries.

moments.description: The 1999 OECD figure of GBIF's original vision.
Why GBIF's scope was narrowed and who filled the gaps.
The provocation: 'Is that enough?'
Donat Agosti on literature data already flowing into GBIF.

title: For the Birds: Adapting Archives and Extracting Data for the Biodiversity Heritage Library
session: BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Reimagining BHL: Foundations, Partnerships and Future Infrastructure
summary: Amanda Boczar and Sydney Jordan described the University of South Florida Libraries' environmental archives and its new BHL partnership. Anecdotes illustrated the stakes: digitised ornithological records helped establish the American flamingo as native to Florida, while nearly 100 years of Egmont Key records were likely destroyed by Hurricane Milton. After being turned away while BHL was closed to new members, USF joined the consortium in December and has spun up a redundant instance of the Macaw ingest platform on its AWS cloud, with public launch planned for mid-October. Sydney described the FLENH collections (38 archival collections, SORA's 87,000 articles, 112,000 records and 6.7 million downloads), rights and accessibility (WCAG 2.1) obligations, and early tests showing AI extraction of handwritten tabular field data introduces significant errors requiring human correction.
takeaway: USF is strengthening BHL's infrastructure via a redundant Macaw ingest instance while working to bring vulnerable Florida environmental archives and their data into BHL.
whyItMatters: Shows how a partner institution can underpin a transitioning infrastructure, and highlights both the value and the difficulty of extracting data from handwritten archival field records.
keyPoints: USF holdings are mainly historical ornithological and marine science records collected on paper.
Florida's climate, storms and unstable funding threaten archives stored in attics, storage units and marina lockers.
Macaw redundancy adds a third ingest route alongside Smithsonian and BHL Australia; first onboarding planned for November.
USF adopted the Searchable Ornithological Research Archive (SORA) when its host could no longer sustain it.
108 items (~2,800 pages) uploaded during early testing.
Field notes and warden reports mix qualitative and quantitative data in non-standard formats and often prose.
Aggregated published datasets often omit variables like temperature and tides found in raw field notes.

moments.description: Macaw redundancy hosted at USF.
Early AI extraction errors on handwritten tables.
Kearney on USF being first to support BHL during the transition.

title: BHL and the Planetary Knowledge Base: Structuring Biodiversity Literature for the Next Generation
session: BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Reimagining BHL: Foundations, Partnerships and Future Infrastructure
summary: Qianqian Hiris Gu described NHM London's work making BHL machine-readable and connecting it to the NHM's Planetary Knowledge Base. Building on Neil Brummitt's decade of trait extraction from English-language BHL literature (about 700,000 trait terms across 81 standardised traits), an AWS prototyping sprint of four weeks on under 40,000 pages of a botanical journal combined modern OCR with computer vision for article title-page detection (~98%, ~100% with a table of contents), entity extraction (taxa, people, localities, institutions, habitats; F1 ~96%) into a knowledge graph and GraphRAG search. Benchmarking with BHL-provided ground truth showed printed text reaching human-level transcription, and word-level confidence from OCR models can gate what goes back into BHL. The work is now in production: re-OCR of the whole corpus by around January 2027, an open gold-standard dataset in early 2027, and an Explorer interface in Q2 2027.
takeaway: NHM is re-OCRing all of BHL with modern models and extracting entities into a knowledge graph, with confidence gating to protect BHL data quality.
whyItMatters: Turning BHL's 64 million pages into structured, linkable data could unlock huge amounts of trait, taxon and specimen information for research and infrastructure links.
keyPoints: Four pages of a 2002 publication contained 142 data points; BHL has about 64 million pages.
Previous trait extraction covered only English literature and 17% of accepted flowering plants.
Earlier pipelines needed a separate model per task; LLMs/VLMs allow more in one pass.
Article segmentation via title page detection enables assigning DOIs and references.
Word-level OCR confidence creates a barrier against ingesting hallucinated text into BHL.
Production also extracts specimen identifiers to link back to GBIF and stratigraphy data.

moments.description: Scale of data locked in literature: 142 data points in four pages vs 64 million pages.
Article detection and entity extraction accuracy.
Word-level confidence as a barrier against hallucinated data.
Production timeline to 2027.

title: Possibilities to enhance the semantic navigation of BHL: further developing the 'unit of work'
session: BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Reimagining BHL: Foundations, Partnerships and Future Infrastructure
summary: Nicky Nicolson, starting from Kew's IPNI (funded by Darwin's legacy) which indexes names to the exact page, argued that BHL has been built primarily as a library (volumes, pages, then articles via BioStor), whereas as a biodiversity data source its pages are richly structured, containing people directories, multilingual glossaries and gazetteers that are not best reached via articles. She contrasted bottom-up entity discovery across 64 million pages with top-down, community-driven subsetting, and proposed that BHL learn from GBIF's hosted portals: branded, pre-filtered views that let communities and funders see their slice (e.g. DiSSCo UK), which could also address contributors like Madrid who keep content out of BHL's viewer for branding reasons. Comments from Donat Agosti (GBIF hosted portals for journals) and a TaxonPages developer (need for BHL API endpoints) followed.
takeaway: Letting user communities carve BHL into branded, pre-filtered 'hosted portals' could serve diverse needs, satisfy funders and drive innovation.
whyItMatters: Rethinking BHL's units of navigation beyond volumes and articles could expose the structured entities in literature to the communities that need them.
keyPoints: IPNI indexes to the exact page and structured data, not just the article.
BHL was populated as a library: scanned volumes, OCR, then post-accession article identification.
Name indexing is to name strings, not the structured entities they represent.
Pages often function as printed databases: people, glossaries, gazetteers.
GBIF (25) vs BHL (20): GBIF used later years to stitch data together (e.g. clustering) and build hosted portals.
Funders want acknowledgement ('does it acknowledge my investment?') and users ask 'is it relevant for me?'.

moments.description: BHL as a library vs a biodiversity data source.
Lessons from GBIF hosted portals.
Call for BHL APIs to enable mashups.

title: SYM08A closing discussion: sustaining and connecting the BHL ecosystem
session: BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Reimagining BHL: Foundations, Partnerships and Future Infrastructure
summary: In the short general discussion, an audience member drew an analogy with eBird, which deliberately excluded species identification until Merlin was built separately and later connected, arguing that GBIF's and BHL's early focus on core requirements explains their success. The challenge now is sustaining all the pieces: they suggested MCP servers so agents can stitch infrastructures together, leveraging institutions with overlapping missions (like USF), and each stakeholder articulating value statements to convince their institutions to sustain the relevant parts.
takeaway: Focusing on core functions made GBIF and BHL successful; sustaining the connected ecosystem now requires clear value statements and machine interfaces such as MCP servers.
whyItMatters: It connects infrastructure scope decisions with long-term sustainability and future AI-agent access.
keyPoints: eBird kept identification out initially; Merlin was developed separately and later connected, a model for iNaturalist.
GBIF scaling back to its core was why it succeeded; BHL likewise focused on being a library.
Others (e.g. NHM) now build knowledge graphs on BHL.
MCP servers could let agents connect the infrastructures.
Users and funders need to understand how infrastructures enable their work.

moments.description: eBird/Merlin analogy for focusing on core scope.

title: Biological occurrence data from historic scientific correspondence: enabling automated approaches for structured data extraction from body text
session: BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Transforming BHL: Data Extraction, Semantic Navigation and Future Interfaces
summary: Christian Bölling presented a Museum für Naturkunde Berlin project building an annotated reference corpus of historical scientific correspondence and articles from MfN journals (Deutsche Entomologische Zeitschrift, Zoosystematics and Evolution, Fossil Record and predecessors), to evaluate whether machine learning can reliably extract occurrence data at scale. A tag set (taxon, place, date, habitat, quantity, person, material, plus org/ID) aligned to Darwin Core annotates occurrences anchored at the taxon name; the first campaign found nearly 1,600 occurrence reports in 165 articles using INCEpTION. Places were matched to Wikidata (1,215 of 1,333) and taxa to GBIF IDs (1,041 of 1,154), and data serialised in RDF. He highlighted difficulties with document retrieval, erratic publisher APIs, annotation consistency and historical place names, and suggested BHL add entity recognition for persons and places and richer journal relationship metadata.
takeaway: A Darwin Core-aligned annotated corpus from MfN journals provides a reference for evaluating automated occurrence extraction from historical texts.
whyItMatters: Legacy reports contain largely untapped occurrence data; a gold-standard corpus is needed before AI extraction can be trusted.
keyPoints: Historical society meeting reports (e.g. Berlin Entomological Society 1915) detail dozens of observations.
A valid occurrence requires a taxon name plus place and/or date.
Places appear in almost all instances; dates, persons, quantities and materials in about a third; habitats and specimen IDs rarely.
681 distinct place entities and 741 distinct taxa were identified.
Full-text coverage for some journals was much lower than articles published; new OCR was needed for many pre-1970 articles.

moments.description: Occurrence annotation tag set.
Entity linking results.
How BHL could support such work.

title: A closer look at steps needed to extract research-ready biodiversity data from legacy literature
session: BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Transforming BHL: Data Extraction, Semantic Navigation and Future Interfaces
summary: Gerwin Kasperek surveyed the obstacles to extracting research-ready data from legacy literature, using a 1969 German botanical article as an example. OCR errors propagate through NLP stages, and OCR quality evaluation itself is hard; synonyms are numerous (The Plant List had 44% synonyms and 33% accepted names) and abbreviated genus names are ambiguous across groups; taxon concepts shift over time (e.g. Linnaeus' Quercus robur) and modifiers like sensu lato/stricto matter; homonyms span taxa and places (Liparis, Paris); coreferences (C. viride, 'var. nanum') span sentences; and documents mix languages including Latin. He called for coordinated technical solutions (better OCR and its evaluation, domain-aware NLP, nomenclatural ontologies, per-sentence language detection) and taxonomic rigour (stronger backbones, Taxon Concept standards, temporal disambiguation).
takeaway: Legacy literature data can only be unlocked by combining better OCR/NLP with taxonomic rigour that accounts for synonymy, shifting concepts, coreference and mixed languages.
whyItMatters: Clarifies why AI extraction from historical texts is harder than it looks and which standards and tools are needed to get research-ready historical baselines.
keyPoints: Historical baselines of biodiversity need literature data.
OCR errors reduce keyword search reliability and degrade NER further.
Abbreviated names like E. rubiginosa can refer to plants, worms or fungi.
Shifting taxon concepts are more challenging than synonymy.
Coreference resolution needs general transformer NLP plus nomenclatural ontologies.
Many NLP tools assume one language per document; Latin is low-resource.

moments.description: OCR error propagation and difficulty of OCR evaluation.
Shifting taxon concepts.
Call for a coordinated technical and taxonomic approach.

title: Multimodality for Knowledge Extraction from Historical Entomology Literature
session: BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Transforming BHL: Data Extraction, Semantic Navigation and Future Interfaces
summary: Jana Hoffmann and Sefika Efeoglu of Senckenberg's new Semantic Data Systems and Knowledge Engineering group presented a prototype linking text and illustrations in historical entomological literature, using Maria Sibylla Merian's 1679 'Der Raupen wunderbare Verwandlung' (50 plates, digitised and published on Zenodo, soon in BHL). The workflow uses olmOCR for text, an ontology of concepts, detection of visual entities, relations and attributes in illustrations, annotation of text entities using those visual entities, merging into a multimodal sub-knowledge graph, and verbalisation into evidence-grounded captions, since historical plates often lack captions. Next steps are scaling to all 50 articles, provenance, and expert human-in-the-loop validation.
takeaway: Aligning text and illustrations in a multimodal knowledge graph can generate evidence-grounded captions and recover knowledge lost by text-only extraction.
whyItMatters: Illustrations carry complementary morphological, life-stage and interaction evidence that text-only pipelines ignore.
keyPoints: Text describes organisms, host plants and feeding interactions; illustrations show morphology, developmental stages and spatial relations.
Merian volume from the Senckenberg German Entomological Institute library in Müncheberg.
Generated captions are restricted to what is supported by the graph; freer generation adds hallucinated content.
Aim to provide a reusable workflow for other historical sources and downstream BHL uses.

moments.description: The Merian case study.
Workflow from OCR to caption generation.
Grounded vs more hallucinated captions.

title: Future interfaces for BHL
session: BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Transforming BHL: Data Extraction, Semantic Navigation and Future Interfaces
summary: Rod Page previewed live demos for Thursday's BHL interfaces workshop, emphasising he could not promise BHL would adopt them. He covered viewing (the decade-old non-mobile BHL viewer vs PDF, responsive and annotated viewers), full-text search failures (the exact 'Aphrophila gen. nov.' match ranked fourth), taxonomic name search false positives (Scutellum, Argentina), tracking name usage over time (e.g. sperm whale names), LLM-based OCR (e.g. Datalab) which he argued makes OCR essentially solved except for cost, geographic exploration (BioStor points for BHL Australia, polygon search, Allmaps georeferencing of historical maps), and image similarity and text-to-image search over ~200,000 BHL Australia pages. He hoped to have an MCP chatbot over a BHL RDF knowledge graph by Thursday and asked which ideas the community found useful.
takeaway: Modern AI tools make new BHL interfaces feasible now (better OCR, image and map search, chatbots); the community must decide which are worth building.
whyItMatters: Discoverability is as important as access; these prototypes show concrete ways BHL could become more usable and connected.
keyPoints: The classic BHL interface has not changed in about 10 years and does not work on mobile.
BHL full-text search ranked the exact phrase match fourth.
Name indexing conflates taxon names with anatomy terms or country names.
LLM OCR extracts tables, figures and captions; 'to a first approximation, OCR is solved' and cost is the barrier.
Image search allows finding illustrations of a photographed species or a paper reproducing a specimen, and text queries (glacier, phylogenies, red flowers, first pages).
GBIF is now available in RDF, inspiring a BHL knowledge graph.

moments.description: Poor ranking in BHL full-text search.
BHL OCR vs Datalab OCR comparison.
Image similarity and text-to-image search over BHL Australia.

title: SYM08B discussion: extracting geography and articles from BHL
session: BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Transforming BHL: Data Extraction, Semantic Navigation and Future Interfaces
summary: The closing discussion began with an audience provocation: if GBIF and BHL are both in RDF, could an LLM use GBIF as a gazetteer to extract geographic information from all BHL pages, including the old BHL field journals project whose expedition notes could form rich information graphs? A second participant asked why BHL still lacks article-level indexing. Kearney explained content is uploaded at volume level; BioStor and later the Persistent Identifier Working Group added article data and DOIs (about 450,000 articles), but the paid work was paused during the Smithsonian transition, and she urged contributors to supply article metadata. Page added that articles could be found with a complete bibliography of life or by having AI read BHL for article pages, as NHM's work does. Kearney closed by noting BHL's need for fundraising and new ideas.
takeaway: Article-level discoverability and geographic extraction are key BHL gaps that AI may now make tractable, but resourcing remains the constraint.
whyItMatters: Highlights practical priorities for BHL (articles, places, field notes) and the link between discoverability and sustainability.
keyPoints: Idea: use GBIF as a gazetteer with LLMs to extract localities across BHL.
BHL field notes project: expedition journals could yield rich information graphs.
About 450,000 journal articles in BHL have article data, enabling discoverability and DOIs.
Paid article-data work was put on hold in April of the previous year during the transition.
Article discovery needs a complete bibliography of life or AI reading BHL pages.
BHL is new to fundraising and philanthropy.

moments.description: Provocation about GBIF as a gazetteer for BHL.
Kearney explains volume-level uploads and article data.
Closing remarks on BHL's potential and fundraising.

title: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) for RASD: The Flemish Biodiversity Portal Approach
session: To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
summary: Dimitri Brosens described how the Flemish Biodiversity Portal, an adaptation of the Atlas of Living Australia's Living Atlas software, gives different users different views of the same data. Access is not managed by the two-person portal team: users log in through the Flemish government's access-management gateway, and each institution decides which of its employees get the 'high resolution' role. He compared the portal as seen by an anonymous citizen (1 km gridded data) and by a user with high-resolution rights (exact locations), and showed that the flags are carried in dataset dynamic properties. Only the first five minutes or so of the talk were recorded because of the sound failure.
takeaway: The Flemish portal implements restricted access through role-based access control, with institutions rather than the portal team deciding who may see high-resolution data.
whyItMatters: Shows a lightweight way for a small regional portal to serve both open and restricted data by delegating identity and role management to an existing government authentication service.
keyPoints: The Flemish Living Atlas (adapted from the ALA Living Atlas) holds about 38 million occurrences, information on about 27,000 species, about 320 occurrence datasets and about 100 species lists.
The original driver was not sensitive species but a data provider that wanted its data shown publicly only as gridded data, which led to two versions of the data.
Login uses the Flemish government's central access-management gateway (eID or itsme token); institutions manage access rights for their own staff, so the two-person portal team does not have to.
Anonymous users see a generalised dataset on 1 km grid squares; users with the high-resolution role additionally see a separate high-resolution dataset with exact locations.
Role-based access flags (for example 'RBAC allowed is high resolution') are recorded in the dataset's dynamic properties.
Species pages likewise differ depending on the user's role.

moments.description: Side-by-side view of the portal for a normal citizen versus a user with high-resolution rights.
RBAC flags stored in dataset dynamic properties.

title: Restricted access species data in Finland
session: To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
summary: The recorded portion of Will Morris' talk explains how FinBIF applies Finland's government-maintained restricted species list (first published 2015, updated 2025, a little over 150 species) to all data it mediates. Restrictions range from full concealment to generalisation to 1-100 km grids and may be limited by region, season or specific sites; field notes are withheld and multi-record events are unlinked so co-observed species cannot reveal locations. Restricted data are published through a public portal and API, while a logged government authorities portal gives unrestricted access and a request service lets others ask providers for restricted data. He noted that GBIF-bound Darwin Core Archives only use informationWithheld and dataGeneralizations, and that much of the restriction information has no standard home yet.
takeaway: FinBIF applies an authority-maintained restricted species list to all mediated data, but lacks a standard way to share what it restricted and why.
whyItMatters: A national-scale implementation showing both the mechanics of restricting data (generalisation, unlinking events) and the gap that motivates the TDWG RASD extension.
keyPoints: A working group of government authorities (e.g. Finnish Environment Institute, Parks and Wildlife) maintains the list of restricted species and the restrictions to apply; the list was first published in 2015 and updated in 2025.
FinBIF conservatively applies these restrictions to all data it mediates, not only government data.

The list has just over 150 species and mirrors taxonomic bias: about half are birds (about a third of Finland's breeding birds), nearly all bats, some reptiles, amphibians, butterflies and a moth, and many vascular plants (largely orchids).
Restrictions include full concealment or generalisation to 1, 5, 10, 25, 50 or 100 km grids, possibly limited to parts of Finland, seasons (breeding, wintering) or specific sites.
Field notes that might reveal locations are withheld, and multi-record events are unlinked so an unrestricted co-observed species does not reveal a restricted one.

A public portal, API and bulk download service (with persistent identifiers) serve restricted data; a separate logged authorities portal gives unrestricted access to government employees; others can use a data request service mediated between users and providers.

Data published to GBIF use Darwin Core informationWithheld and dataGeneralizations, but the sensitive species checklist is only an Excel spreadsheet and information about restricting entities and access routes is not shared via any standard.

moments.description: Overview of the kinds of restrictions applied (concealment, grids, region, season, site).
Unlinking multi-record events to protect restricted species.
Gap: restriction information not shareable in any standard.

title: Restricted Access Species Data: The Swedish Model
session: To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
summary: Johan Liljeblad traced Sweden's handling of restricted species data from a simple role table in the first citizen-science observatory (2000) to the UserAdmin role system launched with Artportalen 2 (2014) and a federation system harvesting other datasets (2021). About 1.5 million of 158 million records, belonging to 111 species, are protected in diffusion classes (5, 25 or 50 km squares), with users also able to hide or diffuse their own records. He explained authorised access via contracts, three access systems and 'signal search', which tells authorised users whether any sensitive records exist in an area without revealing species, and noted the trend is to restrict less over time.
takeaway: Sweden combines a long-running role system, diffusion classes and a yes/no 'signal search' to manage 1.5 million protected records while gradually restricting fewer species.
whyItMatters: Illustrates a mature national approach with practical tools (signal search, logged searches, delegated role management) and identifies the need for standardised authorised APIs and verification categories to exchange sensitive data.
keyPoints: Timeline: 2000 citizen observatory with one role per account; offline sensitive observation database until 2008; 2014 UserAdmin with Artportalen 2 allowing role switching; 2021 federation system harvesting other Swedish datasets via APIs; new version of UserAdmin a few years ago.
About 158 million records in total, of which about 1.5 million are protected, belonging to 111 species; the list is published as an Excel spreadsheet.
Protection classes generalise to 5, 25 or 50 km squares; users can hide their own observation until a future date (treated as class three) or privately diffuse it.
The system is revised roughly every five years, and the trend is to restrict less, because hidden observations can't be protected if nobody knows about them.

Access routes: ask authorised staff, signal search, or sign a contract giving access to certain classes, usually for a region and taxonomic group; accessed through Artsök, Navet (Swedish Forest Agency) and the Centre's own system.

County administrative boards grant roles to their own staff, so role management is not centralised; searches are logged so leaks can be traced, though leaks usually come from Facebook groups or research papers.

Signal search answers yes/no for whether sensitive data exist in an area for a list of species, with at least a one-year date window; large diffusion areas (e.g. nesting eagles) make it say yes for much of southern Sweden.
Harvesting sensitive data from iNaturalist and observation.org needs authorised APIs and standardised verification categories so verified records can be returned to source.

moments.description: Scale: 1.5 million protected records out of 158 million.
How signal search works.
Need for standards for harvesting sensitive data and returning verifications.

title: Toward RASD Implementation in Brazil: Integrating Conservation, Open Data, and Traditional Knowledge Safeguards
session: To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
summary: Clara Baringo Fonseca explained that Brazil's national biodiversity information system currently handles sensitive data only by generalisation, informationWithheld and splitting data into private and public datasets.
