She identified three areas needing distinct rules: endangered species, ongoing research, and socio-biodiversity data and traditional knowledge. Focusing on the last, she argued that communities must control their data, that it is often attributes such as uses, local names or preparation methods rather than the species that must be restricted, and that semi-restricted access (for example for the patent office) and traceability are needed.
takeaway: Protecting traditional knowledge requires community-controlled, attribute-level and semi-restricted access, not just hiding species locations.
whyItMatters: Brings Indigenous and traditional knowledge into the RASD discussion and shows that restriction needs go beyond location obfuscation of threatened species.
keyPoints: Brazil's system is growing fast and is trying to repatriate Brazilian data held in repositories outside the country.
Currently only dataGeneralizations, informationWithheld and separate private/public datasets are used.

Three topic areas with different risks and access rules: endangered species (hunting, trafficking), ongoing research, and socio-biodiversity data/traditional knowledge (misappropriation via biopiracy).
International law is not enough; systems must carry community-defined conditions at data level and within a legal framework.
Traditional territories are underrepresented in repositories, but without restriction mechanisms there is little point collecting more data; FAIR and CARE principles should both apply.

Needs include appropriate public metadata, community authorisation of what is shared, semi-restricted access (e.g. patent office can check whether a species has associated traditional knowledge) and traceability.
Use cases: religious or sacred use (kept only for preservation), species use (attributes restricted), and hunting inside protected areas that managers want to monitor.
Restrictable attributes include scientific or local names, type of use, preparation method, time and location; control must always rest with the community.

moments.description: Three categories needing different access rules.
Three traditional-knowledge use cases.
It is the attributes, not the species, that need restricting.

title: The Edge: Insights into problems that arise from implementing data solutions for restricted access (sensitive) species data
session: To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
summary: Convener Cameron Slatyer presented the Atlas of Living Australia's experience of edge cases that arise when implementing RASD treatments across more than 184 million records using government-supplied lists. Taxonomy was the biggest problem: undescribed species, disagreements between states, and mismatch between subspecies-level sensitivity and species-level data force precautionary generalisation at higher ranks or whole species. Data errors (wrong coordinates outside a treatment polygon, names or locality in the wrong field, as common with eDNA data) can expose restricted data, and AI mining makes such leaks easier, including an experimental ALA AI tool that exposed a locality recorded in the wrong field.
takeaway: Plan RASD treatments carefully, because taxonomy, data errors and associated records can silently defeat simple rules like 'generalise to 10 km'.
whyItMatters: Practical lessons from one of the largest RASD implementations, directly relevant to anyone automating sensitive-data treatments.
keyPoints: Reasons for RASD range from conservation to discouraging entry to bombing ranges and protecting biosecurity eradication sites for trade reasons.

The ALA applies treatments (withholding records and images, generalising, modifying fields) to over 184 million records, driven by lists from state, territory and Commonwealth governments, plus data-provider requests.
Main message: plan the approach - what is being restricted, flow-on effects, and risks.
Taxonomic problems: undescribed RASD species, disagreement among states over current names, and sensitivity at subspecies level while providers supply species-level data (or vice versa).

Rule of thumb: when taxonomic resolution can't be resolved, go up a level; species absent from the backbone attach at genus, so genus-level records get generalised; populations can't be delineated, so the whole species is generalised.
Data errors can expose RASD: erroneous coordinates outside a treatment polygon, scientific names in the wrong field (common in eDNA data with BIN numbers), and locality in the wrong field.
AI makes such errors easier to mine; an experimental ALA AI tool mining iNaturalist data exposed a sensitive species because locality was in the wrong field.

moments.description: Taxonomy as the biggest RASD implementation problem.
Three common taxonomic edge cases and how the ALA handles them.
Data errors and AI mining exposing restricted data.

title: Using wildlife trade data to support proactive RASD decision-making
session: To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
summary: PhD researcher Charlotte Lassaline argued that RASD lists, which rely on formal conservation assessments, are biased towards well-studied vertebrates and miss poorly known, range-restricted invertebrates that are increasingly sought in wildlife trade. Using the Kangaroo Island pygmy trapdoor spider, whose public data were restricted within about two weeks of a reported poaching incident, she contrasted reactive and proactive approaches. She proposed a wildlife trade species sensitivity framework combining trade-demand measures with weighted biological sensitivity factors into a vulnerability index to flag species for data protection before formal assessment.
takeaway: Wildlife trade data can act as an early warning system to protect species' locality data before formal conservation assessments catch up.
whyItMatters: Offers a practical, evidence-based way to prioritise species for data restriction, particularly for invertebrates that formal lists overlook.
keyPoints: Wildlife trade is predicted to affect one in five species worldwide; poachers use public occurrence data to locate species.
RASD lists are largely informed by formal assessments (IUCN Red List, CITES, government lists) that are slow and data-hungry.
Only about 1.4% of insects and just over 1% of arachnids have been evaluated by the IUCN Red List, versus most vertebrates.
Invertebrates are often newly described, range-restricted and data deficient, yet increasingly desired by collectors; public occurrence data may be the only information on where they occur.
There is a 'window of vulnerability' between exploitation starting and formal recognition and legal protection.
Kangaroo Island pygmy trapdoor spider: nationally endangered after bushfires but data still public; a poaching incident reported to the ALA led to restriction within about two weeks (reactive).

Proposed framework: trade demand (number of adverts, individuals traded, market value) plus weighted biological sensitivity factors (distribution, population size, reproductive output, dispersal) produce a vulnerability index.
High-index species already protected should be considered for RASD listing; unassessed ones are candidates for investigation; data should be obscured not removed, available on request, and reviewed.

moments.description: IUCN Red List coverage gap for insects and arachnids.
Kangaroo Island pygmy trapdoor spider case.
The wildlife trade species sensitivity framework.

title: A new standard for restricted access (sensitive) species data
session: To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
summary: Tania Laity presented the work of the TDWG Sensitive Species Extension Task Group (convened by the ALA, GBIF and Gaia Resources), which arose from a 2023 Hobart workshop and is building on Arthur Chapman's work. The group has drafted hierarchical vocabularies of RASD reasons (privacy, sensitive location, harm, biosecurity, species attributes, usage restrictions, First Nations cultural significance) and treatments (coordinate obfuscation, attribute generalisation, date generalisation, withholding and embargo). She showed how treatments attach to records in Darwin Core Archives (as a star-schema extension) and Darwin Core Data Package (via join tables), walked through the treatment fields, and demonstrated a cave case study with a troglobitic spider, fossils and undescribed mites.
takeaway: A proposed Darwin Core extension would record why data were restricted and what treatment was applied, in a one-to-many way similar to MeasurementOrFact.
whyItMatters: Would give data users visibility of restrictions and reasons across providers and aggregators, supporting FAIR handling of restricted data; submission to TDWG was planned by end of year.
keyPoints: Task group first met in September 2024; conveners from ALA (Cam Slatyer, Tania Laity, Simon Sharon), GBIF and Gaia Resources; members from government, universities, data providers and aggregators in several countries.
The group prefers 'restricted access species data' over 'sensitive' because 'sensitive' makes people reluctant to share.

Reason vocabulary: personal information and privacy; sensitive species location; potential harm to people or property; biosecurity risk; species attributes (e.g. roosting or nesting sites); usage restrictions (legal contracts); First Nations cultural significance.

Hierarchical treatment vocabulary: coordinate obfuscation (truncation to grid, snapping to polygon centroid, randomising), generalising attributes (taxon level, locality text), generalising dates (month, year, decade), withholding records/attributes/datasets and embargoes.
A treatment needs a reason; one reason may need several treatments; a record may have several reasons - applied one-to-many like the MeasurementOrFact extension.
In Darwin Core Archive, treatments are an extension pointing to the core; in Darwin Core Data Package, a treatment class is joined to events or occurrences via join tables (e.g. event-treatment).

Treatment fields include target field, treatment reason, treatment type, free-text description, start and end dates (for embargoes), treatment organisation and a contentious 'treatment in effect' flag.
Draft documentation for the TDWG maintenance process was being prepared for submission by the end of the year.

moments.description: RASD reasons vocabulary.
Hierarchical treatments vocabulary.
Implementation in Darwin Core Data Package via join tables.
Cave spider, fossils and mites case study.

title: SYM23 panel discussion on restricted access species data
session: To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
summary: Two panel Q&A sessions chaired by Cameron Slatyer: an impromptu one on the first four talks when the session ran ahead of schedule, and a longer one with all speakers after the final talk. Topics included the real cost of managing sensitivities (several FTE in Sweden, monthly list updates at the ALA, opportunity cost), breaches (none known), personal privacy of collectors, whether generative AI already exposes locations, obfuscation on request of data collectors (e.g. pest hunting and Indigenous datasets), taxonomic upscaling, names that reveal localities, correlated fields such as collector and date, historical data, informationWithheld usage, and the feasibility for global collections like the Smithsonian. It closed with the argument that much RASD reflects expert preciousness rather than real threat and that restriction should be justified formally.
takeaway: Restricting data is costly and imperfect; panellists argued for targeted, 'shrink-wrapped', well-justified restrictions handled centrally rather than blanket redaction.
whyItMatters: Captures practitioners' candid views on the costs, risks and unintended consequences of RASD, including the conservation harm of over-restriction and the new threat of AI mining.
keyPoints: Cost: Sweden has about three FTE handling access contracts; FinBIF sees a large hidden human cost and opportunity cost; the ALA updates RASD lists monthly but estimates about a million records came in only because RASD treatment was available.
No panellist knew of data breaches; Will Morris argued habitat loss, not knowledge of locations, is the main threat and 'security by obscurity' is a poor conservation tool.
Collector privacy (Kew question): Sweden requires contactable reporters but allows hiding observations; INBO sometimes attributes data to a team rather than individuals.
Generative AI (Gemini, ChatGPT) could already reveal where the Kangaroo Island spider lives because the data were mined years ago, though a long-restricted species was refused.
Entire datasets may be generalised as a condition of sharing, e.g. vertebrate pest data (to deter illegal hunters trespassing) and Indigenous datasets.

ALA generalises only records attached at genus level, not all species in a genus; privacy-obscured iNaturalist records not shared with government led to an area with a highly endangered species being cleared.
Names can reveal localities (e.g. a species named after Studley Park); the extension allows withholding the taxon name while keeping the record discoverable.
Obfuscation is a trade-off: related fields (collector, date, sequential identifiers) can re-identify localities; effort must stop somewhere.
No cutoff date for historical data according to the ALA (30% of ALA species' latest record is over 50 years old); mobile species like nesting birds differ.

Global collections can't annotate every record; in Australia collections rely on the ALA to generalise centrally. Cameron argued about 80% of restrictions stem from experts being precious about taxa (e.g. 2,000 sensitive orchids) while actually poached taxa go unprotected.
Many ALA and GBIF users don't realise generalised data exist; better ways to represent generalised data are needed.

moments.description: Question on the cost of handling sensitivities.
'Security by obscurity is a really poor conservation tool'.
Are we too late because AI has already indexed the data?
iNaturalist privacy records leading to habitat destruction.
Argument that most RASD reflects expert preciousness rather than threat.

title: Open Digital Curation Needs: openness, interoperability, provenance
session: Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
summary: Deborah (Debbie) Paul, from the team behind TaxonWorks, Catalogue of Life work and Global Names, argued that open digital curation - built on openness, interoperability, provenance and identifiers - empowers wider participation and shortens the path from spotting an error to fixing it. Examples included Bionomia profiles that keep deceased collectors' expertise attributed, an iNaturalist user fixing names directly in the Orthoptera Species File, and TaxonWorks features letting projects search and clone each other's controlled vocabularies linked to ontologies. She welcomed agents (including LLMs) with roles in the Darwin Core Data Package, raised questions about what provenance we must now track for AI use, and asked how shifting openness (API keys, CC0 to CC BY, logins) will affect interoperability.
takeaway: Open digital curation increases transparency, agency and trust and reduces latency, but needs new provenance practices for AI.
whyItMatters: Frames the symposium's themes and poses concrete open questions for standards around AI provenance and openness.
keyPoints: Her team works on TaxonWorks, Catalogue of Life and Global Names; about 25% of Catalogue of Life names reaching the GBIF backbone come from TaxonWorks workbenches.
Openness, interoperability and provenance all depend on identifiers and TDWG standards; most interoperability pieces now exist.
Bionomia lets expertise of people no longer active continue to be credited; an early-career researcher's Zenodo dataset updated via the Bionomia API has been downloaded over 1,000 times.
Human-mediated round-tripping: an iNaturalist user reports Orthoptera name issues directly in the Orthoptera Species File GitHub repo, shortening the time to fix.
TaxonWorks lets projects create controlled vocabulary terms linked to ontology URIs (e.g. 'petiole' in plants vs insects), and search and clone other projects' terms.
Darwin Core Data Package agents can be LLMs; agents need identifiers and roles, which aligns with TaxonWorks' person-role model.
Journal policies (e.g. Pensoft) ask authors to state AI use in methods and forbid reviewers putting unpublished manuscripts through AI.

Open questions: do we need to record model, deployment (institutional vs public ChatGPT), prompts? How will API keys, CC0 to CC BY moves and logins affect interoperability? What if AI didn't hallucinate?

moments.description: Human-mediated round-tripping from iNaturalist to Orthoptera Species File.
The 'petiole' example for ontology-linked vocabularies.
What provenance do we need to track for AI?

title: Machine-Ready Botanical Data: Mapping Integrated Collections and Traits with Darwin Core Data Package
session: Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
summary: Nathan VanderKraats presented a draft mapping of Missouri Botanical Garden's collections to the Darwin Core Data Package, used as an integration layer across independently developed living collections, herbarium and trait data. He highlighted the value of a semantic graph (queries that work whether or not a system has Tropicos' intermediate 'collection' level) and walked through living collections, herbarium identifications and a detailed specimen traits section distinguishing material assertions, media, regions of interest, traits and ML features with human and AI agents. He argued that capturing which traits drove an identification is a separate problem outside the data package, and invited community input to turn the draft into a botanical profile.
takeaway: Darwin Core Data Package can serve as a semantic integration layer for a botanical garden's diverse collections and trait data, and MBG's draft mapping is offered for community refinement.
whyItMatters: Gives a concrete, institution-scale application of the newly ratified Darwin Core Data Package, including AI-relevant trait and media modelling.
keyPoints: The mapping is explicitly a draft; he asked the community to help make it a firmer botanical standard.
Boxes show both the official DwC-DP class and a convenience label (e.g. 'specimen' for Material).
Tropicos has an extra 'collection' layer (duplicates from one plant/population) between collection event and specimen; graph queries can answer 'how many specimens from this event?' regardless.
DwC-DP as an integration layer across independently developed databases, with a warehouse-like relational layer on top; knowledge graphs can improve LLM querying of large databases.
Some constraints must be enforced externally, e.g. accession numbers shared between organism and seed material, and only one accepted identification per occurrence.
Identifications link to materials and media (specimen, DNA sequence, photograph) as evidence.

Traits section: material assertions by humans on physical specimens; media file vs media content; regions of interest and transformations; traits vs ML features; human and AI agents; hyperspectral classes (see Matt Austin's talk).
Controlled vocabularies and identifiers for fields are the next area needing community alignment.

moments.description: Why a semantic graph helps across differing implementations.
Specimen traits section including human and AI agents.
Identifications and trait attribution are a separate problem.

title: From Images to Structured Data: A Scalable AI Workflow for Natural History Museums
session: Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
summary: Anne Koivunen, head of digitisation at Luomus, described a pragmatic AI pipeline for tackling a backlog of 10 million undigitised specimens with fewer staff and a goal of full digitisation by 2045. Label images go to Gemini 2.5 for verbatim transcription, then again with a prompt and schema for structured data saved into the Kotka collection management system; for messy vascular plant and moss labels an 'intent' step asks the model what the writer meant. AI output never overrides human-transcribed fields, is flagged, and run metadata (model version, prompts) is stored. She stressed that winning collection staff's trust was harder than the AI itself.
takeaway: A simple 'just do it' AI transcription pipeline with schema prompts, an intent step and full provenance can make label digitisation scale.
whyItMatters: A realistic, production-oriented example from a mid-sized museum showing both technical choices and the organisational change needed to adopt AI transcription.
keyPoints: Luomus (University of Helsinki) has about 14 million specimens, about 10 million invertebrates; about 4 million digitised in ~10 years of mass digitisation.
Strategy goal: digitise everything by 2045, requiring about 30% faster digitisation despite staff cuts.
Scalability means variety as well as volume: taxon-specific label types, handwritten/typed, multilingual (Finnish, Swedish, Russian), corrections and differing collection traditions.

Pipeline: images -> Gemini 2.5 verbatim transcription (1-5 hours per batch) -> post-processing -> Gemini with prompt and schema for structuring -> Kotka CMS; the schema is the most important part of the prompt.
Complex labels get an extra 'intent' step interpreting what the writer meant, giving near-correct output even for heavily corrected labels.
Field names were partly invented rather than strict Darwin Core terms because this gave better results.
Verbatim text is stored in a dedicated field; structured data goes to specific fields, flagged as AI-generated, never overriding human transcription; model versions and prompts are stored.
Case study of 30,000 specimens with 600 (2%) reviewed; future review may drop to 1% focused on difficult labels.

moments.description: The simple Gemini-based pipeline.
Intent step for messy labels.
Gaining collection staff acceptance was the hardest part.

title: Closing the Loop: The DiSSCo Annotation Validation Framework for Trustworthy Data Round-Tripping
session: Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
summary: Wouter Addink, DiSSCo technical director, framed the problem of a curator swamped by thousands of AI annotations that could override records and lose provenance. DiSSCo's planned annotation validation framework runs machine annotation services centrally for all collections and places annotations in layers: an untouched institutional base layer, a community enrichment layer for unvetted annotations, and a curated consensus layer. Annotations pass automated technical validation, then are routed by type and impact: low-impact corrections are auto-promoted, medium-impact ones need a two-agent condition or a trusted agent, and high-impact ones (new identifications, type status, catalogue numbers) need managed expert review. A public consultation was extended to 16 October with an online meeting on 22 October.
takeaway: DiSSCo proposes impact-based, layered validation so trusted annotations are promoted automatically and only high-impact ones need expert review.
whyItMatters: Addresses how to absorb large volumes of human and AI annotations without losing institutional control or provenance, a key prerequisite for AI-assisted curation at scale.
keyPoints: Scenario: a museum builds an AI annotation service that produces thousands or millions of annotations; directly writing to the CMS loses sovereignty and provenance.
Machine annotation services run in the DiSSCo infrastructure so they can be applied to all participating collections; anyone with ORCID can annotate.
Layers of trust: institutional base layer (untouched), community enrichment layer (unvetted), managed review, and curated consensus layer holding the latest digital specimen version.

Validation flow: submission with persistent identifier and agent ID; automated technical validation (schema, content policies, e.g. no malicious content or exact locations of protected species); automated routing; promotion creating a new version.
All versions are stored, making the system resilient to errors in automated promotion.
Comments and quality flags go to the enrichment layer; delete proposals need administrator review.

Edits are assessed for impact: low (error corrections, measurements) auto-promoted; medium needs two agents agreeing or a trusted agent with a good track record; high (new identification, type status, catalogue number) needs expert review, where experts may also be trusted machines.

Three documents (general concept, technical specifications, governance/policy framework) are under public consultation, extended to 16 October; online meeting 22 October; finalisation by year end, then implementation.

moments.description: The layers of trust.
Impact-based routing flow.
Call to action on the public consultation.

title: Geonomia: Metadata and Community for Georeferencing
session: Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
summary: Nicky Nicolson presented Geonomia, a Kew project to make specimens' textual localities computable. Only 13% of Kew's 6.3 million digitised specimens appear on GBIF maps, yet analysis of download predicates behind citations showed two-thirds of users filter spatially, discarding most of Kew's data. Using density-based clustering of collector number and date (collectors move forward in time and space), the team groups specimens into collecting trips across all herbaria's GBIF data, finds outliers, and passes trip-level batches to an LLM to summarise itineraries, habitats and regions, publishing results with Datasette. She argued collecting trips are a useful entity between GBIF's related records and Bionomia's collector careers, and that georeferencing should be shared community work.
takeaway: Clustering specimens into collecting trips makes georeferencing and AI enrichment more efficient and should be done as a community effort.
whyItMatters: Tackles the large share of specimen data invisible to spatial queries and offers a reusable approach for batching records meaningfully before applying AI.
keyPoints: Kew has digitised 6.3 million specimens, but only 13% have coordinates on GBIF; many predate GPS and only have place descriptions.
Analysis of GBIF download predicates for citations of Kew data showed two-thirds used spatial predicates, discarding most Kew data; the same analysis is possible for any GBIF dataset.
Collector number plus date traces a collector's path; density-based clustering finds adjacent collecting events, groups variant locality strings and reveals transcription outliers.
Clusters give context for human georeferencing and tighter context batches for AI.
Used GBIF SQL downloads (vascular plants, species level, one country) to pre-process on GBIF's side, including screening recordedBy values like 'collector unknown'.
Processing ran on a shared HPC facility at the Crop Diversity Institute; LLMs summarised habitats, itineraries (linear traverse vs hub-and-spoke), place names and regions per trip.
Results published as a SQLite database with Datasette; example: a 1964 trip of almost 2,000 specimens with only about a third georeferenced, drawn from many institutions' datasets.
Collecting trips sit between GBIF related-records (event level) and Bionomia careers; hypodigms (specimens cited by taxonomists) are another logical grouping.

moments.description: Two-thirds of users query spatially, throwing away most Kew data.
Clustering by collector number and date.
Datasette view of a collecting trip with LLM summary.

title: From satellite embeddings to Darwin Core: an open, ensemble-AI workflow for Prosopis juliflora mapping and reusable training-dataset generation
session: Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
summary: Pranav Jha described mapping the invasive Prosopis juliflora (Neltuma juliflora) across India, especially about 1.1 million hectares in Kutch, Gujarat, using satellite data and geospatial foundation model embeddings. The workflow combines Sentinel, hyperspectral and NISAR radar data with ground truthing, AlphaEarth embeddings, NDVI and slope checks, reaching about 91% accuracy, and uses 3 m hyperspectral signatures to distinguish Prosopis from similar natives. Ground teams validate predicted clusters through drop, curation and refined zones to build reusable training datasets, and the model is being extended to Lantana camara and mangroves.
takeaway: Satellite embeddings plus hyperspectral signatures and ground validation can map invasive Prosopis at scale and generate reusable, attributable training data.
whyItMatters: Links remote sensing AI to biodiversity data reuse, with a focus on transparent, reusable evidence for invasive species management.
keyPoints: Prosopis juliflora is among IUCN's top invasive species and has spread across APAC and sub-Saharan Africa; in Kutch it covers about 1.1 million hectares, harming native species and pastoral communities, and has spread to 20+ agroclimatic zones.
Satellite mapping is needed to understand invasion at scale, over time (multi-date imagery), where to look next and what it displaces.
Density is mapped at 10 m resolution to guide ground teams to hotspots.

Inputs: Sentinel, hyperspectral (e.g. AVIRIS and others), NISAR SAR data and ground truth; AlphaEarth geospatial foundation model embeddings train a classifier, followed by NDVI and slope/elevation checks.
Current accuracy about 91%; working with Google DeepMind to include it in Google Earth.
Prosopis resembles native Prosopis cineraria and acacias; 3 m hyperspectral spectroscopy separates them.
Ground workflow of drop, curating and refined zones produces reusable datasets; goal is transparent, attributable, reusable evidence.
Next: Lantana camara in northern India and mangroves in sub-Saharan regions.

moments.description: Data sources and workflow.
Distinguishing Prosopis from look-alike natives with hyperspectral data.

title: Open Digital Curation and Round-Tripping Biodiversity Data Enhancements Across Collection Infrastructures: Six Years and 50 Million Links in Bionomia
session: Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
summary: In a pre-recorded talk, David Shorthouse questioned calls for taxonomists to train AI identification models without credit, and highlighted that 60% of preserved specimens in GBIF lack any identifiedBy value. He reviewed six years of Bionomia: services for individuals (alerts when specimens are used in research, Zenodo archives with DOIs) and for organisations (frictionless data packages of CSV files, badges), and the potential of the collector social network for attribution suggestions. He identified unstable occurrence identifiers as the main barrier to round-tripping, noted no CMS can record third-party attribution provenance, and discussed the Darwin Core Data Package's agent terms, predicting recordedByID and identifiedByID will become obsolete and calling for a TDWG task group on an agent role vocabulary.
takeaway: Round-tripping is much harder than expected, and data managers must fully populate identifiedBy so taxonomists' expertise is credited.
whyItMatters: A reflective, data-backed critique of how collections credit expertise and how AI and round-tripping can erode or build trust.
keyPoints: A 2025 paper trained a herbarium-image identifier to 90% accuracy and recommended taxonomists train models, which he framed as working oneself out of a career without credit.
About 60% of preserved specimens published to GBIF have no identifiedBy content, undermining efforts like the EU TETTRIs project.
Bionomia is in its sixth year; anyone with ORCID can link specimens to collectors and determiners; interface in seven languages; ~320 million records re-downloaded monthly from GBIF.

DwC-DP will let over-prescribed terms (recordedBy, identifiedBy) be expressed as agent-role-action relationships; he predicts recordedByID and identifiedByID will be deprecated, questions the 'preferred' prefix in agent name, and calls for a TDWG Attribution Interest Group task group to ratify agent roles (perhaps modelled on the OBO Contributor Role Ontology).
The co-collector social network can boost candidate matches and could support a lightweight attribution utility within a CMS.

User services: email alerts when one's specimens are used in research; Zenodo snapshots with DOIs for CVs. Organisation services: frictionless data package of CSVs (users, missing attributions, date conflicts) and HTML badges.
Main barrier: unstable occurrence identifiers from dataset deletions, splits and migrations; catalogue number is often the more stable key.
No organisation can absorb full provenance of volunteer-made links; DwC-DP's provenance table may get close.

moments.description: 60% of preserved specimens lack identifiedBy.
Prediction that recordedByID and identifiedByID will be deprecated.
Unstable occurrence identifiers as the greatest round-tripping problem.
Closing messages on round-tripping and responsibility.

title: Type specimens in Wikidata
session: Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
summary: Siobhan Leachman presented a proposed Wikidata data model for type specimens, developed with Auckland Museum, Te Papa, the Bioeconomy Science Institute and Wikidata editors to fix inconsistent modelling. Wikidata is intended as a non-canonical finding aid bridging sources and identifiers, with references and edit history supporting transparent reuse by AI applications. The model was built from existing items, likely queries and a crosswalk to Darwin Core; new properties (collector, specimen classifier, collection date, location collected) were proposed, and a trial batch of New Zealand Arthropod Collection holotypes was uploaded via OpenRefine from GBIF data. Documentation is on a WikiProject, Wikimedia Commons and a Zenodo community; future work includes GBIF occurrence ID, basis of record, preservation method and biocultural notice properties.
takeaway: A consistent Wikidata type specimen model lets anyone link type specimens to collectors, publications, taxa and identifiers as a transparent finding aid.
whyItMatters: Improves findability and interoperability of type specimens and gives AI applications a well-referenced, provenance-rich source.
keyPoints: Motivation: inconsistent modelling of existing type specimen items; helping institutions translate Darwin Core data into Wikidata; supporting the digital extended specimen.
Wikidata tracks references per statement and all edits, supporting transparency and provenance for AI reuse.
Wikidata data are not canonical; they are a finding aid linking to the holding institution's data.
Approach: compare existing items, review standards including Darwin Core, design for likely queries, be pragmatic for institutions already publishing to GBIF.
New properties proposed for collector, specimen classifier, collection date and location collected.
Trial batch: holotypes of the New Zealand Arthropod Collection extracted from GBIF, cleaned and reconciled in OpenRefine, uploaded to Wikidata.
Documentation on a WikiProject, Wikimedia Commons and Zenodo (including the OpenRefine spreadsheet); exemplar items include a holotype first observed on iNaturalist and one linked to a DiSSCo DOI.
Future: GBIF occurrence ID property (under discussion), basis of record property, preservation method, and biocultural/Local Contexts notices once GBIF and Darwin Core support exists.

moments.description: Wikidata as a transparent source for responsible AI.
Trial upload of NZ Arthropod Collection holotypes.
Known gaps and future property proposals.

title: Here, There, and Everywhere: Modelling Research Expeditions in Wikidata
session: Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
summary: Sabine von Mering presented on behalf of the TDWG Research Expeditions task group (Collection Descriptions Interest Group). Expedition data are fragmented across institutions and lack persistent identifiers, hindering provenance and historical, including colonial, contextualisation. The group has a draft definition of a research expedition, promotes Wikidata QIDs as identifiers for expedition parent events, and proposes a lightweight, extensible Wikidata schema with minimum properties, links to holding collections and archives, and knowledge-graph visualisation (e.g. Scholia for the Harriman Alaska Expedition). Recommendations: create or enrich expedition items, use minimum properties, and record QIDs in collection management systems.
takeaway: Treat research expeditions as first-class entities with Wikidata identifiers so distributed specimens, people, publications and archives can be linked.
whyItMatters: Improves discoverability and provenance of expedition-derived collections and supports historical and colonial-context research.
keyPoints: Expeditions were often transdisciplinary, so specimens, ethnographic objects and archives are scattered across institutions.
The terms research/scientific expedition are not unproblematic given colonial, economic and military entanglements.

Working definition: an organised, time-bounded field activity by one or more people at one or more locations, affiliated with an institution, for research purposes, distinct from routine collecting (still a draft).
In GBIF an expedition can be an event, linked via parentEventID; some datasets already use Wikidata QIDs; longer-term explicit Darwin Core support is being considered alongside DwC-DP.
Minimum recommended Wikidata properties: instance of, start/end time, country, participants, collection items at, archives at; extensible with funder, field of work, itinerary etc.
Links to holding collections can reference specimen PIDs; archival material (logbooks, field books, correspondence) and finding aids are recorded.
Scholia knowledge graph of the Harriman Alaska Expedition shows participants, publications and collections.
Recommendations will be finalised and published; institutions are encouraged to contribute, including hidden contributors visible only in archives.

moments.description: Working definition of a research expedition.
Harriman Alaska Expedition item.
Recommendations to institutions.

title: Digital curation across the biodiversity data lifecycle, at the node level (SiB Colombia), aggregator level (GBIF) and how to incorporate user feedback
session: Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
summary: Esteban Marentes described curation as a circular process with feedback loops at node, aggregator and user levels. At SiB Colombia, every dataset receives human 'acompañamiento' - a semi-automatic review with OpenRefine, the GBIF API and QGIS of metadata and 30-40 Darwin Core elements - before publication. GBIF interprets names and other fields and exposes flags through the Data Validator and annotated downloads. Of about 700 helpdesk messages in three months, 45% of taxonomy issues and about 37% of data-content issues were fixed; an LLM in GitHub Actions summarises taxonomic feedback into JSON (edited by staff about 70% of the time) and a deterministic script checks the Catalogue of Life extended release to close resolved issues.
takeaway: Curation feedback works at every stage of the data lifecycle, and about a third or more of reported issues do get fixed; AI is used cautiously to summarise feedback.
whyItMatters: Quantifies how user feedback flows back to data and shows a careful, human-reviewed use of LLMs in aggregator operations.
keyPoints: Data flow: publisher -> node/data manager feedback -> GBIF feedback -> users providing feedback to GBIF, nodes or publishers; nodes differ in approach.
SiB Colombia reviews every dataset before GBIF publication using OpenRefine, the GBIF API and QGIS, recording fixes and required changes in an Excel report; publication only after fixes.
GBIF interprets names, elevations, dates and vocabularies and raises flags (fuzzy taxon match, invalid date, invalid coordinates).
Publishers can use the GBIF Data Validator; users can see issues in annotated downloads and dataset-level summaries.
Roughly 700 helpdesk messages in Q1: mostly general help, then IPT, then taxonomy; 46 about data content.
About 45% of taxonomy feedback fixed, largely via the Catalogue of Life extended release; about 37% of data content issues fixed by publishers.

An OpenAI LLM in GitHub Actions summarises taxonomic feedback into categorised JSON; staff edit about 70% of outputs; a deterministic script re-checks each issue against the latest CoL extended release monthly.
Q&A: no community feedback yet on the AI use; SiB Colombia is exploring AI to speed up reviews; models improve quickly.

moments.description: SiB Colombia's pre-publication acompañamiento.
How much feedback actually gets fixed.
LLM plus deterministic checks for taxonomic feedback.

title: Closing Gaps in Specimen Metadata: A Collaborative Annotation and Feedback Platform for Natural History Collections
session: Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
summary: Szu-Hsien Lee showed GBIF data trends indicating that specimen records increasingly lag observation records in completeness, because imaging is fast but transcription needs experts (including for Western and Japanese-era labels in Taiwan). After using students and AI within one institution, he built a system over the Taiwan Biodiversity Information Alliance (TBIA) aggregate (about 2 million specimen records) where anyone can fill missing terms with AI-assisted transcription and human correction, storing both for later evaluation. He also demonstrated collector trip views and links to historical botanical literature, and aims to return corrections to providers, arguing 'an untranscribed image is not a failure, it's an invitation'.
takeaway: A national collaborative annotation platform with AI-assisted transcription can close metadata gaps across many Taiwanese collections.
whyItMatters: Addresses the widening completeness gap of specimen data and offers a model for institutions lacking digitisation resources.
keyPoints: GBIF data trends show specimen records growing but lacking completeness (dates, identifications, coordinates), with the gap widening globally and in Taiwan.
Imaging takes seconds; transcription of old handwriting (including Japanese-era labels) needs trained experts and funding.
The museum's collection management system is shared with other Taiwanese institutions lacking resources; images without metadata are effectively hidden.
College teachers assigned transcription as student homework; later AI was used, but this only helped one institution slowly.
TBIA aggregates biodiversity data from institutions and government in Taiwan (also published to GBIF); about 2 million natural history specimen records.

Flags: about 30% missing identification (often name-matching issues, resolved via the TaiCOL checklist), over 65% missing coordinates (often with verbatim locality), and missing media is the biggest barrier.
Platform integrates an AI API for transcription; AI handles English handwriting well but struggles with Chinese and Japanese, so humans correct; both versions are stored for later evaluation.
Future: route accepted corrections back to data providers and encourage undigitised institutions; sync collector names with Bionomia and Wikidata.

moments.description: Completeness gap between specimen and observation data.
The annotation platform interface.
'An untranscribed image is not a failure, it's an invitation'.

title: Responsible and GreenAI: Does our community need Gigantic Data Centers to deliver?
session: Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
summary: Patricia Mergen reflected on AI compute needs and trustworthy AI based on her work in the EU AI Factories project. Contrasting SETI@home with today's investment race in data centres and GPUs (US, EU, China), she noted EU sovereignty levels are utopian and trustworthy-AI requirements can block research, while compute dependency disadvantages poorer countries. Although digitising billions of specimens could need millions of GPU hours, researchers she interviewed mostly train on laptops; data cleaning and AI-readiness is the real bottleneck, so she argued for biodiversity thematic data labs and a TDWG role. She closed on environmental costs, including PFAS in data-centre cooling, urging people to think twice before using AI.
takeaway: Biodiversity researchers mostly need AI-ready data rather than giant data centres, and AI use should be weighed against its environmental cost.
whyItMatters: Challenges assumptions behind large AI infrastructure investment and points to data standardisation as the community's main AI need.
keyPoints: SETI@home-style volunteer computing would be unlikely today due to data scale, cyber-security fears and desire for autonomy.
Massive investment in data centres is a competition between US, EU and China, with few analyses of actual community needs.
EU sovereignty certificates (levels 0-4) require fully EU components at the highest level, which is currently unrealistic.
Trustworthy AI requirements sometimes block research; UNESCO discussions highlight compute dependency of countries without their own infrastructure.
GPU targets: Amazon claims 2.5 million GPUs in 2025; EU hopes for 1.2 million by 2030; China 1.6 million by 2029.
ChatGPT estimated analysing 3 billion specimen images might need up to 500 PB and 1-50 million GPU hours, but researchers (e.g. TETTRIs cascade grants) mostly run models on laptops.
The main time cost is finding, cleaning and making data AI-ready; AI Factories plan thematic data labs, and she is pushing for a biodiversity lab where TDWG standards could play a role.
Data-centre sustainability: large electricity, CO2 and water use expected to triple; recirculating cooling systems may release PFAS.

moments.description: SETI@home analogy.
Reality: researchers train on laptops.
Data preparation, not compute, is the bottleneck.
Take-home: think twice before using AI.

title: Agentic AI Systems for Specimen Interaction and Camera-Based Observation
session: Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
summary: Jack Hollister tested whether an off-the-shelf, locally hosted 32-billion-parameter vision language model, with only a prompt and harness, could identify morphological features of insect specimens. Using a 3D-printed rotating scanner driven by a Raspberry Pi to take 40 images per specimen and Dell GB10 compute, the model drew bounding boxes and counted wings, legs and antennae, reported colour, and detected damage; features were stored in an interactive graph network.
takeaway: Off-the-shelf local vision language models can pick out and count specimen morphology and spot damage with minimal guidance.
whyItMatters: Shows a low-guidance, locally hosted route to extracting morphological data and condition information from collections.
keyPoints: Local hosting on Dell GB10 machines (~£7,000) which can run up to 200B-parameter language models (400B clustered); the largest usable VLM was 32B.
No fine-tuning; only a prompt and harness describing tasks and inputs.
3D-printed scanner rotates specimens 360° and tilts the camera ~150°, controlled by a Raspberry Pi; 40 images per specimen.
Asked simply 'what can you see', the model counted and boxed wings, antennae, legs and pins and identified damage.
Features stored in a graph network for interactive querying.

moments.description: Model identifies and counts features with bounding boxes.
VLMs are good at understanding morphology.

title: Rediscovering Archives - Using LLM's for the Transcription and Extraction of Ecological Data from Historical Archives
session: Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
summary: Phoebe Santos presented master's research (NHM, ZSL, UCL) testing whether a single LLM transcription approach generalises across different historical record types. Using British Library colonial-era India records and NHM mammal osteology table records, a closed-weight Claude Sonnet model and open-weight Qwen 2.5-VL 32B were prompted to classify page structure (text, mixed, table) and transcribe while preserving structure, with zero-, one- and few-shot and dataset-specific examples. Both did well on text; Claude was significantly better especially on tables and was robust to prompting, while Qwen improved with more and dataset-specific examples.
takeaway: Off-the-shelf multimodal LLMs can transcribe varied handwritten archives well, with closed models more robust on structured tables.
whyItMatters: Evidence that LLM transcription is a viable, affordable route to unlocking historical ecological archives.
keyPoints: Goal: test generalisation of one approach across collections with different handwriting, format and structure.
Structure matters for meaning; models often failed to reproduce page formatting.
Datasets: British Library 18th-19th century British Colonial Office India records; NHM handwritten mammal osteology tables.
Models: Claude Sonnet (closed weights) and Qwen 2.5-VL 32B (open weights), temperature 0.7, no other changes.
Prompt asks the model to classify each page as text, mixed or table and apply matching structure instructions.
Both good on text; Claude significantly better (small absolute gap) and much better on structured records; Claude consistent across prompting; Qwen improved with more, dataset-specific examples.
Claude costs suggested LLM transcription may be cheaper than commercial services; limitations: only English, left-to-right scripts.

moments.description: Structure-classifying zero-shot prompt.
Results comparing Claude and Qwen.

title: KakraCards: An AI-Assisted Pipeline for Liberating Six Decades of Seabird Heritage Data
session: Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
summary: Kristjan Adojaan described digitising about 9,000 catalogue cards recording nearly 60 years of breeding data for common gulls on a small islet in western Estonia. Scanned cards are sent simultaneously to several LLMs with a card-specific prompt; agreeing answers are accepted and disagreements resolved by a human, producing a ground truth used to benchmark more models (Gemini models performed best, Mistral among the worst) for about $50 over 3,000 decodings. Data will go into PlutoF and GBIF.
takeaway: Multi-model consensus with human adjudication builds ground truth and picks the best LLM for transcribing standardised historical cards.
whyItMatters: A cheap, replicable approach for liberating long-term ecological monitoring data held on paper.
keyPoints: Monitoring on the islet (Kakrarahu) began in the 1960s; methodology changed little, so cards are consistent.
Cards have a header, ringing data, yearly nest observations and handwritten recovery notes.
Images are sent to several public LLMs; identical answers accepted, differences reviewed by humans, creating ground truth.
Benchmarking more models: Gemini best, Mistral among the lowest; about $50 for 3,000 decodings; per-card-part effectiveness computed.
Next: analyse confusion points, run on all ~9,000 cards, store in PlutoF and publish in GBIF.

moments.description: Multi-model consensus pipeline.
Benchmark results.

title: Data Quality in Focus: Bridging the Biodiversity Data Gap for Sustainable Finance
session: Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
summary: Emma Granqvist, director of SBDI, presented work from the Finance to Revive Biodiversity (FinBio) programme. The finance sector assesses biodiversity mostly top-down with global models or proxies; using high-quality arthropod eDNA survey data from Sweden and Madagascar with environmental covariates, the team showed that machine learning predictions of essential biodiversity variables degrade heavily at sites without local data, leading to wrong site rankings. They propose a biodiversity data hierarchy with quality scores modelled on carbon accounting standards, to be refined in phase two.
takeaway: Biodiversity assessments for finance need local data; a tiered data-quality hierarchy like carbon accounting could make them credible.
whyItMatters: Connects TDWG-style data quality to decision quality in sustainable finance, a growing user of biodiversity data.
keyPoints: Planetary boundaries show seven of nine limits exceeded; finance flows more to harmful than beneficial activities.
Finance typically uses top-down global predictive models or proxies; bottom-up local data such as eDNA are needed alongside.
Study: year-long bulk arthropod eDNA surveys in Sweden and Madagascar plus environmental covariates; ML predicting five EBV-like summary measures, evaluated within and at new sites.
Predictive performance drops heavily at sites with no local data, leading to many wrong decisions (e.g. site rankings for protection or exploitation).
Proposal: a biodiversity data hierarchy with quality tiers modelled on carbon accounting and linked to reporting frameworks; phase two starts in January.
Data quality here means informativeness for a decision, not just correcting observations.

moments.description: Risk of assessing without local data.
Proposed data quality hierarchy.

title: Robots Rapidly Writing Records: Machine Annotations at Scale with DiSSCo
session: Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
summary: Soulaine Theocharides explained that DiSSCo harmonises collections data from many institutions so machine annotation services, adapted once, can serve all partners, avoiding duplicated development. Pilot services include plant organ detection (LeafMachine), links to GBIF/ENA/GeoCASe, georeferencing with GeoPick, and label transcription to Darwin Core using a vision model; DiSSCo can now run services over entire datasets at once. The envisaged pipeline ingests only images, runs services, lets remote experts annotate, and returns verified data to institutions. In Q&A she explained that data come from member countries under CC0 or CC BY.
takeaway: DiSSCo can now run adapted machine annotation services over whole datasets, pointing to an image-to-verified-data digitisation pipeline.
whyItMatters: Shows how shared infrastructure lets institutions reuse AI services at scale instead of building their own.
keyPoints: Digitisation is getting harder to scale; institutions work independently and duplicate effort.
DiSSCo brings institutions' data into one structure so services can be reused by all partners.

Pilot machine annotation services on the sandbox: LeafMachine plant organ detection, linking to GBIF, ENA and GeoCASe, GeoPick georeferencing, and label transcription into Darwin Core; none developed by DiSSCo, all adapted.
New: running services over entire datasets at once rather than per specimen.
Pipeline goal: ingest images, run services, remote human experts annotate, verified data returned to institutions (export exists; return in development).
Virtual hackathon next month for connecting services; DiSSCo is becoming an ERIC to enable service level agreements.

moments.description: Pilot machine annotation services.
Envisaged digitisation pipeline.

title: From Collection Drawers to AI - A One-Week Recipe
session: Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
summary: Arianna Salili-James described a collaboration with NIBIO (Norway) in which a team built a digitisation rig in one week from recycled parts (a BugDome box, cheap lights, two borrowed cameras and a rotating platform, inspired by NHM's ALICE). They photographed bark beetle specimens and took 360° videos (useful for label reading), trained a YOLO model for genus- and species-level classification using GBIF and in-house images, and built 3D meshes from video with COLMAP for outreach. A refined three-camera version with one-button software and label extraction is in development; in Q&A she estimated 20-40 seconds per specimen and very low costs besides cameras.
takeaway: A useful AI-ready digitisation setup can be built in a week from recycled materials and borrowed cameras.
whyItMatters: Demonstrates a low-cost, rapid path to digitisation and AI classification for smaller collections.
keyPoints: NIBIO's entomology collection has about 200,000 pinned insects; focus on Coleoptera (bark beetles).
Plan: prototype rig, one week of photography, AI species identification, 3D reconstruction.
Rig built from a BugDome box, foam, zip ties, cheap lights, two borrowed cameras and a rotating platform (inspired by ALICE).
360° videos gave excellent label views and may feed automatic label extraction; videos are temporary.
GBIF data filtered by an AI tool plus NIBIO and NHM photos used to train a YOLO model for genus and species classification with good results.
3D meshes created from video using COLMAP for outreach.
Refined three-camera box with one-button capture software and label extraction under development; the team seeks a name for it.

moments.description: Building the rig from recycled parts.
360° video gives excellent label views.
Cost and speed of the setup.

title: Semantic Governance and Knowledge Organization in AI-Augmented Biodiversity Infrastructures
session: Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
summary: In a pre-recorded talk, Andrew Jones argued that as AI generates annotations, classifications and links probabilistically, the key question becomes how to govern the meaning AI creates. He identified challenges of semantic ambiguity, inconsistency, provenance and institutional trust, and proposed AI-assisted rather than AI-directed curation: outputs mapped to established vocabularies, checked against community standards and accompanied by provenance, with governance built into technical architecture. He called on TDWG to define provenance-aware, semantically transparent, interoperable and community-governed practices, pointing to the Image Quality and AI Readiness Task Group.
takeaway: AI-generated biodiversity knowledge must be provenance-aware and anchored in shared vocabularies, making AI-assisted rather than AI-directed curation.
whyItMatters: Articulates governance principles for AI annotations that complement technical frameworks like DiSSCo's validation layers.
keyPoints: AI can enrich records, find relationships and improve discoverability, e.g. across Tulane's millions of specimen records.
AI can generate an answer without generating an agreed-upon meaning.
Challenges: semantic ambiguity, inconsistency between systems or runs, provenance of machine-generated content, institutional trust.
Existing standards and vocabularies provide shared semantic commitments that generative AI lacks.
AI-assisted curation: map outputs to vocabularies, check against standards, record provenance, note human review.
Recommended principles: provenance-aware, semantically transparent, interoperable, community-driven governance.

moments.description: Four challenges of AI-generated meaning.
Four recommended principles for TDWG.

title: kabr-tools: A Modular Workflow for Automated Video-Based Behavioral Monitoring Across the Autonomy Spectrum
session: Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
summary: In a pre-recorded lightning talk, Jenna Kline introduced kabr-tools, which grew out of the KABR (Kenyan Animal Behavior Recognition) drone video dataset collected at Mpala Research Centre in 2023 (about 10 hours of footage, 900+ annotated videos, ~200,000 Hugging Face downloads). The modular workflow runs from drone or camera-trap video collection through model-agnostic detection, tracking and behaviour annotation with manual oversight, to ecological analyses such as time budgets, behaviour transitions and individual behaviour patterns, and has been used for African wild dog studies.
takeaway: kabr-tools offers a modular, model-agnostic pipeline from drone or camera-trap video to ecological behaviour analysis.
whyItMatters: Helps ecologists process video datasets too large for manual analysis while choosing their level of automation.
keyPoints: KABR dataset: three species, about 10 hours of footage, over 900 annotated behaviour videos, about 200,000 downloads on Hugging Face.
Workflow stages: detection, tracking and behaviour annotation, all model-agnostic with adjustable autonomy.
Supports time budgets, behaviour transitions, land-use comparisons and individual identity tracking.
Used by collaborators for camera trap and drone studies of African wild dogs; scripts, data and preprint available online.

moments.description: Three ML stages of the workflow.

title: LT17 closing Q&A: AI hallucinations, validation and lightning-talk format
session: Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
summary: After the lightning talks the moderators opened questions. Besides questions to individual speakers (captured with those talks), an audience member asked whether speakers found hallucinations when reviewing AI outputs. The answer (apparently from a collaborator of Jenna Kline) was that non-generative ML tools don't hallucinate but misclassify, and accuracy should be evaluated at the ecological task level because of distribution shift; Jack Hollister acknowledged validating vast LLM outputs is an unsolved problem; a relayed comment argued ML behaviour annotation beats humans. The session closed with feedback that Q&A in lightning sessions needs better support.
takeaway: Validation of large-scale AI output remains open; for ML classifiers, accuracy should be judged on the ecological task rather than benchmark metrics.
whyItMatters: Highlights evaluation practices for AI in biodiversity and practical lessons for running lightning sessions.
keyPoints: Question to all: have you found hallucinations, and does not finding any mean none exist or they were undetected?

Answer: non-generative ML has no hallucinations but has expected misclassifications; evaluate accuracy at the ecological task level because ML accuracy is misleading once deployed under distribution shift.
Jack Hollister: LLM outputs are too large to validate fully; how to find small hallucinations is an open question.
Relayed from Jenna Kline: ML-based behaviour classification can be better than human analysis; latent-space approaches (Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior) address unnamed behaviours.
Audience feedback: the one-minute format and app made asking questions hard; moderators suggested better aids listing talks at the end.

moments.description: Question on hallucinations in AI digitisation.
Validation of massive LLM outputs is unsolved.

title: A community-curated controlled vocabulary for fossil collections using dwc:materialEntityType
session: Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
summary: Holly Little explained why the new Darwin Core terms materialEntityCategory and materialEntityType (from the Darwin Core Data Package work) give paleontology collections a chance to go beyond basisOfRecord = FossilSpecimen. Using examples (insects in amber versus compression fossils, bivalves in matrix, forams as bulk samples, picks, slides or macrofossils, trilobite mass-mortality slabs) she showed that early values such as macrofossil/mesofossil/microfossil are too coarse for search, research and imaging planning. The group proposes a first-level controlled vocabulary drawn from terms collections already use, with an informal second level, and is seeking community feedback via a QR-linked document before formal proposal to Darwin Core.
takeaway: A granular, community-derived vocabulary for dwc:materialEntityType would let users filter fossil records by what the material actually is, which basisOfRecord cannot do.
whyItMatters: Fossil records in aggregators like GBIF are hard to filter by the kind of physical material; a shared vocabulary improves discoverability for researchers and planning for collections staff (e.g. imaging workflows).
keyPoints: basisOfRecord = FossilSpecimen only separates fossils from other record types; it cannot distinguish e.g. an insect in amber from a compression fossil.

materialEntityCategory would carry 'fossil'/'fossilized', while materialEntityType can be more specific; early proposed values (macro-, meso-, micro-, oversized fossil) were judged not granular enough.
Feedback was gathered from the Paleo Data Working Group, researchers, a session at the Smithsonian NMNH, the TDWG Earth Sciences and Paleobiology Interest Group and a US collections workshop.
The vocabulary prioritises terms the paleo community already uses; some perceived overlap between terms is intentional.
Proposal is hierarchical: a formal first level plus an informal nested second level for institutions wanting more detail.
It covers paleontology only; geology material types are handled by a separate vocabulary Ben Norton is developing.
Other terms (dwc:preparations, counts, taxonomy, Latimer Core terms) help but are uncontrolled, not indexed or not in Darwin Core; a morphology term does not yet exist.

moments.description: Amber vs compression fossil insect example illustrating the filtering problem.
Proposed vocabulary document (QR code) and two-level hierarchy.

title: Extending Specify 7 for geological collections (GeoSpecify)
session: Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
summary: Theresa Miller presented GeoSpecify, the SwissCollNet-funded collaboration (Natural History Museum Bern, Specify Collections Consortium, Ben Norton) that extended the existing Specify 7 data model for geology rather than building a separate system. After requirements gathering with Swiss museums and an advisory committee, Specify gained an improved chronostratigraphy tree with start/end ages and biostratigraphy flags, a tectonic unit tree, an extended Geologic Context table, one-to-many relative and absolute age tables, and an 'extended age query' that searches all age fields by name or numeric range with strict or non-strict matching. Collection object types, discipline default forms, collection object groups (discrete, consolidated, drill core) and components allow mixed rock, mineral and fossil collections in one system, with Darwin Core Archive export planned to include the mineralogy extension.
takeaway: GeoSpecify brings geology into the same Specify data model as biological collections, with purpose-built age, stratigraphy and composite-object features.
whyItMatters: Institutions with mixed biological, paleontological and geological holdings can manage them in one standards-aligned system and publish geology data via Darwin Core.
keyPoints: Project led by Beda Hofmann (NHM Bern), James Beach (Specify) and Ben Norton, funded via the Swiss Academy of Sciences' SwissCollNet; phase 1 (from 2023) built a conceptual model and classification, phase 2 defined requirements and implementation.
Requirements came from four Swiss collections (Bern, Basel, Geneva, Lausanne), a GeoSpecify advisory committee and an on-site requirements trip; needs included warnings for heavy or toxic specimens.
Chronostratigraphy tree shows start/end dates, links to the International Chronostratigraphic Chart, stays ordered by age and can flag biostratigraphy nodes.
Lithostratigraphy and a new Tectonic Unit tree are populated locally because terms vary by region.
Geologic Context links to all stratigraphic trees and supports start and end chronostratigraphic periods; relative and absolute ages are one-to-many (e.g. deposition and metamorphism ages).
Extended age query searches geologic context, relative and absolute ages together, converting period names to numeric ranges and supporting strict/non-strict range matching.

Collection Object Types let one collection hold minerals, rocks and fossils with different trees, forms and numbering; Collection Object Groups (discrete, consolidated, drill core) and components capture composite specimens.
Data can be exported as Darwin Core Archive/RSS; the mineralogy extension will be an export option once accepted by GBIF.

moments.description: Explanation of the extended age query, the speaker's favourite feature.
Collection Object Groups: discrete, consolidated and drill core.

title: Improving access to Earth science collections data via GeoCASe and the European Open Science Cloud (GeoDARA)
session: Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
summary: Laura Tilley described GeoDARA, a six-month (May-November) EOSC Gravity small project by the CETAF Earth Science Group and partners exploring how earth science collection data can be made more FAIR through GeoCASe and connected to the EOSC thematic node DataTERRA. Three case-study datasets (Quaternary pollen records from Estonia, 7,500-year tree-ring isotope records from the University of Helsinki, and HMS Challenger foraminifera from NHM London) are being used to assess metadata such as object type, taxonomy, origin, age, depositional environment and provenance. A key finding is the mismatch between specimen-level standards (ABCD-EFG, Darwin Core) and DataTERRA's dataset-level DCAT, so the project is mapping between them and will deliver a demonstrator, guidance and an online training workshop on 28-29 October.
takeaway: Linking specimen-rich GeoCASe records to dataset-level DCAT descriptions could let deep-time collection data feed modern environmental observation infrastructures.
whyItMatters: Earth science collections hold deep-time environmental records that are largely invisible outside the collections community; connecting them to EOSC could support climate and environmental research.
keyPoints: Earth science collections allow interdisciplinary, deep-time research but have low visibility, inadequate metadata and limited access.
GeoDARA is funded as a six-month small project under EOSC Gravity and aims to connect GeoCASe to DataTERRA, an EOSC thematic node for environmental and observation data.
Case studies: Estonian pollen records, Finno-Scandinavian tree-ring records (University of Helsinki) with oxygen/carbon isotopes, and HMS Challenger foraminifera (NHM London).
Collections use ABCD-EFG or Darwin Core at specimen level, whereas DataTERRA uses DCAT at dataset level, which cannot carry individual specimen information.
Next steps: complete the metadata assessment, improve datasets and possibly the GeoCASe data model, publish via GeoCASe, map to DCAT and produce a demonstrator plus guidance.
An online training/demonstrator workshop is planned for 28-29 October.

moments.description: Mismatch between specimen-level standards and dataset-level DCAT.
Online training demonstrator workshop on 28-29 October.

title: Improving geospecimen provenance and findability in the National Museums Scotland Scottish mineral collection
session: Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
summary: Sarah Stewart, a computational chemistry PhD student, reported on a two-month internship improving provenance for the roughly 18,000-specimen Scottish mineral collection at National Museums Scotland. She merged transcribed historical ledgers with modern museum records, parsed locality strings into hierarchical levels, standardised names to IMA species and Dana/Strunz classes, and matched unique localities to Mindat to add coordinates, using Python scripts plus manual review. The pipeline exposed record problems (26,000 records for 18,000 specimens, about 1,000 without IDs, 15,000 duplicates needing triage) and resulted in 16,000 validated specimens, while the museum contributed new species occurrences and almost 2,000 new localities back to Mindat.
takeaway: A scripted, reviewable workflow can quickly reconcile legacy mineral records and enrich them with Mindat coordinates, while giving data back to the community resource.
whyItMatters: Shows a transferable, low-cost approach for georeferencing and cleaning geological collection data, and a two-way model of exchange with crowdsourced databases like Mindat.
keyPoints: The collection spans about 200 years; locality precision ranges from mine depth to just 'Scotland'.
A dual legacy problem: historical ledgers (transcribed) and modern digitised records each contain information missing from the other.
Localities were split into hierarchical levels (country, county, region/loch, town/parish/hill, quarry/mine) to preserve detail that external databases often flatten.
Mindat localities were evaluated for feature type and how coordinates should be treated (e.g. mine entrance vs mountain summit).
Scripts took about a day to run/write; the whole project took two months.

Gave to Mindat: about 900 new species occurrences, 475 existing localities and almost 2,000 new localities; gained just over 5,000 Scottish specimens' worth of locality information and mineral coverage data.
Coverage analysis found 366 minerals recorded from Scotland not held in the collection, and 11 held by the museum not otherwise known from Scotland.
Scripts are openly available on GitHub; the workflow is transferable to other collections.

moments.description: Record reconciliation statistics.
Two-way exchange with Mindat.
Handling ambiguous mine names.

title: Bridging domains: how SESAR supports Earth and biodiversity digital extended specimens
session: Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
summary: Andrea Thomer introduced SESAR (System for Earth and Extraterrestrial Sample Registration), a nearly 20-year-old registry at Columbia University that mints IGSNs (now DataCite DOIs) for physical samples and holds over five million samples from more than 1,800 users, including a growing number of biodiversity records. She previewed a major migration under way that week: a redesigned search portal, sample landing pages with maps and sample 'family' links, an improved Workbench, and adoption of an application profile of the iSamples Earth and environmental material vocabulary (thousands rather than hundreds of terms). SESAR supports digital extended specimens by storing IGSNs, other identifiers and semantically rich links to related resources that propagate to DataCite Commons, and is developing a Darwin Core crosswalk and profiles for other communities.
takeaway: Persistent sample identifiers plus linked metadata propagated to DataCite let samples be connected to their derived research products across Earth and biodiversity domains.
whyItMatters: Shows how a mature geoscience PID infrastructure can support biodiversity collections and the digital extended specimen vision.
keyPoints: SESAR was founded in 2004 by Kerstin Lehnert and fully operational since 2009; it is the birthplace of the IGSN.
IGSN (International Generic Sample Number) is now effectively a DOI managed by DataCite, giving unambiguous links from papers and datasets to samples.
The new system has a redesigned search portal, landing pages with maps and links to parent/sibling samples, and an improved Workbench with registration, usage metrics and team permissions.
SESAR metadata stores the IGSN, local catalogue/field numbers and explicit semantic links to related digital resources, which are propagated to DataCite Commons for network traversal and metrics.
Adopts a lightly edited application profile of the iSamples Earth and environmental science material vocabulary (by Steve Richard).
The new architecture eases extension vocabularies; a SESAR-to-Darwin Core crosswalk and Darwin Core sample profile are in development, with Illinois Natural History Survey herpetology as a test case.
Planned profiles for marine/lacustrine core repositories, astromaterials/meteorites and tephra.
NSF and IMLS grants support hackathons, webinars, tutorials and roadmaps for sample metadata sharing.

moments.description: What an IGSN is and why it is better than a catalogue number.
How SESAR supports digital extended specimens.

title: Developing and implementing a relational mineral taxonomy model in EMu for Museums Victoria's mineral collection
session: Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
summary: Oskar Lindenmayer described moving Museums Victoria's 57,000-specimen mineral collection (about 2,500 species, 131 type specimens) from classification stored locally in each EMu catalogue record to shared mineral taxonomy records in EMu's taxonomy module. The model adopts IMA hierarchy terms (species, subgroup, group, supergroup, plus other rank/value), keeps Dana class/code for legacy while adding Strunz-Mindat classes, handles solid-solution series such as wolframite via a multi-valued series field outside the hierarchy, and separates ideal formula and ideal elements. Catalogue records were linked to shell taxonomy records holding Mindat IDs before the new fields existed, then populated rapidly via the OpenMindat API, with about 150 non-standard records created manually.
takeaway: Linking catalogue records to shared, Mindat-populated mineral taxonomy records makes mineral identification data consistent and queryable.
whyItMatters: Gives mineral collections a template for relational, standards-aligned classification data in a common CMS, reusing infrastructure built for biological taxonomy.
keyPoints: Previously group and class were stored per catalogue record, producing inconsistencies across records for the same species.
New taxonomy records (e.g. vanadinite) are shared by all catalogue records; some fields are mirrored back to the catalogue for querying.
IMA 2009 hierarchy terms are used; other rank/value handles non-standard cases and the amphibole supergroup's fourth level.
Dana classification has not been updated since 1997, so Strunz-Mindat class/code are recorded alongside it.
A multi-valued series field lets a search for 'wolframite' return ferberite, hübnerite and series-level records without the whole wolframite group; series can span groups.
EMu cannot render subscripts/superscripts, so a plain-text human-readable formula convention was adopted.
Legacy data were copied into a locked field first; shell records with EMu IRN, Mindat ID and name allowed linking before implementation.
IMA status and status date capture discredited names without overwriting historical identifications; varieties remain in the catalogue record.

moments.description: Handling solid-solution series with a separate series field.
How records were pre-linked and populated from the Mindat API.

title: Understanding geological specimen use for effective digitisation strategies
session: Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
summary: Rachel Walcott presented early results from pooling data from three institutions (National Museums Scotland, Smithsonian Mineral Sciences and NHM London) to quantify how abiotic geological collections are used, as input to digitisation priorities. Smithsonian inquiry forms show MIDS-level basics dominate searches but subcollection-specific fields have a substantial long tail; loans show meteorites and minerals are heavily sought while rocks decline over time; NHM loan purposes show about 40% 'predicted' uses (exhibition, outreach) and a wide variety of others, with very little for climate change. She concluded that images are used more than expected, MIDS elements are essential, and geological context (e.g. hydrothermal veins, pegmatites) is a key subject-specific element the mineralogy extension should support.
takeaway: Evidence from inquiries, loans and publications shows geological specimens have diverse, sometimes unexpected uses, which should shape which data are digitised first.
