whyItMatters: Provides rare quantitative evidence for prioritising what to digitise in abiotic geology collections, including challenging the assumption that climate research is a major user.
keyPoints: Geological (non-paleo) collections are small in object numbers but diverse; mineral specimens usually contain several species plus analytical daughter samples.
Evidence sources (paper records, inquiry books, database mining) each have biases and are hard to link.
Uses include both predicted reuse (exhibition, teaching, calibration standards sent worldwide by the Smithsonian) and new uses (e.g. heavy rare-element concentration).
Smithsonian inquiry forms: basic MIDS-level elements are most requested, but subcollection-specific options show a long tail of use.
Loans: meteorites are highly sought (small samples used), minerals often, rocks increasingly less.
NHM loan purposes (850 loans): about 40% predicted uses; many diverse uses from medical to archaeological to materials science; climate change is a very small share.
A nearest-neighbour analysis of 100 Smithsonian publications shows use from archaeology to new mineral characterisation to solar system formation.

moments.description: Inquiry-form results by MIDS level.
NHM loan purposes and the small share for climate research.
Digitisation takeaways: images, MIDS, geological context.

title: Session discussion: mineralogy extension and MIDS geology rules
session: Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
summary: In the closing discussion slot Ben Norton thanked the many people and institutions behind the four-year effort that began with GeoSpecify in 2022, noting that institutions share whole databases despite worrying their data are 'not clean', and announced the Darwin Core mineralogy extension was two to three weeks from approval by the TDWG Executive, with terms usable beyond minerals (e.g. hazard type). Adam Mansur urged geology collection holders to take part in the upcoming public review of MIDS, whose geology-specific rules would benefit from more perspectives, including on the importance of systematic imaging for abiotic collections. Ben added that MIDS includes a geology discipline with two terms pending ratification in Darwin Core.
takeaway: Geology collections now have concrete standards moments to engage with: the mineralogy extension ratification and the MIDS public review.
whyItMatters: Signals the point at which geology is being formally integrated into TDWG standards and asks the community to shape it.
keyPoints: The effort started with GeoSpecify in 2022 and has involved dozens of institutions contributing databases.
The mineralogy extension was expected within two to three weeks, pending TDWG Executive approval; some terms (e.g. hazard type) apply beyond geology.
MIDS will go to public review soon and includes geology-specific rules that had only expert review so far.
Open question: how important is systematic imaging for abiotic geology collections?

moments.description: Call to take part in the MIDS public review of geology rules.

title: The United States contribution to the global taxonomy of the Catalogue of Life in the first quarter of the 21st century
session: National & Global Taxonomic Backbones
summary: Yury Roskov opened with a tribute to Frank Bisby, co-founder of TDWG and the Catalogue of Life (Species 2000), then summarised growth from 200,000 species in the first 2001 edition to 2.2 million accepted species from 158 expert global species databases (GSDs), plus an extended release adding over 220,000 species. His analysis shows US-based GSDs and US-hosted platforms contribute about 820,000 species (36%), with ITIS supplying the management classification and over 158,000 species, and Species File and other TaxonWorks-hosted checklists contributing substantially. He closed with a vision of a global infrastructure where persistent identifiers for names, specimens and references are passed unchanged between databases and aggregators, each adding metadata, possibly using blockchain-like transparent transactions.
takeaway: US experts and platforms supply over a third of the Catalogue of Life, and the next step is an identifier-based infrastructure passing unchanged IDs between databases.
whyItMatters: Documents how the global taxonomic backbone is built and argues for provenance-preserving identifier infrastructure rather than repeated dataset copying.
keyPoints: Catalogue of Life base release reached 2.2 million accepted species over nearly 25 years; the extended release launched publicly this year adds over 220,000 species mainly in gaps.
158 GSDs curated by experts are arranged in a management classification; about two thirds of the catalogue is updated each year.
US-based GSDs contribute about 820,000 species (36%); initially ITIS supplied about half.
ITIS provides the global management classification that avoids overlaps and reveals gaps, and supplies over 158,000 accepted species.
12 Species File checklists maintained in TaxonWorks contribute over 81,000 accepted species; other TaxonWorks-hosted and processed datasets include ScaleNet, Systema Dipterorum and others.

Vision: pass global unique identifiers for names, specimens and references unchanged along the chain (nomenclator -> taxonomic database -> CoL -> GBIF), extending metadata at each step, so changes propagate and providers see usage metrics.

moments.description: US contribution: 820,000 species, 36% of CoL.
Vision for a global identifier-based taxonomic infrastructure.

title: A knowledge organisation system for taxonomic data
session: National & Global Taxonomic Backbones
summary: Niels Klazenga argued that problems with taxonomic checklists are data-quality issues that are fixable, and presented a layered data model developed as a reference implementation for his flora following ratification of TCS 2 (Taxon Concept Schema) last December. The model separates concerns into semantics (taxon concepts), syntax (names, typification, usages), authority (references, agents), governance (taxon trees and revisions) and narrative (profiles), plus identity, infrastructure and extension layers, using 'sidecar' patterns to keep taxon concepts immutable. He mapped layers to TCS, Plinian Core and Darwin Core, noted that governance is not covered by any standard, and proposed a conceptual model for taxon data developed with the Darwin Core maintenance group.
takeaway: Separating taxon data into layers with immutable taxon concepts at the centre gives a practical path to implementing TCS and fixing checklist quality problems.
whyItMatters: Offers a concrete reference architecture for taxon-concept-based systems and identifies gaps (governance, conceptual model) in current TDWG standards.
keyPoints: TCS was ratified last December; reference implementations are needed for uptake.
Taxon concepts (scientific hypotheses) are central; names sit in a separate syntax layer, following David Remsen's distinction between syntax and semantics.
Authority (references, agents) links to all layers; governance holds taxon trees, nodes and revisions; narrative holds profiles and most flora content.
Identity (external IDs such as IPNI, Tropicos, MycoBank), infrastructure and extension layers support the system.
Sidecar extensions (name types, reference roles) and functional sidecars (tree node, profile) keep taxon concepts immutable.
Maps (name usages, relationships) are used in tabular data but are not entities with identifiers.
Phylogeny had to be core rather than an extension since it expresses domain semantics.
The Darwin Core Taxon class tries to shoehorn a whole domain into a single entity.

moments.description: Walkthrough of the layered model centred on taxon concepts.
Mapping layers to TCS, Plinian Core and Darwin Core.

title: Managing observations when taxonomy changes: the case of Artportalen and Dyntaxa
session: National & Global Taxonomic Backbones
summary: Johan Liljeblad explained how Sweden's 26-year-old citizen observatory Artportalen stays aligned with the national taxonomic database (Dyntaxa, started 2004), which uses stable taxon-concept identifiers rather than names. Taxonomy is published continuously and harvested nightly, but Artportalen applies changes every two months with news notes: name changes need no action, lumps move observations to the new taxon ID, and splits keep observations on a 'collective taxon' unless information (e.g. geography or phenology) allows assignment to one segregate. Edge cases include chained lumps, excluded taxa and fully revised concepts, so the process remains semi-manual with expert review, which is manageable at about 100 new taxa and 10-15 reassignments per cycle.
takeaway: Concept-based taxon IDs with traceable history let a large observation system absorb taxonomic change pragmatically.
whyItMatters: A working national model for keeping millions of observations consistent with an evolving taxonomy, relevant to any portal linked to a changing backbone.
keyPoints: Every taxon has an ID and at least one recommended name; the ID stays stable to the concept while names change, and changes are traceable.
Taxonomy is harvested nightly (Darwin Core file) but applied to Artportalen every second month to manage changes and inform users.
Not every taxon in the database is reportable; a filter controls what can be reported.
Lumps move observations to the replacing ID; splits keep observations on a collective taxon unless extra information allows reassignment.
Complications include multi-step lumps, taxa later excluded from Sweden, and totally revised concepts with no single target.
Around a million records are added per two months; about 100 new taxa and 10-15 reassignments per cycle are checked by organism-group experts.
Sweden has about 60,000 species in the database and observations of about 40,000.

moments.description: How lumps and splits are handled with collective taxa.

title: Modernizing Brazil's taxonomic backbone: how ChecklistBank supports biodiversity and genetic heritage systems
session: National & Global Taxonomic Backbones
summary: Clara Baringo Fonseca described how GBIF Brazil uses ChecklistBank to build a single taxonomy for three national systems: the legally mandated genetic heritage and traditional knowledge system (SisGen), the national biodiversity portal and the protected-area research permit system. The monthly-updated Flora and Funga of Brazil (since 2010, 700+ specialists) and the Taxonomic Catalogue of the Brazilian Fauna (since 2015, 800+ specialists) are cleaned, merged with invasive species, Catalogue of Life microorganisms and GBIF fungi in ChecklistBank projects, and exported as Darwin Core Archives, some with and some without microorganisms. The taxonomy drives processing in the Living Atlas Brazil portal, versioned republication with DOIs in the IPT, and data-gap maps relevant to Global Biodiversity Framework targets 20 and 21.
takeaway: ChecklistBank lets a small national node assemble one consistent taxonomic backbone for legal, portal and permitting systems.
whyItMatters: Shows how a megadiverse country operationalises national checklists for policy and legal compliance, and the workflow gaps between species description and national lists.
keyPoints: Brazil has about 120,000 animal and 67,000 plant species; national catalogues are updated monthly by hundreds of taxonomists.
A 10-year plan aims to create a Brazilian Catalogue of Life merging flora, fauna, fossils and microorganisms.
Three national systems (genetic heritage/traditional knowledge, national portal, protected-area permits) must share the same taxonomy.
ChecklistBank is used to clean duplicates and mis-mapped Darwin Core fields, merge lists, and add Catalogue of Life microorganisms and GBIF fungi.
Living Atlas Brazil processes occurrence taxonomy against the official backbone, showing original vs processed names.
Versions are republished in the IPT with DOIs, not sent onward to avoid duplication.
Maps of taxonomic/occurrence knowledge show major gaps in marine areas and Amazonia.

moments.description: Workflow combining catalogues in ChecklistBank for the three national systems.
Using literature-extracted new species to fill national list gaps.

title: Building a taxonomic reference authority for conservation: the Digital Catalogue of Biodiversity of Poland
session: National & Global Taxonomic Backbones
summary: Piotr Tykarski presented the Digital Catalogue of Biodiversity of Poland, built from 2021 under the Polish Biodiversity Information Network (SIBP) by more than 120 specialists from over 20 institutions and now reaching the stage where authors can edit checklists online. It covers all eukaryotes and cyanobacteria recorded for Poland (over 65,000 species in 107 chapters), each backed by at least one reference and a presence status, using an ITIS-based taxonomy model with role-based permissions. Each chapter is published to GBIF and synchronised to ChecklistBank; a portal offers interactive summaries and graphical views, and plans include DNA barcodes, printed publications and a Europe-wide network of comparable national checklists.
takeaway: Poland now has an expert-maintained, fully referenced national checklist published through GBIF and ChecklistBank.
whyItMatters: A national taxonomic reference authority supports conservation agencies and could, if replicated, enable comparison of biodiversity across European countries.
keyPoints: Launched 2021 with government subsidies; more than 120 cooperators from over 20 institutions.
Over 65,000 species (more than expected) in 107 chapters supervised by authors.
Every species has at least one bibliographic reference (publication or expert opinion) and a status (present, absent, needs confirmation).
Taxonomy tables follow the ITIS data model; keywords/attributes attach extra information.
Checklists are published as GBIF checklist datasets, synchronised with ChecklistBank; the team hopes governmental agencies will adopt it.
Portal provides checklist perspectives, Excel download, interactive taxon summaries and sunburst-style views with adjustable depth.

moments.description: Scope and structure of the catalogue.
Proposal for comparable national checklists across Europe.

title: National Biodiversity Information Action Campaign production process: a case study of Taiwan
session: National & Global Taxonomic Backbones
summary: Chun-I Chang described how Taiwan produced its 2026-2030 national Biodiversity Information Action Campaign, shifting from the 2021-2025 focus on building basic systems and data exchange to long-term resilience. The plan was co-developed via review, problem identification, a two-day workshop of a 10-person cross-institution working group mapping national data flows, and nine online meetings. Four vulnerabilities (governance, data flow, monitoring, sustainability) led to five directions including interoperability through shared taxonomic references; a 2025 data-gap campaign filled 852 grid cells and added over 3.8 million records.
takeaway: Taiwan's second national plan reframes biodiversity information infrastructure around resilience, with shared taxonomic references as a cornerstone of interoperability.
whyItMatters: Provides a replicable process for co-developing national biodiversity data strategies and a concrete example of mobilising partners to fill data gaps.
keyPoints: 2021-2025 built basic database exchange and talent; 2026-2030 focuses on open data, integration and network building.
Lessons: cross-domain collaboration is valuable, coordination takes time, participants have capacity constraints.
Vulnerabilities identified: inter-agency governance, data flow, monitoring use, and sustainability (funding and people).
Five directions: system interoperability (APIs plus shared taxonomic references), data openness and quality, network sustainability, inter-agency collaboration, data usability.
The 2025 gap-filling action mapped geographic, temporal and taxonomic gaps and mobilised alliance partners.
The alliance (16 government institutions under an MOU) is moving toward a formal organisation able to receive participant fees.

moments.description: Four vulnerabilities and five strategic directions.
Gap-filling achievements.
Methodology for identifying data gaps.

title: Metadata matters: perceptions on the implementation of Darwin Core in the biocollections cyberinfrastructure
session: Digitizing Collections & Legacy Data
summary: Wade Bishop, a social scientist, presented results of a survey (57 responses, about 98% from the US) of collections staff on Darwin Core implementation, building on earlier interviews and focus groups. Respondents were mostly senior collection managers or curators in academic settings who largely learned data skills on the job; 82% deposit data in GBIF. Open responses on challenges were coded into simplification of complex data (e.g. trawl start/end locations, host-microbe relationships, dynamicProperties flattening), lack of community guidelines, limited capacity, and other mapping issues, and most respondents were unsure how their data were licensed.
takeaway: Standardisation through Darwin Core can mask nuance, and practitioners report complex data, missing guidelines and limited capacity as the main implementation barriers.
whyItMatters: Evidence from practitioners on where Darwin Core implementation breaks down can guide guidelines, training and standard development.
keyPoints: Earlier microfossil research found a gap between metadata users need for fitness-for-use and what is provided.
57 survey responses, about 98% from the US; 71% collection managers or curators; most in role for 10+ years; 75% academic; about half with PhDs.
Most learned their data skills on the job.
82% deposit data in GBIF; storage spans cloud, institutional servers and local drives.
Challenging elements include record-level metadata, occurrence, event and location terms.
Challenges coded as simplification of complex data, lack of community guidelines, limited capacity, and others (e.g. administrative 'bookkeeping' metadata).
Most respondents were unsure how their data are licensed, which matters for machine-actionable reuse.
Next step is studying end users; a paper is under review and a Fulbright proposal would extend the work internationally.

moments.description: Coded challenge categories with example quotes.
Licensing uncertainty among respondents.

title: Pinned insect digitization conveyor: image and data transcription workflows
session: Digitizing Collections & Legacy Data
summary: Jessica Bird described the Smithsonian NMNH Entomology conveyor project digitising pinned pollinators (bees, beetles, butterflies, moths, flies), funded for an estimated 360,000 specimens, in a collection of about 35 million specimens that would take 20 people 67 years to digitise traditionally. Pre-curation vets taxonomy in EMu and prints unit-tray header labels with QR-embedded taxonomy and identifiers; on the conveyor, labels are staged, specimens barcoded and three focus-stacked views plus label images captured, with metadata in JSON. Images pass QC in the open-source OSPRY tool, enter the DAMS, generate skeletal EMu records published to GBIF via IPT, while label images feed a separate contracted human transcription workflow.
takeaway: An industrial conveyor workflow with QR-encoded metadata and automated skeletal records makes mass digitisation of pinned insects feasible.
whyItMatters: Demonstrates throughput, cost and QC practices for mass digitisation of one of the hardest specimen types, relevant to anyone planning large entomology projects.
keyPoints: USNM Entomology is the second-largest entomology collection (about 35 million specimens, over 21 million pinned).
Project started 2025 on pinned pollinators, funded for about 360,000 specimens.
Header labels with QR-embedded taxonomy and unit tray identifiers streamline later record creation; drawer IDs name image folders.
Silhouette determines imaging sphere/resolution; three focus-stacked views (about 30 slices each) and a composite label image are taken.
QC in OSPRY samples 10-40% of images per folder with standardised error phrasing.
Skeletal records are created automatically in EMu and published to the collections website and GBIF.
Label orientation could not be automatically corrected, so label transcription was split into its own contracted human workflow.

moments.description: Time-lapse video of the conveyor in action.
Summary statistics of throughput and images.
Cost per specimen.

title: X-raying wild plant seeds: preparing images for future AI-driven global biodiversity research
session: Digitizing Collections & Legacy Data
summary: Robert Turner explained how Kew is migrating 21 years of Millennium Seed Bank seed X-ray images (used for non-destructive seed quality testing: healthy, empty or infested seeds) from a network drive into its digital asset management system and linking them to collections data. As part of Kew's 2021-2026 digitisation programme and new Integrated Collections Management System (Earthscape, occurrence-centred with links to WCVP/POWO and Index Fungorum), Python tools add a resolution-based grid and scale bar to each image, validated against physical seed measurements. Images go into the Digifolia DAMS, are exposed via S3/CloudFront URLs linked in Earthscape, and will reach users through the Kew data portal and the future Seed Pod portal, subject to checking material and data agreements.
takeaway: Adding scale and linking legacy seed X-rays to collection records turns an inaccessible archive into AI-ready research data.
whyItMatters: Seed X-rays could support AI research on identification, viability and damage across the world's largest ex situ seed collection.
keyPoints: X-raying is non-destructive, rapid and suitable for small seeds, unlike destructive cut tests.
The Millennium Seed Bank holds about 105,000 seed collections of 40,000 species from 191 countries.
21 years of X-ray images were stored on a network drive inaccessible to most staff and external scientists.
Potential AI uses include taxonomic identification, morphology, germination/viability and infestation/damage detection.
Python tools read DPI from image metadata or DICOM files to compute grid spacing and add scale labels.
Earthscape separates collection objects from occurrences so herbarium, seed and living collections from one event share an occurrence.
Data sharing is constrained by material agreements with countries whose alignment with data agreements must be checked.

moments.description: Healthy, empty and infested seeds in X-ray images.
Grid and scale bar generation.

title: Next-generation digitization: integrating spectral reflectance into the online mobilization of herbaria
session: Digitizing Collections & Legacy Data
summary: Matthew Austin described how Missouri Botanical Garden, with philanthropic support to digitise its roughly eight million herbarium specimens, is adding spectral reflectance as a 'third layer' of digitisation alongside images and transcribed labels. After imaging and barcoding, a spectral team takes three point measurements per leaf surface on selected specimens (leaves liftable onto a black background, free of glue or pathogens, woody taxa with in-house curatorial expertise), recording rich per-scan metadata under the protocol of iHerbSpec, a 30+ institution working group. Data are linked in Tropicos by barcode; about 1.55 million specimens have been imaged and 16,000 have spectra, and clade-specific species identification models trained on expert-identified spectra achieve accuracies around the 90s, even identifying sterile specimens.
takeaway: Spectral reflectance can be captured at scale during herbarium digitisation and supports accurate species identification from leaves alone.
whyItMatters: Extends the digital extended specimen with chemistry/phenotype data and shows a standardised cross-institution protocol for making it reusable.
keyPoints: Spectral reflectance encodes chemical and physical properties and can infer functional traits and aid identification.
The project also funds a curatorial mentorship programme pairing 18 digitisation staff with curators.
Transcription is outsourced to MAX Communications with in-house QA before upload to Tropicos.
Measurements are point spectroscopy (three per leaf surface), not full-specimen imaging.
Metadata include leaf surface, developmental stage, perceived preservation and contamination.
iHerbSpec developed the first standardised protocol for herbarium spectral measurements, with file naming and metadata conventions; it meets annually in person and monthly online.
Spectral files link to specimens by barcode with a Tropicos UI to fix unmatched files.

moments.description: Spectral measurement workflow and criteria.
Confusion matrix for Pleurothyrium species identification.
Calibration for preservation and leaf condition.

title: Experience of collaborative management of the World Auchenorrhyncha Database in TaxonWorks
session: Digitizing Collections & Legacy Data
summary: Dmitry Dmitriev described how the World Auchenorrhyncha Database (leafhoppers, planthoppers, cicadas and relatives) grew from a largely single-person project into a collaborative one after migration to TaxonWorks, now with 66 registered users. He toured the TaxonPages public interface: species pages with synonymy, nomenclatural history, type information, specimen- and country-level distribution maps, downloadable distribution records, host-plant associations, iNaturalist images, interactive and dichotomous keys generated from morphological matrices, and pictorial image matrices built from contributors' 28,000 images. Data flow to the Catalogue of Life and GBIF, and iNaturalist now pulls the classification directly from the TaxonWorks API; feedback arrives through GitHub issues.
takeaway: TaxonWorks turned a personal taxonomic database into a collaborative, well-connected resource feeding Catalogue of Life, GBIF and iNaturalist.
whyItMatters: An example of how a modern taxonomic platform supports collaborative curation, identification tools and downstream data sharing for a large insect group.
keyPoints: TaxonWorks is an open collaborative platform for taxonomy, collections, identification tools and bibliography; the Species File Group also works on TaxonPages, Catalogue of Life and Global Names.
66 registered users; some join mainly for the advanced filtering tools.
Higher-taxon distributions are aggregated from included species; all data are downloadable.
Dichotomous keys can be built from morphological matrices; image matrices provide pictorial keys.
A contributor uploaded 28,000 images in about two years.

Comparison with the CoL extended release shows about 200 extra species (down from 500), likely misspellings or historical combinations; CoL validations partly complement TaxonWorks' nomenclatural validation.
iNaturalist harvested web pages until pointed to the API; it now uses the TaxonWorks classification directly.

moments.description: Tour of TaxonPages species pages.
Keys generated from morphological matrices.

title: Digitising heritage for science: the Medical Entomology Museum as a platform for entomological biodiversity research and vector-borne disease surveillance
session: Digitizing Collections & Legacy Data
summary: Eunice Jamesboy presented the century-old Medical Entomology Museum at South Africa's National Institute for Communicable Diseases, rooted in the 1925 entomology department's response to malaria. The museum holds about 60,000 medically important insect specimens, including about 12,000 Anopheles, and about 80% of the mosquito collection is digitised through a workflow of inventory, transcription, taxonomic standardisation, georeferencing and quality control aimed at FAIR, interoperable data. She argued that digitised vouchers provide historical baselines that strengthen contemporary vector surveillance, stressed rescue of orphaned collections and training, and summarised the approach as 'preserve the specimen, mobilize the data, extend science'.
takeaway: Digitised historical mosquito vouchers become reusable evidence that gives context to current vector surveillance.
whyItMatters: Shows a direct public-health use case for natural history collection digitisation in malaria-affected regions.
keyPoints: The Department of Entomology was established in 1925; early mosquito surveys in malaria areas generated the core collection.
About 60,000 specimens including around 12,000 Anopheles; pinned, slide-mounted and fluid specimens, type material and vouchers.
About 80% of the mosquito collection, including Anopheles, is digitised.
Workflow: inventory/accessioning, label transcription, taxonomic standardisation, georeferencing, QC, publication.
Museum data do not replace contemporary surveillance but provide historical context and verifiable vouchers.
Orphaned collections need condition assessment, accessioning, metadata recovery and integration.
Sustainability depends on training people in taxonomy, curation, georeferencing and informatics.

moments.description: Linking historical vouchers with current vector surveillance.
Central message: preserve the specimen, mobilize the data, extend science.

title: How is digitisation doing? Monitoring the increase in digitised collections using MIDS
session: State of the Collections Description Interest Group. What's Happening and What's Not!
summary: Elspeth Haston reported a MIDS-based analysis of ten years (since 2016) of preserved-specimen records of biological taxa in GBIF, using full-GBIF Darwin Core downloads partitioned with DuckDB into Parquet and scored with a version of the MIDS calculator (2017 excluded for data problems). Progress was real but not steady: record numbers reaching MIDS 1 and 2 grew, yet the percentage stayed fairly flat as total records grew, with a big jump in MIDS 1 after 2016 driven by GBIF enforcing licences and more datasets providing modified dates. Newly arriving records vary a lot, some cohorts decline (one institution's datasets dropped organisation data for two years), enhancement tools have uneven impact, kingdoms differ in data completeness, and big datasets have big effects.
takeaway: MIDS can monitor global digitisation progress, and GBIF data show completeness improving unevenly and sometimes going backwards.
whyItMatters: Provides the first longitudinal, standard-based view of how complete published specimen data are and what interventions (e.g. mandatory licences) actually move the needle.
keyPoints: GBIF snapshots lacked full specimen metadata, so the team used Darwin Core archives from users who downloaded all of GBIF.
Big files need big computing resources; one record had over 60,000 coordinates.
The large MIDS 1 increase after 2016 came from licence enforcement and more modified dates; name and identification are high due to the GBIF backbone.
People identifiers started appearing, showing the effect of dedicated enhancement work, though without raising overall MIDS levels.
Recent years show fewer records arriving below MIDS 0 and more at MIDS 1, driven by organisation and modified fields.
2016 records fell from MIDS 0 to -1 by 2018 because five datasets from one institution dropped organisation data, corrected by 2019.
Animalia more often record object type; Plantae lead on media and media IDs (possibly IIIF); collecting numbers more common in plants and fungi.

moments.description: Effect of GBIF licence enforcement on MIDS level 1.
Differences between kingdoms in data completeness.

title: The Latimer Core standard and the Global Registry of Scientific Collections
session: State of the Collections Description Interest Group. What's Happening and What's Not!
summary: Marie Grosjean explained how GRSciColl, the community-curated registry of scientific collections and institutions maintained by GBIF, uses Latimer Core. Collection descriptors are flat tables that fill the gap between textual collection descriptions and specimen-level occurrences, using Darwin Core (dwc:) or Latimer Core (ltc:) headers; GRSciColl currently indexes Latimer Core biome type and object classification name, enabling searches such as marine algae collections by country. Latimer Core is also used as an import/export format and in editor training, but limitations include GRSciColl fields without Latimer Core equivalents (forced into measurementOrFact) and missing descriptors in exports, which will be revisited as Latimer Core's structure is formalised.
takeaway: Latimer Core gives GRSciColl a common language and exchange format for describing collections between free text and specimen records.
whyItMatters: Collection-level description lets undigitised or geological collections become discoverable, and GRSciColl is a key real-world implementation of Latimer Core.
keyPoints: GRSciColl registers collections, institutions, codes and identifiers, curated by 70+ editors with Index Herbariorum as a main source; it has an API and can be embedded in GBIF hosted portals.
Collection descriptors capture lists of taxa, collectors, statistics etc. and can include unmapped columns that are displayed but not indexed.
Indexing Latimer Core biome type and object classification name allows finding non-monophyletic groupings like algae collections.
Missouri Botanical Garden's page is an example of a complete descriptor based on a survey.
Many GRSciColl fields must be modelled as measurementOrFact, which users cannot reproduce without knowing the types.
Plans to revise the Latimer Core export to include descriptors and follow the latest Latimer Core structure.
A modelling exercise in the editor curriculum, tested at a DiSSCo Flanders workshop, shows Latimer Core's flexibility.

moments.description: What collection descriptors are.
Limitations of the current Latimer Core implementation.

title: Once and future Latimer Core: status update and open conversation
session: State of the Collections Description Interest Group. What's Happening and What's Not!
summary: Sharon Grant updated the room on the Latimer Core maintenance group, which meets monthly and describes intentionally grouped things ('Latimer Core is to groups as Darwin Core is to individual occurrences'). Users asked for structure to implement it, which required identifiers; the group discovered that term IRIs obtained at ratification were duplicated with different meanings because of its generic 'has identifier' structure, conflicting with TDWG's globally scoped IRIs. After the group asked TDWG whether standards could formally include structure, TDWG agreed, following Darwin Core DP and Camtrap DP, so Latimer Core is building an LTC DP structure layer for public review later in the year (after MIDS), with a conceptual/relationship layer still to come.
takeaway: Latimer Core is being restructured as a data package with unique term IRIs, enabled by TDWG now accepting standards with formal structure.
whyItMatters: The change affects how TDWG standards are defined generally and determines whether collection-level data can be implemented in machines like GRSciColl.
keyPoints: The group moved from task group to maintenance group, meets monthly and has 15 open issues; MCZbase and another system are exploring implementation.
URIs, IRIs and persistence were explained: persistence requires someone to maintain the string and a resolving service, which costs money.
TDWG issues IRIs for vocabularies, documents and terms; Latimer Core found some term IRIs duplicated with different meanings.
TDWG agreed to formalise how standards document structure (grouping and repeating terms, IRIs for statistics as in MIDS).
LTC DP will define how terms hang together; a new ratification round and public review is planned, after MIDS.
A conceptual layer and term relationships remain future work.
The standard is named after Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer and the coelacanth Latimeria, deliberately honouring a woman who managed a collection.

moments.description: Discovery of duplicated IRIs.
TDWG agreeing to standards with formal structure.

title: Assessing record quality and completeness in geoscience collections
session: State of the Collections Description Interest Group. What's Happening and What's Not!
summary: Adam Mansur compared the Smithsonian's internal Collection Digitization Reporting System (CDRS) with MIDS for assessing record completeness in the Mineral Sciences (about 500,000 records, largely digitised) and Paleobiology (about 800,000 records against an estimated 10-13 million needed) collections. CDRS rules vary by department, are conditional and opaque, and barely move with large projects, whereas MIDS scores are consistent but cluster tightly around MIDS 1 because of the large jump required to reach MIDS 2. He argued that element-level breakdowns (e.g. via the MIDS calculator) are more useful for targeting work: Mineral Sciences lacks stratigraphic context in most records regardless of acquisition decade, while Paleobiology has gaps in names and object type concentrated in particular collections.
takeaway: Element-level views of MIDS information elements are more useful than raw scores for targeting data improvement in large geoscience collections.
whyItMatters: Offers practical guidance for using MIDS to plan digitisation and enhancement work, and highlights needs such as signalling checked-but-null values.
keyPoints: NMNH holds an estimated 140 million objects across seven departments, two geology-focused.
Geology metadata resembles biological metadata plus geologic context (unit, age).
CDRS measures completeness against a 'standard record' by presence/absence checks per primary collection.
Departmental CDRS rules are inconsistent, conditional and hard to interpret; big projects barely change collection-wide scores.
Departments mostly treat media as an enhancement, unlike MIDS; CDRS also includes internal elements like storage location and accession number.
MIDS scores cluster around level 1, so they are only sensitive to large changes.
Stratigraphic context is present in only 5-20% of Mineral Sciences records across acquisition decades, an intrinsic feature of incoming data.
Paleobiology's revamped primary collections make element gaps (e.g. ~20% lacking taxonomic names) actionable.

moments.description: Heat map of how departments map MIDS elements to CDRS levels.
Using MIDS calculator element breakouts to target work.

title: Sustainability and collaboration in a time of uncertainty
session: Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
summary: Libby Ellwood introduced the International Partners for the Digital Extended Specimen (IPDES) and framed the symposium around sustaining the biodiversity data ecosystem. She presented the Digital Extended Specimen as a unifying architecture and identified three sustainability needs: technology and infrastructure, people, and funding. She argued that sustainability will come from a diverse, resilient funding portfolio rather than a single replacement source, and described how IPDES is taking this session to several conferences before synthesising the outcomes in a webinar.
takeaway: Sustaining biodiversity data infrastructure requires treating technology, people and a diversified funding portfolio as one interconnected system.
whyItMatters: It sets out the framing used by the whole symposium and makes the case that preserving servers and software is insufficient without the people and funding that keep the connections working.
keyPoints: IPDES aims to coordinate a globally integrated network of stakeholders through technical and social infrastructure: data, tools, standards, people and working practices.
The Digital Extended Specimen combines North American 'extended specimen' and European 'digital specimen' ideas: physical specimen, digital record, and links to further information and relationships.
Three sustainability needs emerged: technology and infrastructure, a resilient and inclusive community, and funding.

Funding should come from a diverse portfolio: long-term public investment, philanthropy, international partnerships, existing organisations and new models recognising the socioeconomic value of biodiversity data.
Versions of the session were run at the iDigBio Digital Data conference, SPNHC, TDWG and ICOM-NatHist, to be synthesised in a later webinar.

moments.description: The three sustainability needs: technology/infrastructure, people, and funding.
Argument for a diversified funding portfolio rather than a single replacement source.

title: GBIF after 25 years
session: Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
summary: Joe Miller explained how the GBIF Secretariat approaches sustainability: stable GDP-based national contributions from about 40 member countries, leveraged with European Commission grants, foundations and special funds so the budget has doubled in five years. He described DOI-based citation tracking showing data reuse in science and policy, and how about a quarter of the budget flows back out through BID and CESP programmes. He emphasised aligning with policy and funding mechanisms such as the CBD, GEF 9 and the Global Biodiversity Framework Fund, and previewed a pilot indexing South African data with the national taxonomy.
takeaway: GBIF sustains itself by leveraging stable national contributions into additional funding and by embedding itself in the biodiversity policy and funding architecture.
whyItMatters: It offers a concrete, working model of how a global biodiversity infrastructure demonstrates value and secures long-term funding, including the policy links now being built with CBD and GEF.
keyPoints: GBIF is an intergovernmental organisation in its 25th year, with around 40 member countries paying annually.
DOIs on downloads allow tracking of data use; about eight peer-reviewed publications per day use GBIF-mediated data.
31 of 32 key messages of the 2023 IPBES invasive alien species assessment drew on literature using GBIF-mediated data.
Contributions are GDP-based under a five-year MoU; leveraging this stability, the overall budget has doubled, giving roughly two euros of work programme per euro contributed.
About 25% of the budget goes out to BID, CESP projects and contractors around the world.
GBIF is working with the CBD, GEF, World Bank and UNDP; the CBD Executive Secretary encouraged all parties to join GBIF.
Two thirds of seventh national reports to the CBD mention GBIF, but there are disconnects between national focal points.
A pilot indexes South African botanical data against South Africa's own national taxonomy, to be shown at COP17.

moments.description: Worked example of a Togo specimen traced from BID funding to a publication.
Tracking GBIF data into the IPBES invasive species assessment.
Pilot showing South African data indexed with the national taxonomy.

title: Unifying Natural Heritage for a Resilient Future
session: Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
summary: Wouter Addink used Shackleton's Endurance expedition as a parable of resilience (acting immediately and protecting the most precious assets) before presenting DiSSCo. He explained that only about 10% of Europe's estimated 1.5 billion specimens are digitised, and that DiSSCo aims to industrialise digitisation and create one FAIR, machine-actionable European virtual collection built around the Digital Extended Specimen as a citable FAIR digital object with a DOI. He argued that the ERIC legal model, with member-state financial and governance commitments, frees data from project-cycle dependency.
takeaway: DiSSCo's ERIC model and FAIR digital specimen objects are intended to make Europe's specimen data resilient beyond short-term project funding.
whyItMatters: Specimens provide evidence for biodiversity loss, climate change and health research, and a long-term legal and funding structure is presented as the answer to data loss when project funding ends.
keyPoints: Resilience means taking immediate action and focusing on preserving the most precious assets, illustrated by Shackleton's expedition.
Specimens are evidence for biodiversity loss, climate adaptation and pathogen/health research.
Only about 10% of an estimated 1.5 billion European specimens are digitised.
The DiSSCo digital specimen is a FAIR digital object with a DOI, containing catalogue data and links to derived and related data.
The ERIC model provides long-term governance and financial commitments from member states, beyond project-cycle dependency.
DiSSCo has submitted its step-two ERIC application, with six founding countries, aiming to launch next year; over 400 institutions from 23 countries are involved.

moments.description: Link from the Shackleton story to resilience of the community's assets.
The DiSSCo digital specimen as an actionable, citable FAIR digital object.
The ERIC model as the route out of project-cycle dependency.

title: Requirements of Sustainability Models for Geo-Biodiversity Data Cyberinfrastructure
session: Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
summary: José Fortes asked how cyberinfrastructure design changes when sustainability is a first-order requirement, using music streaming (radio to Spotify) as an ecosystem in which aggregators and distributors route revenue back to content creators. He argued that biodiversity funding will become a hybrid of central grants, subscriptions, pay-as-you-go and partnerships, while stressing he supports open, free data for science. Because every model requires reporting use, cyberinfrastructure must add 'economic orchestration' (tracking who uses what, charging and distributing revenue), which needs community standards; ChatBio's usage tracking was offered as an early example.
takeaway: Cyberinfrastructure sustainability and ecosystem sustainability go hand in hand, so infrastructure must be designed from the start to track use and support economic orchestration.
whyItMatters: It reframes sustainability as a design requirement for infrastructure and raises open questions about what the community would charge for and how revenue could reach small providers.
keyPoints: Sustaining infrastructure is only possible if the ecosystem of providers and users is sustainable, and vice versa.
Funding is shifting from funders distinct from users towards hybrids including subscriptions, advertising, pay-as-you-go and industry partnerships.
All models require reporting of use, so infrastructure must track use of data and services and how revenue is distributed.
Beyond technical orchestration, cyberinfrastructure needs an economic orchestration component; TDWG-style standards would be needed for it.
Open questions include what to charge for: records, images, bytes or services.
Small providers cannot build this themselves and need ways to interface with the ecosystem.
ChatBio uses agents to access multiple resources and tracks which data sources were used, by whom, per session.

moments.description: The music streaming ecosystem analogy.
Economic orchestration as a new cyberinfrastructure component.
ChatBio usage tracking example.

title: From preservation to perseverance: bridging disciplines for data resilience
session: Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
summary: Andrea Thomer described how Earth science data infrastructures in the US moved from the passive threat of invisibility to active threats in 2025, when NOAA and other agency resources were taken offline and many staff lost their jobs. She presented three resilience efforts at different timescales: SESAR rescuing NOAA's Index to Marine and Lacustrine Geological Samples (IMLGS), the ESIP Repository Crisis Scorecards for self-assessment against four crisis scenarios, and an AGU-led, Hewlett-funded international initiative building roadmaps, business models and mutual aid networks. She concluded that resilience is about prioritisation, doing the best with what we have, and called for advocacy to keep infrastructure appropriately visible.
takeaway: Data resilience in a crisis is about prioritisation and mutual aid rather than perfection, and infrastructures need to be kept appropriately visible to be funded.
whyItMatters: The Earth science community's experience of sudden defunding offers biodiversity informatics tested approaches (data rescue, crisis scorecards, mutual aid) and an invitation to collaborate.
keyPoints: Infrastructure is invisible by design (Bowker and Star) and only noticed when it breaks, which makes maintenance hard to fund.
In 2025 over 20 NOAA databases and data resources were taken offline after US federal budget cuts; half of her ESIP colleagues lost their jobs.
SESAR mints IGSN persistent identifiers for physical samples and is being redesigned to serve biodiversity samples.
Phase one of the IMLGS rescue recreated the portal as it was in January 2025 inside SESAR using GeoParquet; phase two will integrate the records into SESAR.
The ESIP Repository Crisis Scorecards (a Qualtrics survey on ESIP's site and Zenodo) assess preparedness for natural disaster, loss of funding, cyber attack and loss of personnel.
AGU's task groups work on business models, shared technical solutions, crisis preparedness kits and mutual aid agreements to take on one another's data.

moments.description: Shift from passive to active threats to data infrastructure in the US.
The IMLGS data rescue into SESAR.
ESIP Repository Crisis Scorecards.
Prioritisation over perfection and a call for advocacy.

title: NEON, Community Standards, and the Hyper-Extended Specimen
session: Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
summary: Chandra Earl presented NEON's design for resilient, interoperable data and samples: 81 sites across 20 ecoclimatic domains, over 400 TB of data a year, and about 100,000 samples a year curated at the NEON Biorepository. She described provenance tracking, issue management, modular pipelines, digital-born sample data, DOIs/IGSNs and external audits, and showed small-mammal vouchers as a 'hyper-extended specimen' linking occurrences, images, tissues, traits, molecular and pathogen data. She closed with questions about citation and impact tracing, who sustains standards and crosswalks, getting commercial users to contribute, and round-tripping of value-added data.
takeaway: NEON was built for interoperability from the start, but sustaining standards, crosswalks and value-added links needs community-level solutions.
whyItMatters: NEON is a large, standards-aligned observatory whose hyper-extended specimens show both the power and the complexity of linked data, and its open questions set up the session discussion.
keyPoints: NEON is an NSF-funded, Battelle-operated observatory with 81 sites in 20 ecoclimatic domains, a planned 30-year lifespan and about seven years in.
It combines automated sensors, airborne remote sensing and observational sampling: over 400 TB a year, 650 million sensor readings a day and 2.5 PB stored.
Around 100,000 samples of about 65 types are archived yearly, representing over 8,000 taxa, mostly at the NEON Biorepository at Arizona State University.
Sample data are born digital (barcodes replaced handwritten labels) and accessioned samples receive DOIs for use tracking.
Data are audited for quality (Bob Mesibov) and AI readiness (ESIP).
NEON uses EML, Darwin Core, MIxS, ENVO, USA-NPN phenophases, IGSNs, dataset DOIs, ORCIDs and RORs, and is testing the Humboldt Extension and Darwin Core Data Package with GBIF.
NEON data are used beyond ecology: food security, drinking water safety after Hurricane Maria, permafrost pathogen sequencing and AI benchmark datasets.

moments.description: The hyper-extended specimen example of NEON small mammal vouchers.
Closing questions posed to the audience for discussion.

title: Canada’s need for synthesis for Adaptation and Resilience to Climate Change
session: Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
summary: James Macklin drew lessons from GenARCC, a large Canadian cross-departmental project using genomics to assess, predict and adapt to climate change, which will add about 20,000 whole genomes across 30 species largely from existing samples and specimens. He showed how the DINA research data management system captures standards-based metadata linked to material samples and sequences, and new pipelines push data semi-automatically to ENA and then associate ENA records with rich metadata in GBIF, compensating for poor metadata searchability in INSDC repositories. He stressed that relied-upon repositories carry funding risk, and that researchers undervalue the 'boring' work of connecting and standardising metadata needed for reuse and decision-ready results.
takeaway: Genomic data can only support climate adaptation synthesis if metadata are captured with standards from the start and linked to discoverable infrastructures like GBIF.
whyItMatters: Environmental genomic data are growing rapidly, and the talk shows a practical pipeline (DINA to ENA to GBIF) for making sequence data findable while highlighting cultural barriers to reuse.
keyPoints: Public genomic data are estimated at 70+ petabytes; environmental metagenomics is a rapidly growing, highly diverse slice.
Canada has genome-level data for about 0.5% of its 80,000 species, biased toward economically and culturally important species.
GenARCC will add about 20,000 whole genomes across 30 terrestrial, marine and freshwater species, using existing samples via MTAs.
DINA captures a standards-based metadata snapshot with flexible managed attributes for terms not covered by standards.
About 740 salmon genomes were pushed from DINA to ENA via a semi-automatic pipeline.
INSDC repositories hold only core metadata searchably; a new workflow links ENA records to rich metadata in GBIF.
Researchers prioritise novel sequencing and analyses over metadata curation, reproducible code and reusable pipelines.

moments.description: Managing data from the beginning with DINA.
New workflow linking ENA sequences to rich metadata in GBIF.
Risks in the infrastructures the project relies on.

title: Architecting the National Biodiversity Information System: Standards-Driven Workflows for South Africa’s Botanical and Zoological Data
session: Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
summary: A SANBI presenter described the National Biodiversity Information System (NBIS), which integrates botanical data managed in BRAHMS and zoological data in Specify, uses TaxaMatch fuzzy matching against an authoritative backbone, and applies staging instances with automated quality checks and ETL synchronisation. NBIS implements the Digital Extended Specimen through persistent identifiers linking specimens to descriptions, literature, names, uses and media. Most of the talk set out a diversified sustainability model: a legislative mandate under NEMBA securing baseline funding, project grants, a proposed biodiversity information fund, alignment with national priorities, a co-investment consortium, a multisectoral steering committee, paid value-added services with open core data, and monitoring to demonstrate return on investment.
takeaway: SANBI sustains NBIS through a statutory mandate plus a roadmap of diversified funding, partnerships and demonstrated return on investment.
whyItMatters: It shows a national biodiversity institute combining technical standards workflows with a concrete, multi-pronged sustainability roadmap.
keyPoints: NBIS integrates data from institutional partners using BRAHMS (botanical) and Specify (zoological).
TaxaMatch fuzzy matching resolves misspelled or variant names against an authoritative taxonomic backbone; SANBI distributes authoritative taxon and gazetteer dictionaries.
Data flow via staging instances with automated QC, then production, synchronised by ETL packages.
The NEMBA mandate provides baseline infrastructure-grant funding; external grants fund functional extensions.
SANBI is investigating a dedicated biodiversity information fund to receive donor funds without financial year-end clawbacks.
Proposals include a co-investment consortium with universities, science councils and SANParks, a multisectoral steering committee, and paid analytics services while keeping core data open.
The roadmap: secure core funding, align with national priorities, co-invest, diversify, demonstrate value, preserve capability.

moments.description: TaxaMatch-based taxonomic harmonisation.
Six-step sustainability roadmap.

title: Symposium discussion: funding models, open data and sustaining biodiversity infrastructure
session: Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
summary: The discussion centred on José Fortes's proposal for economically aware infrastructure. Andre Zerger (ALA) described shared-cost models in research infrastructure and asked for exemplars; Joe Miller warned that institutions charging for data could collapse global aggregation and pointed instead to biodiversity credits and a New Zealand pilot; Chandra Earl suggested banking and medical informatics as governed parallels. Further threads covered a Spotify-style payout model to incentivise publishing, large-scale storage (look to astronomers), whether science infrastructure should be publicly funded like roads and water, regulation requiring private sector data sharing (Colombia, France), outsourcing IT to the cloud, and inviting economists and social scientists into these conversations.
takeaway: The community broadly agreed that core data should stay open, but that products, services, credits, regulation and partnerships must become part of sustaining the infrastructure.
whyItMatters: It surfaces the key tensions in funding biodiversity infrastructure (open data vs. cost recovery, public vs. market funding) and concrete alternatives being tried.
keyPoints: Charging for data at individual institutions risks collapsing global aggregation and citation tracking; products and services are more appropriate targets.
Fortes: hybrid models need not eliminate free access; credit or virtual-currency schemes (as in US supercomputing) can preserve it, but commercial services such as LLMs will cost money.
Around 70 countries are discussing biodiversity credit schemes; GBIF is piloting with New Zealand for nodes to act as data repositories for credit schemes.
Banking standards are paid for through transaction fees; medical informatics is far more governed than biodiversity informatics.
A Spotify-like payout model could incentivise publishing and good metadata for currently unshared data.
Astronomers generate around 70 PB per month and are a source of storage solutions.
Science infrastructure may be better treated like public infrastructure (water, power, roads) than market-driven.
Regulation drives private sector data sharing: Colombia and France require it.
Economists, marketing and communication specialists and social scientists should be invited into these discussions.

moments.description: Joe Miller challenges the idea of charging for data.
Biodiversity credits as an opportunity for GBIF nodes.
Argument that science infrastructure should be publicly funded like roads and water.
Regulation as the counterpoint: Colombia and France require private sector data sharing.
Wrap-up and invitation to join IPDES.

title: FAIR ancient environmental DNA data in practice: developing and implementing interoperable metadata standards in AEGIS
session: FAIR data in practice - eDNA, modelling and biodiversity concepts
summary: Joana Pauperio described metadata work for the AEGIS ancient environmental genomics programme, in which ancient DNA from sources such as lake sediment cores flows through ENA and MGnify to the AEGIS data portal. The team mapped AEGIS metadata to the ENA data model and to the MInAS community standard, working with the Genomic Standards Consortium and FAIRe, and created an interim ENA ancient DNA checklist of 48 attributes including past environmental context and age inference. With MInAS now incorporated into MIxS version 7, ENA will transition to the MIxS ancient checklist, and experiment metadata work is aligning with a GA4GH core checklist.
takeaway: Community-driven ancient DNA metadata standards, now in MIxS, can make paleogenomic data FAIR and reusable across biodiversity infrastructures.
whyItMatters: Ancient eDNA provides long-term records of ecosystem resilience, and standard metadata (including past environmental context and age) are needed for it to join wider biodiversity data ecosystems.
keyPoints: AEGIS is a seven-year programme using ancient environmental DNA to understand ecosystem resilience and inform sustainable food production.
Reference genomes (via the Earth BioGenome Project standards) support interpretation of ancient eDNA.
Ancient eDNA metadata map to ENA's study, sample, experiment and run model, including ancient-specific fields such as age estimate and past environmental context.
An interim ENA ancient DNA checklist has 48 attributes, 13 mandatory and 17 checklist-specific.
MInAS was incorporated into MIxS version 7 this summer; ENA will move to the MIxS ancient checklist.
Experiment metadata work with GA4GH yields a core checklist that maps well to INSDC mandatory fields.
GBIF already ingests sequence-based data from ENA, and ancient DNA occurrences may flow there too.

moments.description: Creation of the interim ancient DNA checklist.
MInAS incorporated into MIxS v7.
Question on taxonomic resolution of ancient eDNA.

title: Rethinking “absence” in biodiversity data collection and modeling
session: FAIR data in practice - eDNA, modelling and biodiversity concepts
summary: Rob Stevenson presented the outcome of a working group (with Abby Benson, Ruben Perez, Deborah Arlt, Yiming and Wesley Hochachka) on confusing 'absence' terminology. He argued presence and absence are asymmetric (presence is a fact, absence a question) and absence is only meaningful against an expectation frame such as a Humboldt Extension survey target. Surveying methodology and analysis texts, the group found the museum (presence-only) and biological survey (repeated, effort-based) communities use different data and models, with detectability as the unifying concept. The main outcome was the TDWG Executive's approval in May of changing Darwin Core occurrenceStatus values from present/absent to detected/not detected.
takeaway: Separating observation from inference means recording 'detected' and 'not detected' rather than presence and absence.
whyItMatters: The occurrenceStatus vocabulary change affects how every data manager records and interprets non-detections, and clarifies terminology for distribution modelling.
keyPoints: Many overlapping absence terms exist in the literature (confirmed absence, zero count, pseudo-absence, etc.).
Presence and absence are asymmetric: presence is a fact, absence is a question.
Absence is meaningful only against a model of what should have been present; survey targets in the Humboldt Extension provide that frame.
Survey methodology books rarely define absence terms in data-sharing terms; Hill et al.'s handbook was most useful.
Museum data (presence-only, Bioclim/GARP/MaxEnt niche models) and survey data (repeated surveys, occupancy and hierarchical models) come from different communities.
Detectability, from mark-recapture, distance sampling and occupancy models, is the key clarifying concept.
Darwin Core occurrenceStatus changed from present/absent to detected/not detected.
Recommended terms: 'opportunistic detection-only data' instead of presence-only, and 'detection/non-detection' data for standard surveys.

moments.description: The asymmetry of presence and absence.
Adoption of detected/not detected in Darwin Core.
Online question about GBIF and OBIS implementation.

title: Challenges and Opportunities for FAIR Marine eDNA Data Publication Workflows
session: FAIR data in practice - eDNA, modelling and biodiversity concepts
summary: Berenice Talamantes Becerra presented preliminary results of a community survey on where marine eDNA data publication workflows get stuck, framed by CSIRO's Marine National Facility and the OBIS-AU node. Respondents most often cited data formatting (about 71%), differences in standards or protocols and metadata formats across repositories (about 58% each); 74% said publication involves too much manual effort and only about 27% found the steps clear. Preferred solutions were a web portal to prepare, validate and submit datasets, automated submission to NCBI, GBIF and OBIS, automated metadata checks and better repository interoperability.
takeaway: Making marine eDNA data FAIR is as much about clear, practical, less manual publication processes as about technology.
whyItMatters: It provides evidence on real bottlenecks in eDNA data publication to guide tool and guidance development, and invites community input.
keyPoints: CSIRO operates Australia's Marine National Facility (RV Investigator) and runs the OBIS-AU node, including Australian Antarctic Program data.
Keeping links between sample, sequencing information, metadata and final observations is essential for eDNA.
Survey covered stakeholders and governance, metadata and standards, technologies, workflow management and capacity building.
Top challenge: data formatting (~71%); then differences in standards/protocols and repository metadata formats (~58%).
~74% agreed publication involves too much manual effort; almost half disagreed QC procedures are clearly defined; ~27% found steps clear; ~36% had technical support when needed.
Priorities: reduce manual work, better validation and guidance, and test interoperable workflow components with users.

moments.description: Preliminary survey results on biggest challenges.
Solutions respondents want.
Survey still open with QR code.

title: Visualising specimens as event chains on the Australian Reference Genome Atlas
session: FAIR data in practice - eDNA, modelling and biodiversity concepts
summary: Kathryn Hall described how the Australian Reference Genome Atlas (ARGA), an index rather than repository, modelled provenance chains from a wild organism through collection, museum registration, tissue subsampling, DNA extraction and lab runs to deposited genomic data products. Because Darwin Core is flat and genomic data derive from many nested material derivatives, ARGA built linked back-end tables keyed on organism IDs, an RDF-based ETL layer, a relational core with GraphQL access, a taxonomic DAG aligning ALA, WoRMS and NCBI taxonomies, and operation-based CRDTs recording every database action. The result lets users see, for example, 31 derived data products from one specimen with tissue, molecule, file type and custodian preserved.
takeaway: Modelling genomic data as event chains from organism to data product preserves context and provenance that flat records collapse.
whyItMatters: Provenance is the 'data seatbelt' that matters when a sequence or phylogeny looks wrong, and ARGA shows a working model for linking specimens to genomic data at fine grain.
keyPoints: ARGA was a partnership of the Atlas of Living Australia, Australian BioCommons and Bioplatforms Australia, with ARDC; the project concluded earlier this year.
Genomic data come from amplicons from extracts from subsamples; one organism can yield hundreds of amplicons and thousands of fragments.
Back-end tables (organism, live state, collections, registrations, tissues/lab samples, data products) are linked by organism ID.
Organism ID tracks provenance even when tissues were never formally registered in collections.
A taxonomic directed acyclic graph aligns ALA, WoRMS and NCBI taxonomies without flattening rank shifts.
Operation-based conflict-free replicated data types atomise records and preserve a full history of actions.
Aim was a sufficiency of metadata to reconstruct the chain, not every possible detail.
A Next.js interface walks users through the chain as narrative cards.

moments.description: Why genomic data don't fit flat one-entity models.
31 data products from one specimen.
The 'data seatbelt' argument for provenance.

title: Bridging Biodiversity Data Standards and Predictive Ecology: Operationalizing Interoperable Workflows for Species Distribution Modeling in West Africa
session: FAIR data in practice - eDNA, modelling and biodiversity concepts
summary: Peter Ugege reported a controlled experiment asking whether standards-informed processing of occurrence records changes species distribution model outcomes for six West African timber species. Starting from 46,941 records, the standards pathway removed 106 records (placeholders, duplicates, a fuzzy and absent records), but after domain restriction and spatial deduplication both pathways converged on identical 36,407 presence units, so no pathway-specific predictive effect was identifiable. Geographic cross-validation gave ROC-AUC of about 0.66-0.75, far below random cross-validation (~0.99), showing random validation overstates transferability.
takeaway: Standards change what enters a modelling pipeline, but workflow design determines whether that difference survives and validation design determines what claims can be made.
whyItMatters: It gives a rigorous, reproducible test of the downstream effect of data standards on SDMs and a clear warning about optimistic random cross-validation.
keyPoints: Three levels of effect were distinguished: record representation, numerical SDM information and predictive inference.
Pathway A (minimal processing) kept 46,941 records; pathway B (standards-informed fitness-for-use rules) kept 46,835, a 0.23% difference.
Within the West African domain the difference fell to 70 records, concentrated in three species and 16 locations, all already represented in pathway B.
After common spatial deduplication both yielded 36,407 presence units and the same 96,407-row modelling matrix.
Models: logistic regression, random forest and histogram gradient boosting, with strict geographic cross-validation.
Random CV mean ROC-AUC ~0.99 vs ~0.70 under geographic hold-out (mean difference 0.28).
No species was best on every robustness dimension, so no composite score was used.

moments.description: Central result: pathways converge after spatial processing.
Random vs geographic cross-validation comparison.
Three-statement interpretation.

title: The future is the future - thought about access to data in publications
session: Planning the Libroscope: creating research ready biodiversity from scientific publications
summary: Donat Agosti introduced the Libroscope and the Disentis roadmap goal of making 100% of major biodiversity publications open, FAIR, machine-actionable and AI-ready by 2035, using a use-case-driven approach. He described Plazi's current pipeline, in which PDFs or XML are processed so that data reach GBIF, Zenodo and dashboards within a day of publication, with provenance down to the exact position in the text, and noted 1.2 million treatments extracted and a steady ~10,000 new species a year across roughly 200 journals processed. He argued the community should also move beyond extracting from PDFs toward digital-first description of unknown and dark taxa.
takeaway: Liberating data from literature works, but the future lies in use-case-driven, digital-first publishing that also targets the undescribed majority of species.
whyItMatters: Literature holds much of what we know about biodiversity yet remains the least open data type; this talk frames a roadmap for making it trusted, AI-ready data.
keyPoints: Estimates: 500 million printed pages, ~2,000 taxonomic journals, 20-50 million treatments, and only 10-30% of species data accessible.
The 2024 Disentis meeting produced a roadmap to make all major biodiversity publications open and FAIR by 2035.
The Libroscope is use-case-driven: target specific data rather than everything at once.
Around 30 GBIF hosted portals are dashboards from publications; material citations link back to exact text positions via persistent identifiers.
Zenodo communities (e.g. for fruit flies) and the Biodiversity Literature Repository collect publications for processing.
Lag from publication to GBIF has fallen from years to under a day in the best case.
1.2 million treatments extracted; ~200 journals processed over 10 years show a flat rate of ~10,000 new species a year.
Bias toward well-known taxa means new approaches (DNA plus optical data) are needed to describe dark taxa.

moments.description: The 2035 roadmap goal.
From publication to GBIF in under a day.
Bias toward described taxa and the need to address dark taxa.

title: Realtime Access to Data in new Taxonomic Publications
session: Planning the Libroscope: creating research ready biodiversity from scientific publications
summary: Guido Sautter detailed Plazi's pipeline turning new taxonomic publications into FAIR data within hours. XML from Pensoft (TaxPub via RSS) needs structural normalisation, while PDFs must be obtained from publishers and decoded, with document structure detection being the main quality-control cost. The workflow tags names, citations, material citations and treatment sections, links names to Catalogue of Life and accessions to ENA, and exports to Zenodo, GBIF, ChecklistBank, Biodiversity PMC, RefBank, OpenBiodiv and others, receiving identifiers back to interlink everything.
takeaway: Plazi can deliver interlinked, machine-actionable data from new taxonomic papers within hours, and XML-first publishing removes most of the costly effort.
whyItMatters: It explains concretely where effort goes in literature data liberation, supporting the argument for semantic-first publishing.
keyPoints: 'Real-time' means same day or within a couple of hours, barring quality control.
Data in publications: the PDF, named entities (names, occurrences, specimens, sequences), treatments, figures and tables.
Figures and tables receive DOIs in Zenodo so they can be cited directly.
Pensoft XML (TaxPub/JATS) is pulled via RSS but needs paragraph-nesting normalisation.
PDF intake depends on publishers (MNHN journals upload directly); structure detection dominates QC effort.
Names are linked to Catalogue of Life, new species to ZooBank; ZooBank names without treatments get 'treatment stubs'.
Exports return identifiers (GBIF dataset keys, Zenodo DOIs) that are disseminated back across repositories.

moments.description: Intake routes for XML and PDF.
Overview of export and identifier return.
PDF structure detection as the main cost; XML as the way forward.

title: Biodiversity literature as FAIR and AI-ready data by design (and how to get there)
session: Planning the Libroscope: creating research ready biodiversity from scientific publications
summary: Chris Le Coquet argued that the next step is not liberating more literature but changing how it is published. Rather than creating PDFs that must later be mined, XML-first single-source workflows (e.g. MitoTaxa, annotated in JATS TaxPub via GoldenGate) capture structure, references, semantic markup and persistent identifiers during production. Shared standards provide a common grammar, PIDs make entities unambiguous, and together they make publications FAIR by design, part of the Libroscope network and genuinely AI-ready.
takeaway: Don't just liberate biodiversity literature, publish it liberated.
whyItMatters: Stopping the creation of new PDF backlog would free liberation effort for legacy literature and give AI trustworthy, structured inputs.
keyPoints: Publications are infrastructure through which knowledge is validated, connected and reused.
Plazi has liberated more than one million treatments from legacy literature; the question is whether this should remain the way we publish.
In XML-first workflows, machine-readable structure exists from the start and many outputs derive from one source.
References become structured objects that can be matched and resolved, preserving relationships for knowledge graphs.
Semantic markup turns material citations into explicit entities and relationships.
Machine-readable is not interoperable: standards (JATS TaxPub, Darwin Core, ontologies) give a common grammar and PIDs give identity.
AI readiness is a consequence of good semantic publishing; the challenge now is scale and community convergence.

moments.description: Legacy vs prospective distinction.
Standards as the grammar of interoperability.
What AI-ready really means.

title: Building digital-native species: Transitioning from PDF liberation to semantic-by-design publishing
session: Planning the Libroscope: creating research ready biodiversity from scientific publications
summary: Laurence presented the 'digital-native species' workflow, noting that it takes on average 21 years from specimen collection to publication and that current practice erases structured data into PDFs only to re-extract it later. In the new model, bulk samples become a biodiversity knowledge graph linking specimens with barcodes, images and genomic data, exported as JSON to Zenodo and carried through an XML-based, semantically enhanced manuscript and peer review to multi-format publication with bidirectional links. She also showed dashboards monitoring institutions and journals, arguing that measuring a journal's FAIRness matters more than impact factor, given that taxonomic references average around 50 years old.
takeaway: Keeping data linked and structured from specimen to publication yields FAIR, trusted data on the day of publication.
whyItMatters: It proposes a way to shorten the long description lag and to produce certified data that can reduce AI hallucination.
keyPoints: On average it takes 21 years from collecting a specimen to publishing about it.
The old model erases data into PDFs, which then must be rescued with conversion errors.
Digital-native species link physical specimens to digital specimens, DNA barcodes, images and genomic data from the outset, exported as JSON to Zenodo.
An XML-based manuscript retains semantic links and identifiers through editing and peer review.
XML-first yields FAIR-born, trusted data at the day of publication with bidirectional links.
Dashboards (institution, GBIF hosted portal for journals, TreatmentBank) monitor impact and journal FAIRness.
The average age of references in taxonomy is about 50 years, making 2- or 5-year impact factors irrelevant.

moments.description: Old model versus digital-native model.
FAIR-born, trusted data at publication.
Impact factor irrelevant for taxonomy.

title: Literature triage to support Island Biodiversity Monitoring
session: Planning the Libroscope: creating research ready biodiversity from scientific publications
summary: Patrick Ruch presented literature triage: instead of Boolean search, users supply a few hundred relevant papers, from which binary classifiers screen the Biodiversity PMC universe and deliver ranked digests. Evaluations for island biodiversity (BioMoQA) and IPBES assessments showed an ensemble of BERT-type models reaching precision around 90-92%, on par with human inter-rater agreement, far cheaper than generative LLMs; domain-specific biodiversity models did not help. He costed a system at roughly 25K and outlined next steps: ingesting Unpaywall/OpenAlex, LLM-generated regex patterns for post-triage entity extraction (99% species precision), question answering, BioC offset-grounded evidence and downloadable agents.
