takeaway: Classifier-based literature triage matches human curators at a fraction of LLM cost and is worth investing in for recurring curation tasks.
whyItMatters: Scalable, affordable triage helps curators and assessments like IPBES avoid missing relevant literature in rapidly growing volumes.
keyPoints: Triage learns from a set of relevant papers and classifies the whole Biodiversity PMC collection, which is larger than PubMed and includes treatments.
Keep track of negative examples when building triage systems.
Ensembles of BERT-type models were best and about 3,000 times cheaper than generative chatbots.
Island biodiversity precision ~90-92%, consistent with inter-rater agreement; IPBES tasks showed even higher agreement.
Building a system costs roughly one to two person-months plus a few thousand a year hosting, ~25K total; worthwhile for recurring tasks.
Real LLM costs are subsidised and may rise tenfold; frugal AI is chosen for cost.
LLMs generate regex patterns from seed keywords for post-triage extraction; a Spanish government pilot extracts species, habitats and fieldwork from environmental assessments.
Processing speed is about 28 ms per document; next step is agentic triage.

moments.description: How triage replaces search equations.
Ensemble BERT results and cost comparison.
Post-triage extraction and question answering GUI.

title: Literature usage in IPBES - Past, Present and Future with Libroscope
session: Planning the Libroscope: creating research ready biodiversity from scientific publications
summary: Rainer Krug, an ecologist and data user involved in IPBES, described how IPBES literature searching moved from tedious, non-reproducible Web of Science and Scopus web-interface searches to scripted, transparent OpenAlex API searches after IPBES adopted a data management policy in 2020. OpenAlex is open, free and downloadable, handles millions of works on a desktop and supports snowball citation searches, whereas a Web of Science licence for one assessment would have cost over a million. Remaining gaps are content inside papers, languages, shrinking abstract availability and grey literature, which the Libroscope could address through semantic extraction and ingestion on demand.
takeaway: Open, scripted literature search via OpenAlex transformed IPBES practice, and the Libroscope could close remaining gaps by making paper contents and grey literature searchable.
whyItMatters: Transparency of evidence is essential for intergovernmental assessments approved by governments, and this shows how open infrastructure and content extraction serve that need.
keyPoints: IPBES assessments synthesise existing knowledge, so literature is central and must be fully transparent to governments.
Earlier web-interface searches in Web of Science and Scopus were tedious, error-prone and not reproducible.
The 2020 IPBES data management policy requires data management reports documenting source data, processing and code.
OpenAlex is open by design, free at typical use, offers API and Parquet snapshots; 4.5 million works handled on a desktop.
Web of Science licensing for the transformative change assessment would have cost more than a million.
Gaps: data inside papers, keyword searches limited by language, reduced abstract availability, and grey literature.
Proposed: search by content and facts, snowball searches over knowledge graphs, and ingestion on demand from OpenAlex into Biodiversity PMC.

moments.description: IPBES data management policy and transparency.
Cost comparison with Web of Science.
Proposal for ingestion on demand.

title: Species trait literature mining to support integrative biodiversity distribution modelling
session: Planning the Libroscope: creating research ready biodiversity from scientific publications
summary: Robert Waterhouse presented a Swiss National Science Foundation project using text-mined species traits and genomic population structure to improve species distribution and taxonomic richness models. Manually curated trait catalogues are laudable but unscalable, so the project extracts species-trait-value triples from Plazi/TreatmentBank treatments and newly prioritised publications, grey literature and supplementary material, using NER trained on community gold-standard annotations. Trait layers support joint SDMs (e.g. predator-prey) and genomic SDMs recognise population structure and dark taxa; the aim is a demonstrative use case showing funders the value of literature infrastructure.
takeaway: Demonstrating research use cases like trait-informed distribution modelling is key to persuading funders to support literature mobilisation infrastructure.
whyItMatters: Adding traits and genomic structure to SDMs could substantially change predictions, and the project connects literature mining directly to ecological research questions.
keyPoints: Trait information links species concepts to both genomic and literature knowledge.
Curated trait databases exist for popular taxa but are not scalable.
Target: species-trait-value triples extracted from treatments and other literature.
Trait layers enable joint species distribution modelling; genomic structure enables genomic SDMs.
Taxonomic name uncertainty and dark taxa affect trait use and modelling.
Taxonomic groups range from well-studied to uncertain (e.g. ~400 amphipods).
Gaps include undigitised treatments, grey literature such as field guides, and data in supplementary materials.
GBIF API access for many taxa required pre-registration.

moments.description: Why traits and genomics improve SDMs.
Text mining workflow.
Use cases as the argument for infrastructure funding.

title: Mapping geographical distributions in the World Register of Marine Species
session: From WDSRPD to GeoSchemes: Recording Biodiversity Distributions for Science and Policy
summary: Serge Gofas explained why WoRMS needed a standard set of marine geounits: species distributions were recorded with haphazard units. Neither EEZs (too uneven) nor Marine Ecoregions of the World (ignoring borders) were adequate, so the TDWG GeoSchemes marine task group published a hierarchical proposal with five oceans, ~200 level-two and 577 level-four units, coastal areas split country-wise and high seas based on Watling et al. He raised the unresolved issue of how to write English 'definitions' required by the TDWG standards specification for spatial units, proposing reference to maps in Marine Regions, and outlined uses including national checklists, cross-checking GBIF/OBIS points and global analysis.
takeaway: A country-aware, hierarchical marine geoscheme will let WoRMS and others record and query distributions consistently, pending a solution for defining spatial units in a TDWG standard.
whyItMatters: It extends a widely used TDWG geographic standard to the oceans, enabling national marine checklists and literature-based distribution records.
keyPoints: WoRMS is curated by 300+ experts and hosted at VLIZ; its distribution tab suffered from inconsistent geounits.
EEZs work for small countries but large or multi-coast countries need subdivision.
MEOW ignores country borders, making locality assignment ambiguous.
Level one: major oceans; level two: coastal areas by biogeographic region plus high seas; level four: 577 units.
High seas use Watling et al. with a 3,500 m threshold between bathyal and abyssal.
Unit codes are unique across terrestrial and marine parts and can serve as controlled vocabulary strings.
Unit sizes (100,000-500,000 km2) are comparable to five-degree grids.

moments.description: Why MEOW and EEZs alone were inadequate.
Open problem of defining spatial concepts in words.
Expected outcomes of the marine geoscheme.

title: Marine Regions as a backbone for the TDWG Marine GeoScheme
session: From WDSRPD to GeoSchemes: Recording Biodiversity Distributions for Science and Policy
summary: Britt Lonneville introduced Marine Regions as the backbone for the marine geoscheme: a gazetteer of nearly 65,000 marine places with persistent MRGIDs, taken from authoritative sources and hierarchically related, openly licensed maritime boundary datasets digitised from UNCLOS legislation, and other geospatial layers such as IHO S-23 sea areas and MEOW. Marine Regions provides base data to the task group, works on development and standardisation with WoRMS, and will host and maintain the resulting units.
takeaway: Marine Regions supplies the identifiers, boundaries and hierarchy that make a marine geoscheme maintainable.
whyItMatters: A persistent, maintained gazetteer is what makes geographic standards usable and updatable over time.
keyPoints: Three pillars: a gazetteer, open maritime boundary datasets, and relevant geospatial layers.
The gazetteer is the geographic counterpart to WoRMS, with nearly 65,000 features and MRGID identifiers.
Names come from authoritative sources (WGSRPD, MEOW, GEBCO, national gazetteers), mapped to one identifier.
Parent-child relations allow hierarchies, including alternative parents.
EEZs and other UNCLOS zones are digitised from legislation under CC BY and updated for new legislation, rulings and feedback.
Final GeoScheme units will be added to the gazetteer and available for download.

moments.description: What a gazetteer is.
Digitising UNCLOS boundaries.
Comment on alternative hierarchies.

title: The new World Geographical Scheme for Recording (not only) Plant Distributions: process, progress and challenges
session: From WDSRPD to GeoSchemes: Recording Biodiversity Distributions for Science and Policy
summary: Paco Pando described updating the WGSRPD, conceived by Dick Brummitt as a politically neutral, four-level scheme following political borders with phytogeographic sense. The terrestrial task group reviewed changes since 2001, now referencing UN naming conventions and precise polygons (prepared by the Pl@ntNet team from OpenStreetMap coastlines) rather than the Times Atlas; about 50 changes were needed and 34 issues resolved, yielding 9, 52, 369 and 617 units at levels one to four. Remaining meta-issues include one or two standards, where polygons live (Marine Regions, Zenodo), the name (GeoSchemes?) and open polygon formats (GeoJSON, FlatGeobuf).
takeaway: The terrestrial update is complete and the standard is nearly ready for public review, with packaging, naming and polygon hosting still to decide.
whyItMatters: WGSRPD is the most widely used TDWG standard after Darwin Core, so its modernisation and extension to all taxa affects many databases.
keyPoints: WGSRPD is used by Plants of the World, IUCN, USDA GRIN and cited 300+ times since 2022.
It is not a biogeographic standard; that role is played by the older Takhtajan floristic regions standard.
The Interest Group (2021) has two task groups: terrestrial update and new marine scheme, coordinated to avoid duplicate identifiers.
References move from the Times Atlas to UN naming conventions and the UN country names database; definitions become actual polygons.
Around 50 changes in names or borders; 34 issues resolved; terrestrial work considered complete.
Next: publish tables as CSV, public review, ratification; also a crosswalk from the old version and guidance.

moments.description: What is changing from the 2001 edition.
Outstanding meta-issues for finalising the standard.
Question on disputed territories.

title: Digitising Plant and Fungal Collections at Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: Applying International Standards to Support Data Sharing and Geospatial Analysis
session: From WDSRPD to GeoSchemes: Recording Biodiversity Distributions for Science and Policy
summary: Udayangani Liu presented how Kew applied WGSRPD in its Integrated Collections Management System after a four-year mass digitisation that imaged over six million herbarium and fungarium specimens. Selecting an ISO country semi-automatically populates TDWG levels, while transcontinental countries, multi-country archipelagos and changed boundaries need level-by-level handling. Analysis of 7.9 million records spanning five centuries showed ISO codes are well captured but only just over 50% have levels three and four, with about 1.5 million records lacking a continent; challenges include historical data, missing hierarchy, language and variable user familiarity with the scheme.
takeaway: WGSRPD enables cross-collection geospatial analysis at Kew, but historical, heterogeneous data leave half of records without fine-level assignment.
whyItMatters: It is a real-world large-scale application of the standard being revised, surfacing practical issues the new version must accommodate.
keyPoints: Kew holds over 8 million items across 12 collections; ICMS manages them in one system following TDWG, Darwin Core and other protocols.
Over six million records were added in the mass digitisation project.
Choosing an ISO country auto-populates TDWG levels; large countries require state/province choice.
About 70% of records capture collecting year; dates span five centuries with dips during the World Wars.
Just over 50% of records capture TDWG levels three and four; ~1.5 million (20%) lack continent.
Data shared via Kew Data Portal, GBIF, DiSSCo UK, Genesys and the Svalbard Seed Vault.

moments.description: Semi-automated TDWG level assignment in ICMS.
Coverage of ISO and TDWG levels.
Key challenges.

title: Collaborative Development of an Institution-Wide Controlled Vocabulary
session: From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
summary: Caitlin Thorn, a data manager at the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin, described how an interdisciplinary working group built a shared controlled vocabulary for about 30 million objects whose sub-collections used different terms for the same thing (object type, preparation type, availability). Instead of a dedicated thesaurus system they chose a structured Excel spreadsheet: collection staff already know Excel, and the list can move to a dedicated system later. The work ran from January 2024 workshops through a Collection Cafe presentation and specialist review to implementation as Specify pick lists. Q&A covered hierarchies, whether the list will be shared, governance, and alignment with Darwin Core.
takeaway: A shared vocabulary across a large museum depends as much on familiar tools, trusted forums and ongoing governance as on the terms themselves.
whyItMatters: Many institutions migrating to a shared collection management system hit the same terminology problem. This talk gives a low-tech, people-centred recipe that others (Naturalis said it is about to try the same) can reuse.
keyPoints: Collections used different terms for the same thing, or the same term for different things, e.g. for object type, preparation type and availability.

A thesaurus was treated simply as a list of terms with definitions; the group's main effort went into writing disambiguating definitions (e.g. 'lost' means permanently gone, 'missing' means it may reappear).
Commercial thesaurus systems were evaluated, but a structured Excel sheet (English, German, Latin where relevant, definitions in two languages) was chosen for accessibility.
The internal weekly 'Collection Cafe' forum and institution-wide emails were used to build participation and credibility.
The final vocabulary was aligned with Darwin Core lists and implemented as Specify pick lists, with a process for requesting changes.
The group has no authority over collections: nearly every term a collection asked for was included, and only ambiguous terms were negotiated.

moments.description: Decision to use an Excel spreadsheet instead of a dedicated thesaurus system.
Disambiguating 'lost' versus 'missing' in the availability vocabulary.
Lessons learned on compromise, familiar tools, trusted forums and governance.

title: From Silos to Standards - Advancing Standardised Collection State Documentation for Institutional Continuity and Coordination
session: From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
summary: Christiaan Steenkamp described how South Africa's NSCF supports a network of about 23 partner institutions, many without data managers, in documenting the state of their collections. Tacit knowledge about readiness, risk and conditions usually sits with individual staff. A 2021 community collection management and conservation manual led to a national collection assessment. Its first tracking tool, built on Google Forms, Apps Script and Looker Studio in 2025, was then refactored with agentic development into a standalone system. The new system scores implementation, documentation and risk, links specimens to jars, preservation batches and storage conditions, enriches records from GBIF with IPT-ready export, keeps audit trails and generates handover documents. It works alongside Specify and BRAHMS.
takeaway: Standardising how collection state (readiness, risk, conditions) is recorded turns tacit curatorial knowledge into shared, comparable institutional memory.
whyItMatters: Collection state and curatorial history are largely missing from current standards. This work shows how a national network with thin staffing can capture them, and it points to a gap beyond Latimer Core.
keyPoints: The NSCF network covers about 23 partner institutions, from full teams to single staff members, built over nine years.
Darwin Core describes occurrences and Latimer Core describes collections, but collection state, readiness and risk are not captured in shareable form.
A community collection management and conservation manual (2021) led to a national assessment scored with taxon experts and observers.
The first Google Stack tracking pipeline (Forms, Apps Script, Looker Studio) was view-only, tedious to update and hard to scale.
The refactored system scores implementation, documentation and risk, lets institutions customise questions, and uses role-level security.
It links specimens to jars, preservation batches, fluids and environmental conditions, keeps an audit log and generates customisable handover documents for staff continuity.
GBIF data can be pulled in, edited with tracking, and exported in IPT-ready format; the system works alongside Specify and BRAHMS rather than competing with them.

moments.description: Tacit knowledge: 'We can know more than we can tell' (Polanyi) applied to collection state.
Scoring of implementation, documentation and risk in the refactored system.
Handover documents to preserve institutional memory when staff leave.
Audience asks about gaps relative to TDWG standards.

title: Bridging the Gap: Strategies for Integrating Person Identifiers into Collection Databases
session: From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
summary: Frederik Berger set out a still-conceptual strategy for linking person name strings in MfN collection data to persistent identifiers via Wikidata. About 30,000 people in Wikidata are linked to collections via property P11146, around 15,000 have Bionomia IDs and 13,500 are referenced from Entomologists of the World. MfN's own data yields about 800,000 name occurrences, 200,000 distinct strings and roughly 13,000 clusters, suggesting about 15,000 people. Only about 1.6% are currently linked to a PID in the central CMS. He compared prioritising frequent names against complex clusters, and proposed a web names directory that reconciles against the collection-related subset of Wikidata, with experts making the final decision.
takeaway: Wikidata's community-built person data can be used to pre-structure candidate matches, but expert judgement and institutional priorities remain essential for identifying collectors.
whyItMatters: Agent disambiguation is a major bottleneck for linking specimens. The quantified gap, prioritisation options and restricted-reconciliation idea are directly reusable by other collection-holding institutions.
keyPoints: No specimen exists without an agent; Wikidata can broker links between institutional databases and other collection information.
About 30,000 Wikidata humans are linked via 'collection items at' (P11146); about 15,000 people with Bionomia IDs and 13,500 from Entomologists of the World are also represented.
The MfN WikiProject 'MfN Berlin Names' (led by Sabine von Mering) lists about 1,100 people.
MfN name data: about 800,000 name strings from about 30 tables, deduplicated to about 200,000 and clustered into about 13,000 groups, suggesting about 15,000 people.
Only about 1.6% of people in the central CMS have an unambiguous PID (about 10% if distributed lists are included).
About 1,500 agents account for up to 90% of collection objects, so prioritising frequent names maximises impact; tackling complex clusters improves authority data quality instead.
Next step: a web-based names directory mapping clusters, strings, sub-collections and candidate Wikidata QIDs, reconciling only against people already linked to collections.

moments.description: The identification gap: only 1.6% of people in the CMS have a PID.
Two prioritisation strategies: frequent names versus complex clusters.
Proposed names directory and restricted reconciliation example (A. White).

title: Confronting legacy data for primary type specimens
session: From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
summary: The presenter traced the USNM Entomology primary type catalogue through handwritten ledgers (since 1896), the in-house INQUIRE type database (1980s), CRIS (mid-1990s) and EMu (migration 2007, full use by 2011). Poor field mapping from INQUIRE meant every migrated type record carried a public disclaimer as an 'INQUIRE type'. Migrated CRIS transaction records lacked objects and had odd dates. Barcodes were duplicated, and some types were never catalogued or linked to acquisitions. The department launched a multi-year, 100% specimen-level type inventory: curators compare EMu spreadsheets with specimens, and transaction discrepancies are resolved against paper records.
takeaway: Decades of database migrations left the second-largest insect collection's type catalogue unreliable, and only a full physical inventory is fixing it.
whyItMatters: The talk is a frank case study of how legacy migrations degrade data and what a sustained, phased remediation looks like. Collections facing similar INQUIRE/CRIS/EMu-style histories can learn from it.
keyPoints: The USNM Insect Collection (est. 1881) holds about 35 million specimens, over 400,000 species and over 130,000 primary types, with a small staff.
Type ledgers in use since 1896 recorded catalogue number, name, sex, locality, year, sender, collector and entry date.
INQUIRE (1980s, in-house) was kept separate from CRIS; both were migrated to EMu in 2007, and INQUIRE fields mapped badly.
All migrated INQUIRE records carry a disclaimer until reviewed; a 'complete' record needs review, a USNM ENT barcode and an image.
Other problems: uncatalogued types, duplicate barcodes from an external printer, and workflow gaps leaving acquisitions unlinked.
Phase 1: curators check EMu spreadsheets against specimens. Phase 2: transaction linking and loan matching. Phase 3: vetting INQUIRE data and type citations. Phase 4: imaging.
Progress: almost 3,500 existing type records completed and over 500 new types added.

moments.description: History of the type catalogue from handwritten ledgers to EMu.
INQUIRE migration problems and the public data disclaimer.
Launch of the phased 100% type inventory project.

title: From Legacy Database to Cloud: Challenges in Migrating Legacy Collection Data to a FAIR Collection Management System
session: From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
summary: Marije Timmermans, the first data manager at SDEI (since February 2026), described preparing for migration to the DINA collection management system, which Senckenberg's central Data and Modelling Centre implements across eight institutes. SDEI's five entomology sub-collections use separate Corel Paradox database instances with diverging schemas, plus card catalogues and personal spreadsheets. Collection data is treated as a management tool rather than research infrastructure, and there is no formal data governance. She acts as liaison, runs one-on-one sessions and workshops, and proposes mappings. Her working method is design-thinking prototypes that domain specialists test.
takeaway: A dedicated data manager who acts as liaison and uses iterative prototypes can make a small institute's move to a shared CMS workable despite fragmented legacy practices.
whyItMatters: It shows the organisational side of CMS migration: divergent schemas, missing governance and the value of empathy-led prototyping. Several audience members picked this up in the discussion.
keyPoints: Senckenberg has about 900 staff, eight research institutions and seven locations; SDMC implements DINA for all of them.
SDEI was founded in 1886 in Berlin, joined Senckenberg in 2009 and has about 35 people including volunteers.
Four of five sub-collections use Corel Paradox instances (from the 1990s) on individual computers; one manager keeps a card catalogue backup and another uses personal spreadsheets.
Schemas have diverged as managers added, moved and renamed fields; practices like putting subspecies in the species field hinder sharing.
There is no formal data governance or ownership, and decision power varies between technical assistants and scientific heads.
Her role: data life cycle documentation, legacy structure assessment, training, liaison with SDMC, and workflows for enrichment, mapping and migration.
Treating work as prototypes (design thinking) and letting specialists test them builds ownership.

moments.description: Four obstacles to smooth migration at SDEI.
Treating data management work as design-thinking prototypes.
Audience comment on standardising empathy.

title: A framework for aligning collections data with the global data ecosystem from data creation to extension in the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History Department of Paleobiology
session: From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
summary: Holly Little presented the Paleobiology department's new five-year, gift-funded 'paleo digital framework' for the world's largest fossil collection. The collection holds about 42 million objects, 800,000 records, and needs an estimated 10–13 million records. The framework covers the data life cycle from capture to enhancement, extension and publishing. It uses imaging-first capture, adaptable specimen surveys for core data points, material entity type and MIDS, and verbatim preservation before AI text extraction. It also aligns taxonomy and geological context with external sources and feeds corrections back to them, and uses Darwin Core Data Package profiles. The informatics team grows from one person to five. She asked the community for workflows and challenges to test.
takeaway: Making paleo collections work in the global data ecosystem needs an iterative, full life-cycle framework, not one-off digitisation.
whyItMatters: It is a concrete institutional roadmap for implementing years of community standards work (material entity type, DwC-DP, geological context). The team explicitly offers to pilot and share solutions.
keyPoints: A 2018 analysis showed low use of Darwin Core terms in paleo collections due to misunderstandings, missing terms and unlinkable resources.
The NMNH Paleobiology collection has about 42 million objects and about 800,000 records; an estimated 10–13 million records are needed.
The informatics team was one person until 2025, then two, with three more staff funded by a gift for a five-year project around 1,000 significant objects.
Principles: work iteratively, image first, share data widely and often, don't wait for perfection, align with global standards and FAIR.
Capture only core data points per specimen type and reuse ledgers (e.g. a locality shared by thousands of specimens) instead of re-transcribing labels.
Enhancement aligns taxonomy (WoRMS, Paleobiology Database, Catalogue of Life) and geological context with external sources and feeds issues back.
DwC-DP mapping showed that different publishing profiles suit different material types (e.g. organism relationships vs cores crossing horizons).

moments.description: The 2018 graph of low Darwin Core term implementation in paleo collections.
The paleo digital framework across the data life cycle.
DwC-DP mapping shows value of different publishing profiles.
Using AI to transcribe ledgers and link by number.

title: SYM29A panel discussion: working with collection managers, documentation and institutional strategy
session: From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
summary: The panel first discussed how to document regions of interest on fossil slabs and pollen slides, then whether collection managers resist new data approaches. Answers ranged from supportive departments to staff who see data work as a burden, and stressed involving managers, continuous support and written procedures. Audience members urged making data management work visible (ticketing boards, published progress and documentation). They proposed a data managers' support group, noted the joint TDWG–SPNHC conference next June, and argued that institutional strategy, not just bottom-up empathy, is needed. The final topic was who maintains CMS documentation, including version control, storing manuals safely, and AI-assisted documentation pipelines.
takeaway: Bridging cabinets and clouds depends on people: engaging collection managers, making data work visible, institutional strategy and durable documentation.
whyItMatters: It brings together practical lessons on change management from several institutions and led to a concrete follow-up: a data managers' email group.
keyPoints: Documenting regions of interest for multiple organisms on one slab or pollen slide is unsolved at NMNH Paleobiology; slabs use catalogue-number suffixes.
Resistance varies: some collection managers see data management as a burden on their core work, while others are supportive if shown it makes life easier.
Keeping collection managers in discussions, decisions and workflows, plus more implementation capacity, helps win them over.
Collection managers are custodians, not owners; initial enthusiasm fades without continuous support.
Making data management work visible (ticketing boards, published progress, documentation) builds understanding.
Without institutional strategy, data managers and curators lack authority to resolve disagreements.
Documentation should be versioned, stakeholder-reviewed, stored in known places (including physical copies), and part of onboarding.

moments.description: Question to the panel on resistance from collection managers.
Suggestion to make data work visible with a ticketing board.
Proposal for a between-conference data managers' community.
Argument that institutional strategy is the missing element.
Old manuals thrown away leave legacy data questions unanswerable.

title: Drawers in the dark harboring data that could spark - finding the sweet spot in collection digitization and mobilizing metadata from museum's collections
session: From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
summary: Nora Lentge-Maaß described MfN's state-funded plan to digitise about 30 million objects holistically: condition assessment, conservation, inventory, digitisation and preparation for the move to a new building. Four digitisation managers and five scan operators were hired. Her showcase was DORA, a malacology digitisation station built with Fraunhofer IAO. It has four cameras with focus stacking, reads QR codes and outputs JSON metadata, and has processed about 170,000 of 260,000 lots (about 85% disclosed). A 2023 cyber attack took systems offline until July 2024 and forced reorganisation into a digitisation-on-demand office, the DCI team and an innovation lab. The lab's new Fides station images insects from several angles. Her take-home: plan for the easy 95%.
takeaway: Plan digitisation for the easy 95%, capture a minimal dataset, and decide when good enough beats perfection.
whyItMatters: It gives practical lessons from one of the largest museum digitisation programmes, including recovery from a cyber attack, with transferable guidance on minimal datasets and workflow design.
keyPoints: MfN's holistic approach combined condition assessment, conservation, inventory, digitisation, QA and new storage, driven by user demand.
Holdings were split into four categories with dedicated digitisation managers; 80% of objects were in historical cabinets.
DORA station: four built-in cameras, focus-stacked tray images with colour chart and scale, label capture, QR-code file naming, and JSON metadata output.
About 170,000 of about 260,000 malacology lots (about 7 million objects) processed; about 85% of the collection disclosed by 19 September.
A 2023 cyber attack destroyed back-end systems; MfN was offline from October 2023 to July 2024.
New structure: coordination office for digitisation on demand (with a request form), the digital catalogue infrastructure (Specify, media repository, data portal) and an innovation lab (ELIO).
The Fides station (with a small company) uses consumer cameras and multi-angle imaging for entomology, but captures media only; AI label transcription runs separately.

moments.description: The DORA malacology digitisation station.
Impact of the 2023 cyber attack on MfN's digitisation.
Take-home messages on digitisation planning.

title: Accelerating specimen identification through Virtual Collections while promoting collaboration
session: From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
summary: Melanie de Leeuw showed how the DiSSCo platform Disscover is turning from a passive lookup tool into an active workspace through Virtual Reference Collections (VRCs), funded by TETTRIs. VRCs pool digital specimens from multiple institutions into one virtual drawer. Three use cases were given: remote curation (e.g. Naturalis hawk moths identified only to family), expert-validated machine-learning training sets, and virtual field guides for rare taxa. Each VRC gets a DOI, aggregates across institutions, keeps two-way specimen–collection relationships, and supports expert annotation. Screenshots of the acceptance environment showed public browsing and ORCID-authenticated creation.
takeaway: Virtual reference collections with DOIs let experts identify and curate dispersed digital specimens remotely instead of shipping material or travelling.
whyItMatters: It turns existing digitised specimens into a collaborative identification resource and suggests a route to citable ML training data. It also raises the unresolved question of feeding annotations back to physical collections.
keyPoints: Taxonomy is stuck in a cycle: physical distance limits experts, and digitised data stuck in silos doesn't help.
VRCs pool digital specimens from institutions such as Naturalis, London, Paris and Oslo into one workspace.
Use cases: curation at a distance, ML training datasets, and virtual field guides for rare or fragile taxa.
Four pillars: a DOI per VRC, cross-institutional aggregation, dynamic entity relationships and active remote curation.
Browsing is open without login; creating a VRC requires ORCID login and an appropriate role.
Next steps: user-group involvement, VRC modification while preserving stability, and an annotation validation framework.

moments.description: Use case one: remote curation of Naturalis hawk moths.
Four pillars of virtual reference collections.
Screenshots of VRCs in Disscover.
Who updates the physical collection after remote annotation?

title: Managing high-volume specimen movements in the entomological collection of Naturalis with a new type of record
session: From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
summary: Myriam van Walsum explained a workload problem in Naturalis's pinned insect collection (about a third of 45 million specimens, only about 10% individually digitised). Records exist mainly at drawer level, with a table of identifications per storage unit. When taxa shifted between drawers, staff had to delete and manually re-enter identifications, so moves were often not recorded. Instead of disruptive independent taxon records, Naturalis introduced a 'lot' record: specimens of the same lowest determined taxon stored in one contiguous location. It is created by migrating existing storage-unit records, so moving a taxon only means updating the lot's link. A Catalogue of Life API lookup also reduced entry errors. She asked how lots should map to Darwin Core or DwC-DP and whether GBIF or DiSSCo want such records.
takeaway: A 'lot' record linking taxa to storage units makes high-volume physical moves cheap to record and tells staff where each taxon is.
whyItMatters: It is a practical data-model fix for a common curation bottleneck in drawer-level digitised collections. It also raises an open standards question about publishing lot and storage-unit records.
keyPoints: Naturalis holds about 45 million specimens; over a third are pinned insects, only about 10% individually digitised (mostly bees).
The zoology/geology CMS is from a Dutch vendor not designed for natural history, so Naturalis writes its own ABCD-aligned requirements.
Taxonomically ordered storage creates many-to-many relationships between taxa and storage units.
Manual delete/re-enter of identifications caused backlog, errors and lost locations, despite a legal obligation to know where specimens are.
Lot definition: specimens of the same lowest determined taxon in one contiguous location; each specimen belongs to exactly one lot.
Lots were created by data migration from existing storage-unit records; no new digitisation was needed.
Catalogue of Life API integration in identifications reduced data entry errors.

moments.description: The digital friction of recording physical moves.
Definition of the lot record and its cardinalities.
Open question to the audience on publishing lot records.

title: Everything is coded: How to prevent a game of telephone in a system full of interfaces
session: From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
summary: Franziska Schuster framed MfN's digital catalogue infrastructure work through the 'game of telephone': standard formats like Darwin Core alone don't keep data meaning intact across professional hand-offs. Developer Jasper then described migrating about 600,000 insect specimen records with 2.5 million images, digitised by a Picturae conveyor pipeline, into Specify after the cyber attack fragmented the data. Requirements unclear from the start made his mapping code slow and hard to verify. Taxon 'NURIs' (internal identifiers) turned out to be non-unique, with up to 2,000 IDs for one taxon, test entries and drawer IDs reused as taxon IDs. Schuster closed with Scrum as a 'don't panic' strategy with three-week sprints and stakeholder feedback.
takeaway: Shared understanding of what data means must be established at the start of a pipeline; standard formats alone won't stop meaning drifting between people.
whyItMatters: It is a candid case study of how identifier semantics break down in mass digitisation pipelines, and it shows how agile methods can manage infrastructure rebuilds.
keyPoints: Coded systems narrow meaning only if sender and receiver share an understanding of the code.
The Picturae conveyor pipeline digitised just over 600,000 specimens with over 2.5 million images, about 5,000 specimens per day, over roughly 2.5 years including development.
After the hack the data were fragmented; deduplication and consolidation came before mapping to Specify.
Iterative feedback from Specify and collection managers made the mapping code increasingly slow and opaque; a month-long rewrite followed after publishing about 22,000 records.
Taxon NURIs were not unique: up to 2,000 IDs per taxon, empty taxa with IDs, and test entries.
Pragmatic fix: accept a taxon NURI only if unique; otherwise keep it in the determination for findability.
Key missing question: is the data sufficient at this point to assign an identifier?
Scrum with prioritised backlogs (must/should/could/won't) and three-week sprints with stakeholder feedback helps the team avoid panic.

moments.description: The game-of-telephone metaphor for data hand-offs.
Discovery of non-unique taxon NURIs.
The missing question: is the data sufficient to assign an identifier?
Scrum as a 'don't panic' strategy.

title: SYM29B panel discussion: publishing lot records and agile development
session: From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
summary: An audience member asked whether lot or drawer numbers should go to GBIF and DiSSCo, distinguishing asset information from collecting metadata. Myriam van Walsum answered that the key researcher question is whether a taxon is held at all, so lot-level records are valuable, while exact storage details stay internal. Nora Lentge-Maaß noted that in malacology the lot is the catalogue unit, and individuals get identifiers related to it. Franziska Schuster explained Scrum: a prioritised backlog with must/should/could/won't labels, three-week sprints, and feedback after each feature.
takeaway: Lot-level records are worth publishing because they answer 'do you have this taxon?', but the definition of a lot differs between collections.
whyItMatters: It clarifies why partially digitised collections may still want aggregators to index lot or storage-level records.
keyPoints: Researchers' main question is often whether a collection holds a taxon, which lot records can answer.
Where exactly a lot is stored stays internal to collection managers.
In malacology the lot number is the catalogue number and manageable unit; individuals get identifiers related to the lot.
Scrum: backlog prioritisation with must/should/could/won't, three-week sprints and stakeholder feedback.

moments.description: Should lot or drawer records be published to aggregators?
Short explanation of Scrum backlog and sprints.

title: From Specimens to Networks: Darwin Core Data Packages in Practice
session: Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
summary: John Wieczorek explained that Darwin Core has moved from a 'bag of terms' to a standard with a conceptual model defining relationships between classes, focusing on MaterialEntity. Material entities can be part of or derived from other material entities. They take part in collection, sampling and derivation events, serve as evidence for occurrences and identifications, and connect to geological context and chronometric age. They can also underpin nucleotide analyses and sequences. Agents, media, assertions, identifiers, references, provenance, protocols and usage policies attach to classes via role and link tables. He closed by demonstrating the Darwin Core Data Package Designer, which generates a datapackage.json from selected tables.
takeaway: The Darwin Core conceptual model and Data Package give material entities a rich, relational context that flat Darwin Core Archives could not express.
whyItMatters: It is the foundational explanation of DwC-DP semantics that several later talks in the session mapped against. The Designer tool offers a practical starting point for mapping CMS data.
keyPoints: Darwin Core was a 'bag of terms'; the conceptual model now adds semantics at the level of classes as part of the standard.
MaterialEntity: identifiable, persists for some time, consists wholly or partly of physical matter (organism, part, non-biological material, environmental sample).
Two self-referential relationships: part of (physically connected) and derived from (no longer connected).
Material entities take part in collecting, sampling and derivation (lab) events, and are evidence for occurrences and identifications.
Geological context and chronometric age separate today's collecting event from the inferred past occurrence.
Molecular data: material (even used-up material) is the basis for nucleotide analyses and sequences.
Agents (people, institutions, software/AI) link via role tables; media link via material-media and event-media tables; assertions generalise measurements or facts.
The Darwin Core Data Package Designer visualises relationships and generates a datapackage.json.

moments.description: From 'bag of terms' to a conceptual model.
Part-of and derived-from relationships for material entities.
Darwin Core Data Package Designer tool.

title: Aligning An Evolving Global Data Model To Software With Global Ambitions: GBIF x TaxonWorks
session: Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
summary: Matt Yoder compared TaxonWorks' API-first data model with the new Darwin Core Data Package (DP). He found the conceptual overlap 'uncanny' after years of independent development. DP's many media, identifier, protocol and reference link tables collapse into single polymorphic annotation tables in TaxonWorks. TaxonWorks lacks a primary Survey concept and full nucleotide analysis, while DP lacks precise anatomy links and physical container hierarchies. He proposed recording mappings (broader/narrower) in SSSOM, merging them in RDF into a 'data mapping of all data mappings', and exposing /vocab endpoints. His observations: partial alignment and lossy exchange are the norm, both models have competing 'fuzzy buckets', and DP's role as an exchange format is unclear.
takeaway: TaxonWorks and DwC-DP have converged conceptually, but exchange between rich models will always be lossy, so mappings should be recorded explicitly.
whyItMatters: It is a concrete software–standard alignment exercise with ideas (SSSOM mappings, /vocab endpoints) that could help many CMSs map to DwC-DP. It also flags practical issues like duplicate extension buckets.
keyPoints: TaxonWorks serves taxonomists first and now about 10–11 large collections; it is API-first and set up for human and agentic contributions.
It already offers Darwin Core import/export, a built-in IPT-like GBIF endpoint, EML persistence and lossless DwC import; an Orthoptera project round-tripped over a million GBIF records.
Conceptual overlap with DwC-DP is remarkable; TaxonWorks models one image depicting many concepts via a single annotation pattern.
Gaps in TaxonWorks: Survey as a primary concept, full nucleotide analysis; gaps in DP: precise anatomy, physical containers, loans, stronger geo-reference primacy.
Mappings can be expressed as broader/narrower relations and persisted in SSSOM, merged in RDF.
Both models have two 'buckets' for fuzzy data (resource relationship vs assertions; observations), which will confuse users.
Needs identified: equipment and configuration, experiments, genomes, more strongly typed agents; comments used as definitions cause confusion.

moments.description: Take-home: TaxonWorks and DwC-DP overlap is uncanny.
SSSOM and a 'data mapping of all data mappings'.
Partial alignment, lossy exchange, schema convergence and AI questions.

title: Material Samples and Occurrences in Darwin Core Data Packages: Practical Experiences from DINA
session: Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
summary: Jonas Grieb asked whether the Darwin Core conceptual model and DwC-DP fix a long-standing problem: CMSs that only hold material and event data have had to invent occurrences to publish to GBIF, producing unstable occurrence IDs. The DINA data model represents material object histories as material samples linked by processes and to collecting events, with organisms carrying determinations. Two worked examples showed good fit. A bat specimen, tissue and molecular extract chain maps to derivedFrom relationships. A mud shrimp and clam preserved together map to partOf relationships, though organism sex and life stage have no place on Material without creating an Occurrence. DINA therefore aims to publish DwC-DP without occurrences and let consumers such as GBIF derive them, which needs agreed conventions.
takeaway: DINA's material-sample model maps well to DwC-DP, so DINA wants to publish without synthetic occurrences and needs community conventions for consumers to derive them.
whyItMatters: It tests in practice whether DwC-DP ends the 'material entities are not occurrences' problem, and pinpoints the remaining gap (sex and life stage on material) and a governance question for GBIF.
keyPoints: A large share of GBIF records have material-entity bases of record (preserved, fossil specimens, material samples).
Generating occurrences from material data causes unstable identifiers and incomplete events.
DINA (consortium since 2014, governed by an MOU) models material samples, processes (collecting, subsampling, extraction) and organisms with determinations.
Derivation chains map cleanly to MaterialEntity with derivedFromMaterialEntity; open question whether only the parent needs an event link.
Mixed-organism samples map to partOf relationships, with some semantic blurriness.
Sex and life stage cannot be placed on Material; options are a synthetic Occurrence (not favoured), non-schema fields, or Material Assertions (discoverability concerns).
DINA plans to publish DwC-DP without occurrences.

moments.description: Worked example: derivation chain from a bat specimen.
The sex and life stage problem for material without occurrences.
Publish DwC-DP without occurrences; conventions needed.

title: Sharing Extended Specimen Data from Symbiota Portals using Registered Extensions
session: Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
summary: Katie Pearson described how Symbiota, open-source software serving as both CMS and mini-aggregator, stores and shares extended specimen data. It underlies 60+ portals, about 52 hosted at the University of Kansas Symbiota Support Hub, used by over 2,000 collections. Keeping a low barrier to entry, Symbiota stays occurrence-centred but supports registered GBIF/Darwin Core extensions: multimedia, identifications, Extended Measurement or Fact, GGBN Material Sample, Alternative Identifiers and Resource Relationship. Examples include herbarium phenology captured in eMoF linked to ontologies, NEON's DNA and tissue subsample tracking, and the Carlquist project linking field notebooks and photos to specimens. The trade-off is that extended data can no longer go in one CSV upload.
takeaway: Existing registered Darwin Core extensions met each of Symbiota's extended-specimen needs, so look for existing standards before inventing new ones.
whyItMatters: It shows how a widely used, low-barrier CMS can share richer extended specimen data via existing standards, immediately visible on GBIF.
keyPoints: Symbiota underlies about 60+ portals and is used by over 2,000 collections.
Built-in publishing sends data directly to GBIF without an IPT.
Extended Measurement or Fact captured herbarium phenology without a new standard, using ontology IDs for types and values.
The Material Sample extension (mostly GGBN terms) is used heavily by NEON for DNA and tissue subsamples.
Identifiers concatenated in 'other catalog numbers' became a separate table aligned with the Alternative Identifiers extension.
Resource Relationship links specimens to other specimens or external resources, e.g. the Carlquist project's field photos and notebooks.
New import/export tools were needed; the single-CSV upload was discontinued in favour of standards alignment.

moments.description: Phenology captured via Extended Measurement or Fact.
Resource Relationship extension and the Carlquist project.
Challenges and the recommendation to reuse existing standards.

title: Diversity Workbench (DWB) as a Standards-Based Collection Management System for Heterogeneous Research Data and Biodiversity Data Mobilization
session: Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
summary: Birgit Rach, digital collection manager at LIB (Bonn and Hamburg), gave an overview of how LIB has used Diversity Workbench (DWB) for more than ten years to manage very heterogeneous data. This covers zoological, botanical, geological, mineralogical and paleontological collections, a biobank, an environmental sample bank, a historical library, research projects and external data as a GFBio data centre. DWB is an open-source, relational, multi-tenant system with granular rights and a customisable import wizard. It is integrated with a DAM system for media, Geneious for sequences and an ASV registry. Publication runs via BioCASe (ABCD) and IPT (Darwin Core) with DOIs. Challenges: gaps in data types, a complex Windows-only interface (a browser client is in development), custom scripts, and keeping up with external APIs.
takeaway: Diversity Workbench can hold very heterogeneous institutional data and publish it through standard pipelines, but its complexity pushes LIB to build web and API layers.
whyItMatters: It shows how a research museum integrates many specialised systems around a standards-based CMS, with publishing to multiple portals from one source.
keyPoints: LIB is a Leibniz research museum at two sites with diverse collections, a biobank, an environmental sample bank and a GFBio data centre role.
DWB: relational, developed in Munich, open source, multi-tenant, granular rights, customisable import wizard, links to many repositories.
Supporting systems: a digital asset management system for media/PDFs, Geneious for sequence data, an ASV registry.
Publication via BioCASe Provider Software (ABCD) and GBIF IPT (Darwin Core), with DOIs and stable identifiers served as RDF and JSON.
Challenges: data types not covered, complex interface, no macOS/Linux client, custom sync scripts, changing external APIs.
Quality control: controlled vocabulary templates, pre-import checks, reference lookups and portal validators (GFBio).

moments.description: LIB's surrounding system landscape (DAM, Geneious, ASV registry).
Challenges of using DWB.

title: From Client to App: Extending Diversity Workbench with REST and graphical web interfaces
session: Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
summary: Björn Quast described work in progress to connect Diversity Workbench more directly with users. Currently the Windows-only client is organised by data concept and feels complex, and publishing pipelines transform data several times with no way back. LIB's online catalogue offers adjustable filters, suggestions, Boolean queries, table downloads and specimen pages with stable identifiers. A redesign aims at mobile-friendly visual exploration using an Elasticsearch index that respects DWB's multi-level access rights. A REST API with concept-based endpoints, sharing JSON structures with the index, supports variable user interfaces and constraint-based insert/update ingest rules. It is already used to ingest ASV registry data (OTU tables, occurrences, identifications).
takeaway: A concept-based REST API and search index let LIB build flexible web interfaces and ingest data on top of the complex Diversity Workbench database.
whyItMatters: It shows a path for legacy desktop CMSs to open up through APIs and web front ends, including data ingest from other systems.
keyPoints: The DWB client is Windows-only and structured by data concept, which confuses users.
Publication pipelines filter by access rights, project and collection through multiple format transformations, with no way back.
The online catalogue offers adjustable filters, suggestions, Boolean sub-queries, CSV download and specimen pages with stable identifiers.
Redesign goals: mobile-friendly, chart-based visual exploration backed by Elasticsearch with DWB's access rights.
The REST API uses concept-level endpoints (e.g. four collection-event tables in one schema) sharing JSON with the index.
Ingest rules (insert, update, insert-if-not-exists, attach) are decided via database-style constraints.
The API is used to ingest ASV registry data into DWB.

moments.description: Decision to put a REST API on the DWB database.
Using the API for ASV registry ingest.

title: Mapping the Relational Data Schema of the Diversity Workbench (DWB) to the Darwin Core Data Package Data Model to fit better to GBIF´s New Data Model
session: Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
summary: Tanja Weibulat explained that GFBio data centres chose ABCD because early Darwin Core couldn't express DWB's complex relations. Their pipeline exports and filters DWB modules (withholding restricted data, anonymising people, rounding coordinates) into PostgreSQL, then maps to ABCD via BioCASe for GBIF and NFDI4Biodiversity. Limitations were that GBIF didn't display multiple identifiers, persons, roles or relations, and data papers needed manual entry. They prototyped mapping the same PostgreSQL tables to DwC-DP in a test IPT: observations and physical specimens split into Occurrence and Material, event, identification and agents shared, and analysis and processing combined into Material Assertion. Next steps are a GBIF sandbox comparison, metadata mapping and extending to the GFBio portal.
takeaway: DwC-DP promises to carry the relational richness that previously pushed GFBio centres to ABCD, and a first DWB-to-DwC-DP prototype via the test IPT works.
whyItMatters: It is a concrete ABCD-to-DwC-DP transition test that matters for the many German data centres still publishing ABCD.
keyPoints: DWB publishing used ABCD because Darwin Core was 'too slow' to capture relations.
Pipeline: DWB modules → filtered export (withhold, anonymise, round coordinates) → PostgreSQL per data package → BioCASe → ABCD XML harvested by GBIF and NFDI4Biodiversity.
GBIF did not display multiple global identifiers, persons with roles, or relations present in ABCD; data papers needed manual entry.
Only a test version of the IPT currently supports DwC-DP; source tables were accessed directly via SQL.
Mapping required splitting observation vs specimen data into Occurrence and Material and combining analysis/processing into Material Assertion.
Dataset metadata must still be entered manually in the IPT.

moments.description: Limitations of the ABCD pipeline in GBIF.
Mapping DWB tables to DwC-DP in the test IPT.

title: The More Extended, The More Open: Semantic Integration of 3D Natural Heritage Data into Biodiversity CMS
session: Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
summary: Yeeun Lee argued that specimens bridge natural history and heritage, because they record biological evidence along with histories of collection, curation, research and exhibition. Existing services (GBIF, BHL, Smithsonian 3D, DiSSCo) cover parts of the task in separate systems, and 3D data are often low quality. The project combines AI-assisted photogrammetric 3D capture of specimens from seven institutions, sized from insects to large mammals, with a semantic model of data, metadata and paradata layers. The model is aligned with openDS, Dublin Core, Europeana and CIDOC CRM, and visualised in Neo4j as a knowledge graph of about 2,400 nodes and 3,600 relations. Example applications are CMS integration, recommendations and map-based views.
takeaway: Treating 3D specimen models as entry points in a knowledge graph that includes heritage context and digitisation paradata makes them reusable knowledge assets.
whyItMatters: It links biodiversity and cultural heritage standards and argues for recording 3D production paradata, which matters as 3D specimens are used for exhibitions, citizen science and AI.
keyPoints: Specimens carry both natural history evidence and heritage value formed through human curation and interpretation.
Natural heritage information is distributed across institutions with differing quality, and 3D data are often low quality.
Photogrammetric 3D production in four stages: capture, multi-point imaging, registration and meshing, with setups adapted to specimen size.
The semantic model has three layers: data (nature, specimen, occurrence), metadata (heritage, resource) and paradata (project, institution, item).
It is aligned with openDS, Dublin Core, Europeana and CIDOC CRM via one-to-one mappings.
The Neo4j knowledge graph has about 2,400 nodes and 3,600 relations.

moments.description: Three-layer data/metadata/paradata model.
Neo4j knowledge graph visualisation.

title: Old habits and new visions: Exploring the RECODE data model, future integration and data enhancement
session: Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
summary: Steen Dupont gave an update on NHM London's RECODE programme (since 2019) to replace a 20-year-old CMS, with go-live expected early next year on the Doxis platform. The data model was heavily normalised: about 70 object record types and 54,000 fields were reduced to about 6,500 in use and then 600–700 fields in four collection object entities (biological, geological, extraterrestrial, human-made). The new system uses true relationships, separates objects from processes, and enforces stricter taxonomy and location hierarchies. Videos of the UAT environment showed a data model viewer, agent relationships, a workflow engine (parallel acquisitions, sequential loans, silent movement control) and a bulk-ingest template builder that outputs CSV/JSON with dynamic errors.
takeaway: Normalising decades of flat CMS data into relational entities and workflow-driven processes gives NHM a foundation for integrations and AI, but it needs institutional governance.
whyItMatters: It is a rare look inside a large museum's CMS rebuild, with concrete numbers on field reduction and design choices other institutions can learn from.
keyPoints: RECODE began in 2019; the system is in UAT and expected to go live at the start of next year.
Current system: about 70 object record types and about 54,000 fields, reduced to about 6,500 used, then about 600–700 fields.
Four target collection object entities: biological, geological, extraterrestrial, human-made.
True relationships replace value fields; objects are decoupled from processes; stricter taxonomy and location hierarchies are enforced.
Workflow engine supports parallel processes (acquisition), strictly ordered processes (research loans for compliance) and silent processes (movement control with history).
A bulk template builder generates CSV and JSON with dynamic error handling for ingest, update and fixes; the JSON can feed other APIs.
Business studio admin layer exposes integrations, AI, the data model and search fields; governance is needed to avoid new silos.

moments.description: The scale of field normalisation.
Data model viewer video.
Workflow engine: parallel, sequential and silent processes.
Bulk ingest template builder.

title: The Unruliness of Higher Geography: What is it doing for us?
session: Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
summary: Erika Krimmel argued that Darwin Core's handling of higher geography is unruly. The dwc:higherGeography term is loosely defined and often a concatenation of other fields. Physical geography (oceans, drainage basins, mountain ranges) and many human regions (parks, EEZs, historical countries) lack explicit terms. A US freshwater mussel study used only georeferenced records and so missed 51% of the data, even though many historic records named drainages precisely enough for the question. GBIF indexes higherGeography and waterBody as text, so finding Atlantic Ocean records takes several searches. Boundary changes over time (Valencia/Cibola County, New Mexico) add confusion. She proposed a Darwin Core Maintenance Group task group.
takeaway: Darwin Core needs more explicit, time-aware ways to share human and physical geography so data without coordinates can still be discovered and used.
whyItMatters: Much historic specimen data can't be georeferenced but has meaningful higher geography. Better terms could unlock it for conservation research.
keyPoints: Higher geography contextualises localities and is a useful first-pass filter.
dwc:higherGeography is open to interpretation and becomes a 'trash basket or treasure trove'.
Physical geography is treated much less explicitly than human geography in Darwin Core.
Freshwater mussel study: 51% of records (ungeoreferenced historic specimens, including a holotype) were excluded despite having drainage information.
GBIF indexes higherGeography and waterBody as text strings, so concept-based search (e.g. Atlantic Ocean) needs several queries.
Geography changes over time (e.g. Cibola County carved from Valencia County in 1981), so concepts are most useful with a time.

moments.description: Freshwater mussel study and drainage as the unit of analysis.
Searching GBIF for the Atlantic Ocean.
Proposal for a Darwin Core task group on higher geography.

title: Mobilizing rich, interoperable, and secure fossil data from underserved collections using Symbiota
session: Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
summary: Erika Krimmel described a project (started 2023) to make Symbiota work for fossil collections, which are underrepresented despite Symbiota's popularity with small, under-resourced collections. A new Paleo Data Portal serves as testbed. Enhancements released in Symbiota 3.4 include GBIF GeoTime–based chronostratigraphy entry with auto-populated hierarchy, and staging scripts for stratigraphic and morphology remarks. There is inclusive numerical-time search, a Macrostrat geology map layer (also in georeferencing), and taxonomy sourced from Catalogue of Life XR via ChecklistBank to trace errors. Other additions: default 'FossilSpecimen' basis of record, description fields for material type, and relationships such as part/counterpart and slab-with. Features are documented in Symbiota Docs and a new Paleodata Knowledge Hub, and collections are being onboarded.
takeaway: Targeted Symbiota enhancements around geological context, taxonomy and relationships make a low-barrier CMS viable for under-resourced fossil collections.
whyItMatters: It extends the benefits of a widely used, low-cost platform to paleontological collections and improves how geological time data reach GBIF.
keyPoints: Symbiota's pre-2023 paleo module had undocumented custom fields, and geological context was not searchable or exportable publicly.
Chronostratigraphic entry now uses a controlled vocabulary aligned with GBIF GeoTime and the International Chronostratigraphic Chart.
Search over geological time is inclusive using the vocabulary's numerical timescale, based on researcher feedback.
Macrostrat API geology layer is available in map search and georeferencing.
Taxonomy is sourced from Catalogue of Life Extended Release in ChecklistBank, allowing tracing and reporting of incorrect higher taxonomy.
Collections can set FossilSpecimen as the default basis of record.
Relationships document part/counterpart pairs and slab associations with uncatalogued material; links to MorphoSource, MorphoBank and BHL.

moments.description: Chronostratigraphy via GBIF GeoTime vocabulary.
Taxonomy from Catalogue of Life XR via ChecklistBank.
Part/counterpart and slab-with relationships.

title: SYM42 discussion: DwC-DP profiles, deriving occurrences, ABCD's future and system boundaries
session: Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
summary: Wieczorek answered a chat question on registering DwC-DP profiles (e.g. a GBIF profile requiring occurrences): none exist yet, but community-created, community-vetted profiles could become standard products. Grieb discussed who should derive occurrences, and a GBIF participant asked what rules GBIF should follow; the panel called for community-driven, rule-based conventions. Weibulat said German data centres must still decide on ABCD's future. Dupont confirmed RECODE's strong API. Yoder noted agentic pull requests from students and the public, and Macklin reflected on how far CMSs should manage links versus rely on external services. Participants suggested core-versus-plugin architectures, and Yoder warned most links die within ten years.
takeaway: Richer relational models bring the community together but raise hard governance questions about profiles, occurrence derivation, system scope and link persistence.
whyItMatters: It captures open design questions for the DwC-DP transition and for CMS architecture as AI-assisted development and linked services grow.
keyPoints: There are no DwC-DP profiles now because early feedback asked for a single model, but communities have since asked for tailored profiles.

The latest Darwin Core public review incorporated GBIF cores and simple extensions (measurement or fact, identification history, alternative identifiers, Humboldt, chronometric age) into the standard; OBIS and GGBN extensions await conversations.
DINA would prefer to publish without occurrences and let GBIF derive them if technically feasible.
GBIF asked whether derivation should use explicit flags or rule-based logic (e.g. event + identification + material).
German NFDI data centres still use ABCD and must decide whether to switch.
Agentic coding creates a flood of pull requests; semantic-layer changes need strict control, UI changes less so.
Suggestion to separate core from blessed plug-ins to manage community contributions.
Link rot: most links don't last longer than ten years, so systems must decide what to persist locally.

moments.description: Registry and governance of DwC-DP profiles.
GBIF asks what rules to use when deriving occurrences.
Agentic development and controlling the semantic layer.
Macklin on relationships and how far systems should go.
Link rot: most links don't last ten years.

title: The BMD Cubing Engine: Harmonizing Biodiversity and Earth Observation Data
session: Operationalizing Biodiversity Digital Twins within Data Space Ecosystems
summary: Mathias Dillen presented the cubing engine built in the Biodiversity Meets Data (BMD) project as the central harmonisation layer between BMD's data catalogue and analytical tools for Natura 2000 site managers. He described a modular Python back end (base grid class, raster/vector engines, a data cube orchestrator with one child class per data source) and a slim front end that takes a YAML 'recipe' and returns harmonised raster and vector files on a common master grid, plus a STAC description and a provenance record. He covered supported sources (GBIF, CHELSA climate data, Earth observation data), GBIF-specific options including Monte Carlo resampling of occurrence uncertainty, and plans to add sources, publish a package and deploy the engine as an API service within BMD.
takeaway: BMD's cubing engine turns a declarative YAML recipe into reproducible, provenance-documented data cubes that harmonise GBIF occurrences with climate and Earth observation data on one grid.
whyItMatters: Harmonising heterogeneous biotic and abiotic data reproducibly is a precondition for decision-support tools; a recipe-driven, extensible engine with STAC and provenance output makes these cubes discoverable and reusable rather than one-off analyses.
keyPoints: The cubing engine is BMD's central harmonisation layer, feeding harmonised data via an API to analytical tools aimed mainly at Natura 2000 site managers.
It builds on the B3 project's GBIF SQL API 'cube' functionality, which resamples occurrence data and makes heterogeneous data safer to use.

Back end: a base grid class (currently EEA grid, a global equal-area grid and WGS84), raster and vector engines for pure geospatial transformations, and a data cube orchestrator with abstract raster/vector cube classes; each data source is a child class, so adding a source means writing one class.
Front end: a single BMDCube class reads a YAML recipe (global, spatial/temporal and source-specific configuration) and runs the harmonisation without users needing to code.

Output: a data tree of harmonised raster and vector files on the same master grid, a STAC file describing the cube, and a provenance record (runtime, engine and dependency versions, hardware); files can be streamed rather than downloading the whole cube.
Stack: Python with GDAL, GeoPandas, xarray (central data model), Dask/DuckDB; outputs GeoParquet for vectors and NetCDF or Zarr for rasters.
Current sources are GBIF, CHELSA climate data and Earth observation data (being moved to direct access to Copernicus S3 storage).

GBIF options include taxon keys and aggregation ranks, default/min/max coordinate uncertainty, excluding GBIF issue flags, and Monte Carlo resampling of points with fractional grid-cell output or point clouds.

moments.description: Architecture of the cubing engine: modular back end and slim front end.
Walk-through of the YAML recipe file and source-specific parameters.
Question on extending the engine to other survey designs and sensor data.

title: BMD workflow engine: FAIR workflows, RO-Crate and FAIR Signposting for a European biodiversity data space
session: Operationalizing Biodiversity Digital Twins within Data Space Ecosystems
summary: Lena Perzlmaier presented the workflow engine developed in Biodiversity Meets Data, motivated by letting a Natura 2000 site manager reuse a scientist's species distribution model. She argued that scientists should share code, containerise it, and define a workflow (BMD mainly uses Argo), described with Workflow RO-Crate (prospective provenance) and Workflow Run RO-Crate (retrospective provenance). A central RO-Crate service links user interfaces, execution engines (Workflow.earth on Destination Earth, and the BMD platform's engine at LifeWatch ERIC) and registries, and runs are exposed as FAIR Digital Objects by combining identifiers, RO-Crates and FAIR Signposting.
takeaway: Packaging containerised workflows and their runs as RO-Crates with FAIR Signposting lets non-technical users run models remotely and get machine-actionable, citable results.
whyItMatters: It shows a concrete path from 'share your code' to reusable, remotely executable and provenance-rich workflows, which is the practical substance behind data space rhetoric.
keyPoints: Motivating example: an ecologist's species distribution model reused by a Natura 2000 site manager interested in invasive species spread.
Steps asked of scientists: share code, containerise it, and define a workflow of inputs, steps and outputs; BMD mainly uses Argo and has considered CWL.
Workflow runners can execute on remote infrastructure, so site managers need not run models on limited local hardware.

Workflow RO-Crate adds licence, authorship, description, language and formal inputs/outputs (prospective provenance); Workflow Run RO-Crate adds a CreateAction with agent, actual parameter values and output files (retrospective provenance).

A central RO-Crate service unpacks submitted crates, sends manifests to workflow engines and repackages run results as run crates that can be published to registries (BMD data space, WorkflowHub, Workflow.earth).
Workflow.earth, deployed in Destination Earth, was the first implementation, focused on agricultural digital twins; the BMD platform's engine runs at LifeWatch ERIC.
FAIR Signposting exposes metadata to machines in HTTP headers; combined with a unique identifier and RO-Crate, runs become W3C-style FAIR Digital Objects.
The BMD interface lets users pick a workflow, choose species from a list and an area on a map, and view results in a dashboard or download the run RO-Crate.

moments.description: Scientist and Natura 2000 site manager example motivating workflow reuse.
Architecture of the RO-Crate service linking interfaces, engines and registries.
BMD user interface: choosing species and area, submitting, viewing a results dashboard.

title: Beyond Data Integration: Ecological and Semantic Interoperability in Coastal Digital Twins
session: Operationalizing Biodiversity Digital Twins within Data Space Ecosystems
summary: Laura Slaughter presented a landscape analysis of how far existing standards, data models and interoperability approaches support integrating land and sea data for coastal digital twins, and where the gaps remain. She distinguished digital models, digital shadows (what most demonstrators actually are) and full bidirectional digital twins, noting that SINTEF aims for 'learning twins' that can amend model structure. She then ran through categories of land-sea problems: spatial reference and boundaries (horizontal CRS and vertical datum mismatches, shoreline and boundary definitions), scale and resolution, semantic interoperability, units, technical interoperability, missing data (the 'white ribbon'), provenance and governance.
takeaway: Coastal digital twins expose a long list of unresolved land-sea interoperability gaps, from vertical datums and shifting shorelines to missing cross-domain ontologies.
whyItMatters: Anyone building digital twins that span terrestrial and marine domains will hit these problems; a structured map of existing support and gaps helps decide where to invest.
keyPoints: Norway's long coastline has produced several coastal twin projects (coastal change, storm simulators), where marine and terrestrial data 'clash'.
Work was a landscape analysis: derive digital twin requirements from the literature, then map land-sea integration problems, who works on them and remaining gaps.
Digital model (no automated link), digital shadow (automatically updated from the physical system but not acting back) and digital twin (bidirectional) are distinct; many demonstrators are shadows.
The goal is learning twins that can recommend interventions and amend both state and model structure, which raises requirements such as dynamic data integration and handling missing data.

Spatial issues: horizontal CRS mismatches (partly addressed, e.g. by OGC), vertical datum mismatch between land elevation and marine depth, dynamic shorelines, land-sea boundary semantics and geometry mismatches.
Semantic issues: incomplete cross-domain feature mappings, one concept with different names or definitions, need for cross-domain ontologies; units remain a problem.
Technical issues include schema, format and API incompatibilities; static integration becomes outdated, so dynamic integration with minimal information loss is needed.
The 'white ribbon' is the coastal zone too deep for terrestrial surveys and too shallow for ships, where data are largely missing.

moments.description: Research question of the landscape analysis on land-sea integration for digital twins.
Digital model vs digital shadow vs digital twin.
The 'white ribbon' coastal data gap.

title: From Buzzwords to Blueprints: What It Really Takes to Operationalise Biodiversity Digital Twins
session: Operationalizing Biodiversity Digital Twins within Data Space Ecosystems
summary: Sharif Islam used the Gartner hype cycle to argue that buzzwords like 'digital twin' and 'data space' help win funding but do not help once projects start. His blueprint places the real work in a middle 'control plane' of context, discovery, governance and contracts between fragmented data sources and the consumers (media, funders, policymakers) that buzzwords address. Drawing on BioDT, he said FAIR digital twins boil down to metadata profiles and cross-domain mappings; for BMD he described a STAC-based catalogue with GeoParquet and cloud-native formats so users can query and fetch only the slices they need, including the cubes from the cubing engine.
takeaway: Use buzzwords to get funded, then break them down into concrete blueprints: metadata, catalogues, governance and stewardship in the middle layer.
