whyItMatters: It gives a pragmatic framing for turning digital twin and data space funding language into implementable components, and names governance and stewardship as work that must be resourced.
keyPoints: Digital twin peaked on Gartner's 2018 hype cycle; by 2025 it had been replaced by agents and physical AI, while BioDT (2022) and DTO-BioFlow (2023) were funded on the term.
Buzzwords help proposals but when real work starts teams must still define what a digital twin or data space actually is.
The blueprint: fragmented sources on one side, consumers on the other, and a middle layer of context, discovery, governance and contracts that can be centralised or federated.

BioDT experience: FAIR for digital twins boils down to metadata; human communication issues (e.g. 'model calibration' vs 'model training') required mandatory metadata profiles (model version, datasets, inputs/outputs) and mappings.

In BMD, heterogeneous inputs (Natura 2000 boundaries, EEA species checklists, camera trap and eDNA surveys) are brought together via the cubing engine and a centralised metadata catalogue, plus access control for restricted species.
STAC is a simple static-JSON metadata catalogue with a common API and search; with GeoParquet it can index many S3 objects and supports geospatial and metadata queries.
Cloud-native formats let users take only the slice they need instead of downloading huge CSV files; cubes can likewise be sliced for different audiences.
TDWG standards are foundational, alongside OGC and other standards; governance and stewardship of data and models must be part of the blueprint.

moments.description: 'Punchline' blueprint slide: the middle layer of context and discovery.
STAC catalogue approach for BMD.
Buzzwords for funding, blueprints for work.

title: Digital Twins as System-Optimization Tools: Provisioning Edge and Cloud Infrastructure for Biodiversity Monitoring at Scale
session: Operationalizing Biodiversity Digital Twins within Data Space Ecosystems
summary: Tanya Berger-Wolf argued that biodiversity digital twins should model not only nature but also the sensing system itself, so that deployments of drones, camera traps, acoustic sensors, GPS tags and supporting compute, power and network infrastructure can be planned and optimised. Using a summer deployment at The Wilds conservation centre in Ohio (over 400,000 data points across five modalities), she showed a mock-up in which camera trap positions and drone flight plans can be moved within the twin. She called for bringing robotics and sensor-system standards into the same conversation as data standards and AI readiness, pointing to simulators such as WildWing.
takeaway: Digital twins should close the sim-to-real loop for the sensor systems too, letting teams plan where and how to deploy multimodal monitoring before going into the field.
whyItMatters: At-scale monitoring (e.g. the newly announced Amazon.ia effort) depends on deploying complementary sensors in the right place and time; treating the cyber-physical system as part of the twin makes that a solvable optimisation problem.
keyPoints: Remote sensing, autonomous vehicles, on-body sensors, camera traps, acoustic recorders, eDNA and citizen science capture complementary signals at different spatiotemporal scales.
At-scale monitoring requires cross-modal coordination and provisioning of compute, energy, infrastructure and sensor deployment ('sensing everything, everywhere, all at once').
Current practice stops at data analysis; the loop should return to system refinement, using digital experiments in the twin to plan future deployments.

The Wilds (Ohio), a large conservation science site with endangered species, was instrumented over a summer, yielding over 400,000 data points across GPS tags, camera traps, acoustic sensors, drone flights and citizen science.
A mock-up twin lets users reposition camera traps and edit drone flight plans with full sensor details to see what the system needs to provision.
Standards now exist for biodiversity data and AI readiness is being discussed; robotics and sensor aspects need to join the same conversation.
Simulation environments already exist for drones, e.g. the WildWing software for drone mission planning in biodiversity settings.
A FAIR4AI drone data standard was to be presented virtually by Jenna Kline later the same day.

moments.description: Argument that twins must include the sensing system infrastructure.
Mock-up twin with movable camera trap placements and drone flight plans.
Question about commercial hardware in open research.

title: How to operationalize large-scale aerial biodiversity monitoring?
session: Operationalizing Biodiversity Digital Twins within Data Space Ecosystems
summary: Peter Desmet explained how European weather radars, which scan the sky continuously for precipitation, also detect nocturnal bird migration, and how the vol2bird algorithm extracts altitude, speed, direction and density of 'meat in the sky' (no species information). The radar aeroecology community has produced the VPTS CSV standard (Frictionless table schema), a maintained radar metadata list, open-source packages and the Aloft data portal, archiving derived vertical profile data for 24 countries and 173 radars back to 2012, updated daily and archived on Zenodo under CC0. He outlined an aerial-habitat digital twin for migration forecasting (collision prevention, avian flu) modelled on the US BirdCast, and noted obstacles: filtered data from meteorological institutes, lack of taxonomy, and a small community maintaining infrastructure.
takeaway: Existing weather radar networks already monitor bird migration continent-wide; with open standards and the Aloft archive, they could underpin a European migration-forecasting digital twin.
whyItMatters: It turns an existing sensor network into a biodiversity monitoring infrastructure at no deployment cost and raises the broader question of how to publish probabilistic, non-specimen observations.
keyPoints: Songbirds migrate mostly at night, at high altitude and on a broad front, making them hard to monitor with citizen science or GPS tags.
Weather radars emit microwaves up to about 35 km from the radar; birds are separated from rain by more variable speed/direction and lower reflectivity.
vol2bird extracts altitude, speed, direction and density, converting reflectivity to numbers of average-size songbirds; species are unknown.

Community standards include the VPTS CSV format for vertical profile time series (defined with Frictionless table schema), a format for raw polar volumes, and a co-maintained list of European radars that tracks code changes.

Meteorological institutes typically keep data only about two days, so the community archives derived biological data in the Aloft portal: 24 countries, 173 radars, back to 2012, nearly 5,000 days, CC0 on Zenodo, updated daily with a 1-2 day delay.
Open-source packages support discovery, visualisation and analysis; a visualisation tool shows near-real-time migration, e.g. a radar south of Oslo and Karlskrona.
An aerial digital twin could support migration forecasting for wind turbine and aircraft collision prevention, disease modelling (avian flu), outreach, and a biomass essential biodiversity variable.
BirdCast in the US, using NOAA's unified radar network, forecasts migration three days ahead (e.g. 340 million birds in one night).

moments.description: How weather radars detect birds and how they are separated from rain.
Aloft data portal and the long-term archive.
Near-real-time migration charts for a radar near Oslo.
Discussion of expressing identification uncertainty in Darwin Core.

title: Operationalising biodiversity DT ecosystems through assessment-driven service mapping and reusable tools and workflow integration
session: Operationalizing Biodiversity Digital Twins within Data Space Ecosystems
summary: Syrine Ben Aziza argued that biodiversity digital twin projects keep producing tools that are hard to find, understand and adopt once funding ends, so similar solutions get rebuilt. TNO's 'assessment tech' approach pairs 'what is needed' (purpose, stakeholders, capabilities and maturity) with 'what is available' (solutions and resources) through five steps: define context, compare capabilities with needs, identify gaps and constraints, match goals to options, and check feasibility, iteratively. She described a use case guide in BioDT for teams to assess their twin's maturity and ambition, and in DTO-BioFlow an inventory of existing tools tagged by technicalities, infrastructure needs and limitations matched to demonstrator use cases' needs gathered by questionnaire; next steps are automation in the Digital Twin of the Ocean context and eventual standardisation.
takeaway: A simple, purpose-first assessment that maps a team's needs and capabilities to an inventory of existing tools helps digital twin projects reuse rather than rebuild.
whyItMatters: Tool reuse and sustainability are chronic problems in project-funded biodiversity infrastructure; a lightweight assessment method targets the non-technical barriers of discovery, expertise and adoption.
keyPoints: Tools built 'in a bubble' for specific contexts are difficult to find, reuse and adopt; documentation is often not understood by domain scientists without IT support.
Resource and maintenance requirements deter adoption, leading to duplicated solutions and a cycle of prototypes.
The approach asks 'what is needed' (purpose, stakeholders, capabilities, maturity) and 'what is available' (solutions, resources), then maps them to reveal gaps.
Five steps: define current context; compare capabilities with needs; identify gaps and constraints; match goals to options; check feasibility of implementation, with feedback between steps.
In BioDT, a use case guide let teams assess their twin's state and ambition (e.g. whether a dynamic twin is actually needed) before technical decisions.

In DTO-BioFlow, existing tools were summarised with keyword tags (technicalities, infrastructure needs, limitations), and demonstrator needs were gathered by structured questionnaire and mapped into thematic areas.
Next: make the approach more automated and validated in the Digital Twin of the Ocean / Mission Ocean context (ASR 'Oceanity'), and eventually standardise repeatable patterns.

moments.description: 'What is needed' vs 'what is available' framing.
The five-step assessment process.
Tool inventory and use case mapping in DTO-BioFlow.

title: Post-BioDT lessons and next-generation biodiversity digital twins
session: Operationalizing Biodiversity Digital Twins within Data Space Ecosystems
summary: The convener framed the discussion around the lesson from BioDT that biological and ecological complexity could not be captured by large monolithic twins like Destination Earth's climate twins, leaving many specialised prototypes reliant on GBIF, LifeWatch and DiSSCo, and asked what a next-generation biodiversity digital twin should look like. A BioDT work package lead said twinning nature is naive and the project's lasting outcome was educational: modellers and data communities came to understand each other. Others stressed that users never asked for digital twins and simpler tools may solve problems, that outside Europe work must be decentralised (NEON, LTER, GBIF, iNaturalist, Amazon.ia), that twins risk being 'theatre' offering an illusion of control while habitat is destroyed, and that rapid-response twins for emerging threats could be valuable. It closed with a call to continue at an RDA digital twins session in London.
takeaway: BioDT delivered pilots and, above all, mutual understanding between modellers and data people; the next generation must find real users and real conservation impact rather than chase the digital twin label.
whyItMatters: It is a candid, insider assessment of what a large EU biodiversity digital twin project did and did not achieve, useful for anyone designing follow-on infrastructure or funding calls.
keyPoints: Large infrastructures like Destination Earth excel at continuous climate/meteorological data, but monolithic twins could not capture ecological modelling complexity.
BioDT produced a gradient of pilot twins from simple to complex; they promised pilots and delivered pilots.
The most lasting BioDT outcome was educational: modellers stopped assuming data 'fall from the sky' and data communities began to understand modellers.
Communication between data scientists, biologists and social scientists improved; BMD's cubing work continues BioDT lessons.
No scientist or user asked for a 'digital twin' or 'data space'; simpler tools that solve the problem may be fine and should be advertised as such.
Outside Europe there is little centralised funding; decentralised or semi-centralised networks (NEON, LTER, GBIF, NatureServe, iNaturalist, STRI, Amazon.ia) are testbeds for transferring methods.
Standards have progressed from FAIR data to open code, AI models and now workflows.
Global Nature Watch lacked occurrence data, suggesting occurrence data could fill a gap in large AI platforms.
Twins risk being theatre giving funders an illusion of control while habitats are destroyed; the 'then what' of real conservation impact is unresolved.
Quickly spun-up twins could help respond to emerging threats such as avian flu, invasive crop pathogens and zoonoses.
Open data can be perceived as a threat (e.g. Finnish forest landowners), making data policy interoperability a concern.

moments.description: Convener frames post-BioDT lessons and next-generation twins.
BioDT's lasting outcome was educational.
Decentralised approaches outside Europe.
Warning about digital twins as theatre and illusion of control.
Rapid-response twins for emerging threats.

title: Toward Quantitative AI-Readiness Metrics for Biodiversity Data Infrastructures
session: AI-Readiness Metrics and Metadata for Biodiversity Data
summary: Yasin Bakış defined AI readiness as the degree to which a dataset and its workflows can support a defined AI task reliably, reproducibly and interoperably, and argued it should be task-specific, multi-dimensional, testable and expressed as a profile rather than a single global score. Drawing on work preparing museum fish images from GBIF, iDigBio and museums for machine learning, he described moving from manual to automated metadata capture and feeding task performance (e.g. from a trait-extraction landmarking pipeline) back into the profile. Finding that about 90-95% of their roughly 200 needed terms were absent from Darwin Core, Audiovisual Core, EXIF and PROV, the team built the Fish-AIR platform and vocabulary and a TDWG task group under Audiovisual Core.
takeaway: AI readiness should be a task-specific, measurable profile rather than a single score, and current biodiversity standards lack most of the terms needed to describe it.
whyItMatters: It makes AI readiness operational and exposes a concrete vocabulary gap in TDWG standards for image-based machine learning, with a route to address it via a task group.
keyPoints: Definition: the degree to which a dataset and its associated workflows can support a defined AI task reliably, reproducibly and interoperably.
AI readiness is task-specific, multi-dimensional, testable and profile-based; there should be a readiness profile, not a global score.
Profile dimensions include metadata completeness, semantic alignment, provenance, image (data) suitability, reproducibility, interoperability and task performance.
Metadata completeness is not just the share of filled columns but whether the fields ML practitioners use for filtering and cleaning are present.
Manual metadata capture was too slow and expensive, so automated metadata capture was adopted.
An AI-ready dataset is expected to perform better but does not guarantee good results; task performance scores from a trait-extraction/landmarking pipeline update the profile.
Of roughly 200 terms developed, about 90-95% were new, not found in Darwin Core, Audiovisual Core, EXIF, PROV or other standards.

Fish-AIR supplies data and metadata to ML researchers, iterates on their complaints and generates vocabulary passed to the TDWG task group, Audiovisual Core and data quality groups, then to repositories like GBIF, DiSSCo and Phenoscape.

moments.description: AI readiness as a profile rather than a single score.
Most needed terms were missing from existing standards.
Is Fish-AIR reusable beyond fish?

title: Traits Thesaurus: toward semantic harmonization of FAIR trait-based data on aquatic organisms
session: AI-Readiness Metrics and Metadata for Biodiversity Data
summary: Jessica Titocci presented the Trait Thesaurus, a SKOS thesaurus developed with LifeWatch Italy to harmonise functional trait terminology for aquatic organisms. She described the heterogeneity of trait data (sources, aggregation levels, repositories, structures) and especially semantic heterogeneity, such as 'body size' meaning prosome length for copepods. Four separate domain thesauri (fish, macroalgae, phytoplankton, zooplankton) were merged by manual and automated ontology alignment into a unified resource of over 1,500 concepts (now five schemes including macrobenthos) published on EcoPortal, with URIs, synonyms, definitions, units and SKOS mappings to existing resources. It is used for semantic annotation in LifeWatch Italy's portal and in projects like PoMP.
takeaway: A community-validated SKOS thesaurus of aquatic trait terms and units can make open trait data genuinely interoperable across taxa.
whyItMatters: Open trait data are not automatically reusable; shared definitions are needed for cross-taxa synthesis and for AI/NLP applications on trait data.
keyPoints: Trait data come from literature, collections, in situ monitoring and remote sensing, at individual, species or community level, quantitative or qualitative, in varied repositories and structures.
Semantic heterogeneity is the hardest problem: different terms for the same thing and the same term with different meanings (e.g. body size vs prosome length in copepods).
Development steps: scoping, term gathering, formalisation (SKOS data model, VocBench editor), then editing and community validation before publication.
Four independent domain thesauri (fish, macroalgae, phytoplankton, zooplankton) were aligned manually and automatically into one Trait Thesaurus of more than 1,500 concepts.
Now five schemes (including macrobenthos); each term has a preferred label, URI, synonyms, definition, scheme membership, units and SKOS closeMatch/exactMatch mappings.
Published on EcoPortal; used for semantic annotation of datasets, metadata and attributes in the LifeWatch Italy data portal and metadata catalogue.
Applied to harmonise plankton datasets in the Polar Ocean Mitigation Potential (PoMP) project and in progress for a coral reef benthic database.
A LifeWatch working group on traits and a SCOR working group for zooplankton are being launched.

moments.description: 'Body size' means prosome length for copepods: semantic heterogeneity example.
Merging four domain thesauri into one unified resource.
Navigating the thesaurus on EcoPortal.

title: Provenance, Lineage, and Auditability in AI-Driven Biodiversity Image Workflows
session: AI-Readiness Metrics and Metadata for Biodiversity Data
summary: Xiaojun Wang presented how the Fish-AIR repository records provenance for AI-derived fish images produced mostly by external pipelines. Fish-AIR holds just over 400,000 source images from 67 institutions plus about 306,000 derived images (bounding boxes, segmentations, landmarks), and each derived record carries a parent ARK (its direct input image) and a batch ARK (the processing run), so following parent links reconstructs lineage back to the specimen image. Batch records (a class with 14 terms in the Fish-AIR vocabulary) store shared run metadata once, and ARKs, parent and batch references travel in exported CSV and RDF downloads. Automated checks of about 359,000 parent links and 763,000 batch links found all resolvable, enabling researchers to trace odd results and compare model performance across collections or batches.
takeaway: Two persistent-identifier links per derived image, parent and batch, are enough to preserve auditable lineage and pipeline context for AI-processed biodiversity images, even outside the repository.
whyItMatters: As AI pipelines generate derived media at scale, lineage that survives export is essential for reproducibility and for diagnosing whether model errors come from source material or processing.
keyPoints: Fish-AIR serves the Biology-Guided Neural Networks and Imageomics projects; derived outputs are produced mostly by external teams' pipelines.

Snapshot: just over 400,000 source image records from 67 institutions and 7 source collections; about 306,000 derived images, including roughly 290,000 bounding box images, 42,000 segmentations and 27,000 landmark images.
A specimen image can pass through bounding box, segmentation and landmark tasks; each output is a separate record in a separate batch, and file names cannot preserve relationships.
Each record has its own ARK; derived images also store a parent ARK and a batch ARK; source images have no parent, and harvested images reference harvest batches.

21 batch records describe AI pipeline runs by the Tulane and Virginia Tech teams; batch is a class with 14 terms (pipeline, institution, creator, project, date, supplement path, code repository, etc.).
The largest batch contains almost a quarter of a million outputs; shared metadata is stored once on the batch record.
Downloads include multimedia and batch CSVs with ARKs, citation information, term definitions and an RDF model (Fish-AIR vocabulary version 3).
Link integrity checks run after each ingest and before every export; an early audit's 29 unresolved batch links all came from test records.

moments.description: One specimen followed through three AI processing tasks.
Parent and batch ARK design.
Link integrity audit results.

title: Unifying Biodiversity Images: Content-Based Identification with the ISCC standard (ISO 24138:2024)
session: AI-Readiness Metrics and Metadata for Biodiversity Data
summary: Wouter Addink introduced the International Standard Content Code (ISCC, ISO 24138:2024) as a content-aware identifier for biodiversity media; nobody in the room had heard of it. He explained why DOIs (location-focused) and cryptographic hashes (break on any pixel, metadata or format change) fall short for images, and how ISCC combines meta, content, data and instance codes so that content codes survive watermarks or format conversion and Hamming distance measures similarity. A beta 'declaration event' binds an ISCC to a signed creator and timestamp using DIDs and an append-only log run on decentralised hubs, enabling content-based discovery, provenance, isolation of AI fakes and annotations resilient to derivatives.
takeaway: ISCC gives images a content-derived, similarity-comparable identifier that anyone can recompute, addressing duplication, broken links and AI-generated fakes.
whyItMatters: Biodiversity media are copied, converted and increasingly faked; a content-based identifier could keep annotations and provenance attached across copies and formats.
keyPoints: Challenges: AI-generated fakes undermining trust, uncoordinated copies, and metadata/provenance lost when files are renamed or converted.
PIDs like DOIs, RORs and ORCIDs work where identifying metadata is easy, but images need their content to distinguish them.
Standard hashes such as SHA-256 change completely with any pixel, metadata or format change.
ISCC works for images, video, audio and text; a full code concatenates meta, content, data and instance units (typically 64 bits each) with self-describing header (main type, subtype).
The instance code behaves like a hash; the data code changes with data changes; the content code stays the same under format conversion or watermarking.
Because ISCC codes carry semantics, Hamming distance between codes measures how different two items are, enabling similarity matching.
Declaration events (beta, not yet in the standard) bind an ISCC to a signature and timestamp as a FAIR Digital Object, using DIDs and an append-only log on self-hostable hubs rather than blockchain.
Codes can be generated locally from content; start with the Hugging Face playground, then the Python software and possibly a local registry node.

moments.description: Show of hands: nobody knew ISCC.
The four ISCC units and why the content code survives format changes.
Declaration events binding creator and timestamp.

title: Robot-ready by construction: an ontology-driven, SHACL-validated submission pipeline for national ecological monitoring data
session: AI-Readiness Metrics and Metadata for Biodiversity Data
summary: Andrew Tokmakoff described how TERN Ecosystem Surveillance moved from a decade-old Android app and Postgres database to EMSA (Ecological Monitoring System Australia), built for the federal government, where a single data model specification drives both the offline-capable field app (a PWA) and the exporter that pushes RDF to Australia's national Biodiversity Data Repository. Protocol steps and attributes are mapped to IRIs, an OpenAPI 3.0 specification generates UI elements (e.g. lookup-table references) and validates JSON on the way in, and the exporter maps flat JSON into the graph-based ABIS and TERN ontologies, resolving vocabularies live via SPARQL and validating output with SHACL shapes. Data therefore arrive 'robot-ready by construction' rather than by later remediation.
takeaway: Driving both field data capture and RDF export from one semantically annotated specification makes monitoring data standards-compliant and machine-ready from the start.
whyItMatters: It demonstrates a working alternative to retrofitting standards onto legacy data: specification-driven collection with validation at both boundaries, feeding a national biodiversity knowledge graph.
keyPoints: TERN is Australia's national terrestrial ecosystem research infrastructure (funded through NCRIS); Ecosystem Surveillance, based in Adelaide since 2011, runs a long-term standardised plot network, mainly in the rangelands.
Legacy system: AusScribe Android app, Postgres and CouchDB; new system: EMSA protocols and software, with a PWA field app and a Strapi headless CMS back end ('Core') on Postgres.
Two routes to standards-compliant data: collect first and map later, or, as with EMSA, start from protocol definitions that drive both collection and RDF creation.
Data are structured surveys, not just occurrences; protocol steps and procedures are mapped to IRIs, making data self-describing.

An OpenAPI 3.0 specification (close to JSON Schema) is a machine-readable contract: the app builds its UI from it (e.g. an x-lutRef veg growth form lookup) and the exporter reads the same key to map codes into the graph.

The exporter maps flat JSON to graph models (ABIS national profile, TERN ontologies, EMSA protocol-specific SHACL shapes), resolving EMSA vocabularies via SPARQL against GraphDB with caching, so it adapts as protocols evolve.
Quality gating at both boundaries: JSON Schema validation in the app and on submission; SHACL validation of RDF on export.
In the national Biodiversity Data Repository, shared IRIs let queries walk from TERN plot observations to other providers' records without complex mapping.

moments.description: System overview: one specification informs client and exporter.
Point-intercept example with a lookup-table reference used by both UI and exporter.
Quality gating at both boundaries with JSON Schema and SHACL.

title: Artificial Intelligence Amplifies Paleontology's Reproducibility Problem
session: AI-Readiness Metrics and Metadata for Biodiversity Data
summary: Brooke Long-Fox, a data curation scientist at MorphoBank and data editor for Historical Biology, argued that AI is entering a field that already has reproducibility problems of availability (data not deposited or on personal websites), documentation (no README, undefined characters) and traceability (unclear links from evidence to result). AI can turn ambiguous or incomplete sources into perfectly formatted, schema-valid tables that get DOIs and feed further AI, improving structure without improving scientific validity. Using morphological character matrices, she showed that a binary score can encode expert judgements about homology, preservation and ontogeny, and proposed adding verifiability to AI readiness: tracing assertions to evidence, recording whether they were transcribed, transformed or inferred, and who validated them.
takeaway: AI can make uncertain paleontological data look clean and authoritative, so AI-ready data must also be verifiable back to evidence and interpretation.
whyItMatters: It distinguishes technical validity from scientific validity, a warning relevant to any biodiversity data being mass-extracted or inferred by AI.
keyPoints: This is not an argument against AI; she uses AI-assisted curation, but AI can amplify existing reproducibility problems.
Paleontology is data-intensive; the digital extended specimen links a specimen to images, occurrences, stratigraphy, measurements, matrices and outputs, so errors propagate further.
Availability problems: data never deposited, manuscripts claiming no data exist, files on personal websites or cloud links, private or incomplete repository records.
Documentation problems: no README or data dictionary, unexplained abbreviations, 3D models without links to specimens, incomplete character definitions; a PID says where a file is, not what it means.
Traceability problems: data statements not matching deposits, scores not linked to sources, matrices modified across studies without documentation, unclear versions.
AI can produce schema-valid, DOI-bearing structured outputs from ambiguous sources (e.g. OCR column shifts, inconsistent translation), which then feed other AI systems.
Technical validity is not scientific validity: a matrix cell such as character 37 = 0/1 may encode reasoning about homology, absence vs non-preservation, ontogeny, polymorphism or inapplicability.
AI-ready data should be machine-readable, FAIR, documented and validated, and for interpretive data also verifiable.

moments.description: Three categories of existing reproducibility problems.
The failure mode: AI makes uncertainty look structured.
Morphological character matrix example.
Practical path toward verifiable robot-ready data.

title: AI Ready Standards with Croissant for Type Specimens Catalog Datasets
session: AI-Readiness Metrics and Metadata for Biodiversity Data
summary: Sefika Efeoglu presented a workflow for turning historical type specimen catalogues into AI-ready datasets: LLMs (e.g. GPT and Qwen) extract structured information from unstructured catalogue text, which is expressed in Darwin Core and then described with ML Commons Croissant metadata in JSON-LD. She showed how Darwin Core fields map to Croissant fields (scientific name as label, genus as taxonomic feature, individual count as integer, catalogue number as identifier, locality, event date, collector, type status) and how the pipeline evaluates FAIR metrics. The approach aims to bridge biodiversity standards and ML dataset platforms such as Hugging Face, Kaggle and OpenML.
takeaway: Combining LLM extraction, Darwin Core and Croissant metadata offers a route from historical specimen catalogues to FAIR, ML-ready datasets.
whyItMatters: Croissant is becoming the metadata layer ML platforms understand; mapping Darwin Core into it could make collection data directly discoverable and loadable in ML ecosystems.
keyPoints: Biodiversity data are used for species identification, named entity recognition, taxonomic knowledge extraction and knowledge graphs, but historical catalogues are largely unstructured text.
FAIRness supports ML reproducibility, clarity, sharing and more reliable model development; the aim is to extend FAIR into ML workflows.

Croissant (ML Commons) is a standardised, machine-readable metadata format for ML-ready datasets supported by platforms such as Hugging Face, Kaggle and OpenML: 'create once, publish anywhere, use everywhere'.
Workflow: type specimen catalogue, unstructured text, LLM-assisted extraction (GPT, Qwen), Darwin Core metadata, Croissant metadata, AI-ready dataset.

Mapping examples: scientificName as label for classification, genus as taxonomic feature, individualCount as integer feature, catalogNumber as unique identifier, locality, eventDate, collector (provenance) and typeStatus.
Records are represented in Croissant JSON-LD with explicit field data types; the pipeline measures FAIR metrics and metadata quality.

moments.description: Proposed workflow from catalogue text to AI-ready dataset.
Darwin Core to Croissant field mapping.

title: Not just another database: building the future of freshwater taxonomy with FADAtims
session: A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
summary: Astrid Schmidt-Kloiber opened with a caddisfly whose accepted name differs between the Trichoptera World Checklist, GBIF/Catalogue of Life and freshwaterecology.info, arguing freshwater biodiversity has a taxonomy problem rather than a database shortage. Geraldine Mertens recounted how the original Freshwater Animal Diversity Assessment produced species lists and a Hydrobiologia special issue but then stagnated, and how the InfraFADA project rebuilt an expert consortium (over 100 experts, 61 animal groups plus macrophytes) with exchanges from WoRMS and TaxonWorks. Astrid then demonstrated FADAtims, the operational curation system with role-based permissions, bulk upload, detail pages linked to GBIF and the IUCN Red List, and exports including DOI-versioned checklists via ChecklistBank, and raised sustainability of people, infrastructure and interoperability.
takeaway: FADAtims turns the dormant FADA checklists into a living, expert-curated and interoperable freshwater taxonomic infrastructure, but its future depends on sustaining experts and systems.
whyItMatters: Consistent freshwater taxonomy underpins occurrence integration, Red List assessment and ecological analysis; FADAtims is intended as the backbone for several freshwater portals.
keyPoints: Example: Lepidostoma basale is accepted in the Trichoptera World Checklist and freshwaterecology.info but treated as a synonym in GBIF and Catalogue of Life.
Freshwater biodiversity has 'not a database shortage, but rather a taxonomy problem'.

FADA started over 20 years ago; its expert lists and a Hydrobiologia special issue were produced, but maintenance stopped when funding ended due to technology limits and poor machine-to-machine exchange.

InfraFADA rebuilt the expert consortium: over 100 experts, 61 animal groups plus a macrophyte chapter; 43 Excel templates (24 received, 19 in progress), with 15 lists expected from WoRMS and 3 from TaxonWorks.

FADAtims supports role-based permissions (expert, expert leader, group member, public), bulk upload, search and filters, and detail pages with taxonomy, environmental information, references and links to GBIF occurrences and the IUCN Red List.
Experts curate names, synonyms, classification, authorships, FADA environmental regions and distribution; edits are tracked.
Exports include PDFs, CSV and versioned checklists that receive DOIs through ChecklistBank via ColDP packages; DOIs are the main incentive for experts.

FADAtims harvests from and links back to WoRMS and TaxonWorks, delivers to Catalogue of Life (and thus GBIF), and will serve as backbone for the FIP data portal and FBIS; a GBIF freshwater tag is still missing.
FADA More, a three-year follow-up, will maintain and enrich data (molecular data, cryptic diversity, parasites and hosts, ecological information).

moments.description: Caddisfly naming conflict across databases.
FADAtims interface walk-through.
Sustainability challenges for people, infrastructure and interoperability.

title: Catalogue of Life and Freshwater species data
session: A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
summary: Olaf Banki marked 25 years of the public Catalogue of Life (over 2.2 million accepted species) and described ChecklistBank, its API-first infrastructure with around 65,000 data sources, including about 1,000 national lists, 400 invasive species lists and 200 global lists. He admitted CoL cannot currently tell which species are freshwater: WoRMS provides freshwater/marine/brackish/terrestrial flags that CoL holds but cannot model or show, lists like freshwaterecology.info are not yet published there, AlgaeBase is not openly licensed, and FADA's 2013 lists are outdated. He pledged that within about a year CoL will ingest FADAtims data and add freshwater, brackish, water-dependent and aquatic designations to its systems and API, which would flow to GBIF.
takeaway: Catalogue of Life pledges to model and expose freshwater designations within a year, fed by FADAtims and WoRMS, finally allowing freshwater species and occurrences to be identified via GBIF.
whyItMatters: Because CoL is GBIF's taxonomic reference, adding habitat designations would solve a 15-year-old problem of analysing freshwater biodiversity from aggregated data.
keyPoints: 2026 is the 25th year of public CoL releases; activities began in 1996. The release has slightly more than 2.2 million accepted species.
CoL now publishes a base release and an extended release adding e.g. Plazi publications, UNITE species hypotheses and Barcode of Life.
ChecklistBank is an open repository for taxonomic, nomenclatural and policy lists, hosts CoL's assembly tooling and comparison tools; all functionality is in the API.
About 65,000 data sources in ChecklistBank, growing monthly mostly through publications from Plazi and Pensoft; roughly 1,000 national lists, 400 invasive species lists and 200 global lists.
CoL cannot yet filter freshwater species in its own product; freshwaterecology.info matches well except phytobenthos but is not published in ChecklistBank.
WoRMS flags marine/freshwater/brackish/terrestrial but CoL cannot model this in its front end; algae coverage is weak because AlgaeBase is not openly licensed.
Four FADA lists from the 2013 assessment remain in CoL and have not been updated; about 1,700 datasets mention freshwater in their title, mostly Plazi publications.

Pledge: connect to FADAtims (which already exports CoL data packages) and add freshwater, brackish, water-dependent and aquatic designations to CoL systems and API within about a year, flowing to GBIF.

moments.description: ChecklistBank data source statistics.
Admission that CoL cannot yet identify freshwater species.
Pledge to add freshwater designations within a year.

title: A species-level taxonomic catalog of Neotropical freshwater insects: building a consensus reference for occurrence data integration and conservation planning
session: A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
summary: Alejandra Correa-Bedoya presented a Darwin Core-compliant species-level checklist of seven orders of freshwater insects for the Neotropics (southern Mexico to Brazil), compiled over six months for her PhD. She showed that names documented for Colombia (about 1,250 species) often have no occurrence records there, due to taxonomic resolution bias and a data supply gap rather than platform failures, verified names against global infrastructures, and noted her list triples known Odonata species for Colombia compared with a national effort. Grounding it in the free-flowing Samaná Norte river, threatened by planned dams and invasive species, she argued that without species names there are no occurrences, no species distribution models and no evidence for protecting rivers.
takeaway: Without a reliable species-level checklist, Neotropical freshwater insect occurrences, distribution models and conservation arguments cannot be built.
whyItMatters: It links taxonomic infrastructure directly to conservation decisions under dam development pressure in one of the world's most biodiverse and data-deficient regions.
keyPoints: Global freshwater populations declined about 83% since 1970 (Living Planet), about 95% in Latin America and the Caribbean; Central and South America are data-deficient hotspots.
Dam expansion is concentrated on the Andean slopes, modifying flows before data exist to assess losses.
The checklist covers seven orders from southern Mexico to Brazil, excluding the southern cone as a distinct biogeographic region; Coleoptera and Diptera are richest.
It is a taxon-core list (names, synonyms, classification) of officially described species, the naming backbone needed before occurrence data can be resolved.
Colombia has the most documented species of these orders (about 1,250), reflecting its position among heterogeneous biogeographic subregions.
Example stonefly: GBIF shows records across its range but none in Colombia at the range centre, indicating nobody has named and looked for it there.

Verification against GBIF found flags such as recent nomenclatural changes (Coleoptera), typographic/algorithmic errors (Trichoptera) and a genus reassignment (Hemiptera); she frames this as a data supply gap, not a platform problem.
In the Samaná Norte basin, about 600 occurrence records of these orders resolve only to genus, which is not interpretable for conservation decisions.

moments.description: Scope and structure of the Neotropical checklist.
Stonefly with no Colombian records despite Colombia sitting at its range centre.
Samaná Norte, the last large free-flowing Andean river in Colombia, under dam pressure.

title: Biodiversity data at your fingertips: open-access freshwater biodiversity information systems for South Africa and Africa
session: A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
summary: Helen Dallas presented FBIS, the Freshwater Biodiversity Information System for South Africa, and its continental scale-up FBIS-Africa. Developed since 2017 through user-centred design for water resource and conservation managers, researchers, consultants and policymakers, FBIS holds over 14 million occurrence records across eight biodiversity modules and has 1,648 registered users. It uses the GBIF taxonomic backbone (with planned FADA integration), links to the IUCN Red List, offers spatial and temporal filters, spatial layers and standardised dashboards, and attaches citation metadata to every record. Separating the engine from the data enabled redeployment for other platforms via a multi-tenant model that improves sustainability.
takeaway: Co-designed, open and interoperable freshwater information systems like FBIS turn fragmented records into decision-ready information, and multi-tenancy helps keep them sustainable.
whyItMatters: It offers a proven, reusable platform model for regional biodiversity data systems in resource-constrained settings.
keyPoints: Freshwater data are fragmented, inaccessible and poorly integrated, and thus underused in decision-making.
FBIS development began in 2017 with a user-centred approach, designing backwards from end users' needs.

FBIS holds over 14 million occurrence records, eight modules (fish, annelids, invertebrates, wetland and riparian plants, algae, wetland birds, water-dependent mammals and reptiles) and 1,648 registered users.
Taxonomy uses the GBIF backbone; integration with FADA is planned; links to IUCN conservation status.

Tools include spatial and temporal filters, spatial layers (catchments, ecoregions, protected areas), standardised dashboards, and downloadable graphs and data; every record carries citation metadata.
Separating the engine from the data allowed redeployment for other, including non-freshwater, platforms and scale-up to FBIS-Africa.
Multi-tenant model: independent governance and branding per tenant, shared costs, shared improvements and increased resilience.
Five design principles: stakeholder co-design, interoperability (GBIF, IUCN), open access, sustained support and partnerships, and multi-tenancy.

moments.description: User-centred design origins of FBIS.
Separating engine from data enabled redeployment and FBIS-Africa.
Five design principles.

title: The FIPbio data portal: towards an integrated freshwater biodiversity data ecosystem
session: A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
summary: Vanessa Bremerich presented the renewed Freshwater Biodiversity Data Portal (FIPbio) of the Freshwater Information Platform, rebuilt on the BIMS engine behind FBIS with funding linked to IGB's investigation of the Oder fish-kill disaster and relying on the InfraFADA taxonomic backbone. The portal will show GBIF freshwater occurrences, Red List status and data gaps per FADA group, implement the GBIF freshwater data publishing guide (including broader 'meta groups'), and link sampling sites to habitat, method, life stage, abiotic sensor and water quality data and remote-sensing time series. Sites are automatically annotated from reference layers and catchment tools (e.g. hydrographr, GeoFRESH, AquaINFRA), with rule-based quality flagging using FADA biogeographic realms.
takeaway: FIPbio aims to make freshwater data publishing and analysis easier by combining FADA taxonomy, GBIF occurrences, site context, abiotic and remote-sensing data, and automated catchment annotation.
whyItMatters: Freshwater analyses depend on catchment connectivity and sampling context that generic portals ignore; FIPbio tries to encode those freshwater specifics while staying interoperable with GBIF.
keyPoints: History: BioFresh (2009-2014) led to the Freshwater Information Platform and a first data portal that became hard to maintain.
InfraFADA's renewed taxonomic backbone is central; funds from IGB's Oder fish-kill investigation programme were used to renew the portal with the Freshwater Research Centre and Kartoza.
Built on BIMS (the FBIS engine); serves FIP partners, FADA and Freshwater BON (GEO BON) data mobilisation, e.g. freshwater EBVs.
It will show all GBIF freshwater occurrences, IUCN Red List status, and data gaps per FADA organism group.
What it is not: not (yet) an OBIS for freshwaters, which lacks a funded global community; not for national/regional assessments; not yet fully in production.

Implements the GBIF freshwater data publishing guide, e.g. 'meta groups' such as macrophytes, macroinvertebrates, fish; freshwater fungi, benthic algae and phytoplankton are not covered by FADA and need other checklists.
Sites carry habitat, ecosystem type, sampling method, life stage and timing, plus abiotic sensor data, water quality and remote sensing (chlorophyll-a, water colour, land use).

Automatic annotation from reference layers (habitat types, lake IDs, Ramsar sites) and catchment tools: snap to river network, delineate upstream catchment; rule-based quality flagging using FADA biogeographic realms with feedback to experts.

moments.description: What FIPbio is not: not an OBIS for freshwaters.
Data entry flow from sampling site to abiotic and remote-sensing data.
Snapping a site to the river network and delineating the upstream catchment.

title: Freshwater data platforms: acronym soup, abundance, classifications and data quality
session: A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
summary: After announcements, Anne Lyche Solheim asked how the many freshwater platforms and acronyms could be integrated and noted that most seem to handle presence/absence rather than abundance. Olaf Banki acknowledged the community's 'acronym soup' and argued for distinct niches connected machine-to-machine, noting sample-based abundance data exist in GBIF; Vanessa Bremerich positioned GBIF as the unifier fed by high-quality published data and mentioned a possible GBIF-hosted freshwater portal. Yuri Roskov suggested using AI search with credible sources to navigate resources and urged freshwater checklists to adopt WoRMS and other aggregators' classifications; the moderator noted WoRMS preserved FADA lists but does not want insect data. Bernhard Askedalen raised the quality of consultancy survey data, prompting ideas of quality control, community flagging and a traffic-light tag for how reliably a species can be identified.
takeaway: The freshwater community prefers connected, specialised platforms feeding GBIF over one system, but must address abundance data, classification consistency and trust in data from diverse providers.
whyItMatters: It surfaces the user perspective (ecologists confused by many platforms) and concrete ideas such as identifiability tags for handling heterogeneous data quality.
keyPoints: Ecologists struggle with a 'myriad' of biodiversity platforms and acronyms.
Most platforms seem presence/absence based, yet abundance and dominance matter for environmental management.
Response: platforms have different purposes and niches but should speak the same language machine-to-machine, human-to-machine and human-to-human.
GBIF can hold sample-based data with abundances; FBIS supports abundance entry and data should be pushed to GBIF.
GBIF is seen as the unifying endpoint; a GBIF-hosted freshwater portal is under discussion once FADA lists are available.

Yuri Roskov: use AI search with a prompt for credible sources to navigate resources; freshwater checklists for groups covered by WoRMS or other aggregators should use their classifications to avoid conflicting classifications.
WoRMS picked up FADA checklists when FADA went into hibernation, but is not interested in harvesting FADA insect data, about 60% of FADA diversity.

Environmental consultancy surveys vary in quality; responses included data quality control mechanisms, community flagging of suspicious providers, and a traffic-light tag for how reliably a species can be identified (expert vs layperson).

moments.description: Anne Lyche Solheim on too many platforms and missing abundance data.
Olaf Banki on 'acronym soup' and connecting niches.
Yuri Roskov on AI search and consistent classifications.
Bernhard Askedalen on consultancy data quality.
Traffic-light identifiability tagging idea.

title: A collaborative perspective on a globally standardised river basin name database
session: A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
summary: Daniel Mietchen argued that river basins are the natural spatial unit for freshwater biology but lack a global, multilingual naming system: geoscience grids and the Pfafstetter coding system ignore biology, naming, karst, flow changes and complex branching. Using Oslo's Akerselva as an example, he showed how Wikidata links the river, its drainage basin (Nordmarksvassdraget) and Norwegian REGINE and ELVIS identifiers, but that Wikidata's drainage basin statements are almost all Norwegian. He listed edge cases (seasonal and split rivers, karst, flow reversal, dams, historic courses and names, oral languages) and asked how TDWG groups, Wikidata and OpenStreetMap could collaborate, proposing an unconference session.
takeaway: Freshwater biodiversity data need a global, multilingual, collaboratively maintained river basin naming system, and TDWG, Wikidata and OpenStreetMap could build it together.
whyItMatters: Being able to state in a standard way which river basin an occurrence belongs to would support freshwater invasions, connectivity and conservation analyses that grids cannot capture.
keyPoints: Geosciences put everything on grids set by measurement methods; biology rarely follows grids, so translation mechanisms are needed.
The Pfafstetter coding system is widely used in geodatabases but knows nothing about biology or names, and ignores karst, water level changes and complex branching.
The talk asks questions rather than giving answers: how can TDWG help express, e.g. in Darwin Core, that a fish record belongs to one basin and not another?
Akerselva example: basin delineation from AquaINFRA-style segment data, and Wikidata items linking river, source, mouth and drainage basin (Nordmarksvassdraget).
Norwegian identifiers exist (REGINE for basins, ELVIS for rivers); Wikidata has 431 items with drainage basin/REGINE statements and 1,066 with ELVIS IDs, almost all Norwegian.
Transboundary rivers carry names in several languages (e.g. Norway, Finland, Russia), raising the question of which to use.

Edge cases: seasonally dry or drought-split rivers, hunger stones, karst, seasonal flooding, flow reversal, groundwater, atmospheric rivers, paleohydrology, dams, historic courses and names, oral-only languages.
Candidate collaborators: relevant TDWG interest, task and maintenance groups; Wikidata; OpenStreetMap.

moments.description: Pfafstetter coding system and its limitations.
Akerselva in Wikidata with drainage basin and Norwegian identifiers.
Catalogue of edge cases.
WISE river basin districts in Europe.

title: From 'Lost in Translation' to Fit-for-Purpose Data: Why Ecologists and Conservation Practice Still Need Groupings and Uncertainties
session: A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
summary: Bernhard Askedalen and colleague Natalie performed a sketch in which a botanist tries to record uncertain water plant identifications (cf., agg., col., sensu lato) and a database cannot store them, so records are either overstated or bumped to genus, losing ecological information. They showed herbarium sheets with multiple conflicting determinations and noted that for some groups initial names can be as low as 6% correct on expert revision. Natalie found cf. in only 0.1% of water plant and 1.1% of benthic algae observations in NIVA datasets, because reporting pipelines drop uncertainty. They asked how systems should represent uncertainty and taxonomic groupings consistently; the audience suggested keeping these qualifiers with the data, flexibility across organism groups, an identification-uncertainty term, and a BIMS-style identification certainty column with include/exclude decisions.
takeaway: Biodiversity data systems must be able to record identification uncertainty and taxonomic groupings, or ecologists face a choice between false certainty and lost ecological information.
whyItMatters: Monitoring data used for ecological status assessments routinely contain cf., aggregates and sensu lato concepts; standards that erase them degrade both data honesty and usability.
keyPoints: Sketch: 'cf.' for a sterile Sparganium angustifolium cannot be recorded, so it is entered as certain; Utricularia vulgaris without flowers is bumped to genus by a red-list data check; 'agg.', 'col.' and 'sensu lato' are not supported.
Genus-level records lose information useful for within-lake trends and ecological condition assessment based on species assemblages (e.g. eutrophication tolerance).
Paying customers provide little incentive to make records verifiable.

Herbarium sheets can carry three to six different names from different people; for some groups the first name given can be as low as 6% correct, with 94% separated as another species on expert revision.
In selected NIVA datasets from the 1960s to last year, cf. appeared in only 0.1% of water plant and 1.1% of benthic algae observations.
Information exists internally but is lost or transformed when reporting to national systems: uncertain identifications reported as certain, reduced to genus, or aggregates handled via pseudo-taxa.
Question posed: how should biodiversity systems represent uncertainty and taxonomic grouping consistently without losing ecological meaning?

moments.description: Sketch: botanist and database developer argue over recording 'cf.'
Herbarium sheets with multiple conflicting determinations.
Frequency of cf. in NIVA datasets.
Question to the audience on representing uncertainty.

title: How does human impact change species diversity and composition in 50 types of inland water habitats?
session: A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
summary: Anne Lyche Solheim presented work for the European Environment Agency (European Topic Centre on Biodiversity and Ecosystems) revising EUNIS inland water habitat types to align with Water Framework Directive and Habitats Directive types: over 20 standing and over 20 running water types, described mainly by altitude, calcium/alkalinity, humic content and size. Using REBECCA and WISER project data (2004-2011) with expert-harmonised taxonomy, the team compared natural and impacted water bodies by NMDS and clustering and identified characteristic, common and dominant taxa. Natural waters showed distinct, textbook communities, while human impact made habitat types more similar, with fewer characteristic species (e.g. loss of chrysophytes and isoetids, more cyprinids and fewer salmonids).
takeaway: Human pressures erase the natural distinctness of freshwater habitat types, making their biological communities converge on degraded states with fewer characteristic species.
whyItMatters: The revised EUNIS types and their biological descriptions underpin European habitat reporting and show biotic homogenisation as a measurable outcome of pressure, relevant to stalled Water Framework Directive progress.
keyPoints: EUNIS is the EEA's European Nature Information System for habitat classification; its freshwater part mixed very broad and very narrow types and needed revision.
Revised types: over 20 standing and over 20 running water habitat types based on WFD broad types, plus rarer Habitats Directive types.
Key type descriptors for biology are much the same for lakes and rivers: altitude, calcium (alkalinity), humic content and size.

Data came from EU projects REBECCA and WISER (2004-2011) covering thousands of lakes and rivers with physicochemical data; taxonomy was harmonised in expert workshops and checked against AlgaeBase and freshwaterecology.info.
Methods: split natural vs impacted water bodies, assess compositional similarity with NMDS and clustering, identify characteristic, common and dominant taxa per habitat.

Natural lakes: richness increases with size and decreases with altitude; e.g. mixotrophic chrysophytes in siliceous, high-altitude and humic lakes; isoetids in siliceous lakes; salmonids in siliceous, high-altitude lakes.

Impacted lakes: types become more similar, fewer characteristic taxa, fewer chrysophytes, fewer isoetids, no characteristic fish species, more cyprinids and fewer salmonids; species richness differences were unclear.
Rivers face multiple pressures; impacts increase similarity between types and reduce characteristic vegetation and invertebrate taxa, with more dominant fish species.
WFD ecological status has stalled at about 60% less than good and 40% good or better since the first river basin management plans in 2009.

moments.description: Revised standing and running water habitat types and their descriptors.
Methods for comparing natural and impacted water bodies.
Human impact homogenises communities across lake types.
WFD status standstill map.

title: SpecifyaaS: Managing Ephemeral Repositories in Collections-Based Research
session: Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
summary: Kevin Holston explained how the Swedish Museum of Natural History runs its own local Specify 7 instances ('Specify as a Service') as ephemeral or semi-persistent repositories for researchers, rather than pushing them straight into the institutional collection database. He distinguished research-group collections of loaned, persistent vouchers from institutional programmes such as biobanks and the environmental specimen bank, whose semi-persistent vouchers are used up over time. As an example, he showed how a researcher's 16 years of Madagascar aquatic insect inventory became a Specify research database with 808 collecting events, organised event images and field sheets. He argued that these instances bring standards in early and act as laboratories of innovation for Specify.
takeaway: Giving researchers their own lightweight Specify instances early in the research process standardises data from the start and eases later exchange with the institutional collection.
whyItMatters: Much specimen data is created in project spreadsheets before it ever reaches a collection database. Giving researchers compatible, low-commitment instances is a practical way to get standards and identifiers in early and to track derivatives and loaned material as their own objects.
keyPoints: NRM runs local Specify installations on its own infrastructure and spins up temporary instances, for example for visiting researchers, that are compatible with the institutional database.
Category 1 (research group/project): material is mostly on loan, vouchers are persistent, and the project repository has little motivation to record where things physically are.

Category 2 (research institution/programme, e.g. biobank, eDNA and environmental specimen bank): vouchers are semi-persistent and subject to depletion, and the repository must reflect the physical collection.
Historically, derivatives have been documented as voucher attributes rather than as independent objects, which limits tracking of objects, attributes and locations over time.

A researcher's Madagascar aquatic insect inventory became a Specify research database with 808 collecting events over 16 years of trips. An unexpected benefit was standardisation and the organisation of event images and field data sheets.
Holston repurposed the Specify storage tree to record provenance, i.e. loans, in his own research database, showing Specify's flexibility.
Instances can be 'furnished' (pre-loaded with collection data, like a furnished house or hotel) to give visitors a head start in digitising.

moments.description: Defines two categories of ephemeral collections: research groups vs research institutions.
Madagascar inventory: 16 years of trips, 808 collecting events, images and field sheets.
House vs hotel analogy for furnished vs unfurnished Specify instances for visiting researchers.
Final assertions: early standards, researcher relationships, instances as laboratories of innovation.

title: Applying Data Standards at the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh
session: Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
summary: Robyn Drinkwater described how RBGE, a herbarium of about three million specimens with databasing since the mid-1970s, uses identifiers in Specify to standardise and link its data. She covered merging duplicate agents (up to four or five versions of a person from the legacy system) with Specify's agent merge tool and storing agent identifiers. She also covered IPNI, MycoBank and World Flora Online taxon identifiers, CETAF stable specimen URIs used since 2012, and forthcoming DiSSCo DOIs. The second half showed how identifiers link the herbarium with RBGE's three other collection systems (IrisBG, Koha, AtoM), with examples of watercolours linked to moss specimens and living plants linked to herbarium vouchers.
takeaway: Identifiers are how RBGE is standardising legacy herbarium data and reconnecting items spread across four separate collection management systems.
whyItMatters: The talk shows why identifiers need to be structured and resolvable, not just stored. It also shows the practical steps (agent disambiguation, field restructuring, cross-system links) that an institution needs to publish linked, citable data.
keyPoints: RBGE has about three million specimens covering all traditionally 'plant' groups including diatoms, algae and oomycetes; about 1.5 million database records have passed through at least four database systems.
The legacy system had no unified agents table, which left four or five versions of some people. The Specify agent merging tool is helping to disambiguate them.
Specify's dedicated agent identifier field allows several identifiers per agent. Link-outs to ORCID and Wikidata are planned to help staff.

Taxon identifiers: IPNI IDs for vascular plants and MycoBank IDs for fungi, with World Flora Online IDs being tested. Both have been stored in the LSID field, and that mixed content prevents link-outs, so restructuring is needed.
CETAF stable identifiers have been used since 2012. They make specimens citable, and staff can link from the barcode field to images in the herbarium catalogue without importing images into Specify.

RBGE runs four systems: Specify (herbarium), IrisBG (living collection), Koha (library and artworks) and AtoM (archives). Identifiers are used to link, e.g., Greville moss watercolours in Koha to specimens, and living accessions to herbarium vouchers.
Next steps: GenBank/BOLD identifiers for DNA extractions, links to sequencing data, getting identifiers into the Darwin Core export, and a possible Scottish data lake.

moments.description: Legacy data had four or five versions of some people; agent merging in Specify.
CETAF stable specimen identifiers in use since 2012 and their benefits.
Four collection management systems at RBGE and why items must be linked across them.
Greville watercolours and moss specimens linked through identifiers in Koha and Specify.

title: From Legacy Data to FAIR Workflows: Standardising Biodiversity Collections Using Specify
session: Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
summary: Siyabonga Zamisa described how the KwaZulu-Natal Museum moved its 11 natural history collections (over 430,000 records) from Access, Excel, catalogue cards and other systems into Specify by 2019. With support from the Natural Science Collections Facility, it then developed shared workflows. He walked through a Darwin Core-based template spreadsheet used by all collections, quality checks in OpenRefine before WorkBench upload, routine specimen-versus-database QA, and a publishing pipeline through the IPT to GBIF. Before this the museum had no collections in GBIF; seven of eleven are now published.
takeaway: Standardised workflows, not just a new database, turned 11 differently managed collections into GBIF-ready data.
whyItMatters: This is a concrete African museum example of procedure and standards, not technology alone, driving data mobilisation, with measurable gains in publishing, cataloguing speed and loan processing.
keyPoints: 11 collections with over 430,000 records, the largest being Mollusca and Insecta. Previous systems included Access, Excel and Rapid, and all collections have been in Specify since 2019.
The problem was inconsistent practice: each collection had its own habits for capturing, tracking and sharing data, which slowed loans and data sharing.
A single template spreadsheet based on Darwin Core terms, with field explanations, is used across all 11 collections to ease WorkBench mapping.
Workflow: capture in template → data technician QC in OpenRefine → Specify WorkBench mapping and validation → upload.
Daily QA: randomly selected specimens are checked against their Specify records and both are corrected.
Publishing: Specify query export → OpenRefine QC → removal of sensitive species → IPT metadata and Darwin Core mapping → GBIF.
Results: from no collections in GBIF to seven of eleven, faster cataloguing and much shorter loan processing.

moments.description: Shared Darwin Core template spreadsheet and import workflow.
Publishing workflow from Specify query to GBIF via OpenRefine and IPT.
From zero to seven of eleven collections in GBIF.

title: Digitize, Standardize, Mobilize: Wildlife Biodiversity Biobanking with Specify
session: Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
summary: Kim Labuschagne presented the SANBI Wildlife Biobank, which holds samples and e-vouchers rather than whole specimens. It has over 250,000 samples from more than 110,000 animals in 46 countries, covering about 1,900 species including many threatened ones. She explained why an extended-specimen data model is needed to link samples, derivatives, permits, storage history, molecular data and publications, and how implementing Specify around 2013 replaced disconnected spreadsheets and records. Key features are the taxon, storage (bank→freezer→rack→box→position) and geography trees, attachments for permits and chain-of-custody photos, and customisable workflows.
takeaway: Specify's hierarchical trees and attachments turned a fragmented wildlife biobank into a traceable extended-specimen data system.
whyItMatters: Biobanks are growing conservation and genomics infrastructure, and their value depends on tracing every aliquot, permit and derived dataset back to the individual animal.
keyPoints: The biobank was established in 1994 and holds over 250,000 samples from more than 110,000 individual animals from 46 countries, spanning 14 phyla and nearly 1,900 species.
Many holdings are threatened on the IUCN Red List, including the extinct western black rhino.
79 different sample types are stored from room temperature down to -196 °C. Every freezer-to-freezer move is a QC point that must be recorded.

The data model has moved from 'tissue sample + catalogue number' to an extended specimen with voucher, field metadata, permits, storage history, DNA extraction, genome sequence, disease screening and publications.
Specify was implemented around 2013, with support from SAIAB, to replace disconnected systems.
The storage tree locates samples down to position in a box. Catalogue numbers plus barcodes prevent searching through hundreds of boxes.
Attachments hold permits (including CITES and disease regulations), data sheets and chain-of-custody photographs.

moments.description: Biobanks keep samples of the elephant, not the whole elephant, plus e-vouchers.
Traditional vs extended specimen data models in biobanking.
Storage tree from bank to freezer to box position.

title: Integrating Specify in broader Science infrastructure
session: Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
summary: Niels Klazenga described how RBG Victoria, a Specify user for over 16 years, embeds Specify as a 'collections hub' among other hubs: a Canto digital asset management system, VicFlora, a documentation hub, a traits hub of Lucid keys, KeyBase, and the Australasian Virtual Herbarium within the Atlas of Living Australia, which is its only dissemination channel. A separate 'bystander' application and a GraphQL API provide what Specify lacks or does differently, such as ZPL label printing, duplicate labels, partial loan returns, an event system and taxonomy syncing. He noted that moving from ABCD to Darwin Core felt like a step back and that a more structured model will help. He also called for Specify to support linking identifications to taxon concepts.
takeaway: Specify works best at RBG Victoria as one component of a wider hub-based science infrastructure, with custom tools filling its gaps.
whyItMatters: Real-world integration patterns, such as a taxon tree as backbone for other systems, a GraphQL API feeding a IIIF image portal, and IPT-to-ALA-to-GBIF delivery, show how a CMS fits into institutional infrastructure and where CMS vendors could improve.
keyPoints: RBG Victoria started with Specify 6.0.1 and chose Specify mainly to deliver high-quality data to AVH.

Hubs: Specify (collections), Canto (media/DAMS), VicFlora (flora of Victoria and horticultural flora of south-eastern Australia), a documentation hub, a traits hub (Lucid keys) and KeyBase (pathway keys).
Specify is not used for dissemination; all data go through AVH/ALA via the IPT, and ALA passes them on to GBIF as Australia's GBIF node.

A bystander app handles things Specify cannot, e.g. starting label printing mid-sheet on sheets of 30, ZPL labels for new printers (PDF quality too low), duplicate labels, partial loan returns and an event system.
The Specify taxon tree is the taxonomic backbone for other applications such as the image portal and living collections database, synced via a GraphQL API that predates Specify's own API.
A IIIF-compliant image portal is under development; Specify data populates the IIIF Presentation API.
Seed bank germination tests and orchid conservation data do not fit Specify and will get separate databases.
Taxon concepts: many are recorded as taxon citations, but identifications need to link to taxon concepts.

moments.description: Overview of the hub-based science infrastructure around Specify.
The bystander app and why some functions live outside Specify.
Call for linking identifications to taxon concepts in Specify.

title: The Good, the Bad, and the Standardised: A Specify Journey Through 200 Years of the MfN Berlin's Biological Collections
session: Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
summary: Marion Depraetere traced how the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin's history shaped its data: colonial expeditions such as Tendaguru, the 1945 bombing, Soviet confiscation and return, Cold War isolation, pandemic-era reliance on personal Excel files, and an October 2023 cyberattack that ended debate and made Specify the sole CMS. All 30 collections are now in one Specify instance, which enables cross-collection reporting. Specify's flexibility supports decolonisation work through a one-to-many historical-events table and a prototype 'Historical Context' collection linking archive letters to specimens. She highlighted the gap between political geography (ISO 3166) and ecological or marine units, and argued that standardisation should respond to a need rather than be imposed.
takeaway: Specify's flexibility lets MfN consolidate 30 historically complex collections into one database while starting to reconstruct colonial and wartime history, but geography and historical events remain unsolved.
whyItMatters: Many large museums face the same combination of legacy heterogeneity, colonial provenance and diverse audiences. The talk shows practical data-model workarounds and the open problem of representing administrative and ecological geography together.
keyPoints: MfN holds about 30 million items across 30 collections and sub-collections, managed by about 60 staff and support people.
History affects the data: colonial expeditions, the 1945 bombing (75% of the collection saved, losses still unclear), Soviet confiscation and repatriation, and Cold War isolation.
Specify was first adopted in 2010 (mammals first). The pandemic reinforced personal tools. The October 2023 cyberattack halted MfN for nearly a year and confirmed Specify as the sole CMS.

All 30 collections sit in a single Specify instance, allowing standardisation while keeping collection-specific features and giving single-query reports (e.g. entries per year, percentage of objects with IDs).
For decolonisation, a repurposed one-to-many table links objects to historical events, and a prototype 'Historical Context' collection links a 1909 letter from Tanga to the objects it mentions.

Political boundaries (ISO 3166) aid interoperability but do not match ecological, biogeographic or marine units. Options are extra locality fields (complex, error-prone) or a second geography tree based on GeoNames or Marine Regions, not yet tested.
Standardisation 'must remain a response to a need rather than a solution to a problem'.

moments.description: The 2023 cyberattack paradoxically settled the decision to adopt Specify.
Using Specify's flexibility for decolonisation: historical events and archive links.
Geography gap between political boundaries and ecological/marine units.

title: Meeting Biodiversity Standards with Specify 7
session: Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
summary: Grant Fitzsimmons presented Specify Collections Consortium work that lets collections keep local flexibility while sharing data in standard form. He described exportable schema-configuration packages, an updated, detached web portal (largely contributed by the Florida Museum), and a new Darwin Core mapping tool built on the Specify Query Builder. The tool supports Occurrence, Event and Taxon cores, every GBIF-registered extension, and custom terms by IRI. It shows term definitions in the app, auto-suggests mappings, starts from existing queries or templates, and enforces GBIF's minimum required terms. Release is expected by the first quarter of next year, and the SCC is joining multi-CMS work on the Darwin Core Data Package.
takeaway: Specify's new built-in Darwin Core mapping tool aims to make publishing from highly customised databases straightforward without giving up local flexibility.
whyItMatters: Mapping local CMS schemas to Darwin Core is a persistent bottleneck for publishing. A mapping tool in the CMS that knows GBIF extensions and requirements could lower the barrier for hundreds of institutions.
keyPoints: The SCC is a non-profit funded only by its member institutions and offers hosting, asset management and workshops.
Customisations (schema configurations) can be exported as packages and shared between institutions, databases or disciplines.

The updated web portal is a detached copy of Specify data that can hide sensitive localities and Red List species. It is free to SCC members and largely contributed by the Florida Museum of Natural History.
The new mapping tool uses the Query Builder interface to map fields to Darwin Core terms, grouped by class, with in-app term definitions, IRIs and examples.
It supports Occurrence, Event and Taxon cores, all GBIF-registered extensions (e.g. identification history, GGBN, Audiovisual Core), unregistered extensions and custom terms by IRI.
Adding a field auto-suggests a mapping. Adding an extension (e.g. Audiovisual Core) maps its standard terms automatically, and the tool flags missing GBIF-required terms.
Release is expected by Q1 of next year. The SCC is also in the multi-CMS Darwin Core Data Package grant project and a planned Leiden hackathon, and all work will be public on GitHub.

moments.description: Framing: how to keep local flexibility while making data consumable downstream.
Introduction of the Specify-to-Darwin Core mapping tool.
Automatic suggested term mapping when fields or extensions are added.

title: From Data Entry to Distribution: Streamlining Biodiversity Workflows with Specify at CSIRO
session: Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
summary: Dan Baker described how CSIRO's National Research Collections Australia migrated five of six collections into separate Specify instances between mid-2021 and end-2025. The collections now hold over two million specimens and more than 150 users. The data management team maintains standards at three levels: field definitions and controlled picklists, collection-specific formatting through a fully used agent table with aggregated views, and holistic minimum-dataset checks in WorkBench templates. They are supported by Excel templates with conditional formatting, a VBA script for collector names, batch edit and Power Query checks. He also covered training, support channels, standard roles, and uptake figures, and ended with a Specify wishlist.
takeaway: Layered standards in templates, roles and training let CSIRO keep five Specify instances consistent while each collection keeps its own outputs.
whyItMatters: Large multi-collection institutions need repeatable ways to enforce standards across many users. This talk gives a detailed practical toolkit and concrete feature requests for CMS developers.
keyPoints: Five of six NRCA collections were migrated to Specify between mid-2021 and end-2025, each taking 12–18 months with staggered go-lives. Subject experts were seconded for at least 50% of their time.
