dlib was chosen for being fast, lightweight, CPU-efficient and extendable from face-landmark models; it uses regression to predict landmark positions.
Pipeline: detect the fish in the museum image, crop, predict landmarks.
Accuracy by Euclidean distance: 95% at 0.02 threshold, 85.3% at 0.01.
Outline landmarks were more accurate than inner-body ones; the eye was very accurate, perhaps because of its distinctive shape.
Per-species accuracy ranged from ~100% (N. chalybaeus) to 65.97% (N. buchanani), about 34% variation.
Low-accuracy cases were curved, folded, dorsal-view or differently photographed specimens.

moments.description: Headline accuracy results.
Examples of high- and low-accuracy landmarking.

title: Contained Agentic Workflow for Literature Analysis and Data Extraction in Museum Collections
session: Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. AI applications, integration, and validation
summary: Steen Dupont demonstrated Kvasir, a prototype built mostly by coding agents (Codex) that runs fully on local hardware. It ingests a personal literature corpus with Docling, stores it in Neo4j and Qdrant, and lets an OpenClaw agent with a local Qwen model answer questions and explore papers. The demo ingested papers into 696 chunks and showed papers broken into sections with their references plotted over time, to characterise papers and trace evidence across the corpus. He argued for local AI for security, noted that optimised local models are improving, and suggested shared edge machines (e.g. a Dell GB10 serving 10-20 users) as institutional infrastructure, with the agent as a pluggable orchestration layer.
takeaway: Contained, local agentic RAG over a literature corpus is feasible on a laptop or shared edge machine, avoiding the security worries of cloud agents in museums.
whyItMatters: Museums worry about releasing agents on institutional data. This prototype shows a low-cost, offline route to experimenting with LLM literature analysis.
keyPoints: The project explores AI on local hardware rather than cloud LLMs; museum IT set up a closed network, but the demo runs offline on a laptop.
Motivation: better visibility of a PhD literature corpus: most-cited works, citation timing, references per section, without reading every paper.
Architecture: OpenClaw agent orchestrator, Qwen 3.6 main model, Docling parsing, Codex-written Python scripts, Neo4j graph and Qdrant vector store, Kokoro for audio.
Demo: two papers ingested, 696 chunks created, a paper view with sections, references per section and their publication years.
Idea: the distribution of references (introduction-heavy vs conclusion-heavy) characterises paper type.
Why local AI: security, improving local models, and pre-processing so the LLM only does the important step.
A GB10-class edge machine could serve 10-20 users on ordinary laptops instead of expensive individual machines.
The agent acts as an orchestration layer, so new Docker-hosted models (e.g. vision) can be plugged in without rebuilding.

moments.description: Architecture of the local agentic stack.
Live demo of Kvasir's paper and reference exploration.
Arguments for local AI and edge infrastructure.

title: Curation through citation: using AI and a knowledge graph to curate DNA barcodes
session: Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. AI applications, integration, and validation
summary: Roderic Page asked what concrete value knowledge graphs deliver, and proposed curation of DNA barcode data as an answer. Using his BOLD View site, he showed BOLD records with bad or missing coordinates, vague or informal names, and names hidden behind GenBank links. Some can be fixed by following links from the barcode to GenBank, the publishing paper's DOI and a holotype, which is more than internal-consistency data cleaning. The barriers are extracting specimen and sequence codes from literature (which Plazi does not do well) and linking barcodes to papers. He pointed to emerging large triple stores (Wikidata, OpenStreetMap, GBIF, BHL, Bionomia; 86 billion triples) as signs that such a graph is becoming real.
takeaway: Linking barcodes, specimens and literature in a knowledge graph could fix many BOLD records, if we can reliably extract the connecting codes from papers.
whyItMatters: Barcode data train widely used identification models while many records lack species names or correct coordinates. Citation-based curation would improve data that downstream AI relies on.
keyPoints: Knowledge graphs need to show 'concrete information you do not already possess' (the Silicon Valley quote).
CurateGPT suggested combining knowledge graphs and chatbots for curation.
BOLD holds ~25 million barcodes; a well-known 5-million-barcode training set is mostly identified only to order or family.
BOLD View is his site for exploring barcode data and noting odd records.

Examples: a Tasmanian-endemic crustacean plotted at Australia's centroid; a record labelled only 'Caudata' that GenBank calls a snake from China; an informal name resolved via GenBank -> DOI -> paper -> holotype.
Data cleaning flags inconsistencies; fixing needs external evidence such as the literature.
Plazi extracts coordinates well but not specimen and sequence codes; a simple ChatGPT prompt gets most of them.
He published a dataset linking ~1,500 barcode datasets to literature; GenBank links to papers are often missing.

moments.description: Framing: what concrete value do knowledge graphs give?
Resolving an informal barcode name via GenBank, DOI and holotype.
Question on getting external corrections back into infrastructures.

title: Integrating Many Data Sources in iChatBio Enables Emergent Scientific Use Cases
session: Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. AI applications, integration, and validation
summary: Michael Elliott presented iChatBio, a public multi-agent AI system for biodiversity data. A chat agent delegates sub-tasks to specialised agents for GBIF, iDigBio, iNaturalist, ALA, OBIS, WoRMS, BHL, NCBI, GloBI, NASA climate data, web search and data processing. Worked examples combined GloBI and GBIF to find predators of the white-throated dipper with records in Norway, and generated descriptions and categories for specimen images. He stressed that chat text can hallucinate but data artefacts are real and traceable, and that more agents create emergent use cases.
takeaway: iChatBio's specialised agents let a conversational interface combine many biodiversity data sources, with traceable, non-hallucinated data artefacts.
whyItMatters: It lowers the barrier to multi-source questions no single portal can answer, and its open SDK invites the community to add data sources.
keyPoints: Public since February 2025 at ichatbio.org; by May 2026 over 2,600 user conversations, 14 agents, 11 data sources, 12 student contributors.
A chat agent interprets requests and delegates to specialised agents; an open-source Python SDK lets others build agents.
Agents cover GBIF, iDigBio, iNaturalist, ALA, OBIS, WoRMS, BHL, NASA POWER, NCBI, Google web search, GloBI, plus processing and map generation.
Vision: data access, processing (filtering, enrichment, statistics, visualisation, FAIR packaging) and inference (Q&A, intelligent cleaning, hypothesis generation), only partly implemented.
Artefacts record exactly how data were retrieved (search parameters, requests).
Example: predators of Cinclus cinclus from GloBI, then GBIF counts in Norway; the chatbot looked at only about 10 species to keep responses short.
Moving toward user-defined repeatable workflows, e.g. describing and categorising specimen images from GBIF.
Climate values from NASA can be joined to occurrence records.

moments.description: Multi-agent architecture and open SDK.
Worked example combining GloBI and GBIF.
Takeaways on hallucination vs traceable data.

title: Reliable LLM-assisted curation of ecological survey data: a deployed agent bridging field collection and data curation
session: Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. AI applications, integration, and validation
summary: Andrew Tokmakoff described a deployed LLM curation agent for TERN Ecosystem Surveillance plot data. The data moved from an older system to a new EMSA-based, schema-driven app, and side-loaded data can bypass app validation. Declarative YAML rules compiled to SQL run first. The model then works through phased briefs and queries the database via a tool harness, surfacing ecologically implausible values (999 m hummock grass, shrubs taller than the canopy, inverted soil horizons). Findings go to a curator dashboard, and nothing is written without human approval. Lessons: adjudicate by class not row, never accept silence as 'no findings', and codify confirmed findings into deterministic rules.
takeaway: An LLM agent that proposes findings for curator approval, with confirmed patterns turned into deterministic rules, catches plausibility errors that schema validation misses.
whyItMatters: It is a rare deployed, cautious example of LLM-assisted curation with clear governance (no autonomous writes) and a practical recipe others can reuse.
keyPoints: TERN is Australia's government-funded ecological research infrastructure; the Adelaide team runs hundreds of revisited plots collecting soils, vegetation and samples.
The new EMSA-based PWA is schema-driven, but a bridge is needed to the old publishing system; side-loaded Excel data lose app validation.
Data can be schema-valid but implausible, e.g. a 999 m hummock grass placeholder. Such errors are rare human factors, not systemic.
Declarative rules in YAML compile to SQL (e.g. point intercept heights > 80 m); rules were themselves created with the LLM.
Phased prompts ('briefs'), e.g. flag a single species across 50+ intercepts and don't reason it away by bioregion (the model once dismissed 76 intercepts as normal for arid regions).
Harness loop: brief and tools -> model requests queries -> harness runs SQL -> JSON rows back -> model reports findings -> findings table -> curator.
Every database write passes through a curator; adjudication is by class, not individual rows.
False positives (a 65 m tree in tall wet forest; 39 forest sites without point intercepts) lead to rule tuning.
Recipe: start from real problems, let the model roam, approve or reject, codify rules, use evals with known datasets.

moments.description: Declarative YAML rules compiled to SQL.
How the harness and model interact.
Takeaways for reliable LLM curation.

title: Enhancing Biodiversity Georeferencing Using Large Language Models and Knowledge Graphs
session: Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. AI applications, integration, and validation
summary: Roselyn Gabud presented a georeferencing pipeline for Manchester Museum herbarium site records from Africa exported from EMu. An LLM, backed by GeoNames and Wikidata, fills missing locality hierarchy fields from narrative site descriptions, with spelling correction and per-entity fallbacks. Geographic entities are then matched from the most to the least specific level and scored by name similarity and hierarchy. A human-in-the-loop tool shows suggestions on a map, lets annotators correct them, re-run georeferencing and export back to EMu. Preprocessing cut records with only one populated locality field from 134 to 10, and records with four or more fields rose from 13 to 142.
takeaway: LLM preprocessing plus knowledge-base matching fills in locality hierarchies and proposes coordinates, with a review tool to keep humans in control.
whyItMatters: Hundreds of thousands of specimen records still await manual georeferencing; semi-automated methods that cope with sparse, ambiguous localities could clear that backlog.
keyPoints: Collections such as Manchester Museum and Philippine biodiversity collections hold hundreds of thousands of records still georeferenced manually.
Many records have only a continent and a narrative site name, so filtering by country or province is impossible; ambiguity comes from outdated names, spellings and overlapping names.

Preprocessing: clean and extract location text, LLM interpretation of the full description, per-entity fallback via spelling correction, GeoNames, Wikidata and LLM, then hierarchy enrichment with confidence ratings.
Georeferencing queries GeoNames, Wikidata or Wikipedia from nearest named place up to continent, scoring candidates on name similarity and hierarchy; no match leaves coordinates blank.

Knowledge bases compared on 100 records (0.1-degree threshold): GeoNames good for administrative hierarchy but limited; Wikidata broader for natural features but noisy hierarchy; Wikipedia most comprehensive but noisy and slow.
On 263 annotated records (50 train, 213 dev), completeness improved markedly after preprocessing.

moments.description: Overview of the georeferencing pipeline.
Comparison of GeoNames, Wikidata and Wikipedia.
Human-in-the-loop correction tool.

title: Validating LLM-Extracted Biodiversity Data to Preserve Scientific Meaning
session: Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. AI applications, integration, and validation
summary: Brooke Long-Fox explained how MorphoBank used an LLM tool, developed with intern Shreya Jariwala over about a year, to restore missing character and character-state definitions to ~600 NSF-funded phylogenetic matrices from PBDB. The tool is now a beta feature for users. It cut per-matrix curation from hours to minutes. Across 400+ papers and ~35,000 character-state entries accuracy was about 90%, but almost every matrix had some error: omissions, misaligned states, fabricated runs of characters, and specialist anatomical terms replaced with common words. Her message was that AI produces a draft and human validation keeps the data scientifically meaningful.
takeaway: LLM extraction speeds up morphological matrix curation enormously, but errors, including fabrications, appear in almost every output, so expert validation is essential.
whyItMatters: Data can look FAIR while silently changing an author's scientific meaning. Error types from real curation show why repositories must build in human validation.
keyPoints: MorphoBank holds 1,500+ phylogenetic morphological character matrices from thousands of published papers.
Matrices are taxa x characters scored 0/1/2 etc.; the meaning lives in character and state definitions.
NSF funding supported adding ~600 PBDB Nexus files; many lacked state definitions, which took 1-2 to 10+ hours per matrix to add by hand.
The AI tool was trained on 20-50 hand-curated datasets; it needed page hints and expected character counts to find the right tables.
Now a beta feature in MorphoBank, with a warning that AI-extracted characters may contain errors (preprint on bioRxiv).
Results: 400+ papers, ~35,000 character-state entries, ~90% estimated accuracy; about three hours of work reduced to three minutes.
Error types: omissions, dense/irregular tables, heading misalignments, fabricated states, ambiguous anatomical terms resolved wrongly.

moments.description: Errors in almost every extraction.
Taxonomy of observed error types, including fabrication.
Validation is needed; AI produces drafts.

title: TDWG 2026 Unconference: pitches, topic voting and breakout report-backs
session: TDWG 2026 Unconference
summary: Organisers explained the format. Eleven proposers gave 90-second pitches: AI for natural history collections (CETAF), botanical legacies and access and benefit sharing, SPNHC-TDWG ties, causal modelling in ecology, controlled vocabularies, trait standards, river basin naming, what makes data AI-ready, Wikidata, project closure ('Closing Time'), and Darwin Core data packages and structured data extraction. After in-room and Zoom voting (interrupted by a Zoom outage), six groups met: controlled vocabularies (31 votes), Closing Time (22), AI readiness (20), Wikidata, AI for collections and Darwin Core data packages. Report-backs included plans for a controlled-vocabularies interest group, a working definition of AI readiness, Wikidata people-identifier issues, a global CETAF AI living document, and GBIF-centred conclusions on Darwin Core data packages.
takeaway: The Unconference showed the community's priorities (controlled vocabularies, AI readiness, project sustainability, Wikidata, Darwin Core data packages) and started several follow-up groups.
whyItMatters: It records community-driven agendas and commitments (a new interest group, an AI-readiness definition, a living AI guidelines document) that may shape future TDWG work.
keyPoints: Pitches: Maarten (CETAF ISTC AI and robotics group) proposed a living document of AI use cases and guidelines for collections.
Quentin proposed discussing access and benefit sharing for digitised herbarium legacies (Nagoya Protocol), to improve a COST Action proposal due in October.
Deb Paul proposed making the SPNHC-TDWG memorandum of understanding more formal, with reciprocal activities each year.

Other pitches: causal modelling in ecology (EcoWeaver), discoverability of controlled vocabularies, trait data standardisation from an aquatic trait thesaurus, standardised river basin naming, defining AI readiness (new IQ-AIR task group), Wikidata for biodiversity, project closure and succession planning, Darwin Core data packages (ChatIPT experiences) and comparing structured-data extraction methods.

Votes: controlled vocabularies 31, Closing Time 22, AI-ready 20, Wikidata ~18, AI for collections 18, Darwin Core data packages 17 (14 + 3 online), botanical legacies 14, causal modelling 13, traits 12 + 1, SPNHC 10, river basins 3, extraction comparison 3.
Controlled vocabularies: the data quality group already listed 100+ active vocabularies; mapping tools exist; GBIF's vocabulary concepts could be improved; an interest group is being formed.
Closing Time: covered adopting physical and digital collections, supporting affected people, sudden disasters such as hacking, and the lack of up-to-date job descriptions and exit interviews.

AI readiness working definition: 'the degree to which a dataset and its associated workflows can support a defined AI task reliably', supported by structure, metadata, terminology, taxonomic backbone, identifiers, FAIRness, reproducibility, task performance, context, authorship, usage history and reliability.

Wikidata: ORCID problems (several per person or shared), adding people identifiers to collection management systems, little use of recordedByID/identifiedByID in GBIF, and a proposed Wikidata property for GBIF occurrence IDs.

Darwin Core data packages: GBIF should focus on finding, trusting, publishing and accessing complex data rather than visualising everything; tooling and visualisation are the blockers; AI helps with good examples and reusable prompts; GBIF for discovery, the IPT for unaltered data.
Deb Paul encouraged making room for unconference and hackathon formats, and Nicky Nicolson suggested 'speed blog' outputs.

moments.description: Explanation of the unconference format.
Start of the 90-second topic pitches.
Voting on topics.
Controlled vocabularies group report.
AI readiness definition reported.
Darwin Core data packages group report.

title: TDWG Treasurer's Report: financial policies and investment proposals
summary: Chandra Earl presented TDWG's finances and a new draft accounting and financial policies document that codifies practice for future treasurers. Membership brings about $18,000 a year and annual meetings roughly $10,000 net of publishing costs, against about $7,500 in regular expenses, so net revenue is about $17,500 a year. Individual membership is stagnant and institutional membership grows by only about 0.8 institutions a year. She proposed keeping $55,500 in operating cash plus an equal emergency fund in money-market funds, creating a $50,000 restricted endowment and investing the remaining $139,000 long term, for an estimated $48,000 a year. The money could support outreach, meeting hosts, member-only programming and named awards.
takeaway: TDWG is financially stable but not growing its membership; the treasurer proposes codified policies, an endowment and investments to fund outreach and sustainability.
whyItMatters: For a volunteer-run standards body, sustainable finances and membership growth underpin all its standards work; the proposals would change how TDWG funds community activities.
keyPoints: A draft accounting and financial policies document codifies current practice so knowledge isn't held by one or two people; it will be public.
Average of about 64 individual and 171 institutional (x5) memberships per year.

Revenue: ~$18,000/year from dues; annual meetings average ~$18,000, or ~$10,000 excluding included publishing costs. Beijing and Kenya lost money; Oslo's apparent $177,000 is because bills are unpaid, and it is expected to break even.
Regular expenditures ~$7,000-7,500/year; Pensoft contract base fee ~$3,000; net ~$17,500/year.
Proposals: 100% operating reserve ($55,500), a matching short-term money-market emergency fund, a $50,000 restricted endowment, $139,000 in long-term investments; projected ~$48,000/year.
Ideas for use: funding outreach and the Time and Place subcommittee (e.g. host honoraria), member-only materials, a named endowment for travel/research awards, community support fund or newsletter.
A donate button is now on the TDWG website.

moments.description: New accounting and financial policies document.
Investment and endowment proposal.
Stagnant membership as a concern.

title: TDWG Business Meeting: elections, subcommittee and working group reports, and TDWG 2027 announcement
summary: The TDWG chair opened elections for secretary, treasurer, the TAG chair (Ben Norton is stepping down), outreach and communications, and several regional representatives, with nominations closing around the end of October. Subcommittee chairs reported: the TAG on Darwin Core Data Package ratification, Latimer Core and MIDS; Time and Place on Montreal 2027 and the search for 2028 hosts; Fundraising and Partnerships on closing TDWG's European branch in favour of an associated-partner model; and Outreach on a rebuilt social media presence. Many of the 19 working groups gave one-line updates, including MIDS public review from 28 September, TCS2 ratification, the completed Mineralogy extension and a recommendation of SSSOM for standards mapping. The meeting ended by announcing TDWG 2027 in Montreal in June (Wednesday-Saturday) with GBIF, OBIS and Canadensys.
takeaway: TDWG is recruiting for key elected roles and subcommittees while reporting a busy standards year and announcing a large joint 2027 meeting in Montreal.
whyItMatters: It records TDWG's governance state, standards milestones and upcoming opportunities to get involved, useful for anyone tracking the standards pipeline.
keyPoints: Elections: secretary, treasurer, TAG chair (open; Ben Norton stepping down), outreach and communications, and Asia, Latin America and North America regional reps; nominations roughly to end of October.
Regional representatives will review community support fund proposals and be asked to run at least one outreach activity a year, especially in Africa and Latin America.
The chair asked people to join functional subcommittees even if they don't want elected roles.
TAG: Darwin Core Data Package ratified; Latimer Core nearly there; MIDS going to public review.
Time and Place: Montreal next; 2028 is the priority, with offers already discussed for 2028-2030.

Fundraising and Partnerships: May workshop; idea of outsourcing administration to an umbrella association; TDWG's European branch closed; TDWG now joins EU projects as an unfunded associated partner (e.g. an AI proposal coordinated by Pensoft).
Outreach: LinkedIn followers grew from ~160 to 1,285; 35 social campaigns and 25 emails; Canva, a short-URL service and a communications brief adopted.

Working groups: MIDS public review from 28 September for ~2 months; GeoSchemes terrestrial and marine about to submit standards; Latimer Core structural/descriptive/terms layers for review early 2027; Darwin Core moving to scheduled public reviews; IQ-AIR task group started; Mineralogy extension finished (35 terms); ABCD term-level documentation; standards mapping to recommend SSSOM; TCS2 ratified; invasive species group proposes four new Darwin Core Data Package properties.
TDWG 2027: Montreal, June, Wednesday-Saturday, with GBIF, OBIS and Canadensys; 800-900 attendees expected.

moments.description: Open positions for the upcoming elections.
Fundraising: European branch closure and associated partner model.
Start of 19 working group one-line reports.
TDWG 2027 Montreal details.

title: Ctrl+Alt+SDD: A Historical Review Toward a Standard Reboot
session: May the Data Be Structured: Linking Descriptions, Identification and AI
summary: A two-part review of TDWG's Structured Descriptive Data (SDD) standard. Elie Saliba traced its lineage from single-access keys and the DELTA format through SDD's development (from 1998, ratified 2005, last updated to 1.1 in 2006-2007) and noted that much of its development record was lost when a wiki disappeared. Adeline Kerner then showed how the Xper software family has implemented SDD and where it has had to bend or extend it, and suggested that the Xper4 redevelopment is a chance to restart community discussion on SDD.
takeaway: SDD is well-documented but dormant and imperfectly interoperable, and the Xper4 rebuild is an opportunity to reopen and modernise it together with the community.
whyItMatters: Structured descriptive data underpin interactive identification keys, and several later talks in the session (Xper-AI hybrids, recording identification sessions) depend on SDD being revived and extended. The talk also warns about how easily standards history can be lost.
keyPoints: Single-access keys (the oldest attributed to Lamarck, 1815) make it hard to express doubt or go back, and get stuck when a character is not visible; free-access keys need formalised descriptions but allow multiple paths, weighting and extra help.

DELTA (Description Language for Taxonomy), developed and maintained by Mike Dallwitz in Australia since the 1970s and endorsed by TDWG in the 1980s, was tied to its own software, so other tools created their own formats; SDD was introduced to restore interoperability.

SDD discussions began at the 1998 meeting, driven by Gregor Hagedorn (who wrote a PhD largely on the topic); SDD 1.0 was approved in 2005 at St Petersburg and SDD 1.1 (2006-2007, prompted by GBIF) was the last public update. It was used in European projects such as EDIT.
Most development documentation lived on a wiki that was lost; the history had to be rebuilt from printed personal archives, and the TDWG GitHub copy needs curation.

SDD has five main classes (described entities/items, descriptors, states, descriptions, groups) and is XML-based. Its flexibility undermined interoperability, it has no provision for AI, captures little metadata and does not store user identification paths.
Xper has evolved from a 1980s standalone program through Xper2 to the free, collaborative, online Xper3, keeping SDD import/export throughout. The Xper3 identification web services consume SDD.
Lucid and Xper both implemented SDD, but a 2008 comparison found their files were not fully interoperable, because of how the XML was structured rather than because of the tags.

Xper specialises SDD constructs (measure subtypes; a rating scale of 1-5 for observation convenience) and converts calculated descriptors, which SDD lacks, into categorical ones, freezing their states and losing information.
Q&A: SDD was 'a bit early', designed for features that software implemented only much later. Twenty years of hindsight make it easier to keep what worked and drop what never did.

moments.description: The SDD development wiki was lost; history was reconstructed from printed archives.
2008 comparison shows Lucid and Xper SDD files were not interoperable.
Xper4 is proposed as the opportunity to restart the SDD discussion.
Why SDD was 'a bit early' and how it could be revived.

title: Structured identification keys complementing AI: closing the corpus bottleneck with AI-assisted digitisation
session: May the Data Be Structured: Linking Descriptions, Identification and AI
summary: Koch argued that image-recognition AI and structured multi-access identification keys complement each other. In his pipeline an image model gives candidate species, which then filter a Clavis-format key so the user answers only a few discriminating questions. He also showed a prototype in which a vision-language model checks which key characters are visible in a photo and explains the identification. To remove the key-building bottleneck, an agentic LLM pipeline extracts characters from printed literature (e.g., Norwegian mammal books) into draft keys for around $10-30 each, which experts then review.
takeaway: AI and identification keys are complementary, and LLM-assisted digitisation of printed literature now makes it feasible to build structured keys at scale for expert review.
whyItMatters: Keys add explanation and education that image classifiers lack, and they ground AI in domain knowledge that is disappearing as taxonomists retire. Cheap draft keys change the expert's role from building keys to reviewing them.
keyPoints: Every occurrence point depends on an identification, so identification underpins most biodiversity data.

The Norwegian image-recognition app is kept low-threshold (no sign-up) and shows uncertainty, e.g. warning users not to eat mushrooms identified by AI; but images cannot capture every diagnostic feature and give no learning.
Digital multi-access keys avoid getting stuck on an unanswerable question. Keys are authored in the Clavis JSON format, and Koch argued that AI makes mapping between formats increasingly trivial.

Pipeline 1: photo, then image AI species candidates, then those candidates filter the key, so the user answers two or three species-specific questions. Some states are already eliminated, which reduces user error. A working dragonfly demo is integrated with the national app API.

Pipeline 2 (not yet scalable): candidate list, key facts and photo are passed to a multimodal VLM, which reports which characters it can see and generates an explanation that includes diagnostic features not visible in the photo.
An agentic pipeline extracts facts only from supplied sources (e.g., rodent traits from Norwegian mammal books) and collates them into a key, possibly one that never existed as a key before.
Draft keys cost under $10 for a single source and about $30 for multiple sources with Claude Opus. Experts now review a working key in an interface instead of starting from an empty spreadsheet.

Clavis is peer-reviewed and narrower than SDD: it breaks keys apart and reassembles them rather than representing them verbatim. Pensoft now supports Clavis import/export, and the key player works simply from a URL to a Clavis file.

moments.description: Pipeline: image AI candidates filter the multi-access key.
VLM explains an identification from key characters.
Agentic extraction of key characters from printed literature.
Cost of AI-drafted keys: under $10 to about $30.
Maturity of Clavis and interoperability with other systems.

title: Beyond traditional identification keys: hybrid deep learning and Xper3 keys for insect identification
session: May the Data Be Structured: Linking Descriptions, Identification and AI
summary: Puissant presented a hybrid identification method. A supervised contrastive metric-learning model trained on photographs of MNHN collection specimens of French ladybirds (Coccinellidae) returns the nearest candidate taxa, which then pre-filter an Xper3 interactive key. The model's top-10 hit rate was about 90% on both unstandardised GBIF images and standardised professional photographs. Pre-filtering cut the mean number of key steps sharply, especially for difficult cases, while leaving the final decision to the user.
takeaway: Deep-learning pre-filtering of an interactive key keeps the key's explainability while greatly shortening identification paths.
whyItMatters: The approach turns digitised museum collections into training data for tools that non-experts, e.g. in large-scale monitoring, can use without handing the final decision to a black box.
keyPoints: Collection specimens give precisely identified images covering broad morphological variation, but such datasets are small, have many classes and are imbalanced.
Automated tools such as BirdNET and Pl@ntNet need large training sets and were described as usually less taxonomically precise than expert-built keys.
Uses supervised contrastive learning (SupCon): a CNN embeds images so that same-class pairs are pulled together and different-class pairs pushed apart, which enables nearest-neighbour identification.
Evaluation metric: hit rate, i.e. whether the correct taxon is among the 10 nearest neighbours. Hyperparameter search selected a deep network with long training and moderate augmentation.
External validation on GBIF images (variable lighting and pose) and on a professional photo website both gave about a 90% hit rate.
In an Xper3 interface the uploaded image filters the key. Performance drops for dark or complex backgrounds, since training images had backgrounds removed.
The average path length fell from 4.2 steps to about one (ASR partly garbled); the longer the original path, the larger the reduction.

moments.description: About 90% hit rate on external datasets.
Path-length reduction with AI pre-filtering.
Perspectives: user testing, background removal, other taxa.

title: Needs for data standards about sharing and analyzing identification tools usage
session: May the Data Be Structured: Linking Descriptions, Identification and AI
summary: Vignes Lebbe proposed extending SDD so that it records how identification tools are used as well as the keys themselves. Drawing on the SPIPOLL citizen-science programme, where Xper3 logged participants' identification pathways in a closed format, she argued that an identification session is more than a path through a key graph: it combines context, observations with uncertainty, navigation including backtracking, and in hybrid cases AI outputs. She outlined a session model made of question, response and result steps and linked it to a planned Xper4 identification service.
takeaway: SDD should be extended so identification sessions (context, uncertain responses, backtracking and AI outputs) become open, shareable data, not just the keys.
whyItMatters: Recorded identification sessions could show where users go wrong, improve keys and provide rich training and evaluation data for AI models, because they capture the reasoning as well as the final name.
keyPoints: Identification has moved from single-access keys to free-access keys, AI tools and now hybrid approaches, used in research, education, citizen science and public outreach.

In SPIPOLL (MNHN citizen science on flower-visiting insects) the Xper3 team recorded identification pathways. This enabled analysis of character choice sequences, errors, feedback and metrics such as backtracking frequency, but only in a closed format.
An identification session is not merely a path through a key graph: it needs who identified what specimen, observations, uncertainty, corrections, backtracking and AI contributions.
The proposal is to add three objects to SDD (identification context, identification session, identification process). The talk focused on the session.

A session is a sequence of steps: question, response or result. Qualitative responses may hold several states with confidence; quantitative ones hold values or intervals with accuracy. Uncertainty must not be lost.
A result leads to a new question, an end, or a backtrack to a previous question. An end may give one or more taxa with compatibility or probability and does not imply success.
For hybrid identification, at minimum store a reference to the trained model and its output (e.g., taxa with probabilities).
Next step: a new identification service linked to Xper4 that offers single-access key generation, free-access keys, hybrid identification and storage and sharing of sessions.

moments.description: SPIPOLL pathway recording example.
An identification session is more than a path.
Proposed step model: question, response, result.
Summary and call for an extended SDD.

title: The Iterative Signal-Based System (ISBS): Structuring Bioacoustic Data for Interpretable Identification
session: May the Data Be Structured: Linking Descriptions, Identification and AI
summary: Pankowski presented ISBS, a hybrid neural-symbolic framework for classifying cetacean vocalisations from passive acoustic monitoring. It works in three phases: detection (manual now, neural detection in progress), description (45 acoustic descriptors plus contextual metadata such as location and recordist), and classification with IKBS, a symbolic knowledge-based system from his lab. A proof of concept on over 500 events from the Watkins marine mammal sound database classified vocalisations into harmonic, impulsive and stationary acoustic domains. In Q&A an audience member explained that Camtrap DP is being adapted as a TDWG standard for bioacoustic data.
takeaway: Describing cetacean vocalisations with explicit descriptors and symbolic classification gives interpretable, taxonomy-like structure to bioacoustic data before large-scale AI.
whyItMatters: Neural classifiers are opaque, and there is no consensus on how to describe cetacean calls. A descriptor-based, interpretable approach could support a shared ontology of vocalisations and studies of how calls vary over time and between populations.
keyPoints: Passive acoustic monitoring yields weeks of recordings with sparse events (e.g., minke whales detectable 100 km or more away), so manual processing is very time-consuming.

Neural networks classify well but lose the information on why a call is classified as it is. Annotators also disagree on how many vocalisations a spectrogram contains, and there is no international consensus.
Detection: neural approaches are acceptable for detection because explainability matters less there. Manual detections supply known cases for the knowledge base, and boat noise is a major problem.
Description: 45 acoustic descriptors (temporal, spectral/frequency, cepstral) plus contextual metadata such as recording location and recordist, together with any expert annotations.
Classification uses IKBS, a knowledge-based system developed about 20 years ago in the lab for corals and turtles and adapted here to vocalisations.

Proof of concept: Watkins marine sound database, seven cetacean species seen around Reunion, more than 500 events, classified into harmonic, impulsive and stationary domains or combinations. Results were described as promising; the transcribed accuracy figure is garbled.
Next: classify vocalisation types rather than species. The long-term hope is individual-level recognition and a consensus ontology of cetacean vocalisations.

Q&A: an audience member reported that Camtrap DP was evaluated for bioacoustics (Safe and Sound project) and is being adapted (Safer and Sounder, starting in December), with a TDWG bioacoustic-ready standard expected in about a year.

moments.description: Overview of the three-phase ISBS hybrid framework.
Proof of concept on the Watkins database.
Audience member explains that Camtrap DP is being adapted for bioacoustic data.

title: The LIB Open Knowledge Space: A semantic architecture for FAIR, CLEAR, and AI-ready biodiversity knowledge
session: Designing Institutional Knowledge Data Science Centres for Biodiversity
summary: Vogt presented the planned LIB Open Knowledge Space, the core infrastructure of LIB's new Centre for Biodiversity Knowledge Science. He argued that FAIR efforts often make only containers (metadata) FAIR rather than content. The architecture combines the Semantic Units framework, in which each humanly meaningful statement is an identifiable, versioned resource with metadata and vector embeddings, with a 'semantic ladder' of progressive formalisation. The ladder runs from raw text snippets through entity-linked snippets and Rosetta statements to OWL or higher-logic models, and the running example was a beetle observed feeding on carrion.
takeaway: Knowledge can enter the LIB Open Knowledge Space as natural language immediately and be formalised step by step, so content becomes FAIR, CLEAR and AI-ready incrementally.
whyItMatters: The approach lowers the entry barrier for semantic knowledge graphs while keeping a route to full formal semantics, and it offers a model for institutional knowledge centres built on natural history collections.
keyPoints: FAIRness is a continuum, not a Boolean; many projects build 'FAIR containers, not FAIR content'.

Semantic units: every semantically meaningful piece of content gets its own identifier, instantiates a type, and carries provenance and technical metadata, source reference, extraction method and a vector embedding.
Ladder level 1: a text snippet linked via a data property, with no formalisation cost. Level 2: entity recognition and linking to Wikidata or ontology terms for basic semantic search.

Rosetta statements use linguistic syntax-tree positions and semantic roles to create formalised, still natural-language statement types, represented in RDF by n-ary reification. They can be queried with SPARQL, validated with SHACL, and rendered as dynamic labels.
Higher levels: OWL-based models reached via schema crosswalks from Rosetta schemas. The approach is technology-agnostic (RDF/OWL, property graph or relational).

LIBTellMe, a RAG chatbot over LIB documents, will let users push relevant answers into the space as text snippet units. Diversity Workbench collection data will be imported at higher formalisation levels.
A vector layer runs alongside the ladder; each rank adds FAIRness and AI-readiness, and content is only pushed up when a use case needs it.
Everything will be open source and aligned with community standards, with federated approaches under consideration.

moments.description: The two pillars: semantic units and progressive formalisation.
How Rosetta statements are derived from syntax trees.
The semantic ladder and the LIBTellMe chatbot pipeline.

title: Strengthening Taxonomic capacity and Biodiversity Information in Education
session: Designing Institutional Knowledge Data Science Centres for Biodiversity
summary: Mergen described how taxonomy and biodiversity informatics are under-represented in education. Taxonomy content is being hidden from course titles, fieldwork is becoming optional, and dedicated biodiversity informatics degrees are rare or have disappeared. She presented outcomes of the EU TETTRIs project (an MoU among six partners and pilot courses) and its successor, TETTRIs Next Level (started this September, running to 2030), which plans a training academy and European certification. She called for reviving TDWG's dormant Biodiversity Informatics Curriculum interest group to inventory training, safeguard materials and describe courses, possibly reusing schema.org Course markup.
takeaway: Taxonomy and biodiversity informatics need to be visible, modern parts of curricula, and TDWG should revive its curriculum interest group to secure training and knowledge transfer.
whyItMatters: Standards and infrastructures depend on people trained to use and maintain them. Losing courses and retiring experts risks breaking knowledge transfer just as AI makes structured data more important.
keyPoints: The public and even biology students often cannot name common local species; Mergen cited UK and German studies (figures partly garbled by ASR).
Identification apps are useful but create dependence on technology.
TETTRIs found taxonomy and nomenclature often remain in courses but are hidden from titles and descriptions to avoid deterring students. Fieldwork is increasingly optional.

TETTRIs produced an MoU signed by six partners on taxonomic and biodiversity informatics training. TETTRIs Next Level (started this September, runs to 2030) aims for an academy, European certification, 'taxonomists for the future' pilots and science-policy training.
Biodiversity informatics is rarely a degree topic; the Sorbonne/MNHN master (Régine Vignes Lebbe, Elie Saliba) disappeared after staff moved on. Most practitioners trained on the job.
Relations between morphological taxonomy and molecular communities have improved through voucher linking, barcoding, eDNA and TDWG standards.
AI master's programmes are proliferating; biodiversity informatics can use AI to gain curriculum space and funding, since TDWG standards make data AI-ready.

The proposal is to revive the TDWG Biodiversity Informatics Curriculum interest group to inventory formal and informal training, archive materials, support mentoring and knowledge transfer, and define curriculum advice, reusing schema.org Course/CourseInstance via Bioschemas collaborations.

moments.description: Taxonomy is being hidden in course titles.
Loss of biodiversity informatics degree programmes.
Proposal to revive the TDWG curriculum interest group.
How to engage app-native students.

title: Enabling machine-readable access to biodiversity data through federated semantic querying
session: Designing Institutional Knowledge Data Science Centres for Biodiversity
summary: Mimouni presented the Semantic Data Cloud, a containerised application that exposes distributed Darwin Core Data Package datasets through a single SPARQL endpoint without copying them into a triple store. Datasets are published as cloud-hosted Parquet files with an EML JSON-LD catalogue entry. The system selects relevant datasets by spatial, temporal, licence or maintenance filters, then rewrites SPARQL to SQL through an OWL 2 QL ontology with OBDA mappings based on the Darwin Core conceptual model, and executes it with DuckDB over HTTP. A live instance at data.qcbs.ca holds over 50 GBIF datasets and exposes an MCP server for LLM agents.
takeaway: Distribute the data, not the infrastructure: cloud Parquet plus OBDA query rewriting gives a virtual Darwin Core knowledge graph without duplicating data into RDF.
whyItMatters: It offers a practical route to semantic, cross-dataset querying of the new Darwin Core Data Package without imposing a full RDF stack on data providers, and it is usable directly by LLM agents.
keyPoints: The ratified Darwin Core Data Package solves DwC-A's conflation of several entities in one table, but its semantics are implicit in table joins and it is hard to expose online.

The Darwin Core conceptual model defines relationships in natural language rather than in a formal ontology. An OWL ontology makes the semantics explicit and lets data be seen as a graph (e.g., a material entity evidencing an occurrence during an event).
Conventional RDF publication costs data duplication, fragile federated queries, a heavy RDF/ETL burden on providers, and schema drift.
Core principle: 'the data should be distributed, not the infrastructure'. Tables are exploded Parquet files on object storage instead of zipped CSVs.
An EML JSON-LD file per dataset carries asset hrefs pointing to the Parquet files (as in STAC catalogues) and supports dataset discovery with filters.

SPARQL is translated to SQL using an OWL 2 QL ontology and OBDA mappings, which guarantees rewritability while remaining a good fit for vocabularies like Darwin Core. DuckDB executes the SQL on remote Parquet over HTTP, so the virtual knowledge graph exists only for the query's duration.
The layers are separate: storage (Parquet), discovery (metadata catalogue), execution (DuckDB remote SQL), and planning/reasoning (SPARQL plus OWL).

The SPARQL endpoint is described via the Model Context Protocol so LLMs can write and run queries. A live instance at data.qcbs.ca holds over 50 GBIF datasets mapped to the DwC Data Package, and the code is on GitHub.

moments.description: Costs of conventional RDF publication.
The Semantic Data Cloud architecture.
MCP description enables agentic use of the SPARQL endpoint.

title: Prototype: The Semantic Units Framework and Rosetta Statements for Knowledge Graph Construction Workflows
session: Designing Institutional Knowledge Data Science Centres for Biodiversity
summary: Al Mustafa presented a prototype pipeline that puts Rosetta statements and semantic units into practice for knowledge-graph construction. Using the PhenObs botanical-garden phenology dataset, users fill YAML templates structured by Rosetta statement slots. A compiler then produces executable RML mappings and SHACL shapes, yielding a knowledge graph with layered statement units, compound units and dynamic human-readable labels. Mappings were about four times shorter than conventional ones, but graph size more than doubled.
takeaway: Rosetta-statement templates compiled into RML and SHACL make semantic-unit knowledge graphs much easier to author, at the cost of larger graphs.
whyItMatters: The prototype shows that the semantic units and Rosetta statement ideas can be implemented with less mapping effort, which matters for bringing institutional research data (e.g., at iDiv) into FAIR, human-readable knowledge graphs.
keyPoints: Going from a spreadsheet row (plant, growing season length) to an RDF knowledge graph is harder than it looks.
Rosetta statements are formalised natural-language statements with syntactic positions and semantic roles (subject, quality, value and unit), with required or optional slots.
Semantic units give identifiers to collections of triples so that they can be treated as units of meaning with a class, metadata and layers of abstraction.
A Rosetta statement template library (geo-indexing, time, scientific observations and more) feeds a compiler that outputs valid RML mappings and SHACL shapes for validation.
Templates cover five dimensions: statement slots, semantic-unit structure, RDF output pattern (akin to ontology design patterns), validation constraints and dynamic labels.
Users fill a YAML representation instead of RML/R2RML; for PhenObs this cut mapping code from about 4,000 to about 1,000 lines.

The resulting graph layers statement units over the base data graph, then compound units (flowering, fruiting and senescence traits; vegetative versus reproductive) and time-series units, each separately queryable.
Graph size more than doubles, and the impact on querying remains to be assessed.

moments.description: Compiler producing RML mappings and SHACL shapes from templates.
Mappings four times shorter.
Graph size more than doubles.
Future work.

title: What is the Role of "AI" in the Centers for Biodiversity Informatics of the Future?
session: Designing Institutional Knowledge Data Science Centres for Biodiversity
summary: Yoder reflected on the sociocultural impact of AI on a biodiversity informatics centre, drawing on the experience of the endowed Species File Group (about 10 staff and about 100 collaborative projects), which is considering growing from a group into an alliance. He set out ten observations: storage rather than compute is the bottleneck; standards matter more than ever; centres must spot and harden community-built AI tools; administrators, the public and researchers are ambivalent about AI; data protection walls are both necessary and futile; AI noise makes 'open' costly to maintain; and risk should be spread across networks of people. He concluded that centres are long-term havens for people who use technology, and that AI should serve life.
takeaway: Biodiversity informatics centres are about people. AI raises the importance of standards, storage, openness and distributed risk, and centres should fuel researchers' curiosity rather than be driven by the technology.
whyItMatters: The talk offers a practical, non-technical view of how AI affects the running, funding, security and mission of long-lived informatics centres.
keyPoints: The Species File Group has been endowed for about 15 years, has about 10 full-time staff and about 100 collaborative projects, and is exploring a move from group to alliance to share risks and benefits.
Mathematics, where AI output can be verified with the Lean system, shows that principles proposed for organisations in response to AI are largely just good principles for any centre.
The biggest bottleneck is storage, not compute. Aggregating data into commercial clouds enables AI models that communities may resent, so the community needs shared or 'infinite' storage.
Standards are more important than ever: to parse data with AI you still need a standard to parse into. Standards are 'a sea of stability' in the AI wave.
Citizen scientists and taxonomists now build long-needed tools with LLMs; centres must notice them and harden them for the long term.
Administrators are enthusiastic but visionary rather than practical; social media and some colleagues (e.g., journal editors) are hostile, and corporate partnerships are contested.
Walls and silos are inevitable, required and pointless: data leak eventually, so hiding protected-species locations is futile, yet Cloudflare-style walls are now ubiquitous.
Open science is not open-ended: LLM-generated pull requests and AI noise raise the cost of staying open.
Amid uncertainty (outages, hacks, collection closures, politics), risk should be spread by getting data back out to individuals and networks.
Centres are long-term havens for people who use technology, and the role of AI is to serve life and fuel researchers' curiosity.

moments.description: Storage, not compute, is the bottleneck.
Standards are more important than ever.
Walls and silos are inevitable, required and pointless.
Take-home: centres serve people, and AI serves life.

title: Discussion: designing institutional biodiversity knowledge and data science centres
session: Designing Institutional Knowledge Data Science Centres for Biodiversity
summary: After summarising the session's talks, the chair asked four questions. What belongs in an institutional centre and what in shared federated infrastructure? What is the biggest obstacle? What should change because of AI? What must institutions agree on to interoperate in 5-7 years? Answers ranged from data-owner-controlled federation, with institutions stewarding shared semantic artefacts, to calls for radical sharing of compute, tools and data against corporate interests. Others raised access inequalities, Indigenous data governance, researcher incentives and journal enforcement, tools that hide semantics, scouting community innovation, embracing messiness, US-Europe differences in AI policy, investing in people, and archival format portability.
takeaway: Interoperable institutional knowledge spaces depend less on technology than on people, shared storage and semantics, incentives and governance.
whyItMatters: The discussion gives a cross-institutional view of priorities and tensions (openness versus governance, European versus US AI policy, incentives) for anyone planning biodiversity knowledge centres.
keyPoints: Vogt: hosting depends on data owners. Some want full control via federated nodes that define allowed queries; others need institutes to host for them. Semantic artefacts (ontologies, schemata) and core services should sit with institutions for long-term sustainability. The chair compared this to GBIF nodes.
An audience member noted that skills (not only data) should be shared, and that recognition of data and software skills is patchy across countries.
Tim argued for radical sharing of compute, tools and resources, since large AI companies and big publishers benefit from secrecy and concentration.

Deb Paul noted access inequalities and her institution's experience that many researchers had never tried AI. She proposed Carpentries-style 'day three' support and alliances to handle staff turnover.
Sharon (Field Museum) urged bringing Indigenous data governance and traditional knowledge into 'make everything open'. A Brazilian participant disputed a claim about smartphone access in Brazil.

Obstacles: Tarek said researchers lack incentives and skills to semantify data, so institutions and computer scientists must build supporting workflows. Another participant said researchers know how but take shortcuts, so journals should require standardised data. Matt said to build tools that hide the semantic layer, and that federated storage is the biggest obstacle. A further point was that reviewers should flag messy data.

On AI: Matt called for small teams trained to spot community innovations and bring them into standards. Tim suggested embracing authentic messiness (citing Journal of Open Source Software practice). Noah flagged a gap between European institutions restricting big-tech AI and widespread US academic use.
The one thing to agree on first: storage, 'invest in your people' (Nikki), and changing management culture to keep staff histories and ensure archival format portability (Pat).

moments.description: Chair's first question: institutional versus federated infrastructure.
Call for radical sharing against corporate AI interests.
Indigenous data governance raised.
Biggest obstacle.
What changes because of AI.
One thing to agree on for interoperability in 5-7 years.

title: Approaches to the Automated Tracking of Taxonomic Research Activities
session: Publishing and Communications Promoting Biodiversity, Natural History Collections, People, Data and Data Standards
summary: David Fichtmueller introduced work package 1 of the newly started EU project TETTRIX, which will automatically gather ongoing taxonomic research activities from many sources into a central database (TaxoTrack), align them with taxonomic backbones and identifiers, and produce outputs such as maps, gap analyses, dashboards and policy briefs. He described how it builds on TETTRIs expertise assessments from publications (OpenAlex, Meise) and GBIF specimen data (Berlin), laid out the partner-led source streams, and asked the audience how their research could be detected. Feedback stressed ORCIDs on publications, registering nomenclatural acts, and institutional evaluation reports as sources.
takeaway: TETTRIX aims to build a machine-run, regularly updated picture of who is doing taxonomy on what and where, and is asking the community which sources it is missing.
whyItMatters: A systematic, repeatable overview of taxonomic research activity could expose understudied taxa and regions and inform funders and policy makers, but it depends on the research being machine-detectable through identifiers such as ORCID.
keyPoints: TETTRIX (successor of TETTRIs) started in September 2026; work package 1 will automatically gather ongoing taxonomic research activities, store them centrally and align them with taxonomic backbones.

Earlier TETTRIs work assessed expertise from publications filtered in OpenAlex (Meise) and from GBIF specimen data (Berlin); the specimen approach was harder because person data in GBIF are ambiguous and rarely carry identifiers.

Planned source streams: taxonomic publication databases incl. sub-article data (Pensoft: BLR, Biodiversity PMC, OpenBiodiv), funding records and project registries (UFZ Leipzig), taxonomic data networks and name registries (Berlin, Meise, Prague with a Central/Eastern European focus), 'dark' pre-naming activity via DNA barcodes, BINs and species hypotheses (NTNU), and expertise/service marketplaces.
All sources feed a central database, TaxoTrack, aligned with identifiers such as Wikidata, ROR and ORCID, to generate maps, taxonomic coverage evaluations, policy briefs and dashboards.
The team does not expect researchers to change workflows; it wants machine-accessible sources so the analysis can be re-run every few weeks or months.
A survey was launched targeting funding agencies and project registries, with an open section for other source ideas.

moments.description: Previous TETTRIs expertise work based on publications and GBIF specimens.
Overview of the TaxoTrack central database and planned outputs.
Speaker asks the audience how their taxonomic research could be detected.
Audience point: ORCIDs on publications and registering nomenclatural acts.

title: Empowering and Expanding Communities from Knowledge to Best Practices in Data Mobilization: The TaiBIF Collaborator Training System
session: Publishing and Communications Promoting Biodiversity, Natural History Collections, People, Data and Data Standards
summary: Melissa Chin-Yi Lu described TaiBIFer, TaiBIF's structured training and certification system that turns workshop participants into paid collaborators to extend the capacity of a small GBIF node team. Participants take a core workshop, complete scored assignments (Darwin Core mapping, sampling-event structuring, test IPT publishing, OpenRefine cleaning, GBIF searching) and a role-specific practical assessment for one of four roles: translator, ambassador, data mobilizer or species name checker. Since late 2022 62 collaborators have been certified; challenges are case management, retention and continuous funding, which TaiBIF supplements with AI and toolkit tools.
takeaway: A tiered, role-based certification pathway linked to paid assignments lets a small GBIF node multiply its support capacity.
whyItMatters: Many GBIF nodes face demand beyond their staff capacity; TaiBIFer offers a concrete, replicable model for building a certified, paid community of practice and a career pathway in biodiversity informatics.
keyPoints: Demand for publishing support, data cleaning, translation and taxonomic validation outgrew TaiBIF's small team.

TaiBIFer, inspired by the GBIF volunteer community model, creates a path from learning to practice: workshop, scored assignments, advanced certificate, role-specific assessment, then eligibility for paid collaboration.

Four roles: translators (localising GBIF resources into Traditional Chinese), ambassadors (workshop mentors, potential trainers), data mobilizers (helping institutions clean and publish datasets), and species name checkers (contributing to TaiCOL).
Separating roles lets people contribute through their strongest skills and lets TaiBIF set role-relevant criteria.
Since late 2022: 11 translators, 21 ambassadors, 11 data mobilizers and 19 name checkers (62 in total); data mobilizer attracts the most applicants but has the hardest qualification bar.
Paid assignments recognise that the services require time, responsibility and expertise, and create a feedback loop into future training.
Human capacity is complemented by 'Digital TaiBIFer', a 24/7 AI helper, and the TaiBIF Open Data Toolkit for dataset templating, validation and cleaning.

moments.description: Overview of the TaiBIFer pathway from workshop to paid collaboration.
Numbers of certified collaborators per role since 2022.
Challenges: case management, retention and funding.
AI helper and Open Data Toolkit used to fill human capacity gaps.

title: Bionomia, Scholia, Wikidata and Zenodo: broadcasting biodiversity data contributions
session: Publishing and Communications Promoting Biodiversity, Natural History Collections, People, Data and Data Standards
summary: Siobhan Leachman argued that Wikidata is 'the one ring to rule them all' for increasing the visibility of biodiversity data and the people and institutions behind it, because it is open (CC0), multilingual, linked and a hub for over 7,500 external identifiers. She showed how Bionomia attributes GBIF specimens to collectors and determiners and auto-archives their records to Zenodo with DataCite DOIs linked to ORCID, how Scholia visualises scholarly profiles and citation links (including to collections via 'uses'/'acknowledges' statements), and how Expeditia maps research expeditions. Zenodo communities were presented as a way to collate outreach and project outputs. Q&A covered privacy and researcher digital traces, and extending attribution to other roles such as conservators and taxon-name authors.
takeaway: Linking people, specimens, publications, datasets and collections through Wikidata and associated tools (Bionomia, Scholia, Expeditia, Zenodo) makes biodiversity contributions findable and creditable.
whyItMatters: It offers practical, free routes for individuals and institutions to document the impact of collecting, identifying, publishing and collection use, which traditional metrics miss.
keyPoints: Wikidata is a CC0, multilingual, human- and machine-readable knowledge base that anyone can edit and that search engines, AI applications and collection systems reuse.
As an identifier hub Wikidata links to over 7,500 other websites, catalogues and databases, enabling round-tripping (e.g. BHL and the CETAF botany pilot pull people data from Wikidata).

Bionomia links GBIF specimen records to Wikidata items (deceased) or ORCIDs (living) of collectors and determiners, generating profiles with maps, co-collector networks and citing literature, and its IDs are added back to Wikidata.
Bionomia can automatically deposit versioned archives of a user's attributed specimens in Zenodo with a DataCite DOI, which can flow into ORCID profiles.
Bionomia dataset profiles give institutions frictionless data packages to round-trip identifiers, spot data errors and find publications using their data.
Scholia visualises Wikidata-sourced scholarly profiles; linking publications to collections or datasets via 'uses' or 'acknowledges' statements credits collections.
Expeditia visualises research expeditions using Wikidata, GBIF, Bionomia and georeference data.
Zenodo communities collate related uploads, e.g. outreach material from the International Botanical Congress 2024.

moments.description: Wikidata as 'the one ring to rule them all'.
Bionomia profiles and attribution of specimens.
Automated Zenodo deposits with DataCite DOIs linked to ORCID.
Expeditia expedition visualisations.
Discussion of researcher digital traces and privacy.

title: Handling evidence: a cross-disciplinary perspective
session: Publishing and Communications Promoting Biodiversity, Natural History Collections, People, Data and Data Standards
summary: Dmitry Schigel argued that TDWG standards treat the registration of biodiversity evidence as a flat layer that mixes primary detections with interpretations. Using examples from direct versus circumstantial evidence and a grammatical-tense analogy (living organism, shed skin, eDNA, eRNA), he showed that different evidence supports different inferences, and noted that specimens and samples span a wide range of evidence types. He surveyed how forensic science (Locard's principle, chain of custody), archaeology (context recorded before interpretation, Harris Matrix) and medicine (evidence pyramids, GRADE) separate what was recorded from what was concluded, and proposed that standards evolve to separate detection terms from interpretation terms and carry explicit confidence for identifications.
takeaway: Biodiversity standards should stop treating what was recorded and what was concluded as the same kind of fact, borrowing evidence-handling practice from forensics, archaeology and medicine.
whyItMatters: As sensors, eDNA and AI inflate the volume of evidence, explicitly separating detections from versioned, attributable interpretations and grading evidence quality would make data more trustworthy for policy decisions such as Red List assessments.
keyPoints: Biodiversity recording involves detection, interpretation and registration; TDWG standards register both neutrally in one flat layer.
Direct evidence varies: an observed organism (present tense), exuvium (past), dry eDNA (present perfect) and eRNA (currently functioning) support different inferences about presence.

In Darwin Core, instrument readings such as coordinates sit alongside interpretive annotations such as scientificName and identifiedBy with equal status; an occurrence is a detection event plus a taxonomic decision.
The flat format was a deliberate, successful historical choice (billions of records), but pressure now grows for richer models such as the Darwin Core Data Package and the Humboldt Extension.
Specimens and samples range from single individuals to tissue, bulk and 'blind' eDNA samples; sequence data inherit evidence from physical samples.
TDWG shares roots with library science but now has little exchange with GSC or ISO, risking professional encapsulation.

Forensics logs every evidence transfer; archaeology records context before interpretation and keeps field records, reports and interpretations as separate citable layers; medicine's GRADE separates evidence quality from recommendation strength.
Proposal: separate detection terms from interpretation terms, make interpretations versioned and attributable, and add terms quantifying confidence in identifications for humans as well as machines.

moments.description: Detection, interpretation and registration as three steps.
Grammar tenses as a lens on different kinds of direct evidence.
Forensic evidence handling and Locard's principle.
Medicine's GRADE framework separating evidence quality from recommendation strength.
Proposal to separate detection from interpretation terms and add identification confidence.

title: A Network That Is Social: A Community-Based Model and Plan for Sustaining MorphoSource, a Scholarly 3D Data Repository
session: Publishing and Communications Promoting Biodiversity, Natural History Collections, People, Data and Data Standards
summary: Julie Winchester presented MorphoSource, a Duke-hosted repository for 3D, 2D and AV media of scholarly objects, and its plan to move from NSF grant funding to a community-supported model. She summarised its scale (over a quarter of a million datasets, 96,000 specimens, 2,900 contributors, 32,000 users, about 3,000 citing articles) and running costs (about $400k/year staff plus $25k storage). The model combines voluntary user pledge drives, scholarly society sponsorships, tiered museum subscriptions for organisation-level management features (with a free tier), journal subscriptions and deposit fees, backstopped by Duke, with longer-term plans for shared infrastructure with the KU Biodiversity Institute.
takeaway: MorphoSource will sustain open access to 3D data by charging museums, journals, societies and depositors, never downloaders, as NSF funding ends.
whyItMatters: It is a concrete, costed example of how a widely used community data infrastructure can shift to community funding without closing access, relevant to many biodiversity data services facing the end of grant funding.
keyPoints: MorphoSource supports 3D meshes, point clouds, CT volumes, photogrammetry series, histology and video, with IIIF-based interactive previews and annotation tools.
Launched in 2013 at Duke, supported by NSF grants since 2017; current funding runway ends toward the end of next year.
Scale: over 250,000 datasets, 96,000 specimens from almost 2,000 collection organisations, 2,900 contributors, 32,000 registered users, over 25,000 taxa.
Impact: over a million media downloaded since 2013, broad non-research use (schools, public, artists), at least 3,000 citing articles (about 640 in 2025), over 100 NSF abstracts mentioning it.
In a survey of 750 respondents, MorphoSource was named as often as aggregated NCBI repositories as a data source.
Costs: four FTE at about $400k/year plus $25k storage, rising $2,500/year; a steady state could run on about $300k.

Revenue model: quarterly voluntary pledge drives (first in October), sponsorship from about 12 scholarly societies, four paid museum subscription tiers plus a free tier, journal subscriptions, and deposit fees; never charging for access or registration.
Museums not subscribing lose management tools in early 2027; Duke provides a backstop; long-term aims include a node network and shared governance with KU.

moments.description: Scale of MorphoSource holdings and users.
Annual operating costs.
The community-based sustainability model and its revenue streams.
Chair comment: the era of infrastructure being provided free is ending.

title: Hit or miss? Creative promotion of biodiversity data and standards for success and recognition
session: Publishing and Communications Promoting Biodiversity, Natural History Collections, People, Data and Data Standards
summary: Shelley James and Deb Paul led an interactive session asking what counts as a publication, whether institutions credit software and datasets, and which audiences the community fails to reach. Audience members described getting credit via Zenodo DOIs and funder CV sections, the long-term impact of taxonomy not captured by short-term metrics, the gap between formal evaluation boxes and informal profiles, and the need to reach the private sector. The presenters promoted the diamond open access journal they edit and BISS at Pensoft, the new ORPHO authoring tool, cheap engaging swag, digitising hidden collections, publishing protocols and creative outputs (art auctions, animated talk illustrations) on Zenodo with DOIs, and registering names in nomenclatural registries.
takeaway: The community should broaden what it counts and publishes as outputs, and deliberately reach new audiences with creative, citable formats.
whyItMatters: Recognition of datasets, software, protocols and outreach shapes careers and funding in biodiversity informatics, and the discussion surfaced both practical tactics and structural barriers in evaluation systems.
keyPoints: Publications can include software, tutorials, datasets, blog posts, grey literature and even collection tours.
Institutions often recognise only formal peer-reviewed outputs, unlike individuals' broader view.
Audience: dataset and software DOIs (e.g. via Zenodo) and funder forms such as Horizon Europe or NSF 'other outputs' sections are routes to credit.
Taxonomic publications may have impact over a century, unlike fast-cycle fields, which short-term metrics miss.
Formal evaluations (tenure, docentship, Academy of Finland) have fixed boxes; 'digital recognition' matters only if that 'market' accepts it.
Deb Paul warned that early-career researchers in the US have faced negative reactions from colleagues for using AI-generated images.
CETAF's strategy emphasises engaging the private sector, a heavy but under-recognised user of GBIF data (e.g. banking).

Tactics: publish in the Pensoft diamond open access journal and BISS, use Pensoft's ORPHO authoring tool, make inexpensive memorable swag, digitise hidden collections, and put protocols, art and animated talk illustrations on Zenodo with DOIs.

moments.description: What do you consider a publication or product?
Schigel on formal evaluation systems and the 'market' for digital recognition.
Deb Paul on early-career researchers penalised for using AI-generated images.
Private sector as an unreached audience (CETAF strategy).
Art auction fundraiser and animated talks on Zenodo.

title: Building a Living Publication Workflow for Long-Term Social-Ecological Monitoring Data: The Taiwan LTSER Experience
session: From Standards to Implementation: Connecting Observation Data in Asia to GBIF Infrastructure
summary: Jhu-Jyun Jhang presented a semi-automated 'living' publication workflow for Taiwan's Long-Term Social-Ecological Research (LTSER) network, which collects ecological, environmental and social data. Research teams fill a co-designed data template and upload to the depositar repository; a robot polls the depositar API daily, validates updated datasets against the template, emails contacts on failure, loads valid data into the LTSER portal, maps them to Darwin Core, syncs to the TaiBIF IPT and publishes to GBIF and TBIA. Four datasets have been published this way so far.
takeaway: Embedding Darwin Core alignment as automated checkpoints in a repository-based pipeline keeps continuously updated monitoring data flowing to GBIF.
whyItMatters: Long-term monitoring data are rarely republished after updates; an automated pipeline lowers the burden on researchers and keeps GBIF copies current.
keyPoints: Taiwan LTSER is a site-based monitoring project combining ecological, environmental and social data to understand climate change and human impacts.
Continuously growing datasets make one-time publication inadequate; repeated extraction and Darwin Core alignment is costly, so data risk never reaching biodiversity infrastructures.
The workflow has three phases: research teams preparing data, an automated robot/script phase, and publication to GBIF and TBIA.
An LTSER data template co-designed with each team specifies field name, definition, data type, controlled values, examples and requirement status, easing later Darwin Core mapping.
depositar provides public data/metadata APIs, multiple formats and persistent ARK identifiers.

A robot checks depositar daily at 3 a.m.; updated datasets are validated, invalid ones trigger an email to the team contact, valid ones go to the LTSER portal, are mapped to Darwin Core and synced to the TaiBIF IPT.
Four datasets have been published through the workflow.

moments.description: Overview of the three-phase semi-automated workflow.
depositar as repository hub with APIs and ARK identifiers.
The automated validation, portal load and Darwin Core mapping steps.

title: Snapshot Japan: A Community-Driven Network for Large-Scale Wildlife Biodiversity Monitoring Using Camera Traps
session: From Standards to Implementation: Connecting Observation Data in Asia to GBIF Infrastructure
summary: Kumiko Totsu presented Snapshot Japan, the only Asian regional initiative of Snapshot Global, which runs a standardised annual September-October camera-trap survey with researchers, citizen groups, schools, NPOs and companies. She described the protocol (at least eight unbaited cameras per site, 200 m-5 km apart, site selection by disturbance level and habitat), participant support (websites, help desk, webinars, camera lending, a participant-only Shiny visualisation app), and the data flow from Wildlife Insights through expert-checked identifications to Camtrap DP conversion with an R tool, publication as data papers in Biodiversity Data Journal and on GBIF. Sites grew from 9 in 2023 to 32 in 2024 and 65 in 2025.
takeaway: Community support plus a simple standard protocol and Camtrap DP publishing let Snapshot Japan scale camera-trap monitoring from 9 to 65 sites in three years.
whyItMatters: It is a practical model for extending standardised camera-trap monitoring and GBIF publication into Asia, where Snapshot Global coverage is thin.
keyPoints: Long-term citizen monitoring needs community maintenance, quality control of identification and protocols, and internationally standardised data formats.
Snapshot Japan was established in 2023 with eight principal investigators; a five-person management team runs it.
Annual cycle: QC and publication of the previous year's data, participant feedback, recruitment, deployment in September-October, tutorials, and uploading by a deadline.
Protocol: at least eight cameras per site, 200 m to 5 km apart, no bait or lures, site selection by combinations of disturbance level and habitat type.

Data are uploaded and tagged in Wildlife Insights, checked by the management team with taxonomic experts, converted to Camtrap DP with an R tool on GitHub, and published as data papers and GBIF datasets; a beginner-friendly converter is being developed.
Sites increased from 9 (2023) to 32 (2024) to 65 (2025), covering Hokkaido to Okinawa, with growing participation from NPOs, companies and high schools.
